It’s a weird time to buy a laptop, but the new MacBook Pro doesn’t skimp on quality

Ars Technica November 06, 2026

It has the best laptop screen we’ve used, but there may be reasons to wait.

Apple’s new MacBook Pro is expensive as hell.

Let’s get that out there right away, because for a lot of people, it will be the only thing that matters. As with so many things in life, though, you get what you pay for. There’s no questioning the quality of the laptop’s display or most of its other hardware components.

But should you buy it? Well, that’s a complicated question in 2026.

We’re in a time of great uncertainty when it comes to buying a computer. Prices are at levels we’ve not seen in recent history, and they may well keep climbing. Meanwhile, users paying close attention to the early developments in both local and agentic artificial intelligence are asking an important question: “What will computing even look like in a few years, and what does that mean for the computer I should buy today?”

Apple’s new MacBook Pro sits at the intersection of all of this uncertainty. In multiple ways, it’s also straddling different worlds.

It arrives amid a changing of the guard in Apple’s leadership, potentially raising questions about the future direction of Apple’s ecosystem. It’s a mass-market consumer product, but configuring it with enough RAM and storage to make it feel future-proof pushes its price into territory mostly only well-funded businesses can afford. It’s firmly rooted in the computing paradigms of the past 20 years, but it shows early signs of flirtation with new AI workflows. It’s a conventional Apple laptop in most ways, but it also has a touchscreen—something that would never have happened in a prior Apple era.

It’s an outstanding, high-quality product, but whether it’s something you should buy depends on you—what you’re doing right now, what you’ll be doing in the future, and what you value.

For most of the specs we look at, Apple isn’t claiming any difference here. The new MacBook Pro promises 24 hours of battery life (though you’d have to use it in a conservative way to achieve that), it has the same ports (three Thunderbolt, one HDMI, one SDXC, and MagSafe), and it has the N1 chip for Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6 connectivity.

And like its immediate predecessor, it offers the M5 Pro and M5 Max chips as options. Running synthetic benchmarks, we found no meaningful difference at all compared to when we ran the same tests on the previous model, so we won’t spend time discussing their performance today. We’ve covered both thoroughly in prior reviews, and you can read up there if you’d like.

The chips are more than fast enough for normal workflows for the foreseeable future, including most 3D work. AI inference is the main area where they may be less future-proof. To be clear, they’re strong enough for now, but the field is evolving rapidly, and there’s reason to expect significant improvements in future chips on this front.

According to Bloomberg, Apple is skipping Pro and Max versions of the M6 chip that was introduced earlier this year to focus its attention on a significant rework for the M7 due in 2027. “The M7 line is designed primarily around major advancements to on-device AI processing,” Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman wrote. The line would emphasize memory bandwidth, which matters for fast, efficient AI inference.

Even without Bloomberg’s report, I’d expect Apple to prioritize those areas in its next high-end chip refresh. That’s partly because there’s another tea leaf to read here: Apple made just such an update with the A20 Pro, which debuted in its latest iPhones several weeks ago. That update brought a substantially improved Neural Engine and a significant increase in memory bandwidth. We also found that the A20 Pro delivered improved 3D graphics performance in some cases.

Similar improvements could come to Macs, meaning it might be worth waiting another year if you’re focused on AI workflows or even 3D applications—especially given the high cost of these machines. That’s part of what makes this such an uncertain time to buy a laptop. We’re in a moment when these companies are revisiting the architecture of these chips because of these new workflows, and we don’t know what the end result is yet.

Here’s one thing that’s not at all uncertain: The display on the MacBook Pro is the best I have ever used in a laptop. If the display is your primary concern, this is a big moment.

Apple calls it a “tandem OLED display,” meaning a panel with two emissive layers. This approach helps achieve a higher peak brightness, but perhaps more importantly, it can reduce the risk of burn-in. Most of the time, the display won’t need both layers running at full power. Instead, they can share the load and run at a reduced current, helping extend the panel’s lifespan.

The new display can achieve up to 2,000 nits of peak brightness on HDR highlights, but it’s rated for 1,000 nits of sustained brightness. In general, I like the way Apple handles HDR for this at the OS level, too.

The brightness matters for HDR content, sure, but what really makes OLED stand out is per-pixel illumination—meaning each pixel can turn on or off independently. That allows for absolute black levels and very strong contrast. The MiniLED display in the previous MacBook Pro offered good contrast for an LCD display, but OLED has a fundamental advantage here, and it shows.

As you’d expect, the screen offers native support for both P3 and Adobe RGB color gamuts. It also has a variable refresh rate from 10 to 120 Hz, just like many of Apple’s other products. As before, the MacBook Pro comes in roughly 14-inch (3,024×1,986 pixels) and 16-inch (3,472×2,226 pixels) variants. There’s also a nano-texture glass option to fight glare, though that will set you back another $150.

It’s one of the most impressive displays I’ve used in any device, and it’s certainly the best I’ve ever used on a laptop. The colors are vibrant, the contrast is outstanding, the blacks are inky, and it can get very bright when it needs to—not just with highlights but full-screen brightness as well. And on the whole, it’s extremely precise. Uniformity appears basically flawless. It’s what you’d expect from an ultra-high-end TV or reference monitor, not a laptop or computer screen, and it’s genuinely striking.

We’ll see about longevity, but OLED has come a long way in recent years, and my first impressions are that Apple has made all the right choices here.

I find myself trying to find something negative to say about the MacBook Pro’s screen to avoid sounding too effusive, but I can’t think of anything substantive. The best I can do is complain that Apple’s proprietary “PROLED XDR” label is silly and eye-roll-inducing.

Branding aside, the screen is the main reason to pay extra for this model.

With its lid closed, the new MacBook Pro looks identical to its predecessor. The dimensions are largely the same. It’s slightly thinner, but you’d have to check the spec sheet or handle them side by side to notice.

Pick it up, though, and you’ll find that it’s noticeably lighter than the last model, by about half a pound. It’s not in a totally different weight class, but you can notice the change, and it’s a nice improvement. The reduction is partly due to the display technology switch; it’s easier to make a light OLED screen than a light MiniLED one.

Open the MacBook Pro and turn it on, and you’ll see one of a few other notable differences, depending on whether you’re behind or in front of it. From behind, you’ll see the Apple logo on the lid now lights up, as it did on MacBooks of yore. It’s arguably a little tacky, but it’s also neat and nostalgic. I don’t hate it.

From the front, you might notice that the already barely there bezels are even more barely there, though that’s subtle. More likely, you’ll see that the top-of-screen camera notch has been replaced by a cutout just like the Dynamic Island Apple introduced on the iPhone.

When I reviewed the first iPhone with a Dynamic Island, I was largely positive about it. No, it’s not ideal to have a cutout on the screen, but Apple has handled it as intelligently as possible, and I would even go so far as to say it has turned what should be an albatross into an attractive feature.

Thanks to the OLED display, it’s possible to make any of the pixels around the camera cutout just as black as it is. Apple has designed live activities, the volume bar, and more to appear as if they are expanding out of and around, and contracting back into, this little dot. It remains ingenious.

When the Dynamic Island first arrived on the iPhone, it helped unify several previously disparate approaches to displaying notifications in iOS, making it especially useful. This time, it doesn’t solve as many problems, but it’s an improvement over the dead weight of the notch. It also helps that the MacBook Pro’s much larger screen means the cutout takes up a small share of the screen’s real estate.

The Dynamic Island works the same with full-screen apps as the notch did. By default, the top of the viewport ends just below the Dynamic Island, so it just looks like there’s a taller top bezel, and it doesn’t cut into the application interface. The menu bar, clock, and other system elements still occupy the space above the application (set against a totally black background) when you move the cursor up there.

I tested a few fullscreen games with it, like World of Warcraft and Cyberpunk 2077. Some behaved by default like the default fullscreen app behavior I just described, but others tried to occupy the whole thing, making the cutout visible. Vitally, every video app I tried avoided the cutout in fullscreen.

This isn’t something to upgrade for, of course. But on the whole, I think it’s an improvement over what we had before.

Apple has finally added a touchscreen to the MacBook Pro. I say “finally” because the possibility has floated around for about two decades. Steve Jobs was famously opposed to the idea; there’s even video of him explaining why he thought it would make for a poor user experience.

A couple of years ago, reliable reports emerged that Apple was moving forward with the idea regardless. When I first heard about it, I imagined what could be a really exciting implementation: a convertible laptop that would let you use it in a tablet-like mode, with Apple Pencil support for drawing and writing.

As a game developer, I imagined quickly sketching 2D game maps with an Apple Pencil, using a local AI model to convert them into 3D geometry, and then switching to a laptop configuration to start testing and coding. I also imagined using it like an iPad to more comfortably watch movies on a flight.

That’s not what we got, though. The laptop has the same form factor as the previous MacBook Pro model—no tablet mode or Pencil support. Instead, it just lets you reach up from the keyboard and trackpad to touch the screen. That feels like a missed opportunity.

Some creative apps have implemented touch features that might justify the touchscreen functionality if you use them a lot. For example, you can play the on-screen virtual piano keys on Logic Pro with multiple fingers, which could be nicer than clicking on them. I imagine many people already have workflows built around other approaches, though.

If you were specifically waiting for a touchscreen on your MacBook Pro, this seems like as good an implementation as you could hope for without turning the laptop into a convertible. Apple has put real care into it. For example, it has re-engineered the hinge so the screen is not particularly wobbly when you touch it. It’s fast, accurate, and responsive. It supports multi-touch gestures like pinch-to-zoom or swiping with three fingers to switch desktop spaces.

There’s one use case I find compelling as a developer. Testing iPhone and iPad apps in the Simulator has always been a minor hassle because of the difference in input methods. You either have to approximate only a subset of the interactions available to users with a trackpad and mouse or connect an iPhone or iPad to test them that way. A touchscreen could provide a more elegant way to test such apps in Xcode, Unity, or whatever else you might use.

Unfortunately, some of the UI elements in macOS are too small for my large fingers, so I have to tap very carefully. I also keep forgetting the touchscreen is even there for hours at a time and go back to my normal habits, partly because there’s nothing you can do at the OS level that you can’t do just as easily with trackpad gestures. And as Jobs predicted all those years ago, my arm got tired while I was using it.

For me, it feels faster, easier, more comfortable, and more natural to use the keyboard and trackpad 100 percent of the time, but I admittedly have decades of muscle memory and habits built around them. There’s apparently a generation coming up with the same kind of familiarity with touch interfaces, so this feature may appeal to them. Plus, touchscreen laptops have been a thing on Windows forever, and some people seem to want to buy them, though I never quite got why without an added tablet configuration.

It’s unlikely to account for a big portion of the device’s cost compared with the rest of the OLED panel, memory, storage, and so on. So, my own bafflement aside, I’m not unhappy it’s here. I imagine it will serve those who want it well enough.

As noted earlier, whether this laptop is worthy of a recommendation depends on you and how you use your machine. That’s always been the case, but it seems more so here.

If you’re a creative professional or a display enthusiast who wants the best laptop screen you’ve likely ever seen, you won’t be disappointed if you shell out for it. And hey, maybe you can show me your workflow and prove me wrong about the touchscreen!

If you’re just looking for a great laptop with strong performance for everyday use, consider the non-OLED, non-touchscreen model that’s still in Apple’s lineup—or even a MacBook Air, which compromises relatively little for most users. And there is, of course, the entire world of Windows and Linux laptops.

If you’re a developer—especially one working at the frontier of AI workflows—well, that’s where things get tricky. Will waiting be worthwhile? So much about how those workflows will evolve and what they’ll demand from your hardware is still so up in the air that I can’t make a confident recommendation. (For what it’s worth, I fit best in this category, and I’m still holding onto my M1 Max machine, though my resolve is wavering.)

All that said, in most ways, this is still the same MacBook Pro we’ve reviewed again and again for the past few years. Touch adds a feature aimed at a particular niche, or perhaps it’s there to roll out the welcome mat for a newer generation. The display is a more substantial update and makes a compelling case for upgrading, especially if you’re coming from an older, pre-MiniLED laptop.

But this is an expensive machine. The configuration I reviewed here (16-inch, M5 Max, 128 GB of RAM, 2 TB SSD) retails for a whopping $7,399, though you could at least shave $1,600 off that by going to a more typical-for-most-people 64 GB. (The cheapest configuration starts at $2,899.)

For the vast majority of buyers, the pre-OLED version that’s still in Apple’s lineup or another MacBook altogether will offer more bang for your buck. If you’re the kind of person who wants OLED or a touchscreen, though, you probably know that already. Based on my time with the new MacBook Pro, both features deliver on their promises, even if the latter isn’t as ambitious as some of us had hoped.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang summoned by Congress over Chinese espionage concerns

Ars Technica November 06, 2026

Lawmakers want answers about Jensen Huang’s ties to an alleged Chinese intelligence asset.

Top Republican lawmakers have asked Jensen Huang to appear before Congress to answer questions after it was reported that US intelligence officials believe Nvidia’s chief executive has been targeted by a Chinese spying operation.

The chairs of the House committees on China, foreign affairs, and intelligence wrote to Huang this week asking him to appear before a joint closed-door briefing for their committees on November 18.

“Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the People’s Republic of China’s access to sensitive US technology and information,” representatives John Moolenaar, Brian Mast, and Rick Crawford wrote.

“The issue of PRC infiltration and access to cutting-edge US technology is core to the investigative work of our three committees this Congress. It is vital that Congress determines the extent to which US national security has been placed at risk,” the lawmakers added.

The New York Times last week wrote that US intelligence officials believed Huang had been the target of a Chinese spy operation. The concerns center on a Chinese woman named Alice Huang, an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based cloud company that has bought billions of dollars of Nvidia’s chips.

Nvidia has rejected the claims and on Thursday would not say if Huang would appear before Congress. “Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job. Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year,” the company said.

“Our regional cloud customers receive ordinary business information—not sensitive Nvidia trade secrets—and zero information relevant to national security,” it added.

The lawmakers said they wanted Huang to discuss the security protocols Nvidia had in place to protect against “foreign adversary espionage.” The company said its chief executive had an “outstanding security team” that travels with him.

The New York Times said Huang had not received a “defensive briefing,” which the intelligence community usually, but not always, provides potential espionage targets to warn them about the activity.

Nvidia said it was confident that the US government would have let the company know if it thought a person was a threat to US industry and that it often receives updates from Washington about people of concern.

The US has previously scrutinized Megaspeed, founded in 2023 as a spin-off from a Chinese gaming company, for potential chip smuggling, although no charges followed.

Nvidia launched its own unannounced on-site inspections at Megaspeed in Singapore when it became aware of the US concerns, but the internal probe found no evidence of its chips being diverted into China, said people familiar with the matter.

The company’s supply chain has come under increasing scrutiny as US export controls have prompted increased smuggling of its chips. Earlier this year Wally Liaw, a co-founder of Supermicro, one of Nvidia’s key supply chain partners, was arrested in the US and charged with smuggling Nvidia chips into China. He denies any wrongdoing and has pleaded not guilty.

No more Cybertrucks; Musk moves on from the angular metallic flop

Ars Technica November 06, 2026

Tesla wanted to unseat the Ford F-150, instead it made the Edsel look successful.

Elon’s Edsel is no more. Last night, Tesla CEO Elon Musk revealed on social media that his car company is ending its failed attempt to wrest control of the American pickup truck market. The Cybertruck will cease production in the middle of 2027, liberating that space in Tesla’s cavernous factory for other uses—more Cybercabs, most likely.

Musk first revealed the Cybertruck in late 2019, back when Tesla was still trading at a theoretically understandable price-to-earning ratio. The pickup’s unusual angular shape owed more to low-res video game models than any concessions to practicality. At the time, Musk made fanciful claims that the truck would use a stainless steel monocoque construction, telling his audience that “the body and bed don’t do anything useful” on a normal truck. While some race cars use carbon-fiber monocoques for strength and lightness, making a pickup truck with a stainless steel monocoque chassis would only make sense if someone had an awful lot of stainless steel lying around and needed something to do with it all.

The truck was supposed to go on sale for less than $40,000, and Tesla made its usual stratospheric sales predictions that (had they been accurate) the bare metal EVs would be as ubiquitous as the Model 3 and Y.

But development of the Cybertruck was more troubled than usual for Tesla, which struggled heavily to bring both the Model 3 and Y into mass production. Musk demanded “Lego-like precision” from the workers assembling the trucks, but achieving the 10-micron tolerances required by the Danish toy company was not evidently successful, based on what we saw when we experienced our first Cybertruck in reality.

That was in 2023, when Cybertruck headlines were mostly about recalls and stop sales. By then, the truck used a conventional unibody chassis—conventional for Tesla, not for full-size pickup trucks. Toward the end of that year, Musk told his audience that “we dug our grave” with the truck, perhaps the first public acknowledgment that annual sales of a quarter of a million Cybertrucks probably wasn’t going to happen after all.

Sales never took off, and the Cybertruck’s divisive shape became an all-too-visible reminder of the CEO’s role in reshaping the federal government to his liking. Even selling thousands of Cybertrucks to SpaceX couldn’t save the pickup. Now, with America having vociferously rejected Musk’s vision of governance, those wishing to drive something that reminds everyone around them of that vision will only have a few months more to purchase one.

Rocket Report: Artemis II literally tore through the atmosphere; New Glenn delay

Ars Technica November 06, 2026

Interstellar Technologies announces more government funding for the Japanese Zero rocket.

Welcome to Edition 9.18 of the Rocket Report! Blue Origin packed a lot of news into one afternoon Thursday with the reveal of a new kick stage for the New Glenn rocket, a new rocket engine design, and the minor and widely expected delay for New Glenn’s return-to-flight mission from December until January. The reconstruction of Blue Origin’s wrecked launch pad at Cape Canaveral, Florida, continues apace after a catastrophic explosion nearly six months ago. There’s a lot of pent-up demand from NASA, Amazon, and the Space Force for Blue Origin to get New Glenn back in action.

As always, we welcome reader submissions, and if you don’t want to miss an issue, please subscribe using the box below (the form will not appear on AMP-enabled versions of the site). Each report will include information on small-, medium-, and heavy-lift rockets as well as a quick look ahead at the next three launches on the calendar.

SpaceX vets work on water-fed propulsion. Three brothers who worked at SpaceX in the Falcon 9 era are now building satellites that run on water, a potentially harvestable resource on the Moon and found all over the Solar System, Ars reports. In late 2022, the three Carlisle brothers founded Argo Space to build infrastructure in space. Their vision was not just in-space transportation but also removing the need to use propellants from Earth to move around the heavens. Argo Space’s satellites will use water not only as a propellant, but also as a coolant and radiation shield.

How does this work? … Argo Space flew its first mission in July, but the spacecraft failed after one of its solar arrays didn’t deploy, and there wasn’t enough time to test the propulsion system. Two more missions are on Argo Space’s schedule for 2027 to demonstrate the company’s water-based thrusters. The propulsion system is basically a small rocket that uses hydrogen and oxygen as propellants. However, instead of launching with separate tanks of liquid hydrogen and liquid oxygen, the satellite carries a reservoir of liquid water. In space, the vehicle uses solar power to split water into hydrogen and oxygen gases and burns them to generate thrust.

JAXA backs small satellite launcher. Japanese launcher startup Interstellar Technologies has secured the backing of the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) for its Zero rocket program, Aviation Week & Space Technology reports. The company said JAXA selected it for its Acceleration of Commercial Rocket Launch Demonstration program under the Space Strategic Fund. The government-funded program supports development and flight demonstrations of private launch companies with grants of up to $76 million per company, with the goal of fostering a growing commercial launch industry in Japan. Interstellar previously raised more than $250 million, with roughly equivalent funds from government and private capital.

Zeroing in … Interstellar is using the money to complete development of its Zero rocket, a two-stage launcher designed to carry up to 1 metric ton (2,200 pounds) of payload to low-Earth orbit. “We have achieved critical technical milestones, including Japan’s first successful firing test of an orbital-class methane engine,” said Satoshi Nakayama, director of the board and president of Interstellar. “We have now reached the stage where we must swiftly turn these proven development results into operational commercial services.” The most recent update from Interstellar indicated a first launch of Zero in 2027.

Launch demand outpacing supply. A new report from analytics firm Quilty Space confirms that, outside of China, the world faces a significant shortage of rockets over the next five years, Ars reports. The firm estimates that between now and 2030, there will be a shortfall of about 150 launches compared to demand from satellite operators and civil space agencies. If demand from the US military is added in—and SpaceX does not extend the Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy program to accommodate increased national security needs—the shortage could be doubled.

Worse than we thought … “What we wanted to get at is to understand how severe this launch crisis is and when will it be resolved,” said Caleb Henry, director of research at Quilty Space. “What we learned is that the launch crisis is more severe than we thought and that it will not go away this decade for sure, and it might not abate until sometime late in the 2030s.” Why is this happening? Quilty puts the blame on several factors: the war in Ukraine taking Russian rockets off the Western market; Amazon Leo demand; developmental delays in a new generation of rockets, from New Glenn and Vulcan to Neutron, Terran R, and Nova; and more recently, the retirement of the Falcon 9 as a rocket for commercial service.

China continues launching mega-constellation. Another 18 satellites for China’s SpaceSail Internet network launched Tuesday (Monday, US time) from a spaceport in the country’s northwestern desert. The mission marked the second launch—and first operational flight—of the Kinetica 2 rocket developed by a Chinese startup known as CAS Space. The SpaceSail constellation, also known as Qianfan, now consists of some 275 flat-panel satellites from a series of launches that began in August 2024. The network’s first phase will number 1,296 satellites.

A mini-Falcon Heavy … The Kinetica 2 is an interesting launch vehicle, with three side-by-side boosters arranged in a manner similar to SpaceX’s Falcon Heavy. But the Kinetica 2 is a much smaller rocket, with three kerosene-fueled engines on each booster instead of nine. Its lift performance to low-Earth orbit is about 12 metric tons (26,000 pounds). CAS Space plans to eventually recover and reuse the Kinetica 2 boosters.

India launches strategic navigation satellite. A Geosynchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle (GSLV) rocket launched on October 30 with a satellite to restore India’s regional navigation system, NDTV reports. The NVS-03 satellite is the third spacecraft in India’s second-generation navigation network. Some of the fleet’s older satellites suffered from atomic clock failures, rendering them partially or totally unusable. NVS-03 carries multiple clocks of different designs in an attempt to overcome the system’s reliability problems.

A “naughty boy” … India’s medium-lift GSLV has now launched 20 times since debuting in 2001. The rocket doesn’t fly as often as India’s smaller launcher, the PSLV, and hasn’t always performed well when it has. Six of the 20 flights ended in total or partial failures, but most of the mishaps occurred early in the rocket’s history. GSLV’s track record earned it the title “naughty boy” from Indian space officials. The most recent launch was a different story. The head of India’s space agency, V. Narayanan, declared that the GSLV’s recent flight was the “most precise launch of any rocket in the world.” We’re not sure what metric Narayanan used to make that claim, but the launch was, indeed, a success.

China reveals roadmap to lunar landing. Chinese space officials confirmed that the Asian nation plans to land its astronauts on the Moon within three years, Ars reports. At the Seventh Manned Spaceflight Conference in Beijing, officials, including Wang Xiang, chief designer for the lunar exploration program, laid out the country’s most publicly detailed plans yet for a series of missions leading up to a crewed lunar landing “before 2030.” China’s lunar landings will involve a lunar-orbit rendezvous similar to what NASA did in the 1960s and early 1970s with the Apollo program. However, lacking a rocket as powerful as the Saturn V vehicle, the crew and lunar lander will launch separately to the Moon.

These are the rockets … China’s Long March 10 rocket family will be the workhorse for the country’s initial crew missions to the Moon. The next big test will be the demonstration flight of a Long March 10A rocket, which flies with a single core booster, and China’s new Mengzhou Moon ship to low-Earth orbit in early 2027. The larger Long March 10, with three boosters connected together, will launch China’s Lanyue lunar lander on an uncrewed test flight to the Moon in 2028. The next year, a follow-up mission will involve the concurrent launch of two Long March 10s, one with an uncrewed Mengzhou spacecraft and the other with a Lanyue lander that will dock together in lunar orbit. Then, before 2030, another dual launch of Long March 10s will occur, this time with crew on the Mengzhou spacecraft, leading to the crewed landing mission.

Blue Origin’s big reveals. Blue Origin announced two significant upgrades to its New Glenn rocket on Thursday, reducing the cost of manufacturing the vehicle and expanding its capacity for payload delivery to geostationary orbit and the Moon, Ars reports. With these upgrades, the company aims to eventually position New Glenn to launch more than 1,000 times a year. One of the announcements involved a new engine, called Northstar, that will eventually replace the BE-4 engine that powers the first stage of New Glenn. The other piece of news was that Blue Origin is developing a hydrogen-oxygen third stage for the rocket to give it an extra kick for high-energy missions.

Blue’s Northstar … The Northstar engine is a simplified but more powerful version of the BE-4 engine. It has half the number of parts and 30 percent less mass, and about 65 percent can be 3D-printed, all while providing a thrust increase over the BE-4. Blue Origin believes it can manufacture the engine at 25 percent the cost of a BE-4 engine. The kick stage is somewhat of an engineering marvel in itself. The stage will use a lightweight composite fuel tank, but officials were not sure the structure could contain leak-prone hydrogen at high pressure. The company recently had a breakthrough at Launch Site One in Texas, when it completed its first composite liquid hydrogen tanking test, giving engineers confidence to move forward with the design.

New Glenn won’t return to flight this year. Blue Origin now plans to resume launches of its New Glenn rocket in January, delaying the much-anticipated flight of the vehicle after a destructive launch pad explosion in May, Bloomberg reports. The Jeff Bezos-backed company had been driving to launch New Glenn again before the end of the year in its quest to challenge SpaceX. But Blue Origin Chief Executive Officer Dave Limp told employees on Wednesday that they are now targeting a flight early in 2027.

What’s a month? … The slight delay is unsurprising, and a January launch would still put Blue Origin well head of initial fears of how long it would take to rebuild its launch pad in Florida. New Glenn has a busy launch manifest after the return-to-flight mission, including a crucial launch in the spring of Blue Origin’s Blue Moon Mark 1 lander, an uncrewed precursor to the company’s future human-rated lander for NASA’s Artemis missions.

Artemis II tore through the atmosphere. The launch of NASA’s Artemis II mission in April caused significant disturbances in Earth’s ionosphere that could have triggered temporary, localized errors in GPS positioning, a new study has found, Space. com reports. The study by a team of researchers from National Cheng Kung University in Taiwan analyzed data from high-precision networks of fixed, ground-based GPS receivers. The researchers used the GPS measurements to reconstruct how the passage of the Artemis II mission’s Space Launch System rocket changed the concentrations of free electrons in the upper atmosphere.

Disturbing the peace … The measurements found that the ionospheric disturbances resulting from the Artemis II launch were more significant than any caused by other rocket launches to date. Curiously, they were up to 10 times more intense than those observed following the test launches of SpaceX’s Starship, which is twice as powerful as the SLS based on liftoff thrust.

Blue Origin says it is building a higher-performing rocket engine at 1/4 the cost

Ars Technica November 06, 2026

“This is going to be a game-changer.”

KENNEDY SPACE CENTER, Florida—Blue Origin announced two significant upgrades to its New Glenn rocket on Thursday, reducing the cost of manufacturing the vehicle and expanding its capacity for payload delivery to geostationary orbit and the Moon.

With these upgrades, the company aims to eventually position New Glenn to launch more than 1,000 times a year.

“There has never been higher demand for launch, ever,” Dave Limp, chief executive officer of Blue Origin, said during the UP. Summit conference at the Shuttle Landing Facility in Florida.

Blue Origin has already begun test firing a new engine, called Northstar, that will eventually replace the BE-4 engine that powers the first stage of New Glenn. Separately, the company also said it was developing a hydrogen-oxygen third stage for the rocket, GS3, to give it an extra kick.

The Northstar engine is a simplified but more powerful version of the BE-4 engine, Limp said. It has half the number of parts and 30 percent less mass, and about 65 percent can be 3D-printed.

Blue Origin believes it can manufacture the engine at 25 percent of the cost of a BE-4 engine and eventually reach the point where each engine can be assembled in less than a day. The company is deep into development and testing of Northstar, having already begun a test-firing campaign.

“To get access to space at a lower cost, we have to look at every part of the vehicle,” Limp said. “This is going to be a game-changer.”

The BE-4 engine powering New Glenn today has a thrust of 640,000 pounds, and Limp said Northstar will have a starting thrust of 715,000 pounds. Like the BE-4 engine, Northstar burns methane and liquid oxygen using an oxygen-rich staged combustion cycle and a single-shaft turbopump architecture.

Limp said the company will continue to manufacture the existing BE-4 engine for United Launch Alliance, which uses two of the engines to power its Vulcan rocket.

Blue Origin is developing a third stage for New Glenn called GS3 (creatively named Glenn Stage 3) to offer direct injection to geostationary orbit and Earth-escape trajectories. The third stage fits within an interstage, preserving the full fairing volume for customer payloads.

The stage can fly on both the smaller 7×2 variant (as in, seven first stage engines and two second stage engines) of New Glenn as well as the larger 9×4 variant. According to Blue Origin, a GS3-equipped New Glenn 7×2 can carry 8 metric tons directly to geostationary orbit and 10 metric tons to translunar injection. Those figures increase to 14 tons and 20 tons, respectively, for the larger 9×4 variant.

As the rocket’s third stage, it needs to be light, Limp said. For this reason, the third stage is made mostly of composites, which are high-performing and lightweight. But there’s a problem with that.

The stage will be powered by the company’s BE-7 engine, already used by its lunar landers. This engine is optimized for in-space operations and uses liquid hydrogen and oxygen propellants. But hydrogen is the smallest atom and therefore leaky. With composites, thermal cycling and mechanical strain can cause cracking, exacerbating losses of molecular hydrogen.

Limp said the company was not sure a large composite tank, 5.5-meter diameter in this case, could be constructed that would contain hydrogen at high pressures.

The company recently had a breakthrough at Launch Site One in Texas, when it completed its first composite liquid hydrogen tanking test. During the test, the tank was pressurized to 100 percent of the maximum force expected during operation for 2.5 hours. It was even successfully tested at 150 percent of this maximum pressure for 10 minutes.

That gave the company confidence that a GS3 based on composite tanks was a concept that could go forward, and now the company is aiming for a debut in 2028 for a government customer.

“We have one customer signed up for cislunar space in 2028,” Limp said. “We are open for business.”

The past, present, and future share a show floor at Pinball Expo 2026

Ars Technica Long form October 21, 2026

Flipping through the highlights in and around Pinball Expo 2026.

It’s October in the Midwest, which means it’s time for the pinball world to descend on a convention center in Chicagoland for the annual Pinball Expo. Once thought to be an entertainment sector slowly bleeding out, pinball has come back in a big way in recent years. I visited one of Chicago’s last old-school manufacturers before heading down the road to see what’s new in the silver-ball universe.

Hundreds gathered on a brisk fall Friday morning outside Stern Pinball’s headquarters in Elk Grove, Illinois, waiting to enter a Wonka-like wonder factory where piles of raw parts become licensed creations from Jaws to the brand-new Fallout. Stern invited me to tour its offices and factory floor before heading off to the convention in nearby Schaumburg, Illinois.

As I stood with my tour group in Stern Pinball’s HQ lobby, mouth agape at the dozens of machines lining the walls, we were greeted by the man himself, Gary Stern, who gave us some background on the company’s 40-year history. After a stop at Gary’s podium, we were ushered to the factory floor entrance, where Stern employee and legendary game designer George Gomez briefed us on the tour rules and answered questions. According to Gomez, “at any given time, Stern controls 90 percent of the current pinball market, and everybody else splits the rest.”

While the industry may be expanding toward something more reminiscent of its glory days, there’s no doubt who still rules the market. With a steady stream of new license releases, Stern has cemented itself as the brand in modern pinball.

What I saw on the expo floor, though, showed me that the remaining 10 percent of the market is doing some really interesting things, and hobbyist projects are booming. From modular home setups to open development kits that let anyone with silver-ball dreams try their hand at game design, there was something for everyone. In short, it’s a very exciting time to be a pinball fan.

Stern’s latest offering, Fallout, stood near the entrance of a convention floor packed with the latest machines from manufacturers like Jersey Jack, Barrels of Fun, Spooky Pinball, and others. I’ve attended this show for the last four years, and each year seems to bring new companies into the fold. Despite more than 25 years of advances in home entertainment, nothing quite matches the tactile thrill of launching a metal ball around a wooden cabinet.

Several companies showed off their latest attempts to bring pinball into virtual reality without abandoning physical controls, letting players wear a VR helmet while pressing real buttons on a pedestal setup. It’s a fun novelty that demonstrates what’s possible, but if the lines at the expo were any indication, most people still prefer walking up to a physical machine and enjoying the tactile controls, visuals, and sounds that come with it.

One of the biggest questions facing anyone buying a pinball machine for home use is what to do when you get bored with a $10,000 game. Until recently, the options were to sell it, find someone willing to trade, or build your own virtual pin setup with screens instead of physical playfields. The Multimorphic P3 team saw an opportunity for another approach.

According to Multimorphic co-creative director Stephen Silver, “The way the P3 is designed is that the lower two-thirds is a ball-tracking interactive display… We have floating mechanisms above the screen, floating flippers, floating slings, floating targets. And the upper third is a swappable play field. We’ve got 10 different play fields now that we can swap and change the entire game.”

As demonstrated by the much-hyped Dungeon Crawler Carl prototype (whose lines never seemed to get shorter), the P3 system uses a playfield screen that can react to ball movement in real time, and the game can change to match player choices. In Dungeon Crawler Carl, for instance, the display layout changes based on which book in the series the player chooses.

“We’re planning on doing seven books in the game… you can play them in any order you want,” Silver explained. ” The idea being that you get to Faction Wars—the events of the seventh book—it’s a perfect wizard mode. When we started this, Faction Wars was the last book in the series. It still feel(s) like a good wrapping-up point for this story that we’re telling. In the future, we could always be open to adding more books, but right now that’s the plan.”

The first two entries in the book series had playable pin versions on the show floor, and Silver says that “every single book itself is the equivalent depth of a ’90s Williams game… It’s like seven really solid games in one,” Silver said.

Dungeon Crawler Carl will enter production “at the end of the year, and then it should be rolling out to delivery early next year,” he said.

The platform’s versatility extends beyond in-house designs. Multimorphic offers a free software development kit (SDK) that lets community members design and distribute their own table creations for the P3 system. Machine owners can swap physical overlay kits or remove them entirely to play original games on the reactive screen.

“There are 30 different games available on the system now because you can do software-only games,” Silver said. “It’s the only third-party development platform in pinball. So anybody can download the free SDK and develop third-party software games… and release it through our store to an audience of P3 owners that are hungry for new content.”

Sitting on one of the more unassuming tables of the PinExpo show floor was Pocket Pinball, a free Android APK that lets users load any Visual Pinball X (VPX) table on their phone or tablet. But the project’s developer, Johnny Zen, had something else to show off: a closed beta for his Pinball Construction Set. An homage to the 1982 classic Bill Budge Apple II game of the same name, the browser-based tool lets users design their own pinball machine with an easy drag-and-drop interface. Multimorphic may have the only free pinball SDK for now, but if Zen has his way, that won’t be true for long.

Whereas most modern pinball designs start at the CAD desk, the upcoming Pinball Construction Set keeps the process entirely within a browser. Zen compares the system to building a coaster in Roller Coaster Tycoon: Users can choose between three styles or start with a blank slate. After selecting a template, such as a standard or wide-body layout, they can add traditional design elements like ramps, targets, and scoops by clicking and dragging them into place.

The program is still in closed beta, but aspiring pinball developers can register their interest to be notified when it becomes publicly available. Zen also plans to add a marketplace where users can commission artwork from freelance artists. “If you needed some artwork for your apron or playfield, you basically look at the artist profiles, then the app will send the artist’s team the exact measurements of what you need,” he said.

One of the most exciting trends in pinball’s modern resurgence is the rise of homebrew design, with passionate hobbyists turning basement-built machines into careers with some of the industry’s biggest players. Often serving as playable resumes, homebrew games give aspiring designers a chance to flex their creative muscles without the licensing restrictions that come with producing commercial machines.

One of this year’s homebrew highlights was Shaolin Flow, an ode to the great Hong Kong action movies that those of us who grew up in the ’90s watched on Saturday afternoon network TV. Complete with an optional Wu-Tang soundtrack, Shaolin Flow lets players choose between traditional flipper-button controls and a more punchy approach. Two fist-shaped sensors sit atop the playfield, to the left and right of the flippers. Players activate the flippers by throwing punches over the sensor.

What initially looked like a gimmick quickly proved to be a great time. Adding a physical element to an already physical game felt more natural than I expected, and the absence of any perceptible input lag made the experience seamless.

As the tools for designing and building pinball machines become more accessible, the homebrew scene continues to grow. Each year brings more entries to the floor, transforming what was once a smaller corner of proudly displayed projects into a dedicated, walled-off section featuring games from the future stars of pinball design. This year’s homebrew showstopper could see its creator designing a licensed table for one of the industry’s major manufacturers by the following year’s show.

Pinball Expo isn’t just an industry trade event; it’s also a celebration of every era of pinball history. Volunteers haul machines from their personal collections to the show floor, where the general public can play them all weekend. And it’s not just balls and flippers. Walk the aisles, and you’ll see artists, merch and crafts vendors, accessories, retro video games, traditional arcades, and enough aftermarket mod kits to turn any pinball machine into a second hobby.

For decades, pinball production was concentrated among a handful of major manufacturers in the Chicagoland area. While the region might still be the industry’s epicenter, newer challengers to Stern’s dominance, like Texas-based Barrels of Fun or European producers like Dutch Pinball, show that things are changing.

Today, aspiring developers can turn a good idea into a playable VPX table without ever putting down their phone. Whether it’s a bedroom developer working with a free SDK or one of the industry’s biggest players, pinball is being made by more people in more places, and fans are all the better for it.

OpenAI, Google pushing new AI models easily tricked into making nudes, researchers say

Ars Technica Long form October 14, 2026

Attack method exposes flaws in OpenAI, Google safeguards against AI nudes.

Safety researchers continue to warn that a large volume of AI-generated explicit content is spreading unchecked, while regulators do little to meaningfully stop it.

This non-consensual content is commonly shared in text and direct messages or stored in private clouds where it’s less likely to be detected or reported, a Google co-authored study of Internet users across the United States, Australia, and the United Kingdom found this July. That’s why the “most critical intervention point” remains at the source: the harmful AI tools used to make the fake sexual images, Google researchers concluded.

Yet red-teaming in recent months suggests that as some of the leading AI image generators from Google and OpenAI become more capable, they may be getting worse at blocking explicit outputs.

Raising the red flag are researchers at White Circle, a public benefit corporation backed by senior leaders and researchers from Anthropic, DeepMind, Hugging Face, and OpenAI. It was founded after CEO Denis Shilov posted one of the most famous universal jailbreaks of leading models in October 2024. Bent on breaking models to conduct thorough safety testing, White Circle helps companies detect and deter threats when implementing advanced AI systems that may not always behave as expected.

Testing how well text-to-image models block banned content categories is a key research direction for White Circle, and Shilov thinks their latest findings are “horrifying” enough to share with the public.

In a little-noticed preprint published last month, White Circle researchers exposed flaws in the guardrails of DALL·E 3, Google’s Nano Banana 2, and GPT-Image-2. In a press release, they explained that “using just off-the-shelf tools, available online for anyone to download, and by sending API calls, White Circle was able to use the novel attack method to bypass the safety filters.” In the best case, on DALL·E 3, about 13 percent of the attack prompts produced images that human reviewers confirmed as explicit. The rate was under 10 percent for Nano Banana 2 and about 3 percent for GPT-Image-2.

“Critically, none of these requests required custom-built or frontier AI models,” White Circle warned.

Researchers reviewed the outputs to verify the bypass rate, which White Circle noted is “the highest of any method tested under the same standard.” The key takeaway, they suggested, is that, “at a time when AI safety has never been under more scrutiny, the defenses leading labs have built are far weaker than they acknowledge.”

By publishing research like this, White Circle is positioning itself as an external evaluator of frontier labs, and it plans to open-source the entire attack pipeline so model makers can understand the true scale of the vulnerability and build stronger protections. Although the company has not widely promoted the research yet, it will share it at a prominent AI conference this November, NeurIPS 2026, which may increase scrutiny on Google and OpenAI later this fall.

White Circle has shared its findings with some frontier AI labs through “mutual contacts,” Shilov told Ars, but neither Google nor OpenAI responded to Ars’ request to comment directly on vulnerabilities found in their models.

Meanwhile, OpenAI and Google have released new models—ChatGPT Images 2.5 and Nano Banana 2.1—and White Circle told Ars that prompt safety testing using the same method showed “both are significantly more breakable than their previous versions.”

Neither company responded after Ars shared these new findings.

White Circle’s attack method can break down frontier defenses in categories, like explicit content, that seem easy to spot, which doesn’t bode well for more serious defense systems currently being updated to block other unwanted AI behavior, like hacking, Shilov told Ars.

“White Circle’s working hypothesis for this is either the newer models are more sophisticated and capable of generating a wider range of content, or that safety has been deprioritized in favor of capability,” White Circle told Ars.

White Circle is also in early talks with government officials about third-party safety testing, Shilov said, which he thinks should be required. Mandatory independent audits could push companies to prioritize safety testing, which analysts have suggested largely takes a backseat as AI firms dump most of their resources into compute and AI infrastructure.

“They should be investing much more into safety measures and security measures around their models,” Shilov told Ars. “And for us, it seems that they’re not actually doing this.”

To expose jailbreaks that are “reusable and transferable”—working across different leading models—White Circle didn’t limit itself to testing one prompt at a time. Instead, researchers sought out “patterns which work across multiple prompts and scenarios” to detect reusable attack strategies that could work across leading models. (Researchers noted that Midjourney wasn’t tested because “it does not provide a public API suitable for controlled benchmarking.”)

The team has dubbed this novel attack method “Red-teaming via Iterative Strategy Evolution” (RISE). It relies on two components: an attacking model that generates jailbreaks and a judge model that verifies if the output is banned content.

The “entire pipeline is built on top of widely available models,” Shilov told Ars. The attacking model is a publicly available version of Qwen3-32B with its safety training stripped out, downloaded from Hugging Face, and the judge model is Gemini 2.5 Flash.

“You don’t need to have frontier models to break defenses of a frontier model, which is very interesting,” Shilov said.

A lot of time was invested in making sure that the judge model accurately flagged explicit content, Shilov said. White Circle research engineer Dmitrii Kharlapenko told Ars that when it comes to testing image generators, the whole field of red-teaming “is very poorly calibrated,” with “literally zero papers” setting up norms. For that reason, it’s an area that remains “completely plagued with reporting issues,” which is concerning to White Circle, as AI companies push to capture markets by releasing ever more eye-catching new models.

For White Circle, the research aimed to build more sophisticated models that could simulate attacks on other models, Shilov explained. That way, they could “help defenders identify and address vulnerabilities before they are exploited maliciously,” the preprint said.

In his ideal world, Shilov thinks AI firms shouldn’t just face mandatory external safety testing but also third-party monitoring, much like the system used to prevent nuclear threats.

Then, entities like White Circle could possibly form a coalition to help detect AI threats in real time, without suffering from biases. Shilov noted that an emerging problem in the AI ecosystem is that basically anyone doing interesting safety work is likely to be contracted by frontier labs, potentially compromising their work.

White Circle has partnered with frontier labs. It previously took part in Anthropic’s bug bounty program, but ultimately found that program was “very constrained in its purpose.”

“The program is focused on universal jailbreaks on domains they care most about, defined by their own specific terms,” White Circle told Ars.

Research like their most recent RISE paper “certainly” wouldn’t have been covered by that program, White Circle said. And conducting that work within Anthropic risked constraining White Circle from sharing it with the public.

Anthropic has proposed going one step further and embedding third-party AI safety evaluators in its labs, which White Circle said would allow them to operate at a much higher level than participating in the bug bounty program. However, the public may not always be able to closely follow that work. On Tuesday, OpenAI and Anthropic urged that restrictive non-disclosure agreements should be required of external evaluators to prevent leaks of trade secrets, Reuters reported.

White Circle would not be willing to sign any restrictive NDAs that might prevent public sharing of critical findings, White Circle told Ars, so if Anthropic requires NDAs, that partnership likely would not happen.

Bad actors who are determined to make AI-generated nonconsensual intimate images (NCII) and child sex abuse materials (CSAM) don’t need frontier models and often use so-called nudifying apps designed for that harmful purpose. But Google’s research found that 20 percent of online users who admitted to making AI nudes did so “for fun” or “as a joke,” while nearly a third were merely “experimenting with tech.” It therefore matters how easy it is to break defenses of the most accessible models. Safeguards should be mandatory, Google’s research said, in order to shut down a “pathway into abuse” for “a subset of perpetrators who might otherwise be deterred by technical friction.”

“A burden of responsibility also falls on developers to implement robust, model-level guardrails, and provenance indicators to prevent the initial generation and subsequent distribution of synthetic sexual imagery,” Google’s research said.

Last week, the Internet Watch Foundation (IWF) warned that urgent action was needed after expert analysts found “more photorealistic AI-generated child sexual abuse images in the first half of this year than in the whole of 2025, including imagery depicting children under two years old.” In total, 6,310 AI images meeting the legal definition of CSAM were found in the first six months of 2026, which is about 40 percent higher than last year’s total findings.

The UK-based nonprofit charity monitors CSAM globally and runs a hotline to support victims targeted. In the UK, they’re calling for regulators to introduce a safety framework that requires AI companies to prevent their technology from being used to generate CSAM, an IWF spokesperson told Ars.

Until then, IWF thinks it’s important for third parties like White Circle to “highlight where companies’ safeguards are failing.”

“Our analysts have seen how advances in AI enable the generation of abusive child sexual abuse imagery with minimal effort, removing the need for technical expertise and significantly lowering barriers to entry,” IWF’s spokesperson said. “AI tools can reproduce and amplify criminal content, accelerating the creation and spread of harmful material at scale. Any friction or step that can be introduced to make it harder to misuse these tools is a positive step forward.”

Just as outside input could help refine filters, IWF thinks that tech companies should also be working more closely with advocates to scrutinize models to better tackle AI-generated CSAM.

“Assessing CSAM is a highly specialized task that requires expert training and welfare support, and is not something for tech companies or machine learning scientists to take lightly,” IWF’s spokesperson said. “But safety must be baked into new technology by design—this includes testing models before they are released to market to make sure they cannot be used to create nude or sexual imagery of children.”

Using a method like RISE, White Circle thinks, could help frontier labs flag more jailbreaks more quickly and rapidly ramp up defenses to block harmful outputs. In addition to testing blocks on explicit images, firms could also use the method to prevent other banned outputs, like images depicting graphic violence or self-harm.

But the labs have not yet come calling for the reproduction pipeline, which will be shared on White Circle’s GitHub to help policymakers assess whether AI safety laws are needed to keep frontier labs in check.

Frontier labs won’t invest seriously in safety testing until it’s mandatory, Shilov told Ars. The preprint argues that existing automated red-teaming tools, which typically rewrite harmful prompts one at a time, are poorly suited to testing today’s hardened commercial models. RISE instead takes reusable natural-language attack strategies and uses them to generate many varied prompts, which White Circle says can help labs find and patch weaknesses faster.

“You don’t need frontier models or proprietary tech to break these systems; you just need a free download and the ability to make API calls,” Shilov said. “And yet the labs building these systems are the ones assessing their own safety, publishing their own results, and setting their own standards. This is further proof, if we needed it, that governments should be pushing for independent, third-party evaluation.”

Correction: This story has been updated to correct several errors. An earlier version described a passage from the RISE preprint as explaining how AI models could block harmful outputs; the passage instead describes the researchers’ attack method. It also said the method bypassed safety filters about 13 percent of the time; that was the highest human-verified rate, achieved on DALL·E 3, and rates for other models were lower. The story also misidentified the judge model, which was Gemini 2.5 Flash, and has been updated to note that the attacking model had its safety training removed.

If you’re looking, here’s a “good deal” for NASA and the European Space Agency

Ars Technica Long form October 07, 2026

“We are in the era of people interested in having good deals, and LISA is a very good deal for the US.”

It’s no surprise that NASA’s new tack toward foreign partnerships—good deals only, please—is challenging preconceived notions of international cooperation in space.

Without a massive budget hike, the US space agency’s emphasis on building a Moon Base and winning a competition for lunar real estate and resources with China will inevitably leave lesser priorities behind.

Gone is the Lunar Gateway, a space station that was to be assembled in orbit around the Moon. For the United States, Gateway was an unnecessary distraction and expense as NASA goes all-in on placing a surface station near the Moon’s south pole.

NASA canceled the Mars Sample Return mission after its budget ballooned beyond $10 billion. It would have cannibalized the agency’s budget for robotic science missions, a funding line already in jeopardy as the Trump administration directs NASA to focus on human spaceflight and a Moon Base.

Before their cancellation, each project involved extensive cooperation with NASA’s international partners, but NASA was the leader on both. It’s not surprising that a nation’s priorities will change with elections and external pressures, like the 21st-century space race taking shape with China.

Going forward, NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said NASA’s international partners must be ready to make “meaningful contributions,” with greater urgency than before. That means they should offer something that NASA or US companies aren’t already doing and deliver the contribution when NASA needs it.

This is creating friction in some areas. It’s most apparent between NASA and the European Space Agency, which is struggling to find a place in NASA’s Moon Base program after the cancellation of Gateway. Isaacman dismissed an ESA proposal earlier this year to develop a European cargo lander to carry supplies for the Moon Base, a role NASA officials expect US-built landers to fill sooner.

So what does a good deal in international spaceflight look like in the Trump era? Isaacman cited a couple of examples: Japan’s commitment to provide a pressurized rover for astronauts on the Moon and Italy’s agreement to build what will likely be the first habitat for the Moon Base.

Here’s another one. Scientists are in the early stages of developing the Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA) mission, the world’s first space-based observatory for detecting and studying gravitational waves.

As currently envisioned, the LISA mission will be led by the European Space Agency, with significant contributions from the United States. The mission will use three spacecraft flying in a triangle formation in heliocentric orbit, positioned nearly 1.6 million miles (2.5 million kilometers) apart to pick up the faint signals of low-frequency gravitational waves. Launch is scheduled for around 2035.

Gravitational waves are a relatively new area of astronomy, using detectors spread across a wide area, like on a continent or in space, to identify ripples in the fabric of space-time generated by cataclysmic events in the distant cosmos. Beginning with the first detection with a ground-based observatory in 2015, astronomers have used gravitational waves rippling across the Universe to reveal the collisions of black holes and neutron stars in faraway galaxies.

LISA will unlock a new wave of gravitational wave science by spreading its detectors over greater distances. Each spacecraft will carry two free-floating gold-platinum cubes inside an internal Faraday cage that protects them from all external disturbances other than gravitation, canceling out thruster firings, spacecraft vibrations, and the almost imperceptible influences from solar radiation pressure and interplanetary dust.

The LISA spacecraft will literally fly themselves around the free-floating cubes inside them, while inter-satellite lasers will measure the exact distances between the test masses. The laser ranging instruments must be sensitive enough to detect a change in distance smaller than the size of an atom to confirm a gravitational wave detection.

Under its agreement with ESA, NASA is responsible for supplying the transmitters and telescopes for the lasers. NASA will also provide charge management devices to reduce the buildup of electric charge on the proof masses inside each spacecraft and support data analysis on the ground to find the sources of LISA’s gravitational wave detections. Europe will build the spacecraft, launch them, and operate them.

This is exactly the kind of international partnership NASA should hold onto, according to Ira Thorpe, a gravitational wave astronomer at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center and leader of the US science team for the LISA mission. NASA isn’t working on its own gravitational wave observatory for space, and the agency likely couldn’t afford it if it wanted to.

“We are in the era of people interested in having good deals, and LISA is a very good deal for the US,” Thorpe said in a recent presentation at the National Academies’ Committee on Astronomy and Astrophysics.

“We are paying for roughly a third [of the mission],” Thorpe said. “We’re getting all of the science data, 100 percent of it. That is very good leverage. We are giving them (ESA) this flagship. If the US was to do LISA on its own, it would probably be a… $3 billion kind of number as an off-the-top-of-my-head guess. For a fraction of that cost, we are getting the same science.”

Thorpe’s $3 billion estimate isn’t far off the mark. ESA approved development of the LISA mission in 2024 with a budget of 1.75 billion euros ($2 billion), but that figure doesn’t include contributions from the United States or individual ESA member states. As it stands today, NASA’s work on the LISA mission is expected to cost around $1 billion, but the agency hasn’t yet established a firm budget commitment.

“I think this is the largest science mission that ESA has attempted to do. Full stop,” Thorpe said. The LISA mission has a long history, with the first concepts for a gravitational wave observatory dating to the 1970.

“It’s bounced back and forth, depending on how the political winds have shifted on both sides of the Atlantic over decades,” Thorpe said. “I think we’re in a very stable system where ESA is going to clearly lead. NASA is going to be the major partner, a critical partner, for the project.”

But the Trump administration injected doubt into LISA’s future last year when the White House proposed canceling NASA’s participation in the project, alongside dozens of other science missions. Congress rejected the cuts and restored funding for fiscal year 2026, but the Trump administration again proposed cancellation in its 2027 budget request released earlier this year.

“That caused some concern in Europe, which I think is understandable,” Thorpe said. “But at the same time, speaking from the project side, we continue to do our work. We try to just focus on making our deliverables. We’ve met every deliverable commitment to ESA so far. We have not missed.”

Congress is expected to continue funding LISA, which has powerful patrons on Capitol Hill and was one of a handful of future NASA science missions with a specific funding line in Congress’s appropriations bill for 2026.

Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.), whose constituency includes NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center leading the US contribution to LISA, is the top Democrat on the Senate subcommittee responsible for writing NASA’s budget. Van Hollen could take over as chairman if Democrats win control of the Senate in this year’s midterm elections. Across the Capitol, Rep. Glenn Ivey (D-Md.), whose district also includes Goddard, sits on the corresponding subcommittee in the House.

“I think we’re in very good shape going forward,” Thorpe said.

The NASA official overseeing all of the agency’s astrophysics missions is Shawn Domagal-Goldman. Despite the White House’s attempt to end NASA’s contribution to the LISA mission, the 2026 budget passed by Congress and subsequently signed into law by President Trump should signal to ESA that Washington supports the project.

“Something this complex is always challenging, but it’s why it’s important that we reaffirm our commitment with the funding that we have in the FY ’26 appropriations bill,” Domagal-Goldman said. “As long as we have a continuing resolution or anything at our current funding levels, we will maintain our commitment to the LISA mission.”

“I’m really happy for that because when LISA launches, it’s going to answer some of these other big questions that you can only do with a space-based gravitational wave observatory,” he said.

LISA’s scientific pursuits include investigating the origins of black holes and galaxy formation. It could potentially be sensitive enough to detect gravitational waves originating shortly after the Big Bang, allowing scientists to test the theories about the birth of our Universe, according to NASA.

“These are propagating disturbances in space-time,” Thorpe said of gravitational waves. “They can carry energy. They can carry momentum, and I think most interesting for astronomers, they can carry information about the systems that produce them, and we can use them to understand the Universe.”

Physicists will use detections from LISA to test Einstein’s general theory of relativity. Some of the most cataclysmic events in the cosmos, such as mergers of supermassive black holes, should produce a very specific gravitational wave signature, according to general relativity. LISA will be more sensitive to lower-frequency gravitational waves than ground-based observatories, like LIGO, corresponding to the kind of waves scientists expect to be generated by the most massive black holes.

“GR gives us an exact prediction for what this waveform would look like, so any small deviation would give you some hint as to what might be going on,” Thorpe said. “I like to think if GR is going to break—and I don’t generally like to bet against Einstein—but if it is going to break, these are the kinds of places where it may break down.”

Another joint science mission between NASA and ESA has, at least so far, survived the White House’s budget ax. NASA has long been on the hook to provide the launch for Europe’s Rosalind Franklin Mars rover, along with a science instrument and retrorockets for the craft that will deliver it to the Martian surface. The Trump administration sought to cancel NASA’s role in the mission, but funding approved by Congress last year was enough for NASA to finally book a launch for Europe’s first Mars rover on a SpaceX rocket in 2028. Notably, Rosalind Franklin is currently the only future Mars rover with any NASA involvement.

Questions remain about NASA’s role in other joint missions with ESA. The New Athena X-ray observatory, scheduled to launch in the late 2030s, is supposed to be the largest X-ray telescope ever built, a successor to NASA’s Chandra X-ray Observatory, still operational after launching in 1999. As with LISA, New Athena was conceived as a European-led mission with major support from NASA.

Domagal-Goldman said NASA is “fully engaged” with ESA on the New Athena mission and remains “fully committed” to the partnership. But New Athena didn’t get a specific funding callout in Congress’s 2026 budget for NASA.

The chances of a major US contribution to ESA’s next mission to Venus, named Envision, are less assured. NASA has its own Venus missions in the pipeline, and although the US space agency has not officially announced that it is pulling out of the Envision partnership, ESA is moving ahead with contracts to begin developing a European-made radar mapping instrument for the Envision orbiter, which was previously supposed to be built at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in California.

As NASA’s support wavered, ESA was on the clock to decide on Envision’s radar because the mission is slated for launch in 2031. With Envision, at least, ESA is ready to strike out on its own.
