Google shouldn’t be pressuring schools to use its AI

New Scientist November 05, 2026

When I was at school, a new technology launched in the form of a magic box that could answer any question you wanted. It was called Google, and my teachers cautioned that we shouldn’t trust everything it spat out, because anyone could put anything on the internet. Three decades later, history is repeating – with a twist. Schools are now begging Google to allow students to access its search engine, but the tech giant says that is only possible if teachers also accept a new kind of magic box, AI.

Google is far more integrated into education than it was in my day, with its Classroom and Workspace products providing teachers and students with a range of tools from email to lesson planning. More recently, Google has incorporated its Gemini AI chatbot into Classroom, to the chagrin of some US school districts that want to be able to decide whether or not students have access to AI. Sure, said Google, you can switch off AI, but then you lose search. “Search and AI are deeply integrated,” Google’s Chris Phillips told The New York Times.

Why I have changed my mind about AI and you should too

At first, I thought this must be a misunderstanding about what we call AI. For most people today, AI means a large language model (LLM) of the type that powers Gemini or ChatGPT. But Google’s search engine has long used AI in the historical sense of machine learning, starting in 2015 with a system called RankBrain that helped relate words to concepts in order to produce search results. The AI Overviews you often see at the top of a search today, which launched in 2024, are the only part of the search results produced by Gemini.

Advertisement

Surely, I thought, what’s happening here is that school districts saying “no AI” simply mean no AI Overviews, while Google is quite reasonably saying it isn’t possible to rip out elements of its search engine that have been operating for over a decade in order to comply with a strict “no AI” request. This can easily be solved by making sure everyone is talking about the same thing, right?

Wrong. Google really is presenting schools with an all-or-nothing choice. “If a school is not comfortable with that and simply wants AI off, then they have the choice to not have search on at all,” Phillips told education news outlet Chalkbeat. This is a product decision, not a technical one. AI Overviews do not appear on every search, and they can be disabled for every search by adding a short code to the URL. Google could surely provide schools with this option, if it wished. When asked to comment, a Google spokesperson sent New Scientist a link to a blog post on AI tutoring with its Gemini product.

We have seen a tech giant use this playbook before. Around the same time that Google was launching its young, upstart search engine in the late 1990s, Microsoft was facing legal action for forcing people to install the Internet Explorer (IE) browser as part of its Windows operating system, in an effort to fight off competitor browsers. At the time, Microsoft claimed that the files for IE were an “integral part” of Windows and could not be removed “without impairing the performance of the operating system”. In 2001, a US court ruled that this integration served to illegally maintain a monopoly, and Microsoft was obliged to make other browsers more accessible. By 2010, Microsoft was forced to offer users a range of browsers, following a European Commission ruling.

Around one-third of AI search tool answers make unsupported claims

There is no suggestion that Google is doing anything illegal in its approach to schools, although the company is currently appealing a US antitrust ruling that found it illegally maintains a monopoly in online search, and commentators have accused it of exploiting that monopoly. “Google is trying to use its monopoly power to force AI into our public schools”, wrote New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani on X. Following the backlash, Google posted on X that for schools, Gemini and search will be off by default and schools can choose to turn on either at their discretion. That doesn’t actually address the issue of having search without AI Overviews, however.

Ultimately, it will probably be for the courts to decide whether Google should be made to offer search without AI, but I am more interested in the question of how and when children should begin to use AI. Google has a 90 per cent market share in search, so it would be naive to think that children aren’t being exposed to AI Overviews, even if they do end up banned in schools. Personally, I know that AI Overviews can be heavily flawed and provide incorrect information, and yet I still find it hard to ignore them at the top of my search results, even while knowing that I should be clicking links to provide websites with revenue if I want them to continue existing.

Research on how LLMs affect learning is still in early days, but the evidence we have is worrying. One study of around 10,000 adults found that people who used an LLM summary rather than a list of links gained a shallower understanding of a topic, seemingly because having the results predigested by an AI required less cognitive effort. Another study of more than 26,000 students in China found that allowing them to use AI drastically improved homework performance, but saw exam results fall – suggesting that the children were letting AI do their homework for them without really learning anything.

Google’s answer to these concerns is its Guided Learning product, which it is adding to search for student accounts. It says the system will pick up when children are looking for help with homework, and walk them through it step by step, rather than simply providing an answer. In tests conducted with around 1800 students in Sierra Leone, Google says this approach provided more than a year of typical learning progress in just eight weeks.

In principle, I am not against the use of AI in schools – it is a modern, useful technology that will surely be part of students’ lives in the future, and they should learn to understand it just as I learned the pros and cons of using Google back in the 90s. The question of how to handle homework assignments in the age of AI, when an essay can be produced in seconds, is thorny and ongoing. One option is to simply scrap homework and require more in-classroom testing, but if Google gets its way and AI ends up being unavoidable there as well, it seems like teachers will have little control. That, to me, is the most objectionable point, as it should not be down to tech giants to set education policy.

Ordering takeaway food, writing emails, reworking presentations: AI assistants are promoted as a way of outsourcing mundane tasks to free up your time for more interesting pursuits. So, what are they actually good for – and what are the risks?

COP climate summits might yet have a useful future – here’s how

New Scientist November 07, 2026

At a certain point, it becomes impossible to convey the urgency of the climate crisis in words. Calls to “intensify efforts” to cut emissions or countries “expressing alarm” at the pace of climate change start to ring hollow after years of rising emissions. At a certain point, you have to ask, what difference will another carefully worded declaration really make?

This is a live question: next week, countries will gather at the COP31 summit in Antalya, Turkey, to progress the global response to climate change. For the seasoned attendee, these gatherings follow a predictable rhythm: some pomp and ceremony at the start when the world leaders are in attendance, followed by a quiet first week of backroom talks, escalating tension and fights over finance in the second week, all rounded off with a late-night showdown as countries argue over the wording of a final agreement.

In the context of ever more dire warnings from scientists and increasingly severe real-world climate disasters, this is an event cycle that is wearing thin. To many of those in attendance – and millions more looking on from afar – it is becoming increasingly clear that COP summits are failing to deliver meaningful progress.

Advertisement

This is a relatively new problem. For decades, the job of a COP negotiator was to forge some kind of global agreement to address climate change. That was no mean feat, and it took years of hard work and dedication to deliver the Paris Agreement in 2015. After the treaty was struck, climate negotiators then spent a few years busily drawing up the rules that would govern how the agreement would work in practice. But with that work largely completed by 2021, since then, COP summits have been left to drift, plagued by arguments over finance and bewildering last-minute disputes over the wording of seemingly uncontentious statements. At last year’s summit, for example, countries couldn’t agree on even mentioning fossil fuels in the final agreement.

COP31 will largely follow the same format. Arguments are already brewing over funding, negotiators are flexing their pens to hammer out details of new bureaucratic mechanisms, and hosts Turkey and Australia are limbering up for fresh disputes over which adverbs to deploy in a final agreement. This is your official warning: COP31 will not be the meeting that saves the world from climate peril.

But there could be one bright spark at the summit. An electrification pledge being touted by the Turkish presidency would see countries promise to increase electricity’s share of their final energy consumption to 35 per cent to 2035.

Focusing the climate effort on electrification is a smart move. In the current landscape, with disinformation rife and a climate denier still in the White House, electrifying stuff is probably our strongest climate weapon. High oil and gas prices and geopolitical instability make the energy security benefits of electrification obvious, while cheap green power could ease cost of living pressures in high-income countries and unlock development in low-income nations.

Electric power is also just so much more efficient than burning fuel. Electricity currently provides about 23 per cent of the energy delivered to consumers, but it powers sectors that make up 46 per cent of the global economy, energy analyst Jan Rosenow pointed out recently. If the world’s economy transitioned to a highly electrified state, powered by renewables, total primary energy use – the raw inputs into the energy system – would fall by almost 50 per cent, Rosenow’s analysis shows. Electrifying stuff is a common-sense move, before you even get to the climate benefits.

Plenty of richer countries are not moving fast enough on this stuff. China and Indonesia are ahead of both the US and the UK on electrifying their economies, while India and Brazil are catching up fast. We could learn a lot by looking beyond our borders. Annual climate meetings should become an opportunity for countries to swap notes and share best practice on the energy transition, not fight over the wording of virtue-signalling statements.

For too long, COPs have been generating a lot of words and not much action. But efforts are under way behind the scenes to redesign these meetings as useful events for the clean energy transition. The push for electrification offers a hint of what this could look like. If it delivers, COP summits might yet have a useful future.

Is a broken jet stream causing extreme weather that lasts longer?

This may include serious public health consequences, a breakdown of vital infrastructure such as transport links and energy grids, crop failures and the collapse of ecosystems.

Governments should urgently start to prepare for more extreme heat events, he adds: “A region like Europe has to prepare for more intense heatwaves in the coming decades.”

A tiny magnet that levitates within a superconductor trap may be the fastest spinning object visible to the naked eye, and one of the fastest spinning objects ever made. In the future, it could be used in experiments searching for mysterious dark matter particles and aid the development of quantum technologies.

Superconductors are materials that conduct electricity with perfect efficiency, and they also expel any magnetic field that tries to permeate them – a phenomenon known as the Meissner effect. Because of this, a magnet placed above a superconductor experiences repulsive magnetic forces and starts to levitate. Tao Wang at the Agency for Science Technology and Research in Singapore and his colleagues have now set one such levitating magnet spinning at an unprecedently fast rate.

A miniature magnet rivals behemoths in strength for the first time

The researchers used a spherical magnet made from neodymium, iron and boron that was about 30 micrometres wide, similar to the width of a fine human hair. They placed it in a cylindrical container made from lead, then enclosed that container in a chamber devoid of air, or a vacuum chamber.

Advertisement

Next, they used liquid helium to cool the whole setup to approximately -269°C (-452°F), only a few degrees above the coldest possible temperature. Under these extreme circumstances, lead behaved as a superconductor and the lack of air meant that the magnet could levitate within it without bumping into any particles. The team set the magnet spinning with a magnetic coil, ultimately pushing this tiny rotor to 138 million revolutions per minute.

Wang says the magnet’s spinning was also very stable: it would take 17 days for its spinning speed to decrease by 50 per cent, something that would typically happen more quickly due to interactions between the magnet and its environment. “In terms of how many turns it makes before slowing down significantly, this is in the same league as the Earth’s spinning,” he says. “This, so far, is the fastest magnetically levitated rotor.” The record for the fastest rotating human-made object is also held by a levitated sphere, but that one was nano-sized, so invisible to the naked eye, and levitated by laser beams.

Physics of light and magnetism rewritten after almost two centuries

Because the rotor experiences essentially no friction, and it is magnetic and cold, its behaviour is very sensitive to its environment, which makes it a promising sensor. The team has already successfully tested it as a gauge of vacuum at very low temperatures. Wang says this could be useful for builders of quantum computers, which often must be kept extremely cold and isolated in order to work.

Benjamin Stickler at Ulm University in Germany says the levitated spinning magnet could also be used to precisely sense and measure magnetic fields.

It could also be a promising platform for tests of fundamental physics, such as looking for effects related to dark matter particles, or sensing gravitational waves at so far unexplored frequencies, says team member Andrea Vinante at the National Research Council in Italy. Additionally, at very low temperatures quantum effects become dominant, so it could even be used for explorations of quantum mechanics and its interplay with gravity at micrometre scales, he says.

Less than 4 minutes of physical exertion a day – such as rushing for the bus or carrying heavy shopping – could halve your dementia risk. People who engaged in short bursts of vigorous movement were up to 48 per cent less likely to develop the condition than their sedentary counterparts in a large study.

“These brief bursts of higher-intensity daily activities are in every nook and cranny of our day-to-day routines, so this creates a really exciting and viable opportunity to find new ways for the everyday person to protect their health,” says Nicholas Koemel at the University of Sydney, who parks his car in a distant space when he gets to work so he has to walk further.

Your brain’s unexpected ability to regenerate and how to harness it

Exercise brings a myriad of benefits, from promoting muscle growth and staving off cardiovascular disease to enhancing mental health. Yet many people find it hard to fit the recommended 150 minutes of moderate-intensity physical activity per week into their routines.

Advertisement

This has caused interest to grow in the benefits of the incidental exercise people get through ordinary exertion, like walking up a hill or playing energetically with children. Recent studies have found that such short bursts of activity can help keep your heart healthy and add years to your life. When it comes to cognition, just a couple of minutes of walking or stretching every hour has been linked to improved memory and attention span.

Focusing on dementia risk, Koemel and his colleagues analysed data from 22,618 adults, who were mainly in their early 60s, from the UK Biobank study. None of the participants had a dementia diagnosis when they strapped on wrist-worn accelerometers to track their activity over seven days between 2013 and 2015.

Free newsletter

The researchers looked in the data for sporadic instances of high-intensity effort, such as climbing stairs, carrying heavy shopping or rushing for the bus. The participants were followed for around eight years after they wore the accelerometer until whichever came first: a dementia diagnosis, death or the end of the follow-up period in November 2022.

During the study, 170 of the participants were diagnosed with dementia. The researchers found that 2.5 per cent of those who did no exercise at all developed the condition. Among people who didn’t set aside time to exercise, but managed a few daily bouts of vigorous lifestyle activity, 0.71 per cent developed dementia. The risk was lowest, at 0.59 per cent, among those who deliberately exercised alongside their daily exertions.

Overall, an accumulation of just 3.7 minutes per day of vigorous routine movement was associated with a 48 per cent lower dementia risk. It was also linked to larger volumes of grey matter in several brain regions, and shrinking of areas of abnormal brain tissue known as white matter hyperintensities. “The results are pretty headline-grabbing,” says Mike Trott at the University of Queensland in Australia.

The study is observational, so it doesn’t prove that bursts of activity directly change dementia risk. It is also possible that undiagnosed dementia caused subtle functional decline that left some people less able to engage in such exercise, says Koemel. Another potential issue is that the study only covered a week-long snapshot of physical activity years before the dementia diagnoses, says Trott.

But previous studies show that, as cardiorespiratory fitness increases, dementia risk drops and grey matter volume increases. “The more we take care of our cardiometabolic health via activities like physical activity, the more we may prolong the health of our brain,” says Koemel.

Physical activity causes a type of brain cell called astrocytes to contract, which then leads to the formation of new neurons, according to a study in mice

The researchers speculate that even tiny vigorous bursts of activity could contribute to better vascular health by lowering blood pressure and reducing arterial stiffness. This reduces the chance of vascular brain injury, which can cause dementia. Energetic physical activity also often requires fast posture adjustments, which means engaging the brain’s cerebellar and sensorimotor networks. This could contribute to the larger grey matter volumes observed in these areas.

But the results don’t mean everyone should suddenly start running up the stairs. “We typically will recommend people gradually increase their physical activity, because radical shifts could increase the risk of certain accidents or injuries,” says Koemel. “A core message is that a little can go a long way here.”

Inflammation of lymphatic vessels, which drain brain waste, may be involved in the onset of Parkinson’s disease. The condition is associated with the build-up of a misfolded protein called alpha-synuclein, which may not be efficiently removed from the brain if the lymphatic vessels are impaired. But the accumulation of alpha-synuclein seems to further damage these vessels, creating a self-reinforcing chain of events where each problem worsens the other.

A dramatic rethink of Parkinson’s offers new hope for treatment

“It is a vicious cycle,” says Justin Rustenhoven at the University of Auckland in New Zealand. This may also help explain why Parkinson’s disease is a progressive condition that worsens over time, he says.

Parkinson’s disease, which affects more than 10 million people worldwide, is characterised by a loss of neurons in brain regions that control movement. This causes symptoms such as tremor and muscle stiffness. The condition is thought to be caused by alpha-synuclein, which occurs naturally in the brain, misfolding and forming clumps that damage neurons.

Advertisement

In 2021, researchers showed that accumulation of alpha-synuclein in Parkinson’s disease may partly result from impaired drainage of brain waste via meningeal lymphatic vessels. These are found in the outermost layer of three membranes, called meninges, surrounding the brain. The vessels receive waste from a network of channels surrounding the brain’s blood vessels, called the glymphatic system, before transporting it to other parts of the body for disposal.

But what causes the lymphatic impairment in Parkinson’s disease was unknown. Rustenhoven and his colleagues wondered whether it may result from alpha-synuclein clogging up the meninges. “No one had really looked at that before,” says Rustenhoven, with most research focusing on changes to the regions that control movement, which are located deep within the brain.

The team analysed post-mortem samples of the meninges from seven people who’d had severe Parkinson’s disease and seven people who hadn’t had the condition. Only the Parkinson’s samples had alpha-synuclein clumps. “For the first time, we showed that these aggregates accumulate at the brain’s borders in people with Parkinson’s,” says Rustenhoven.

Free newsletter

To determine whether such protein accumulation impairs clearance of brain waste, the researchers injected mice with a virus that infected cells called fibroblasts in the meninges. This caused them to continually produce alpha-synuclein at elevated levels, similar to those seen in people with Parkinson’s disease. At such high levels, alpha-synuclein misfolded and formed toxic clumps that spread across cells in lymphatic vessels in the meninges, but not inside the brain.

Two months later, brain imaging revealed that these mice’s meningeal lymphatic vessels drained waste fluid half as rapidly as those of control mice, which were injected with a virus encoding for an inert protein. What’s more, in the former group of mice, immune cells called macrophages had engulfed the alpha-synuclein clumps at the brain’s borders. This caused the macrophages to double in number and produce about triple the amount of TNF-alpha, an inflammatory molecule.

Next, the team exposed sheets of human cells, found in meningeal lymphatic vessels, to either alpha-synuclein or TNF-alpha. Both molecules caused gaps to form between the lymphatic cells, making them leaky, says Rusterhoven.

“The accumulation of alpha-synuclein in the brain borders basically drives an immune response that pokes holes in those lymphatic vessels, making them ineffective at draining,” he says. “We already know from other studies that those lymphatics are important for draining alpha-synuclein, so impaired lymphatic drainage [due to alpha-synuclein] means even more of the protein is going to build up.”

The controversial discovery that our brains can generate new neurons surprisingly late in life is now prompting a rethink of adult brain health, pointing the way to better treatments for stroke, dementia and depression

This feedback loop keeps reinforcing itself, which may cause the worsening of brain damage and symptoms associated with Parkinson’s, says Rusterhoven.

The same mechanism probably applies to other neurodegenerative conditions where proteins accumulate, such as Alzheimer’s disease, says Camille Carroll at Newcastle University in the UK. But this understanding also creates new treatment opportunities. It suggests that “therapies that dampen or modulate that immune response could prevent lymphatic dysfunction to treat Parkinson’s”, says Rusterhoven.

The team now plans to carry out similar experiments where mice are studied after they develop Parkinson’s symptoms, not just its associated brain changes. These mice will also be tracked for longer, he says.

“Their mouse model was appropriate for the question they were asking, which was looking specifically at the effects of alpha-synuclein at the brain border on lymphatics,” says Carroll. “But linking their findings to symptoms will be important.”

In ongoing work, the researchers are collecting more brain-border samples from people who died with Parkinson’s disease of varying severity. This will enable them to determine how often alpha-synuclein clogs up the brain’s borders during the condition and at what stage it may start causing lymphatic impairment.

A pill that induces hypoxia in the brain has been linked to improved symptoms of three neurodegenerative conditions when tested in mice

They are also trialling, in mice and human cells, whether drugs that block TNF-alpha can reverse lymphatic damage during Parkinson’s. A prior study looked at people with inflammatory bowel disease, which is linked to a higher risk of Parkinson’s, and found that those who took drugs that block TNF-alpha were 78 per cent less likely to develop Parkinson’s.

An ongoing trial is also giving people with REM (rapid eye movement) sleep behaviour disorder, which often precedes Parkinson’s disease, a drug that blocks TNF-alpha, to determine whether this affects Parkinson’s progression. “This will be very interesting evidence to support our findings,” says Rustenhoven.

The Hubble Space Telescope is slowly falling out of the sky, and it could burn up in Earth’s atmosphere as soon as 2032. Researchers are urging NASA to rescue it, arguing that the ageing instrument is still vital for science and will leave a stark capability gap if lost.

Hubble was launched in 1990 and, following an infamous design flaw in one of its mirrors that was only fixed in 1993, has provided a wealth of new science ever since. NASA claims that more than 23,000 peer-reviewed scientific papers have emerged from its images.

Stunning first images show the power of the Vera C. Rubin Observatory

But the space-based telescope requires periodic servicing and raising of its orbit, as atmospheric drag causes it to slowly lose altitude. Hubble has gyroscopes that allow it to shift position to image different parts of the sky, but no propulsion of its own.

Advertisement

The last time that Hubble was lifted to a higher orbit was in 2002, when the space shuttle Columbia visited – one of five shuttle missions to the telescope. Since then, NASA has retired the shuttle fleet and no longer has any spacecraft with the capability to carry out the task. NASA estimates that Hubble has a 10 per cent probability of re-entry by September 2032, and a 50 per cent probability by December 2033.

The space agency has put out a call for ideas from the commercial sector, giving companies until 30 November to submit plans for either raising the orbit of Hubble to at least 600 kilometres or safely de-orbiting it and letting it crash into the ocean. The telescope has parts of sufficient density that they would probably survive atmospheric re-entry.

Free newsletter

Such a move wouldn’t be unprecedented. Earlier this year, a NASA-funded mission carried out by commercial outfit Katalyst Space was launched to boost the orbit of the Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory, whose orbit was decaying in a similar fashion to Hubble’s. The mission failed due to a steering problem, but was widely regarded to be possible. Katalyst Space didn’t respond to New Scientist’s request for comment.

Alise Fisher at NASA says the agency is open to ideas from inside or outside the organisation, and isn’t taking anything off the table. “It wouldn’t be appropriate for the agency to speculate about specific potential responses, so we don’t inadvertently limit them, but NASA is looking to explore a range of technologies and approaches, including those the agency may not have considered previously.”

NASA’s call-out explains that a private company would need to supply everything for the mission: the launch vehicle, the spacecraft and, if applicable, the crew. The space agency issued a similar call for ideas in 2022, but did not proceed with any despite reportedly receiving eight submissions. It did investigate a proposal by SpaceX, but the company didn’t respond to New Scientist’s questions on whether it would be submitting a new proposal this time.

Thomas Haworth at Queen Mary University of London is part of a panel of scientists advising NASA on what direction to take with Hubble, which he describes as “the greatest telescope of all time”. He went into discussions with colleagues expecting the focus to be on how NASA could be advised to extract the most science from Hubble before the end of its life, but found that re-boosting its orbit was actually higher on the agenda, he says.

“It’s within the realms of possibility,” says Haworth. “The overall document that we’re coming up with, which still isn’t submitted yet, is going to try and strongly make that recommendation. There is quite a lot of effort to argue for a boost.”

Is an old NASA probe about to redraw the frontier of the solar system?

NASA is likely to make a decision quickly once that recommendation is in, because planning a boost mission will take years, says Haworth. “You need to decide now.”

Stephen Wilkins at the University of Sussex, UK, says Hubble has unique abilities unmatched by any other instrument – including the James Webb Space Telescope, the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope and the European Space Agency’s Euclid telescope.

Hubble can do high-resolution ultraviolet imaging better than anything currently available. NASA aims to launch the Ultraviolet Explorer in 2030, which will cover the same part of the spectrum but with a tenth of the resolution, and the Habitable Worlds Observatory (HWO) may launch in the 2040s and match Hubble’s ability. But if Hubble is allowed to burn up in 2032, this could leave a decade or more of lost science, and if the HWO is cancelled, then that could be a virtually permanent setback.

Launching a mission to physically grapple with the telescope, which is 13 metres long and weighs over 12,000 kilograms, will be no easy task. But it could also bring intangible benefits besides lengthening Hubble’s lifespan, says Wilkins.

“While repair is more complex now that we don’t have the space shuttle, attempting to repair Hubble helps maintain key skills that will be essential for future space exploration or exploitation,” he says. “Whether or not repair makes sense ultimately depends on the cost, but maintaining skills should also be considered.”

Why NASA is sending a probe to Europa – and what it’s looking for

Mark Norris at the University of Lancashire, UK, was previously funded by the Hubble budget to scour archived images for ultra-compact dwarf galaxies. “I’d worked out that, in the archive of these galaxies that Hubble had been surveying for other projects, the things I was interested in were must have been in the images by chance,” he says. “It basically built the foundation of my career. I wouldn’t have a permanent job now if it hadn’t been for that insight.”

Hubble was always designed to be serviced, says Norris, so it is fitted with grapple points for robotic arms to grab hold of. But raising its orbit wouldn’t be a permanent solution and it has begun to show its age.

“The instruments are gradually degrading through exposure to the space environment,” he says. “It’s a bit of a miracle it’s still going, but they over-engineer these things and they did service it so many times – they made sure that when the last service was done, everything was left working. It’s still doing really great science.”

NASA administrators will need to make difficult decisions about costs, as ongoing servicing and ground support will be needed on top of any mission to boost Hubble’s orbit.

“If they can save it, it makes sense, but it depends how much [it costs] and what gets axed in order to save it,” says Hayworth. “Say, for example, if they cut LISA [a plan to build a space-based gravitational wave detector]. This is probably personal and biased, but I think the science from that is so exciting that it would be a shame to lose that for the sake of an old instrument.”

A robot called GIMLI will explore a lunar cave for a future moon base

New Scientist November 06, 2026

In video-game terms, the moon is the first level in an unfathomably giant, never-ending realm. It is the place where we, the players, learn the controls and try very hard not to die, in preparation for safely exploring the rest of the solar system. At a convenient 385,000 kilometres from Earth – a stone’s throw in cosmic terms – our planet’s companion is a great testing ground. And the race is on to claim a piece of it for a base.

Unfortunately for us, the moon is also a preposterously dangerous place to be. The volcanic dust there is adhesive, abrasive and corrosive, able to eat through spacesuits and machinery like a swarm of voracious locusts. Its daytime temperature can reach 120°C, while its benighted craters can plunge to -245°C, which is close to absolute zero, the lowest possible temperature in the universe. There are moonquakes, which (unlike Earth’s own tremors) can last for tens of minutes. And its lack of an atmosphere means that its surface is unprotected from asteroids (which can splatter you) and space radiation (which can give you cancer).

There are so many awful ways to perish on the moon. China knows the risks. So does the US. And yet, these two countries – along with their many friends and enemies – aren’t just keen on sending astronauts to the lunar surface; they are also planning to establish their own nuclear-powered bases, home to rotating astronaut crews.

Advertisement

Asteroid hit the moon and flung rocks 120 kilometres from the crater

I know what you’re thinking: this sounds like the stuff of science fiction, in the sense that you think it will never happen or, if you do, you suspect that it will go horribly, dramatically wrong. But I have been covering these plans for several years now, and I can promise you two things. The first is that, because this new space race is being (partly, perhaps largely) driven by nationalistic zeal, a moon base is much closer to being realised than you might think. The second is that you’re right: if space agencies aren’t exceedingly careful, things could go wrong.

Neither side wants to see a dead astronaut on the lunar surface, which is why these bases must be nothing short of impregnable fortresses. To that end, NASA recently announced that it has selected three new uncrewed scientific missions to the moon, each designed to further the goals of its Artemis programme. The first is a sophisticated seismometer, which will listen out for moonquakes and meteorite impacts. The second will hunt for signs of ice that can be turned into potable water, breathable oxygen and rocket fuel.

So far, so expected. But the third robotic mission really stood out to me, because it is going to investigate a subterranean lava tube.

Yes, you read that right: a tube, burrowed out by actual lava, on the moon.

Lava tubes are extremely cool – and I’m not just saying that because I’m a trained volcanologist. I have walked through several on Earth. They’re serpentine, cavernous things. They often form when a scorching-hot river of molten rock is rushing through a channel. When the river runs out of momentum or magma, the top – exposed to the atmosphere – cools quickly, forming a roof. The rest of the lava drains out elsewhere, leaving an eerie, inky-black hollow behind. Some of them even have nice acoustics, which makes them great alternative gig venues.

The moon is a great big ball of frozen magma. It’s geologically comatose today, but a stegosaurus could have looked up and seen the crimson glow of freshly erupted lava painting the lunar surface. And where there’s an abundance of lava, there are oodles of lava tubes. The problem is that, from the perspective of NASA’s Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter satellite, suspected lava tube sites just look like deep, shadowy pits.

The Marius Hills pit, on the moon’s nearside, is a prime example. It looks like someone punched a hole in the lunar surface, which is why it’s thought to be a natural skylight for a lava tube. Keen to find out for sure, NASA is sending a robotic mission there to scout it out – and not just to settle a few bets between lunar geologists.

Jessica Atkin knows more than anyone else about what it would take to supply food for a moon base. She reveals how to build a lunar farm and what astronauts can expect to dine on

NASA notes that lava tubes offer “natural, ready-made shelters that provide crucial thermal stability and shielding from deadly ionizing radiation and micrometeoroid bombardment”. That’s right: one day, NASA’s astronauts might be living in ancient volcanic vaults to avoid spending too much time on its truly terrible surface.

The mission to the Marius Hills pit – the first plan to explore a lunar lava tube – doesn’t have a launch date just yet. But it does have an excellent name: the Geophysical Instruments for Marius Lunar pit Investigation, or GIMLI. Yes, that one, the warrior dwarf from Middle-earth who loves his axe, despises evil rings of power and frequents all kinds of dangerous caves.

I reached out to Nathaniel Putzig at the Planetary Science Institute, the principal investigator of GIMLI. He swears that the name wasn’t inspired by J. R. R. Tolkien’s Lord of the Rings. He says that he simply wrote down words describing the mission plan and arranged them to make a pleasing sounding acronym.

“At the time, I was only vaguely aware of the Tolkien association, not fully realising that I had happened upon the name for legendary dwarf Gimli, member of the Fellowship of the Ring and the first Lord of the Glittering Caves,” he told me. The name, he said, “won out in the ranked choice voting by team members”. Thank goodness, because it’s literally perfect for this mission.

GIMLI is a joint effort between the Planetary Science Institute, NASA, the Norwegian Space Agency and US tech firm Honeybee Robotics, a subsidiary of Blue Origin. It won’t abseil into the pit itself. Instead, it will land next to it and use its suite of instruments – including a ground-penetrating radar, seismic sensors and a device that measures subtle differences in the moon’s gravitational field – to map out the hidden subsurface, while its cameras take shots of the pit and its walls.

Presuming the skylight does lead to a lava tube, GIMLI won’t just scratch a scientific itch. It will inform NASA’s plans to keep its astronauts from being murdered by the moon.

Car-sized asteroids burn up in Earth’s atmosphere without consequence. But on the moon, they slam, unimpeded, into the ground, and explode like a pile of dynamite. Very rarely – as happened in 2024 – an asteroid the size of a couple of football stadiums crashes into the lunar surface with the force of an atomic bomb. Astronauts are far more likely to be imperilled by pebble-sized asteroids, which sound like less of an issue until you realise that they travel at tens of thousands of kilometres per hour, effectively making them hypersonic space bullets. Fortunately, the roof of a lava tube would handily absorb their impacts.

If the ceiling of frozen lava was thick enough, it would also offer protection from a major solar storm. When the sun is feeling irritable, it can launch a salvo of super-charged particles our way. Earth’s magnetic field and substantial atmosphere deflect and soak up many of them. But the exposed moon takes these bombardments head on. In the event of an especially intense solar outburst, astronauts there could receive a fatal dose and die weeks or even days later of acute radiation sickness. Hiding in a lava tube could save their lives.

Thank goodness, then, that the GIMLI project exists, and can help us answer the many questions we still have. What are the moon’s lava tubes like? Are they roomy? Do they look stable? Could you fit an astronaut habitat in them, or a small nuclear reactor that powers a nearby base? Seeking these havens out is, in NASA’s words, “important groundwork for safe, long‑term living on the moon”.

NASA is targeting the lunar south pole for its upcoming crewed Artemis missions. This is where it wants to establish the first moon base, largely because it is thought to be home to crucial reservoirs of water. Should we expect that base to be at least partly concealed in a lava tube?

“Lava tubes necessarily form in volcanic terrain, and there is little or no evidence of such terrains in the heavily cratered highlands of the south polar region,” says Putzig. So, probably not. But, he adds, “other outposts may well be established elsewhere that lava tubes may be identified”.

Most lava tubes will also require something like rappels, or makeshift elevators, for astronauts to access them. This creates its own hazard: if a clumsy moonwalker trips, falls and gets stuck in a lava tube, or the machinery malfunctions, there’s a chance that they could die down there. Considering all the other ways the moon could take them out, this would be a pretty embarrassing end.

Lava tubes may be a bit of a hard sell: they could be onerous to find, troublesome to access and potentially a bit bleak to live in. I’m willing to bet that, if you’re going to camp on the moon for several months at a time, you would probably prefer to eschew a dark, volcanic labyrinth for a spot on the surface. Even if you’re at risk of being blasted by tiny space rocks, you at least get to see Earth, and the stars cresting the lunar horizon. Even on the moon, the call of the night sky may prove too bewitching a prospect to pass up.

New Zealand Herald November 07, 2026

Opportunity and the overhang are shaping up as the deciders in an incredibly tight election race.

Party leader Qiulae Wong says “stability” will be the most important factor in who her party chooses to work with – if they end up in the kingmaker position.

Te Pāti Māori’s electorate-first strategy seems to have succeeded, with the party on track to win five of the seven Māori seats.

Green leader Chlöe Swarbrick said the overhang strategy and changes to enrolment laws showed “the system has been gamed”.

Use our interactive to see who’s winning in every electorate as votes are counted.

Find out how the overhang works.

The winner of a Christchurch gelato store’s “scoop poll” is in.

Throughout the election campaign, Rollickin Gelato sold flavours based on seven New Zealand political parties.

Every scoop sold counted towards the poll, with results updated each morning on a chalkboard in the stores.

When a party leader visits, the store also gave away their corresponding flavour free for an hour. The David S’more flavour for Act came out on top at 26%, followed by National’s Blueberry Lux at 24% and The Opportunity Party at 15% with Cherry on ’Op.

The Kai Reka Kūmara flavour placed fourth at 13% for Te Pāti Māori, and Orange Choc Chippy flavoured gelato for Labour polled at 10%.

Marama Matcha flavour was at 6% for the Green Party, followed by Allsorts of Winston flavour at 5% for NZ First.

Photo / Anna Heath

Chlöe Swarbrick has challenged newcomers Opportunity to “get off the fence and choose a side”.

The Green Party co-leader said there was a “path to power” after Newstalk ZB’s Heather du Plessis-Allan asked what her gut was telling her about the party’s prospects of forming a Government.

“I think anyone who’s counting their chickens at the moment is going to be a fool in a few weeks’ time”, Swarbrick said.

Pressed by du Plessis-Allan, Swarbrick said she’d made the point in her speech last night that “there is a path to power”.

“And welcome to politics, Opportunity. It is time to get off the fence and choose a side.”

It made sense to choose the side that had the “greatest policy alignment, that clearly actually is willing to center the wellbeing of the planet and regular hardworking people”.

Photo / Jason Dorday

“So yeah, I think that stands in pretty stark contrast to the legacy of the last three years where we’ve seen regular hardworking people go backwards, meanwhile the rich list has pocketed another $27 billion in the past year.

“There is enough in this country if we choose to work together.”

Swarbrick acknowledged the Greens had picked up votes after Te Pāti Māori encouraged supporters to give their party vote to other left of centre parties.

The Greens doubled their share of the Māori electorates’ party votes yesterday, at 40%.

“This was a really upside down election, eh? And I was asked by a lot of people … about the split vote stuff … there’s no such thing as a strategic vote if everybody’s following their own strategy.

“In order to have something strategic, you need a critical mass of people doing things. And I think, yeah, we can see that that did happen to a certain extent obviously with Te Pāti Māori.”

But Māori support for the Greens was also the result of more than 20 years' work by many in the party, including late co-leader Jeanette Fitzsimons and “our Māori MPs, who’ve done the work on the ground”.

National Party campaign chair Simeon Brown said last night was “bittersweet” as his party has a pathway to victory but lost some heavy hitters in the process.

Highly regarded MPs Nicola Willis and Paul Goldsmith are all but certain to lose their jobs, while Chris Bishop is unlikely to make his way back into Parliament.

Brown told Newstalk ZB’s Heather du Plessis-Allan that all three are “key ministers”. He had sent a text to Bishop, who he said had “a tough night”.

What everyone wants most is a National-led Government, Brown said.“That’s why I say it’s bittersweet, right? It is really tough, you know, we all want a National-led government elected for the good of our country. That’s what we campaigned so hard for. But yes, at the same time they are people, and they’ve all got emotions and families and supporters who have worked tirelessly for their campaigns.”

Brown said he was confident National would hold Wairarapa, which has fewer than 150 votes separating the candidates, as well as Hamilton East.

The Wairarapa electorate result is the closest battle in the country, with fewer than 150 votes separating the candidates.

National’s incumbent MP for the area, Mike Butterick, led Labour’s Kieran McAnulty by 139 votes (17,943 to 17,804).

With 100% of the preliminary votes counted, this is the closest race in the country on the Sunday morning after the general election. New Zealand First’s Ron Mark was third with 3555 votes.

McAnulty led Butterick by just 258 votes (12,457 to 12,199) about 10pm on Saturday, with 64.7% of votes counted. By 10.40pm, the result had flipped with Butterick leading McAnulty by 110 votes (12,784 to 12,674).

Five minutes later, McAnulty was leading Butterick again by 474 votes (14,312 to 13,838).

Read more below.

While on Q+A with Jack Tame, National MP and Campaign Chair Simeon Brown was asked if the party had “ultimately benefited from the overhang strategy that [National] campaigned against?”

“No, I think what you see in that is actually our candidates performing incredibly well,” Brown responded.

“Our party vote stayed pretty consistent throughout the campaign, and we’ve always had strength in electorates up and down the country.“Look at East Cape, that was a seat where Dana [Kirkpatrick] has done incredibly well.

“There’s a whole lot of seats which could have run a lot closer, but these are MPs who have worked their electorates incredibly well over three years and deservedly get those results for the work they’ve done.”

“I took over the role earlier this year - it’s been an incredibly challenging time,” National MP and campaign chairSimeon Brown said on Q+A with Jack Tame.

“The price of petrol is running at $3.60 a litre, the economy is recovering but still very challenging out there for New Zealanders, so we always knew it was going to be a challenging election.

“But we made some key decisions to go into this election to fight incredibly hard. We’re pleased with where we’re at," Brown said.

Winston Peters exited the Duke out the back through the kitchen, avoiding media who were out front holding a stand-up with deputy leader Shane Jones.

He would not comment on his party’s poll result when asked by the Herald.

Asked for any reflection on last night’s result, Peters replied: “I said what I said last night.”Pushed for a response, Peters referenced his final public meeting of the campaign in Ōrewa and said, “The next day, there wasn't even a sentence in the Herald. I'm never going to forget that”.

For clarity, the Herald attended Peters’ Ōrewa meeting, live-blogged his speech and question-and-answer session and published a separate article on Peters claiming a foreign government was interested in funding the construction of a modern, fully sized airport in Kaikohe in the Far North.

Shane Jones said he had worked closely with National MP Chris Bishop with Fast Track, describing him as a “very professional, easy guy to work with”.

“Nicola, she was our finance minister, worked closely with her as well," he said.“Gerry was great fun in the house.

“And look, we have our differences, but we were professional politicians, endeavouring to deliver a recipe of success.”Jones said, “All parties go through a period of reinvention”.

When asked by Jack Tame on Q+A this morning if he would consider forming a coalition with the left bloc, NZ First deputy leader Shane Jones had a straightforward answer.

“Negative. No,” he said.

When asked if he would work with The Opportunity Party, Jones noted the special votes still needed to be counted.“Let's just wait until what the specials reveal,” he said.

“We're happy that it appears we're going to have the opportunity to retain the three elements that comprise our coalition government since 2023.

“So any change in that position, it would never be revealed on your programme, for a start.”

McAnulty vs Butterick: Wairarapa election result in the balance

New Zealand Herald November 07, 2026

Labour's Kieran McAnulty, left, and National's Mike Butterick at Hawke's Bay Today's Wairarapa electorate evening at Central Hawke's Bay College. Photo / Jack Riddell

The Wairarapa electorate result is the closest battle in the country, with fewer than 150 votes separating the candidates.

National’s incumbent MP for the area Mike Butterick led Labour’s Kieran McAnulty by 139 votes (17,943 to 17,804) with 100% of preliminary votes counted, the closest race in the country today after the general election.

New Zealand First’s Ron Mark was third with 3555 votes.

McAnulty led Butterick by just 258 votes (12,457 to 12,199) at about 10pm on Saturday, with 64.7% of votes counted.

By 10.40pm, the result had flipped with Butterick leading McAnulty by 110 votes (12,784 to 12,674).

Five minutes later, McAnulty was leading Butterick again by 474 votes (14,312 to 13,838).

The 2026 contest was a National–Labour rematch between Butterick, a sheep-and-beef farmer and Associate Minister of Agriculture, and McAnulty, Labour’s 2026 election campaign chairman.

It’s an electorate often seen as a rural swing seat and its geography stretches across Wairarapa, Tararua and part of Central Hawke’s Bay, with Masterton, Carterton, Featherston, Greytown, Martinborough, Eketāhuna and Waipukurau among its communities.

Eight candidates contested the seat – including former defence minister and twice Carterton mayor Ron Mark for New Zealand First, first-time candidate Lauren Craig for the Greens, Masterton relief teacher and former Navy chef Matt Shepherd for the Opportunity Party, Victoria Ale for Alliance, Barry Young for the NZ Outdoors and Freedom Party and Jared Warren Gardner for Te Pāti Hira.

Only Butterick and McAnulty had a realistic chance to win, with Shepherd, Craig and Mark asking for the party vote.

ALE, Victoria 62 (Alliance)

BUTTERICK, Mike 17,943 (National)

CRAIG, Lauren 1098 (Greens)

GARDNER, Jared Warren 63 (Te Pāti Hira)

MARK, Ron 3555 (NZ First)

McANULTY, Kieran 17,804 (Labour)

SHEPHERD, Matt 474 (Opportunity Party)

YOUNG, Barry 63 (NZ Outdoors and Freedom Party)

In 2023, Butterick won Wairarapa from Labour incumbent McAnulty on the final count, 20,313 votes to 17,497 – a margin of 2816. Turnout was 82.66%.

The electorate party vote was National 17,397, Labour 12,223, and Act 4752.

On election night, Butterick led McAnulty 17,908 to 15,427, or 2481 votes; special votes increased the final margin by 335.

It’s not impossible for the left to win this election, but it looks very difficult – and why Opportunity has a very tough choice

New Zealand Herald November 07, 2026

National leader Chris Luxon says his party has a "pathway" to forming the next government. Photo / Dean Purcell

Two names unlock the truth behind National leader and Prime Minister Christopher Luxon’s election-night speech.

One, Qiulae Wong, was mentioned in the speech. The other name, belonging to Chris Bishop, was not.

The Opportunity leader was praised by Luxon for making history, leading her party into Parliament after three previous attempts had ended in catastrophic failure.

It was a magnanimous gesture from Luxon, who has spent most of the year slagging off Wong and her party.

Less than 24 hours before, Luxon and National supporters had been bopping their heads to an AI-generated attack song lampooning Wong’s alleged desire to tax the life out of the country. Last night, when some of National’s supporters booed, Luxon talked them down: “no, no, we won’t do that, it’s not the Kiwi way”.

What a difference a brush with political death makes. Luxon knows; he’s had two this year already.

That brings us nicely to Bishop, whose name was not mentioned. Luxon ran through every single National MP who had lost their seat that evening in list order, but when he came to Bishop’s name, he skipped it – a clear snub of the man who was not so secretly out to roll Luxon this year, fearing a catastrophic election loss, and who has been proved right by these results.

The coalition may still win the election, but National has quite emphatically lost. While supporters at the election-night party on Auckland’s Viaduct were hopeful that the coalition had a clear path to power, they also knew the party was in serious trouble.

National is a shadow of the broad church of the Key-English-Bridges years, and its large overhang skews heavily in favour of conservative, less diverse candidates.

It has been promising to modernise and diversify since before Tova O’Brien took her camera to the party’s caucus corridor in 2020 and asked the leadership how many Māori sat on its front bench. That modernisation goal looks to have taken a significant step backwards on these results.

And what tight results: Labour is ahead by a minuscule 3650 votes, with 29.36% of the vote compared to 29.21%, making this by far the closest the parties have been in the MMP era.

For all of that, however, National and the coalition wake up today feeling just a wee bit more comfortable than Labour and its leader Chris Hipkins.

You got a sense of that on election night. While Luxon’s speech wasn’t a victory speech, at no point did it grapple with the idea that National might lose.

Hipkins’ speech actually contemplated a loss, noting that were Labour to lose the election, it would “continue to stand up for the people who need a strong voice in Parliament and work every day to earn the confidence of New Zealanders”.

On the election-night numbers, National’s enormous overhang means the coalition can continue to govern, even though Opportunity managed to enter Parliament. That defies some predictions (including from me) that were Opportunity to make it to Parliament, it would be hard for the coalition to govern again.

But that majority is tiny. The coalition has 67 seats of the 66 required to govern in a 131-seat Parliament, a two-seat majority. And yes, you read that right, our Parliament, which should have about 120 seats, has 131 on these numbers, thanks to enormous overhangs on the left and right.

Two of the seats that National is relying on to prop up the overhang are held by tiny majorities. Mike Butterick is just 149 votes ahead of Labour’s Kieran McAnulty in Wairarapa, and Ryan Hamilton is just 456 votes ahead of Georgie Dansey in Hamilton East.

A good rule of thumb is that a majority of less than 300 is easily reversible on special votes, with a majority of 300–500 somewhat vulnerable.

With special votes tending to break left, those two seats could flip. But because National has an overhang, losing both electorates would reduce the size of Parliament from 131 to 129, rather than giving Labour two additional seats. On the current party-vote figures, the coalition would retain a majority, albeit by just one seat.

National’s next most vulnerable seat, Whangārei, has a majority of over 1000, making it less vulnerable to flipping.

The final count, including special votes, will be released on November 27.

Labour, the Greens and Opportunity could all see their party-vote shares rise on special votes, while Act and NZ First could see theirs fall. This reshuffling of the list seats could see, in fact seems likely to see, that coalition majority shift, either in the direction of a hung Parliament or in favour of the Labour-Green-Te Pāti Māori and, maybe, Opportunity bloc – just.

There’s reason to believe the changes after special votes are counted might be smaller this election than in previous elections. The Electoral Commission estimates there are about 399,365 including 96,947 overseas and dictation votes yet to be counted. That compares with over 600,000 special votes in 2023.

Put simply, a lot has to go the left’s way in the special votes to even put the bloc in contention. This isn’t impossible, in fact, if history is any indicator, the special votes will help the left. It’s just difficult, and even if it all goes the left’s way, it will still have a tiny majority even with the help of Opportunity.

This is where the election becomes all about how Opportunity decides to think about forming a government. The party is in both a wonderful and terrible position.

Luxon quite clearly will make the call to Wong to talk about forming a government. He’s said he won’t, but he will. A broad coalition of senior members of his own party, including loyalist Mark Mitchell and disloyalist Erica Stanford, made that clear on Saturday night: either he picks up the phone, or they pick up the knife.

Even if special votes don’t change the final result and National holds on to its majority, it’s far, far too thin for comfort. A loose confidence-and-supply deal with Opportunity would give the coalition some breathing space.

In a way, that would be best for Opportunity too. If Wong has no option to go left, if changing the government is taken off the table completely, then it will be far easier to explain to her supporters why she decided to go right.

It may actually be better for Wong if she weren’t kingmaker this election, if she doesn’t crown as king a man that neither her supporters nor the country at large particularly want to lead them. It may be much safer for her if the choice is simply whether to negotiate a stable or an unstable majority for the coalition.

In fact, it would be proof of concept for Opportunity’s promise to try and extract wins from whoever is in government, a point Wong made during her TVNZ debate when she pointedly told Chlöe Swarbrick about all the things she could have done or stopped had the Greens swallowed their pride and governed with National.

However, if the specials break the way we think they will, there’s a chance that a path opens up for the left too. A leftward swing opens up the prospect of a hung Parliament, with the coalition losing the ability to govern by itself. If the left has a very, very good run on the specials, Labour, the Greens, Te Pāti Māori and Opportunity could potentially form a government with a one- or two-seat majority.

Opportunity quite plainly has more in common with this bloc than the right.

It’s progressive in terms of policy, and the party, campaigning for unity and against division and getting money out of politics, was quite clearly positioning itself against the cashed up, bombastic, often divisive culture fostered by the coalition.

This sort of angry, open, almost daily confrontation is simply not how recent left-wing coalitions, like the one led by Jacinda Ardern in 2017, have tended to do things.

The challenge is that this bloc, even with Opportunity, would likely have the tiniest of majorities after specials, maybe one or, at a stretch, two seats.

In 1996 and 2005, governments were formed with these tiny majorities, but in each case the government of the day had a friend outside the government that could be relied upon if things went pear-shaped. Act could be relied on to help National in 1996 (which it did, eventually) and the Greens might have helped Labour in 2005 if required.

The left doesn’t have that this time. It also has a problem in the form of Te Pāti Māori, which can’t be relied upon for stability.

The party split this term and can’t be relied upon not to split again – two of the MPs in the caucus that will be heading to Parliament openly flirted with joining the rebellion this term. In another world, the left might hope that the party that destabilised the coalition would be booted from Parliament, but Te Pāti Māori’s strength in the Māori seats means it’s a problem the left can’t easily shake. A majority of any size that depends upon Te Pāti Māori isn’t actually a majority at all – it’s a ticking time bomb.

The story of these numbers isn’t so much that the right has a path to power, even though it does. The actual story is that the left really doesn’t have a path, or not a stable one. And rather troublingly for Opportunity, it puts the party in a position of looking like it has a choice when it really doesn’t.

That’s a challenge. Opportunity’s results suggest its supporters want change. The party’s best party-vote performance was in Wellington North, where it polled 15.09%, more than double its national party-vote percentage of 5.96%. Its next-best result was in Wellington Bays, where it polled 12.47%.

It’s reasonable to assume these electorates, battered by the coalition’s public service cuts, voted to change the government and would be none too pleased were Opportunity to prop up the coalition.

Opportunity might not be able to give them the change they crave, although Wong can reasonably argue that had these voters simply gone to Labour and the Greens, they wouldn’t have changed the government either.

There are wins Opportunity could give these supporters: the coalition plans to cut the public service by about 9000 roles in the coming years, saving $2.8 billion. Few think the coalition can actually achieve this in full.

Perhaps the coalition can use Opportunity as an excuse to water down or wriggle out of a difficult promise, and Opportunity can use it as a win for its public service supporters?

But there are so many other challenges. Opportunity wants significant campaign finance reform, but the coalition parties survive on their big donations – they out-fundraised the left considerably this term. Imagine how badly things would have gone if they hadn’t had all that money behind them? Even with all that money, coalition has only just got itself into a position where it might be re-elected. They won’t want to put themselves further at risk.

And then there’s NZ First. Recent days have suggested that Winston Peters might be keen to get Michael Laws out of the party, either by persuading him not to take his seat or waka-jumping him.

Opportunity will like that, but NZ First is basically the political wing of the commercial fishing industry. It’s very difficult to see how the party comes around to working with Opportunity, which wants to slowly ban bottom trawling.

NZ First’s only option here is to turn to its backers and say they’d come off even worse if Opportunity went with Labour.

The fact that these scenarios need stating speaks to the poor performance of both major-party campaigns. Luxon and his campaign chairman, Simeon Brown, will have serious questions to answer about the decisions they made in this campaign.

Its relentless negativity and childishness have driven National to the point at which it may form a government with the lowest party-vote share of any major party under MMP. It’s only managed to do this through the overhang, a weird electoral trick. Neither man should lead National into the next election.

Labour has questions to ask too. Based on polling, it’s shed party vote this year, tumbling from the mid-30s to the high 20s, ending the night less than three points higher than it was after the disastrous 2023 result.

It lost electorates it should have won, like Nelson (largely thanks to the Greens not splitting their votes), and Wairarapa, which was contested by campaign chairman McAnulty. He may still flip the seat on special votes but should have performed better given high-profile NZ First candidate Ron Mark split the vote on the right.

The other big unanswered question about this election is what it means for the future of the overhang. Both Te Pāti Māori and National have exploited it (although it’s unclear whether National’s overhang is a natural byproduct of its party vote crashing or a result of a deliberate campaign).

There’s a strong case for Labour and National to work together to stop overhangs deciding elections in future. Neither side wins if they become a permanent feature of our elections.

But that’s all in the future.

For now, the political landscape ever so slightly favours the right, and the night’s big winner is Opportunity and Wong. She should enjoy the victory. What she’s achieved tonight, getting a party into Parliament that was not an offshoot of one already there, has not happened before in the history of MMP.

But be warned, the minor parties currently in Parliament have found it very, very difficult to stay there.

A thumping repudiation of the major party in a sitting government after one term – Kiri Allan

New Zealand Herald November 07, 2026

Erica Stanford at the National party fucntion at the Viaduct Events Centre in Auckland, New Zealand, on November 7, 2026. Photo / Dean Purcell

Going into last night’s election the only thing Aotearoa New Zealand’s political commentators were united on was that the race was too close to call. And with the half the vote counted, at the time of writing this, the only thing that can be said is that whatever the outcome, there will be some major shakeups this term to the way we do politics.

Thirty years almost to the month since the country’s first MMP election we’re staring down the barrel of our most proportionally representative Parliament yet.

And with that, comes clear winners and losers, and the losers are our two major parties, National and Labour.

In an underwhelming campaign where neither of the Chrises succeeded in presenting a vision of hope that inspired New Zealanders, it’s clear the power is going to rest with the minor parties.

And all the indications are that we have a newcomer. Since 1996, there has only ever been one kingmaker, Winston Peters, who has gone both left and right over the years. But never has there been a political party to challenge the middle ground like The Opportunity Party.

If the momentum holds and Opportunity cracks the political glass ceiling, it will change New Zealand politics as we know it.

Prime Minister Christopher Luxon and his National Party are on track to lose a number of party vote seats. This is a thumping repudiation of the major party in a sitting government, which has only been in for one term.

So what happened?

National, well they have let themselves be wagged by the tail for the duration of the coalition. And it’s cost them. As well as their party vote being down, they could lose some of their most proficient ministers including Chris Bishop and Nicola Willis who last night looked like they will lose their seats in the following Parliament.

As for Chris Hipkins and his Labour Party, they have been out beating the streets encouraging the people to vote two ticks red. But results so far show they failed to ignite the fire in the bellies of those they were trying to convince.

Sitting back watching this election campaign, it felt like groundhog day. Every day was grey and dull. This whole year it has felt like we’ve been watching Labour sit on its hands with the overriding command be ‘do nothing and let the other side implode’.

Qiulae Wong stood up on the stage at 8.48pm to announce they had reached the threshold. It felt premature. Only 31% of the vote had been counted. But Wong may hold the balance of power when it comes to annointing our new Prime Minister.

The Green Party is polling at 14 percent and looking to have their largest cohort going into Parliament. They are easily rolling back into Parliament with a new cohort of eager new MPs.

This has been the election of the junior parties. This needs to be a wake up call to the institutional parties that New Zealanders are no longer satisfied with and their three line slogans for issues that deeply impact our lives.

Kiri Allan is a former Labour Party Minister who held the portfolios of Justice, Regional Development, Conservation and Emergency Management. She was the lead minister for the Cyclone Gabrielle response in Tairāwhiti. She is the founder of renewable energy company Four Directions Fund and runs KLA consultancy firm.

Letters: Drivers using phones deserve tougher fines

New Zealand Herald November 07, 2026

A $150 fine for using a cellphone while driving is hardly a deterrent, says a reader who wants to see tougher penalties.

Drivers using phones deserve tougher fines

How many more deaths and serious injuries must occur before New Zealand gets serious about mobile phone use behind the wheel?

Our current penalty of just $150 is an insult to the seriousness of the offence. Compare this with Queensland, where the fine is A$1295 [$1605], and the UK, where it is £200 [$480] plus six penalty points. Get to 10 and you’re off the road.

The research is unequivocal. Handheld phone use has been shown to increase crash risk by 3.6 times, while dialling a number increases it more than twelvefold. The danger is not simply taking one’s eyes off the road; it is the diversion of concentration from driving to the phone, compromising reaction times and hazard awareness.

Britain has recognised the need for a cultural shift, with the stated ambition of making mobile phone use while driving as socially unacceptable as drink driving.

Why haven’t we?

We need a minimum $500 fine, substantially tougher penalties for repeat offenders and widespread use of phone-detection cameras, as already implemented in Australia.

A $150 fine is hardly a deterrent. We would not tolerate such a token penalty for other behaviour that puts innocent lives at risk.

Driving is a responsibility, not a licence to endanger others.

David Alston, Ōrewa.

Plea to election winner

It was reported last week that one in five New Zealand drivers admitted to using a handheld phone while driving. We must stop that right now to save many lives for the rest of 2026.

Five years ago we increased the fine for using a handheld mobile while driving from $80 to $150. Sounds great but it is such a paltry fine compared to over $1000 for the same offence in Queensland and Western Australia.

We should match it from December 1, by whatever Government ends up winning the election. Will they please make a sound promise to increase the paltry fine.

Murray Hunter, Titirangi.

Taxing realities

Let’s be clear about who pays the tax Eric Faesenkloet claims he has paid in his open letter to Green Party co-leader Chlöe Swarbrick, where he is moaning about tax he may be asked to pay (Nov 6).

Faesenkloet, founder and chairperson of Golf Warehouse, said he paid a combined tax contribution from PAYE, GST, income and company tax of more than $8 million annually. But the people who paid the PAYE tax are the workers who are employed at Golf Warehouse, and he is merely handing on their tax contribution.

And the GST he claims he has paid, has been paid, once more not by him, but by his customers and he is handing that on to the tax system.

None of this was ever his personal money. He is opposed to a proposal for the super-rich tax of 2.5% on net assets above $10m. Well, lucky him if he falls into that category. I am sure the workers who are coughing up the PAYE he claims he is paying are not in the frame for paying any wealth tax, just their fair share of income tax.

Neil Anderson, Algies Bay.

Campaign criticism

Heather du Plessis-Allan (Nov 1) is correct National has taken its attacks on Chlöe Swarbrick too far during this election campaign. Has National never heard the “there is no such thing as bad publicity” saying?

New Zealanders have a very acute sense of what is fair play and what is not, and National’s Chlöe attack has been unfair. The vacuum around National is where are “the proud achievements of the last three years and the vision for the future” they should have been promoting?

Instead, National rolled out the old party hacks to paper over the cracks. Not a very intelligent campaign.

And as Heather wrote “it is the opposite of statesman like”.

Gary Carter, Gulf Harbour.

Minor parties, major notes

Until the MMP rules are changed to reduce the power and influence of the minor parties then it’s a complete and utter waste of time and energy and the hundreds of millions of dollars to run a general election. This money would be far better reallocated directly for health, education, housing and transport etc.

Bruce Tubb, Ngataringa Bay.

A Karangahake Gorge farm full of rare breeds and a passion for keeping them going

New Zealand Herald November 07, 2026

Sue Austen with Nubian goat kids at Bullswool Farm. Photo / Catherine Fry

In secluded bush on the hills above the Karangahake Gorge at the southern end of the Coromandel, Sue Austen is continuing her parents’ legacy on a property owned by the family for the past 40 years.

“My parents, Jan and Keith Austen, bought Bullswool Farm in the mid-80s and knew the 30ha block was never going to be a viable farm, but what they developed was definitely a lifestyle block on steroids,” Austen said.

Jan and Keith bought two goldfish for a pond on a rural West Auckland property, and when they unexpectedly spawned, the couple suddenly found themselves with 1000-odd baby goldfish.

Austen said Jan thought there could be money in this, so she developed a large goldfish farm.

“Which did make some good money for a number of years.”

When they retired early to Bullswool Farm, Jan became immersed in breeding rare farm animals, such as alpacas, llamas, donkeys and miniature horses.

She also bred dogs on a large scale but cut back when the farm park opened.

Austen’s father Keith wrote a book called Bullswool and Barbed Wire, which became a self-published runaway success.

It contained humorous and mainly true rural yarns, set to verse and illustrated by Malcolm Evans.

What they were doing at Bullswool with the rare breeds and the popularity of Keith’s book earned the family an episode on TVNZ’s Country Calendar in the 1990s.

“During this time, I was living overseas, and I kept hearing all these stories about people who wanted to visit the farm and meet Dad, who was becoming a bit of a local celebrity, and see the exotic animals Mum was breeding,” Austen said.

Austen returned to New Zealand in 2003.

Farm parks are big in Britain, and the family decided to open their farm by booking only and with paid entry.

Bullswool Farm Park opened in 2004.

“Quite a lot of work was involved in the initial set-up,” Austen said.

“We made a fenced route around the farm, which includes a bush reserve walk, a viewpoint up the hill, a play paddock, and several sheds were converted into rural life museums.”

The park offered children who may not have had much to do with animals the chance to walk from paddock to paddock and have face-to-face interaction with them, and it still fulfils that purpose today.

“Our museums are an ongoing work in progress, and we enjoy curating displays around how farming life used to be,” Austen said.

“We have a good collection of old implements, tools and machinery from the past.”

Austen continues boutique breeding of rare and high-value animals.

“Animal fads come and go, and my rule of thumb is that if there is no demand for a neutered male of a breed, then it is no longer viable to breed that type of animal.”

Every animal on Bullswool farm serves a purpose.

Breeding is carefully considered, and Austen said donkeys were currently a big thing, especially miniature and Irish donkeys.

“With larger companion animals like donkeys, we want them to leave us as well-handled and trained as possible,” she said.

“This helps ensure they are a pleasure to own, and consequently are always easy to rehome, as is often necessary with such long-lived animals.”

The goats enjoy walks through the bush reserve on the farm and closely follow Austen like dogs.

Apart from the donkeys, Bullswool has Baby Doll sheep, which Austen said were easy to breed with other sheep.

They also have great fleeces and good meat for eating.

At the moment, she is concentrating on breeding Baby Dolls with the typical traits of the breed.

Several coops house chickens, ducks and exotic-looking golden pheasants.

The animals are in paddocks, which are usually breed-specific, with cattle, sheep, Nubian goats, miniature horses, donkeys, kunekune pigs and alpacas.

They are fed a pasture-based diet as close as possible to what they would eat as undomesticated animals.

Austen said the farm had plenty of grass available and the pelletised lucerne the animals get hand-fed by visitors is the cherry on top.

She is always looking for ways to diversify and maximise income sources, as her entrepreneurial parents did.

Austen runs an Airbnb and has the Goats in the Garden coffee and ice cream cart.

“Our next ventures include an adults’ bike track, promoting our feijoa ice cream and expanding our gift shop to have more core New Zealand brands and products.”
