Kem Ormond’s Vegetable Garden: How to attract more birds with a feeder and bath

New Zealand Herald November 07, 2026

Kem Ormond hopes to attract finches with her new homemade bird feeder. Photo / Phil Thomsen

Labour weekend has come and gone, but there was plenty of action happening in my garden.

I enjoy encouraging birds into my garden.

While I appreciate there are both advantages and disadvantages to having them around, the pleasure of watching them flit among the plants and seeing them go about their daily routines far outweighs the occasional nibble they take from my produce.

After all, a little sharing seems a small price to pay for the enjoyment they bring to the garden.

This year I have been enjoying sitting on my veranda watching a tūī enjoying the flowers from an orange-flowering Aloe plicatilis planted close to where I sit.

This led me to make a bird feeder, as I wanted to encourage birds closer to my veranda so I could see more of them.

Basic, and rather what you would call organic, the bird feeder was a great hit, but more so with the blackbirds and thrushes, and I wasn’t that keen on encouraging them.

I wanted to see more of the cute finches.

So, I made version two with a terracotta saucer on top for the larger birds to use as a bird bath and metal pegs underneath, to which I attach apples and bits of banana or kiwifruit.

Hopefully, the smaller birds can get underneath and dine without the thrushes and blackbirds taking control.

Being portable, I hope to gradually move it closer to where I can relax and enjoy the busy little finches.

It is still a work in progress, I might add!

It was great being able to hand out surplus tomato plants to friends over the weekend, as this is a big part of gardening for me.

Families are busy, and growing vegetable plants from seed is not for everyone, but when you can, and you have surplus, share with family and friends.

My tomato plants have only been planted in my tomato house for a week, and the growth is amazing.

By the time they have outgrown their punnets, tomatoes are hungry, so don’t leave them in the punnets too long before planting.

I went to the local river market over the long weekend and bought some fresh asparagus.

What a treat, and if you haven’t tried an asparagus and pea risotto, you need to find a recipe and try it; it is delicious.

I don’t often get garden envy, but I visited a friend in the country over the weekend and they had the most wonderful asparagus plot in their vegetable garden.

Oh, the joys of not being restricted by space.

This week I will be planting my capsicums, chillies, eggplants, cucumbers and courgettes.

I did not have great success with my corn last year so I’m giving it a miss this year, but you can start planting yours soon, along with pumpkins and melons, climbing beans, and remember to plant your carrots, beetroot, silverbeet and continuous radishes if you haven’t already.

Make sure you have plenty of leafy salad vegetables planted, and if you don’t want them to bolt, maybe plant in a cooler spot.

Spinach, coriander and rocket will appreciate this.

Remember, your tomatoes will need staking before long, as will your broad beans, plus potatoes will need mounding.

While retaining water moisture is important, I think using mulch or compost may be a better option than pea straw because of the wind that is expected with El Niño, but I will let you decide.

Remember to add notes to your gardening journal, and this year it will be interesting to compare the difference in crops.

Happy gardening.

Kem Ormond is a features writer for The Country. She’s also a keen gardener.

The results are in, but the country will have to wait to know who can form the next Government.

The results are considered preliminary as they do not include special votes, such as those made overseas or out of a person’s electorate.

The official count, as it’s termed, begins on Sunday and includes checking whether anyone has voted more than once, conducting a second count of “ordinary votes”, allowing time for overseas votes and votes cast outside of electorates to return, removing votes from dual voters or those who have died, counting the special votes and conducting quality assurance checks.

The commission expects to confirm the official count on Friday, November 27.

What happens during the period between election night and November 27 depends heavily on where the numbers fall and who holds the balance of power.

In 2023, National and Act held some preliminary negotiations but it wasn’t until after the official count was returned that coalition talks began properly along with New Zealand First.

Opportunity, which claims to be able to work with either the left or right bloc, has stated it would talk first to the party with the most seats and would not conduct dual negotiations. That means if the first round of talks fail to produce an agreement, another round may be required.

Many of the parties have been quizzed on whether they think a government can be formed by Christmas. Labour recently committed to a government by Christmas but has watered that down, clarifying it can’t control the pace of other parties. Other leaders including Christopher Luxon and Winston Peters have indicated they are comfortable with negotiations taking as long as necessary to achieve a positive result.

No matter what, the politicians need to be sitting in the House by January 14, which is the last day for Parliament to meet after the election.

Adam Pearse is the Deputy Political Editor and part of the NZ Herald’s Press Gallery team based at Parliament in Wellington. He has worked for NZME since 2018, reporting for the Northern Advocate in Whangārei and the Herald in Auckland.

The Nats moved to the right last night, and Sir John Key should be embarrassed – Simon Bridges

New Zealand Herald November 07, 2026

National MPs Paul Goldsmith and Nicola Willis on Election night November 7, 2026. Photo / Dean Purcell

It’s too early to call Election 2026, and specials and the Opportunity Party may decide it. But at the end of last night, we did get a handle on the right and left blocks and each party’s performance.

The right will have to have mixed feelings even if they end up winning. National has lost its most senior MPs and is only still in the game because of the infamous overhang. Let’s be clear, its senior list MPs were generally on the liberal side of the party and with the overhang of electorate MPs who will almost by definition be more conservative and right-leaning, last night was a move to the right for the Nats.

Regarding the overhang, Sir John Key should feel embarrassed. More than Don Brash or Harry Mowbray’s positive work, Key, by preposterously warning people off strategic voting, emblazoned it in bright lights and made every centre right voter ask the question, “So we should be strategic voting should we?” When Nicola Willis wonders why she’s not in Parliament she should talk to him, albeit ironically, he did a lot to help the Nats’ effort to win the election given overhang has clearly been crucial for them.

Act and NZ First both did well, and with bigger results than the election before they also mean it’s a real rightward drift, if with the overhang the current Government hangs on without the Opportunity Party. Act and the Greens had the campaigns of the election, although for very different reasons. Act did well by not promising too much, by parading Paul Henry to good effect, and by keeping David Seymour looking like the adult leader in the room. In doing this they picked up a lot of dissatisfied Nat vote. For its part, NZ First, despite some late PR shockers, did surprisingly well and much better than last time. Winston and Shane Jones are political institutions.

On the left, I think one thing is clear. It’s the economy, stupid. Labour ran a small target campaign, which plenty of armchair naysayers criticised heavily. But it worked in that Chris Hipkins has some possibility of being PM after just one term in Opposition, which would be truly historic and a personal redemption for him.

This is down to cost of living and an economy which for many has failed to fire. Much of this is due to Donald Trump and his war causing global inflation and uncertainty. But it’s also true that Christopher Luxon and Nicola Willis just simply didn’t do enough to reform economically in their first couple of years in the hot seats. A new Finance Minister needs a much stronger agenda and will be the most important person in Parliament.

Objectively, the Greens had a standout campaign. They were less on the woke than previously and more on the wallet. And more than that, they came up with significant policies which, whether you agreed with them or not, were thought through and perfectly on point.

Which brings us to the Opportunity Party. Probably their vote is explained by dissatisfaction with the major parties, a phenomenon throughout the Western world, and a corresponding desire for the shiny and new. My concern isn’t the greenness of their policies but of their inexperience. I hope I am wrong but I worry they’ll be possums in the headlights when they may in fact be deciding the Government. On that basis, sitting on the cross benches for a term may be a smart choice, where learning the ropes can occur and their brand be grown and protected.

As for Chris Luxon, if he’s in a pickle he should call Qiulae, and in fact would have a duty to. And if he can’t in that circumstance, then he needs to let someone else in the party he has led do it instead.

Simon Bridges is the chief executive of the Auckland Business Chamber and was the leader of the National Party from 2018 to 2020. He has also served as the Minister for Transport, Economic Development and Communications. He has also worked as a senior Crown prosecutor in the Tauranga District and High Courts.

Better call Qiulae? National might be forced to save coalition – Editorial

New Zealand Herald November 07, 2026

Opportunity party leader Qiulae Wong speaks to supporters at the party’s election night event held at Eden Park. Photo / Anna Heath

The election result is sitting on a knife-edge.

But what appears to be clear after last night’s neck-and-neck race is the opportunity to form the next Government appears to sit with the new kids on the block.

Many commentators and pundits had predicted throughout what has at times been a tiring campaign, that the fortunes of Opportunity last night would determine the election.

Simply, would the party and its leader Qiulae Wong make it over the 5% threshold or not?

Well, at the time of writing, it appears they have.

The first-time parliamentarians, who have said they can work with both the left and right blocs, will now be the likely kingmakers.

The results as they stood last night could point to a change of government, unless National can find a way of making friends with Opportunity.

David Seymour said a potential National-Act-NZ First coalition will need to “explore every avenue” to keep the left bloc out. He said this included potentially working with the Opportunity Party.

“Our mission’s been clear throughout this campaign: lock Labour out, unlock New Zealand’s potential,” Seymour told the Herald’s Ryan Bridge.

“You shouldn’t let anything else get in the way of that mission. I think ultimately the Opportunity Party will be a bad product for New Zealand. Nonetheless, I think it’s really important that we ensure that we explore every avenue to keep Labour and the Greens and Te Pāti Māori and co out of government.”

National, Seymour believed, will need to “have their own discussions internally as a party about what their position is”.

“But what’s clear is that locking Labour out is a non-negotiable. You can’t campaign on how disastrous Labour would be for New Zealand, and I happen to agree with that, then say we’ll do anything to keep them out except this [working with Opportunity]. So, look, let’s see how it goes.”

Last night, on the initial results, was also not the bloodbath some had predicted for the right-leaning parties.

Act appears to have had a record night for the party.

National, meanwhile, traditionally starts strongly, with booths where the party polls well reporting early.

The blues also retook a spiritual home, Tāmaki, behind candidate Mahesh Muralidhar, fighting to reclaim a seat it held for more than 60 years before losing it to Act in 2023.

The main thing still going in National’s favour was the projected overhang, likely to be several seats.

National was ahead in more seats than its party vote would entitle it to. That means it has an easier chance of getting the majority required to form a Government.

It may be the overhang is the only thing that could save the National-led coalition. Or a phone call to Qiulae.

He stars in the most expensive show ever made, but Ismael Cruz Cordova’s journey to Middle-earth was not easy

Sydney Morning Herald November 08, 2026

Every morning while filming The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power, actor Ismael Cruz Cordova would sit patiently while two make-up artists worked to craft his pointed elven ears. The prosthetics that transform him into dashing warrior elf Arondir are cast to the contours of his cheekbones and match his skin tone so well that Cordova himself cannot see the seam.

But when they are done, there is no longer a reflection of one man in the mirror. Rather, Cordova sees three people looking back: the elven warrior who has become something of a poster boy for the Amazon Prime Video series, the actor, who cut his teeth on The Good Wife, Ray Donovan and The Undoing, and the barefoot kid from the Puerto Rican mountains who washed cars to save money for a used DVD player.

“I absolutely love my ears,” says Cordova. “As an elf, there’s something about these ears that everybody wants. Because elves are so close to humans in form, that little hint of difference, it’s elegant and it’s this magical, mystical thing. I remember the first time that I saw myself with them on, at that moment, when it was complete, I just cried the biggest tears.

“It’s this ritualistic aspect of becoming. I’m a very physical actor, and as I transform into this character, by this point, there’s this sense memory. My voice begins to drop, my accent starts coming in. So for me, it’s this incredible rite of passage.”

The man in the mirror, he says, is a “composite of three things ... these three beings that are inextricably tied. Ismael now, and Arondir on top of that ... but it begins with the little boy that sees the movies for the first time. I grew up in the mountains, a very poor community, very rural, not a lot of opportunities. That little boy has to wash cars, lawns, mow lawns, do any type of errand to find a little bit of money to buy a DVD player and then a DVD.”

The first two DVDs he owned? Moulin Rouge! and The Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring, both released in 2001. “This world opened up to me,” he says. “Moulin Rouge! was one of those movies that I was like, whoa, [it] blew my mind. But it was also the behind-the-scenes component [that came with the DVD]. I got to see what this was about from an abstraction to the reality, and it changed my life.”

And The Fellowship of the Ring? “Truly from the get-go, I wanted to be an elf because the elves are so close to who I was,” Cordova says. “They loved nature, [they are a] contemplative people, like my reverence for sunsets. I was always this precocious kid concerned with beauty and with natural beauty and what nature did. I’m still that way.”

In one sense, those ears – as expensive as they undoubtedly are – are a small line item in a big budget. The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power is one of the most expensive TV series ever made. The five-season commitment will exceed $US1 billion ($1.44 billion) in costs. And we’re just three seasons in.

The series, developed by show runners J. D. Payne and Patrick McKay, is set during the Second Age of Middle-earth, thousands of years before the events of The Hobbit and The Lord of the Rings. It follows an ensemble of characters – the younger iteration of the elven queen, Galadriel, the future ruler of Rivendell, Elrond, and a wood elf warrior, Arondir – as they confront the rise of evil in Middle-earth.

The project began after Amazon secured the television rights from the Tolkien estate in 2017, and it sits in an ever-widening mosaic of Middle-earth-set storytelling. In 2024, under a different deal between movie rights holder Embracer and Warner Bros., Kenji Kamiyama directed an anime prequel, The Lord of the Rings: The War of the Rohirrim, about the history of the fortress Helm’s Deep.

And a new film, The Lord of the Rings: The Hunt for Gollum – set between The Hobbit and The Lord of the Rings in the established cinematic universe of the Peter Jackson films – will feature Andy Serkis as Gollum and Smeagol, Ian McKellen as Gandalf, Jamie Dornan as Strider, Leo Woodall as Halvard, a Dunedain ranger, and Elijah Wood as Frodo Baggins.

All of that, on top of the new third season of The Rings of Power, and two more seasons to follow.

By and large, the television series is faithful to the original works of J. R. R. Tolkien, on which it is based. That said, the television adaptation has ruffled canonical feathers of the diehard Tolkien fans because of some of the liberties it takes.

Most of its characters are drawn from familiar legend: Isildur, the mortal man whom we meet as a boy and who will eventually cut “the ring” from the hand of franchise baddie Sauron, and Celebrimbor, the master ringsmith of the elves, who begins creating the magical rings that are central to the story.

But Cordova’s Arondir is another story. He’s a piece of new canon, though his backstory is steeped deeply in Tolkien lore. The Silvan elves, of whom Arondir is one, are the elves who inhabited places such as Mirkwood and Lothlorien, and known for their connection to nature (that’s why they are called “wood” elves).

Arondir’s role in the story, too – the “watchwarden” of the Southlands – is based on the idea, in Tolkien’s postwar history, that after the defeat of the first Dark Lord, Morgoth, the elves kept a close watch on that part of Middle-earth.

“I’m at the whim and trust of the creators of the show,” Cordova says. “I’ve known that from the beginning. I’ve known that he’s going to go where he goes, and it’s allowed me also to be present. I’ve given my absolute entire soul to each moment that I have, not thinking that I’m going to play an arc of five seasons or anything like that.”

While all art is not necessarily inherently political, it is true The Lord of the Rings as an over-arching “legendarium” deals with some potential political themes. The inevitable corruption of absolute power, Saruman’s transformation of Isengard from a green valley into a crater of military manufacturing, the destruction of Fangorn Forest, and Grima Wormtongue’s poisoning of King Theoden’s mind with misinformation.

“About Tolkien’s [world], I think it’s open knowledge that it was created as a result of his experience during war and wartimes and industrialisation and seeing the landscape change, and seeing nature turned, human against human, and people not being able to see the beauty and the simplicity of things that are right in front of them,” says Cordova.

“All art is political. I do not have a capacity to understand otherwise because existence is political. I am always open and flexible for my views to be challenged. I speak with certainty, the things that I say, but I’m also certain that they might be wrong.”

Growing up in relative poverty in Puerto Rico, he says, “my core as an artist and my formation is the transformative power of art and what it can do for people like us and what it’s done, and how it changed my life. I’m here speaking with you in an almost improbable case of social mobility. The arc of my life is an arc of social mobility that a lot of people do not experience, and it has to do with the power of art.”

The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power streams on Amazon Prime Video from November 11.

Steve Tandy warns Wales to be more ruthless after edgy win against Japan

The Guardian Sat, 07 Nov 2026 20:52:09 GMT

Wales 28-21 Japan

Head coach wants more in New Zealand Test

Steve Tandy has admitted there is no hiding from his team’s below-par performance ⁠in their 28-21 home Nations Championship victory over Japan on Saturday where they looked flat at times and kept their ⁠opponents in the ⁠contest.

Wales ran ​in four tries to collect a bonus point and although it was a third win in five games, the head coach ⁠felt his side needed to be more ruthless.

“It’s a bonus-point win. It’s good to start,” Tandy said. “I can’t run away from the ⁠performance. There are elements we need to improve. I thought we’d be better. We ​weren’t ruthless enough.”

Tandy suggested rust may ‌have been to blame ‌as Wales played their first test since July.

“Getting a hit out for the ‌first time since the summer, it does get clunky,” he said. “It helps to review after a bonus point win. We’ll enjoy it but the beauty of this group is the hunger to get better quicker. We’ll definitely have to do that.”

Next up for Wales are New Zealand next weekend and Australia. Tandy ‌knows his side cannot afford to offer up cheap opportunities in those games.

Richard Lloyd, founding member and guitarist of punk band Television, dies aged 75

The Guardian Sat, 07 Nov 2026 20:06:25 GMT

Known for sophisticated musical style in band that played significant role in emerging 1970s punk rock movement

Richard Lloyd, known for his sophisticated musical style as a founding member and guitarist for the influential punk band Television, has died at the age of 75.

His family confirmed that Lloyd died Saturday morning at his home in Chattanooga, Tennessee. “His loving wife Sheila and his dog Willie Mays were with him at the end,” his family said in a statement to Rolling Stone.

According to his family, Lloyd’s death was caused by cholangiocarcinoma, a form of bile duct cancer that he was diagnosed with in March 2026.

A crowdfunding campaign had revealed that Lloyd had developed tumors in his liver and, crucially, there was one that could not be surgically removed.

Television, which formed in 1973, played a significant role in the emerging punk rock movement that grew up around CBGB, the legendary former music venue on the Bowery in New York City. The group was among the earliest punk acts to perform at the downtown venue, which had previously focused mainly on country and bluegrass music.

During a 2007 interview, Lloyd reflected on his role in shaping the club’s history, declaring: “CBGB’s is the most famous rock ‘n’ roll club to have ever existed and I fucking created it! I was the invisible force behind it.”

Television recorded just two studio albums during its peak in the late 1970s. The band’s first album, released in 1977, was Marquee Moon, which has since earned widespread recognition as a landmark recording. Rolling Stone ranked it No 107 on its 2023 list of the 500 greatest albums of all time. The record is still considered one of the most influential guitar-driven albums in rock history.

In a 2005 review, the Guardian described his performance, writing that “Lloyd’s guitar was the louder in a lopsided sound mix, so it was impossible to overlook the amount of ground he was covering. Crisp, crunchy chords, dextrous fills and torrential Van Halen-style solos tumbled from his fingers.”

There are very few reasons for Unai Emery to leave Aston Villa for Manchester United

The Guardian Sat, 07 Nov 2026 20:00:19 GMT

Spaniard may feel some of Old Trafford’s allure when he goes there on Sunday but he is right in wanting to stay at the club with brighter prospects

On Sunday afternoon, shortly before 4.30, Unai Emery will leave the tunnel at Old Trafford and walk along the touchline towards the bench. Will he glance around the grand old stadium – faded and leaking though it may be in parts – and think that he could have a part in restoring the club to former glories? Will he look at the home bench and imagine himself sitting there – or perhaps more plausibly, scuttling up and down in front of it – as the first Manchester United manager since Sir Alex Ferguson to land a league title?

Perhaps not. Emery is, after all, in “advanced talks” to extend a contract at Villa that already runs to 2029. However frustrating he may find the habitual summer churn, he is good at managing it. He feels the right fit for Villa, and that is arguably the most important factor in determining success. Yet all elite managers share a robust self-belief and there is a paradoxical sense that the worse the situation gets at United, the more appealing the job becomes.

Imagine being the manager who does sort it out. Imagine following in that brief lineage of United title winners: Ernest Mangnall, Matt Busby, Alex Ferguson … me? United remain the eighth wealthiest club by revenue in the world; imagine the resources that would be available if they were actually any good.

That is an allure that very few clubs in the world can match, no matter how good they were in the 1890s, and no matter how much the Villa owner, Nassef Sawiris, may dislike the fact. This is a point that cannot be made too strongly. Villa’s threat of legal action against Jamie Carragher was an outrageous attack on free speech. There is no way Carragher’s comment about the food chain of football could be construed as defamatory and, while it’s true he might have made the comment in less provocative terms, swearing is not a crime. This was a classic case of a legal threat being used to quell criticism and those fans – and, worse, journalists – who cheered it on should be thoroughly ashamed. The partisan blindness and persecution complex shared by fans of so many clubs is one of the most depressing features of the modern game.

But it’s also true United’s allure has come to look distinctly tarnished. No matter how bullet-proof a manager’s self-confidence, it would represent a remarkable risk to make the leap from Villa to United at this juncture. In almost every facet, from infrastructure to personnel, the modern Villa are better run than the modern United. And from Emery’s point of view, it’s not just that Villa are well run, it’s that they’re well run in his way.

He has the coaching staff he wants, while the president of football operations, Roberto Olabe, and the director of football operations, Damian Vidagany, are people he trusts and has worked with before. Emery would not have the degree of autonomy he has at Villa at many other clubs. United’s win over Roma on Tuesday may have eased the most immediate pressure on Michael Carrick, but nobody surely thinks that one good half against a depleted Serie A side cures all ills. (The question, obviously, is slightly absurd: nobody surely thinks Carrick is really the problem at United; it’s just that executives tend to get rid of managers because it’s what you do when there’s been a slump in form; it’s how a director acknowledges that he’s recognised there is a problem, while hoping desperately to deflect attention from his own shortcomings).

It doesn’t help that there is a clear precedent from five years ago, when a popular former United player saw his team come from two down to beat a Serie A side managed by Gian Piero Gasperini; Ole Gunnar Solskjær was sacked a month later.

The United crisis may have eased, but it is far from over. While Sir Jim Ratcliffe shows off architects’ plans and begs for public money to build a new stadium, Villa get on with building the new Trinity Road Stand. While United’s squad sags under the weight of its many contradictions, a weird mismatch of ill-fitting parts, Villa’s begins to take shape despite making 11 signings in the summer – even if the 3-0 defeat by Barcelona in midweek suggests there is still work to be done. They probably wouldn’t ideally have made such radical changes and would have preferred to keep Morgan Rogers and Ezri Konsa but, equally, there was an admirable sense of realism at Villa – a recognition of their place in the food chain, you might say – that when Chelsea or Arsenal come calling and offering huge contracts, there’s not much to be done other than to drive the price as high as possible.

Youri Tielemans is another player Villa might have liked to keep, but once United matched his release clause, the deal was done. Although Tielemans probably appreciates his new contract, it’s far from clear it’s been a good move for him from a football point of view, not least because United’s is a midfield that exposes his lack of mobility. Carlos Baleba was signed from Brighton to address that lack of dynamism in the United midfield but there were concerns about his tendency to drift in and out of games even before he suffered a hamstring injury on Tuesday.

It even feels as though Villa have been smarter about using United players than United have. Victor Lindelöf was brought in on a free transfer in summer 2025 and has excelled since and while Marcus Rashford and Jadon Sancho had less of an impact, Villa only signed them on loan. Rashford’s time, which featured four goals in 17 appearances in all competitions, was probably the more eye-catching, but Sancho made 39 appearances in his season at Villa.

In both cases, Villa got value out of a players whose futures were uncertain but without committing to having to take them on full-time.

It’s pretty hard to imagine at the moment, but at some point, United will start heading in the right direction. It may even be that Tuesday’s win prompts a surge of adrenaline that takes them into the top half of the table. For now, though, Villa look by far the brighter prospect, a club on the up, while United are in barely managed decline.

Wait long enough, and results will come to reflect performances. Manchester City may have won their first seven games of the season, but they always looked vulnerable, and now have lost three in a row. Put the two together, and the outcome was a dramatic regression to the mean. It turns out the stats were right, after all.

Liam Delap scored twice to remind people just what a good striker he can be. Oliver Glasner, after last week’s anger, can breathe a little easier in his job. And Enzo Maresca remains a paradox, a manager obsessive about control whose teams always seem oddly susceptible to direct running.

After last week’s defeat at Brentford, Glasner said he regretted compromising too much in the early weeks of his reign at Forest. Although he gave no precise details as to what that might mean, he elaborated a little on Thursday, speaking of the need for “trust and respect” in the appropriate balance, suggesting there had been too much trust and not enough respect this season at Forest, too much “Woodstock 69” and not enough “high-performance nature of military”.

Glasner’s brave new uncompromising world was ushered in with just two changes to the starting lineup from defeat at Brentford, Ola Aina and Dan Ndoye dropping out for Daniel Muñoz and Ryan Yates, who both came on at half-time last week. It may have been an underwhelming revolution but it soon worked, Jair Cunha dispossessing Josko Gvardiol and running through to opening the scoring after six minutes, Forest’s first home goal since Morgan Gibbs-White’s strike against Bournemouth 34 minutes into the final game of last season, a drought of 510 minutes.

No side this season had underperformed their xG by such a margin as Forest; they began the weekend third in Opta’s expected table but second bottom of the actual table. To an extent that is a matter of misfortune: defeat at Brentford, for instance, was a result of a cross and a shot that both looped in off Nikola Milenkovic; when you concede one shot on target but two goals, you know you’ve been unlucky. And when, on Saturday, three minutes after Forest had taken the lead, a Jérémy Doku shot hit Milenkovic and, rather than looping agonisingly past Matz Sels, cannoned wide for a corner, Forest must really have known their luck was in.

One of the biggest issues for Forest this season has been the form of Delap. A gruelling spell at Chelsea had seemingly sapped his confidence but, 18 minutes in, he surged from inside his own half, ran, as Cunha had for the opener, between Rúben Dias and Marc Guéhi, and thumped his shot over the dive of Gianluigi Donnarumma. With confidence, it turns out, Delap is a very different player.

Guéhi’s form, meanwhile, is becoming a major concern for City. With Dias wary of Xaver Schlager running to his right and potentially becoming a passing option, it was surely Guéhi’s responsibility to close Delap down. As it was, the pair left a huge channel, inviting Delap to keep going to score his second goal since joining Forest. Guéhi and Gvardiol were both withdrawn at half-time.

‘People are active, they are fed up’: young voters fueled the Democratic wave

The Guardian Sat, 07 Nov 2026 17:00:16 GMT

After helping Trump to victory in 2024, young voters swung decisively toward Democrats, helping deliver a wave of midterm victories

The 2026 blue tsunami owes a lot to the youth vote.

According to data from Tufts University’s Center for Information & Research on Civic Learning and Engagement (Circle), which monitors youth civic engagement, early estimates show the second-highest youth turnout in a midterm election in 30 years, second only to 2018, when an estimated 31% of young voters turned out during Donald Trump’s first presidency.

While voters over 45 were roughly split between parties, voters ages 18-29 went for congressional Democrats at a 35-point edge, across race, gender, ethnicity, and education levels. Latino youth went for Trump by slim majorities in 2024; this year, they voted Democrat by margins of +10 to +15. 63% of young white men went for Trump in 2024; this cycle, 54% voted Dem. White young women also switched allegiance from 2024 by +15. Rural voters went from 50% voting for Trump in 2024 to 60% supporting Democratic candidates.

This is something of a return to form for the youth vote, which leaned Democratic by double digits in elections between 2018 and 2022. Indeed, the +35 lean for voters 18-35 parallels that in the 2018 blue wave which elected populist Democrats like Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, said Leela Strong, the director of Circle.

“It was such a soundbite for 2024, about the shift of young white men specifically, and folks without formal college experience,” said Strong. “Now, even though we’re comparing a midterm to a presidential, we’re seeing shifts among those demographic groups switching back to Democrats, overwhelmingly so.”

According to Strong, the data even suggests that 15% of young people who voted for Trump in 2024 voted for a Democratic House candidate this cycle. The outcome has been so decisive that Republicans are openly fretting over heavily Blue youth vote turnout in states like Florida, Georgia and South Carolina.

In battleground states – Florida, Georgia, Iowa, Maine, Michigan, Minnesota, North Carolina, Nebraska, New Hampshire, Nevada, Ohio, Pennsylvania, Texas, and Wisconsin – the estimated youth turnout was, in aggregate, 30%.

“I voted because in my working-class, immigrant neighborhood, families are afraid to go outside, drive to work or pick up their kid from school,” said Motyko Morales, 26, an artist in Miami, who says her family members have experienced “real physical and psychological impact” over attacks on legal routes to citizenship and the threat of third-country deportations. She’s “cautiously optimistic” that congressional Democrats will “hold ICE accountable and reverse course on harmful legislation”.

“For the first time in my life, I got to see a candidate that looked [like] and represented the same values of the Rio Grande Valley that I have,” said Amanda Chapa, 22, a recent college graduate and community organizer from Rio Grande City, Texas, of Gina Hinojosa. The governor-elect won 77% of voters 18-29, based on exit polling analysis from NBC News. In 2024, Trump flipped Starr county on the Texas-Mexico border – where Rio Grande City is located – by over 70 points; this year, despite navigating barriers to the polls, voters flipped it back by over 70 points.

Just over half of young voters ranked the economy and jobs as their top priority, followed by healthcare, Iran, immigration, education and the climate. Chapa’s top issues were reinstating cut funding to Medicaid and fighting ICE and the “brutalization of our community members”.

Sarah John, 26, a law student from Los Angeles, said she’s critical of Democrats, but having witnessed the impacts of Trump’s ICE raids in LA (still being felt), she strongly believed her vote against Republicans would make a difference. On Thursday, Los Angeles elected its first democratic socialist mayor, Nithya Raman – making two of the country’s three biggest cities now run by democratic socialists.

The enthusiasm even reached states without competitive federal races. Patrick Schranck, 27, who manages an independent movie theater in Portland, “identif[ies] more as an independent these days” and is active in his local Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) chapter. He spent Tuesday night at Portland DSA’s election night party celebrating the re-election of their three city councilmembers.

Schranck remains skeptical of congressional Democrats’ ability to “fix everything” with their newfound majorities, but, he said: “I’m just glad to see the Republicans lose and see more socialists and progressives get elected nationally.”

For Jordan Korgood, 24, of Boston, voting in this election was especially personal. The Massachusetts sexual health educator feels so passionately about civic engagement that she filed to run for a state board seat overseeing judicial appointments. But her 41-year incumbent opponent had Korgood tossed from the race on a technicality: Because she was homeless for a few months while in college in 2023, her opponent argued she could not meet the five-year residency requirement.

“Voting was the most immediate and direct way I could still engage with electoral politics in a meaningful way,” said Korgood, whose biggest issues were protecting the first amendment and trans rights. Regardless of who was up for re-election in Massachusetts, she said it felt necessary “at a time when fascists who seek to limit or repress my rights as a trans woman are seated in office in both red states and blue states alike”.

Young people were credited in part with powering Trump’s 2024 win, though just under half of eligible young voters turned out, not hitting the 50% turnout achieved in 2020. Plenty chose to sit out the election over US funding for Israel’s assault in Gaza, as well as the decision by both schools and elected officials to criminalize students in the thousands for protesting it. They also felt that the Democratic party had failed to offer a strong counter to what Republicans had on offer, instead tacking to the center.

In a sign of things to come, a year later, 75% of New York City voters 18-29 chose democratic socialist Zohran Mamdani as the city’s mayor, forming “his strongest supporter [bloc] out of all age groups” in the election tally, according to Circle. Political commentators and national party leaders argued a DSA campaign like his could only win in New York City.

Twenty-six-year-old Elise Joshi runs the progressive campus program More Perfect University and has spent the last several months hosting many of the progressive candidates that won big Tuesday at “Students vs. Billionaires Town Halls” on college campuses across the country. When the program launched this spring, Joshi told the New York Times that it was intended in part as a progressive counterpoint to Turning Point USA, whose existing campus presence has expanded in the year since Charlie Kirk’s killing. She argued that TPUSA “refus[es] to champion working-class issues”, and that youth voters were desperate for candidates who would.

Candidates like Michigan’s Abdul El-Sayed – whose campaign slogan was “get money out of politics, put money in your pocket, and pass Medicare for All,” and who refused to compromise on trans girls in sports – are at the forefront of what Joshi and others are calling a blue tsunami.

“We’ve been in Florida, Maine, North Carolina, and I’ve seen the youth enthusiasm every single time – and not just enthusiasm for a specific candidate: Students who are very inquisitive about the issues and the solutions to those issues they’re dealing with, [from] from healthcare to economic issues to trans rights,” said Joshi. “Young people are active, they are fed up with corporate greed and corruption from Washington, and are ready to be really engaged in politics in all the ways you can be.”

More than a few of the successful candidates promising change, regardless of location, are young people themselves, like Melat Kiros, 29, the newly elected Colorado congresswoman who defeated a 15-term incumbent; many are DSA candidates. This week, Providence, Rhode Island, elected its youngest-ever mayor: 28-year-old David Morales, a democratic socialist. That same day, the city became the largest in the United States to vote in support of divesting from “companies complicit in genocide”, organized by the Providence for Palestine campaign.

In a period of global youth uprising against government corruption and seizing power in elections, it’s a partial answer to anyone questioning when America might see its youth in revolt. It’s also a rebuke to a tremendous amount of Republican campaign spending. Elon Musk alone spent nearly half a billion dollars backing Republicans and attacking candidates like Texas’s James Talarico, especially on trans issues. Talarico went on to win voters ages 18-29 by nearly 50 points.

“With the price of gas what it is alongside a hiring freeze, the only solution offered by the Republican party was to blind yourself with bigotry and pick a God and pray – except it has to be the Christian one, or else,” said model Vivian Wilson, 22, who has been financially independent from Musk, her father, since she came out as trans as a teenager. “Spending hundreds of millions of dollars on ‘trans kids boogieman’ ads makes voters feel like they’re being talked down to or ignored – which they were – rather than focusing on any actual tangible policy for change.”

She sees youth turnout for Democrats as only logical amid economic crisis, war on Iran, military support for Israel, ICE raids, and “the known sexual misconduct of Republican candidates”.

Wilson added: “There have been so many nails placed in this coffin that it’s turning into a Theseus’ ship kind of situation.”

“We feel fantastic,” said Kidus Girma, campaigns director for the Sunrise Movement, the youth climate organization that burst on to the scene in 2018 with a sit-in for the Green New Deal in then-Speaker Nancy Pelosi’s office alongside newly elected Ocasio-Cortez. This week, one of the movement’s cofounders, Will Lawrence, 36, won his race in Michigan, with Sunrise’s support.

Joshi and Girma are clear: It’s not “vote blue, no matter who.” There are plenty of power players still in the party who organizers feel didn’t listen to them outside election years, when they need them to power youth turnout.

Up next: Holding these new electeds – and the Democratic party – accountable. On Thursday, Wilson posted to her Instagram account backing a rising call from the US young left to reject Senator Chuck Schumer and congressman Hakeem Jeffries for leadership positions in the new Congress. By Saturday, a Change. org petition calling for Jeffries’ leadership ouster had attracted more than a million signatures.

Rise in NHS birth centre closures ‘shocking’ denial of women’s rights, experts say

The Guardian Sat, 07 Nov 2026 17:00:16 GMT

Twelve midwife-led maternity units have closed in England since 2019 with six closing since Labour came to power in 2024

NHS officials are shutting growing numbers of birth centres in a “shocking” denial of a woman’s right to have a midwife rather than a doctor oversee their baby’s birth, say campaigners.

Twelve birth centres – midwife-led maternity units – have closed in England since 2019. Birth centres play a key role in ensuring that women can choose whether to have their baby at a unit in a hospital run by doctors, at one where midwives are in charge, or at home.

Six units have shut permanently since Labour came to power in July 2024. Four others have been closed “temporarily” for so long, up to six years, that childbirth groups fear they will never reopen. Two other birth centres closed because the hospitals where they were based have begun to fall apart and will remain out of action for several years until new facilities are built.

Women’s ability to choose where their baby is born is also being increasingly restricted in England and Wales by NHS bodies suspending home birth services for up to 14 months.

The wave of closures and suspensions is occurring because of the NHS-wide shortage of midwives, a falling birthrate, the growing complexity of childbirth and a rise in caesarean sections.

Campaigners say the loss of local childbirth services is denying women their right to choose and forcing them to travel from their home area to give birth.

The Royal College of Midwives said that women’s inability to access midwife-led care on the NHS risks them deciding to pay for private midwifery support or even have a baby at home with no health professional present.

Hazel Williams, the chief executive of Birthrights, said: “Over the past few years we have seen shocking restrictions on women and birthing people’s choices of place of birth, with more and more birth centre closures and restrictions and the option for NHS-supported home birth vastly reduced for many.

“These are not luxury options or nice-to-haves. This is about women and birthing people’s right to choose what happens to their bodies and their birth.”

The six permanent closures during Labour’s time in government have been in Rossendale, east Lancashire; Edgware in north London; Melton Mowbray in Leicestershire; Stafford and Lichfield in Staffordshire; and Pontefract in West Yorkshire. NHS bodies that have decided to close birth centres often stress they do not have enough midwives to staff the service safely.

Tope Medupin, the acting chief executive of the National Childbirth Trust, said: “For women and birthing people the loss of a local service often means longer journeys, higher costs, greater uncertainty and fewer options for care at one of the most important times in their lives.

“Longstanding workforce shortages, crumbling estates and wider pressures on maternity services remain unresolved and women are increasingly expected to travel further for maternity care as a result. That cannot simply become the new normal.”

The Huddersfield birth centre in Yorkshire closed in November 2020 as a temporary measure because of the Covid-19 pandemic. But six years later it has not reopened. “No decision has been made to reopen the service and we are not able to provide a timeframe for any potential reopening,” said the Calderdale and Huddersfield NHS trust which ran it. “Any future decisions will be based on a thorough assessment of clinical safety, workforce sustainability and the needs of local women and families.”

Similarly, Ingleside birth centre in Salford, which opened in 2018, has been shut – again ostensibly as a temporary step – since January 2022.

Midwife-led births at the birth centre in Crowborough, east Sussex, were halted temporarily in October 2025 because staff shortages meant it kept closing at short notice. Maidstone and Tunbridge Wells NHS trust, which runs the centre, said it had completed a review of what it would take to reopen the facility but declined to say what that would involve.

The MP for Sussex Weald, Nusrat Ghani, who is campaigning for it to reopen, said the NHS trust had broken “numerous promises” to review the practicalities of reopening the service.

“We have had thousands of local mums and residents complain at the closure of the service and the trust is ignoring their health needs and choices,” Ghani said. “I am disappointed that the trust doesn’t give weight to the prospect of avoidable complications for mothers who are having to travel for up to 90 minutes to give birth.”

The trust may be continuing to describe the closure as temporary to avoid the formal public consultation it would have to undertake if it were made permanent, Ghani suggested.

Gloucester hospitals trust announced last week that Cheltenham birth centre will reopen in February after being shut since 2022 and that home births, suspended since 2025, will resume in January.

A senior NHS leader recently warned that up to 20 full-scale, consultant-led maternity units at acute hospitals in England may have to close in order to keep women and babies safe.

There are fears that the birth centres at the Queen Elizabeth hospital in King’s Lynn and James Paget hospital in Great Yarmouth could also shut after NHS bosses in Norfolk last week proposed closing their maternity units and instead centralising care for the county at the Norfolk and Norwich University hospital in Norwich.

The maternity unit at North Devon district hospital in Barnstaple has been closed for months, including its home birth service, due to lack of staff.

Hannah Leonard, the chief policy officer and deputy chief midwife at the Royal College of Midwives, said: “Women have the right to choose where they give birth, but that choice is being eroded. The evidence shows that for some women choosing to give birth in a birth centre or at home improves outcomes and experience for the woman and her baby.”

Yvette Cooper, the health secretary, is due to publish an action plan to address the crisis in maternity and neonatal care in England before Christmas.

The Department of Health and Social Care did not respond directly to the closures. A spokesperson said: “Every woman and baby deserves safe, compassionate maternity and neonatal care and the health secretary has made it a personal priority to improve standards across the board. Strengthening the workforce is central to that goal and there are now a record number of midwives working in the NHS, with over 600 added in the past year.”

Scotland trail in All Blacks’ wake once more despite Ewan Ashman hat-trick

The Guardian Sat, 07 Nov 2026 16:27:39 GMT

Scotland 21-43 New Zealand

Townsend ‘frustrated’ as first win eludes Scots again

Scotland never got going; Murrayfield never got going; New Zealand did. Scotland have had some agonising defeats here in recent years, as they chase that first win against the All Blacks. This was not one of them. This was dispiritingly routine.

Despite a hat-trick of tries in the first half for Ewan Ashman, the irrepressible hooker, Scotland could not register a point at all in the second. New Zealand cantered away to a tally of seven tries, two for Beauden Barrett who beetled through Scotland’s outside defences with ease, scoring 19 unanswered points in the second half.

“You obviously prepare to try and win games,” said the Scotland head coach, Gregor Townsend. “But it’s more about delivering a performance we can be proud of, that our supporters can be proud of. And it wasn’t there today. So that’s frustrating.”

We always speculate at this time of year whether it is of advantage to the southern-hemisphere teams to arrive in the north fully match fit, or whether they might be fatigued at the end of their season. No question which team was on it for this one. Scotland looked as if they were disconnected, which might be expected in their first outing of the season, but that has not been the case in those agonising defeats at this same time of year in the past. This flop will prove galling.

Whether it will feel so for the north in general, as the devisers of this weird Nations Championship will hope, remains to be seen. There may or may not be much esprit de corps among the teams of the north, but one thing is for sure, the All Blacks and the Springboks look a class apart at the top of the south’s table. Four wins out of four; four bonus points out of four. Two rounds of round-robin to play.

At times tries seemed almost too easy to come by. That applied to Scotland as much as the other way round in the first half, when seven tries were scored, but the home team could not rejoin the party after the break.

There has been a feeling for a while that lineout-and-drives have begun to dominate the modern game – and the directives issued during the off-season targeting defensive players disrupting these have hardly discouraged teams from going for the corner. All but one of those seven first-half tries featured attacking lineouts from penalties kicked to the corner, four of them directly from the subsequent mauls set up.

Springboks smash Italy

South Africa strolled past an injury-hit ⁠Italy with a 66-7 win in Saturday’s Nations Championship meeting in ⁠Turin, where the ⁠fly-half ​Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu scored the first of nine Springbok tries and added ⁠another 21 points from a perfect kicking display.

South Africa ran in six ⁠tries in an utterly dominant opening half. ​Hooker Malcolm Marx ‌went over ‌twice, adding to scores by Feinberg-Mngomezulu, Morne van ‌den Berg and the captain Siya Kolisi and Damian Willemse, with Feinberg-Mngomezulu kicking all six conversions having opened the scoring with a penalty.

Wilco Louw added another try after ‌the break before Italy finally got off the mark with Federico Ruzza’s ​try converted by Tommaso Allan. Springbok wing Ethan Hooker ran in the final score on the stroke of full-time.

South Africa had ⁠claimed maximum points from their three July fixtures ​to ​top the Southern ​Hemisphere group ahead of New Zealand ​on points ‌difference and ​they ​added to that total against Italy ahead of the All Blacks facing Scotland. Reuters

Two of Ashman’s tries were from neatly executed Scotland lineouts, and those of Wallace Sititi and Codie Taylor were likewise taken for the All Blacks. The visitors held a three-point lead at the break, despite yellow cards shown to Peter Lakai and Sititi. Scotland were actually penalised more in that period, but New Zealand’s offences were committed during peak pressure.

Ashman’s second try was from open play, following the mandatory penalty to the corner after Lakai’s yellow. Huw Jones was held up, and from the dropout Kyle Steyn broke down one wing, Kyle Rowe down the other, and Ashman hit a fine line off Ben White’s pass.

But New Zealand had the bonus point after half an hour. Their second try had followed some fine interplay down the left between Tupou Vaa’i and Josh Moorby. Cam Roigard took a tap penalty after a chase of Beauden Barrett’s chip ahead, and Ethan de Groot drove over from close range. Their fourth, though, came from another attacking lineout, this one spun wide after a few juicy drives round the fringes, where Damian McKenzie put over the most senior of the game’s three Barretts, Beauden, with sweet timing.

New Zealand B Barrett; Jordan (Ioane 53), Tupaea, J Barrett (Tavatanawai 66), Moorby; McKenzie, Roigard (Ratima 61); De Groot (Bower 50), Taylor (capt; Aumua 56), Newell (Tosi 63), S Barrett, Holland, Vaa’i (Lio-Willie 72), Lakai, Sititi (Segner 56)

Tries Sititi, De Groot, Taylor, B Barrett 2, Moorby, Aumua Cons McKenzie 4

Scotland badly needed to make the first move after the break. That they did not.

New Zealand pulled away in the third quarter with ease. Novelly, they chose to scrum an attacking penalty and showed how to score off that set piece, too. Scott Barrett’s long pass was gathered by Moorby for a simple run-in. Rugby shouldn’t be made to look so easy.

Worse was to follow for the Scots. The captain, Sione Tuipulotu, was sent to the sin bin, as they continued to infringe with the All Blacks now constantly on the attack. That penalty was sent to the corner, but the All Blacks showed off a prettier interpretation of the attacking lineout, McKenzie looping round Quinn Tupaea to put Beauden Barrett over for the second time.

Murrayfield was silenced, which was bad given there was another half an hour still to play. Asafo Aumua’s try in the final quarter, New Zealand’s seventh, hardly shifted that vibe. Another penalty to touch, another lineout. This one was far enough out to make a drive unrealistic, so they worked the try another way. The throw went long, and Lakai looped blind to send Aumua clean through.

Easy. Too easy. That first win over the All Blacks looks as distant a dream as ever.

Five European leaders call for closer EU-UK ties ahead of Brussels summit

The Guardian Sat, 07 Nov 2026 15:30:35 GMT

Germany, Belgium, Netherlands, Luxembourg and Denmark say cooperation on clean energy will benefit both sides

Five European leaders have called for closer ties with Britain ahead of a keenly anticipated EU-UK summit.

The leaders of Germany, Belgium, the Netherlands, Luxembourg and Denmark, said deeper cooperation on clean energy would benefit both sides in a letter to Ursula von der Leyen and António Costa.

Von der Leyen, the president of the European Commission, and Costa, who leads the European Council, will meet Andy Burnham on 20 November in Brussels, where they hope to sign deals on food and drink, carbon emissions and youth exchange.

The five countries also want the two sides to speed up work on another strand of negotiations: Britain’s return to the EU’s internal electricity market. “We call on you and the UK to agree during the summit on a path towards the conclusion of these negotiations,” states the letter seen by the Guardian from the German chancellor, Friedrich Merz; the Dutch prime minister, Rob Jetten; Belgium’s prime minister, Bart De Wever; Luc Frieden, the prime minister of Luxembourg; and Denmark’s prime minister, Mette Frederiksen.

Describing the UK as a “close partner in the energy transition”, the leaders said Britain’s integration into the EU’s internal electricity market was “necessary to unlock the full potential of the North Sea area and transform it into the largest clean energy hub in the world”.

The UK and nine other European countries signed a pact earlier this year to accelerate the rollout of offshore windfarms in the 2030s and build a power grid in the North Sea. Britain’s exit from the EU’s internal electricity market is seen as cramping the development of North Sea energy and adding to costs.

Bringing Britain into the internal electricity market could be controversial, however, because the UK would be required to make a contribution to the EU budget, specifically to cohesion funds that promote economic development in poorer regions. British officials are wary of a deal in which taxpayers’ money could be used to fund infrastructure projects in central and eastern Europe.

Last year negotiations on Britain’s entry into a €150bn (£125bn) EU defence fund collapsed over a dispute about the size of the UK’s contribution.

In an attempt to head off another row over money, North Sea member states are stressing the potential for the deal to bring about lower and more stable energy prices for British billpayers. “The UK would not simply be paying into EU cohesion funds,” a EU diplomat said. “The UK would be investing in access to a more integrated, secure and competitive European energy market.

“This will lead to more efficient electricity trading, resulting in lower costs for UK consumers.”

According to figures from the industry body Energy UK, published in 2024, if the current energy relationship remains unchanged, Britain could pay extra costs of £10bn from 2024-29, through higher energy bills and lower Treasury revenues.

The industry group argues that Brexit barriers will become more significant over time, frustrating the UK’s potential to realise the full benefits of growth in offshore wind power.

Since he became prime minister, Burnham has said the government would examine the options in the UK’s relationship with the EU, including a customs union, return to the single market or to “go all the way” with full membership.

“There will be no possibility to have one freedom and not the other. The four freedoms are clearly the four conditions to be inside a single market.”

Labour MPs have supported calls for greater ties. Stella Creasy, the chair of the Labour Movement for Europe, who is campaigning for a de-facto second referendum to be included in the party’s next manifesto said there were “plenty of sensible changes” that could be done in the meantime.

Vetting candidates is a tricky process but Reform can’t seem to get it right

The Guardian Sat, 07 Nov 2026 15:00:14 GMT

Charges against party members and off-piste remarks highlight problems brought about by rapid expansion

Speaking to reporters after unveiling his new defence spokesperson this week, Nigel Farage’s jovial and upbeat mood suddenly switched. Why, he was asked, was a Reform UK councillor who was arrested in January over multiple alleged sexual offences still in his role nearly 10 months later?

“I have no idea,” Farage replied icily. “I was told yesterday, and I wasn’t very happy.”

A later question about Reform’s misfiring processes for vetting candidates did nothing to improve the mood. Why, Farage asked, was wrongdoing in other parties barely covered, when the news that the arrested Reform councillor had been charged prompted a BBC News alert?

In fairness to the BBC, the charges brought against George Madgwick, who was Reform’s leader on Hampshire county council, were many and deeply serious, 35 in all, including 12 allegations of rape. Madgwick has said he is innocent.

But more generally, it is another difficult moment for a party that has had to expand and professionalise at unprecedented speed, a process that its internal structures have at times failed to keep up with.

Little more than a week earlier, it emerged that a member of Farage’s security team, Ryan Dinnage, who was with him during this year’s local elections campaign, was facing a rape charge at the time for which he was later convicted and jailed. Reform UK said they were unaware of the charge and that Dinnage “ceased to be used” by the party when it came to light.

And on Monday, a now suspended Reform councillor on Sunderland city council, Glenn Gibbins, will appear in court charged with making “grossly offensive” social media posts about Nigerians. Gibbins denies the charge.

While such incidents are rare, notably more common has been Reform being called on to disown candidates after the emergence of previous offensive or prejudiced comments, often made on social media.

Perhaps the most prominent example was Robert Kenyon, who Reform had hoped would block Andy Burnham’s return to the Commons in June’s Makerfield byelection.

The local plumber had contested the seat in 2024, but greater scrutiny in the new contest saw comments unearthed in which he expressed scepticism about vaccines and the seriousness of Covid, interacted with far-right figures, and most memorably, endorsed an eye-openingly lewd comment about the TV presenter Carol Vorderman.

Being challenged about vetting is nothing new for Farage, which might in part explain his frustration at the subject. Shortly before the 2024 election he blamed an external company for not doing proper background checks on candidates, hinting that Reform had been “stitched up politically”.

Vetting was then brought in-house, initially under the control of a “business psychologist” and former parliamentary candidate who had once described the Syrian dictator Bashar al-Assad as “gentle by nature”.

It is now run by Paul Nuttall, the party’s deputy chair, who spent a brief period a decade ago as leader of Ukip, one of Farage’s earlier parties, a period which saw Nuttall come under scrutiny over his CV and a claim he had lost close friends in the Hillsborough stadium disaster.

The party is tight-lipped about how its vetting now works. Intemperate social media output is not an automatic bar, with members told last year that the aim was to create a “commonsense” system that struck a balance between the party’s reputation and individual freedom.

Other aspects are more rigorous, with would-be candidates trying their luck at regional events reportedly being made to give a speech and undertake a mock interview without preparation.

One Conservative official with knowledge of Reform’s approach said there was a heavy reliance on prospective candidates being open and honest about their past careers and expressed opinions.

“There is a degree of that in every party,” they said. “With us, we begin by asking people if there is anything about them which could bring the party into disrepute, and if we find out later about something they didn’t tell us, it is very problematic.

“With Reform it seems to be more of a judgment call. People do not necessarily get rejected because of comments they did not admit to.”

Outside scrutiny plays a role in all parties. Conservative candidates for parliamentary seats must submit their full employment and residence history, and face what the official called “tricky conversations” in a subsequent interview.

But there is always at least some reliance on integrity. ITV’s recent undercover documentary about Reform UK, which featured a series of councillors and candidates making offensive remarks, also included footage of a regional chair advising a reporter posing as a possible candidate to delete problematic social media posts.

Similarly, it is not usually possible to know whether someone has been arrested or even charged with an alleged offence if they do not tell you.

Parties must therefore rely at least in part on things such as informal knowledge, intensive questioning, and ultimately a trust in the candidate. When, as with Reform, you are seeking many hundreds of potential councillors and MPs at the same time, things can go wrong.

There is, of course, another possible factor at work. When your party’s offering is based largely on immigration and sweeping talk of supposedly problematic foreign cultures, then it seems inevitable it will attract at least some with off-piste views.

Farage vehemently rejects the idea that Reform’s culture is inherently more toxic than any other party. He now needs a vetting system to match.

The Guardian Sat, 07 Nov 2026 14:00:13 GMT

Dickens character is actor’s first big studio role after years overshadowed by legal battles with ex-wife Amber Heard

“It’s good to be back,” Johnny Depp declares in the trailer for Ebenezer, in which he stars as Charles Dickens’s miserly Scrooge – his first big Hollywood studio production in eight years.

The message is clear: this is Depp’s comeback, after years in which his career was overshadowed by legal battles with his former wife Amber Heard.

Paramount has made a point of invoking Depp’s most famous roles – the trailer opens with references to Captain Jack Sparrow, Edward Scissorhands and the Mad Hatter, before announcing: “The master of misfits returns.”

When the film opens on 13 November, it will be a test – not just of whether Depp can still sell cinema tickets, but whether Hollywood can restore him to the ranks of mainstream leading men.

“I think Ebenezer will serve as a bellwether for the industry as to Depp’s bankability,” said Robert Mitchell, the director of theatrical insights at Gower Street Analytics.

“Depp has proven he’s most bankable in the past when aligned to a specific type of film, essentially those with larger-than-life, almost grotesque characters of the type he began playing for Tim Burton in the 1990s.

“That is what the marketing is leaning into with Ebenezer – Depp in a specific, recognisable mode rather than just Depp the actor.”

In 2020, Depp lost a libel case against the Sun’s publisher, with a judge ruling that the paper’s description of him as a “wife beater” was substantially true.

Two years later, in a separate US defamation trial, a jury found that Heard had defamed Depp in a Washington Post article and awarded him $10.35m (£7.7m) in damages. It also found that one of Depp’s lawyers had defamed Heard, awarding her $2m. The pair settled their appeals in 2022.

Depp was asked to step down from his role as Gellert Grindelwald in the Fantastic Beasts franchise after losing the UK case, with Mads Mikkelsen replacing him in the third film.

His subsequent films included Minamata, which made less than $1m at the global box office, and Jeanne du Barry, whose 2023 Cannes premiere was accompanied by protests over the festival’s decision to platform Depp.

But now Hollywood appears increasingly willing to work with the actor again. His next film, Day Drinker, is due for release in 2027, while the producer Jerry Bruckheimer has said he is in discussions with Depp about a possible sixth Pirates of the Caribbean film.

In Ebenezer, Depp returns to the eccentric, heavily stylised performances for which he became famous. Its director, Ti West, told Entertainment Weekly that Depp brought a particular musicality to Dickens’s dialogue, adding: “He’s the movie, really.”

Depp, 63, has also been central to the film’s marketing campaign. He appeared at San Diego Comic-Con in July, dressed as Scrooge. This week, he appeared in character at New York’s Bryant Park, where he disrupted carol singers and knocked over a Christmas tree.

“Hollywood stars are worth every penny they’re paid when they’re cast in the right role, and they’re worth very little in the wrong role,” said David A Gross, who writes the FranchiseRe newsletter. “We just saw Tom Cruise crash in Digger. It’s a good example – there’s no bigger star than him.”

But he added that Scrooge was a promising fit for Depp: an eccentric, funny and familiar character that played to his strengths.

An August report by the website Puck, based on a test screening in New Jersey, offered an encouraging early indication for Paramount.

The film scored 80 out of 100, compared with a reported historical average of 72, while Depp received a score of 86. Women aged over 35 were particularly positive. However, test-screening figures are no guarantee of box office success.

Paul Dergarabedian, the head of marketplace trends at Rentrak, said enough time had passed since the trial for it not to be uppermost in audiences’ minds. “The reviews and the marketing will matter more than how people feel about Johnny Depp personally,” he said.

While some viewers might avoid the film because of their feelings about Depp, Dergarabedian added, it was difficult to establish a direct link between controversy about a star and a film’s box office performance.

Tanya Horeck, a professor of film and feminist media studies at Anglia Ruskin University, emphasised that Depp had never disappeared from public view, remaining the face of Dior’s Sauvage fragrance while his supporters continued to defend him online.

“The idea that this is Depp’s big ‘comeback’ suggests that he went away somehow,” she said. “In fact, the defamation trial largely elevated his star persona as some kind of misunderstood renegade figure.”

Of Hollywood’s willingness to cast him again, Horeck said: “The heralding of Depp’s ‘return’ is indicative of how male stars accused of misconduct are being rehabilitated for public consumption.”

Heard, meanwhile, has largely withdrawn from Hollywood. She recently appeared in Silenced, a documentary about the use of defamation law against survivors of gender-based violence, which premiered at the Sundance festival this year.
