Thunderstruck: what does the future hold for lightning?

The Guardian Sat, 07 Nov 2026 14:00:13 GMT

Humans have always been awed by the power and beauty of lightning. How does the experience and understanding of it change in a warming world?

In a rock shelter in Kakadu national park in the north of Australia is an image of a being the Bininj people call Namarrkon. His flesh bleached away to reveal the bones beneath, he wears stone axes on his head, elbows and knees, and wields a great band of lightning that runs from his ankles up, over his head.

Namarrkon’s journey from the Arafura Sea to the Arnhem Land escarpment helped shape the landscape, according to the dreamtime stories of the Bininj. And in the great storms that arc and rumble across the landscape during the buildup and the wet season, it is Namarrkon who splits the clouds with his stone axes to create the thunder and lightning and release the life-giving rain.

Around the world there are an average of 60 lightning flashes a second, some extending more than 800km. Each flash can release up to seven gigajoules of energy, the equivalent of 1.67 tonnes of TNT, fleetingly heating the air around it to about 30,000C, five times hotter than the surface of the Sun. This constant discharge of energy plays a vital role in regulating Earth’s electrical field and the ionosphere. It helps drive the nitrogen cycle by cracking open nitrogen molecules in the atmosphere and making them available to plants, aiding in the production of ozone, and helping break down greenhouse gases such as methane. And it underpins the cycles of fire that shape the ecologies of forests, savannahs and grasslands across the planet. Lightning, as the story of Namarrkon captures, is an integral part of life on our planet.

Yet as the planet heats up, not just lightning’s role in these systems but lightning itself may be changing. And the consequences of this could be severe. In July more than 48,000 lightning strikes ignited massive wildfires in Canada and the north-west United States, destroying homes and casting a pall of smoke over cities across North America. During last summer’s British heatwave, nearly 30,000 lightning strikes hit south-east England in a single day.

Already, globally around a quarter of a million people are struck by lightning every year, resulting in about 24,000 deaths. In Australia alone lightning kills five to 10 people a year and injures about 100.

The awesome power of lightning is written deep into human cultures around the world. Frequently it expresses a kind of duality, conjuring beauty as well as terror: from the earliest-known poet, the priestess Enheduanna, describing her goddess as having a “glance like striking lightning” to gods whose domain includes both storms and agriculture in ancient Mesopotamian, Maya and Aztec cultures.

Often those who wield the lightning are protectors of humankind: in the Rig-Veda of ancient India, Indra slays the evil serpent Vritra with a thunderbolt and releases the rains and the rivers, while the Norse thunder god Thor was a guardian of humans. And many Native American cultures across the Pacific north-west, Great Lakes and Great Plains incorporate a powerful being known as the Thunderbird, who safeguards humankind.

Although writers and philosophers have sought a physical explanation for lightning for more than 2,000 years, it was not until the 18th century that the American polymath Benjamin Franklin proved the connection between the discharge of static electricity and lightning. Franklin theorised electricity was an invisible fluid that could be passed from object to object or held in substances such as water vapour.

Scientists no longer speak of invisible fluids. Instead, lightning is understood to be created when warm, moisture-laden air rises into the cold upper reaches of storm clouds. As the temperature falls, the water vapour condenses and forms tiny ice crystals. These collide with particles of soft ice called graupel, passing electrons from the ice crystals to the graupel. Now positively charged, the smaller, lighter ice crystals begin to rise into the upper reaches of the cloud, while the heavier, negatively charged graupel sink. As they move away from each other the resulting electrical field grows more intense, until finally the difference between the two neutralises in a sudden discharge of energy. It’s this discharge we see as lightning.

However, the question of precisely what triggers the discharge is still not yet fully understood. This is partly because the electrical fields generated by this process are only about a tenth as strong as they need to be to generate a spark. Recent research suggests it is cosmic rays that provide the spark, although other studies point to the runaway buildup of “streamers” of ionised air.

More than 80% of these discharges take place over land, and although the distribution of lightning changes with the seasons, it is concentrated in central Africa, parts of South America and the Himalayas. The most lightning-prone place in the world is in Venezuela, in an area known as Catatumbo, or “House of the Thunder” in the language of the Bari people, where warm, water-laden air blowing in over Lake Maracaibo collides with the high ridges of the Andes and can generate thunderstorms on 140 to 160 nights a year. By contrast lightning is extremely rare in polar regions.

But while the bulk of lightning occurs over land, particularly storm-prone areas of the ocean can achieve far higher densities of flashes: in one 1998 storm in the Indian Ocean lightning flashed eight times a second, so often that to the human eye it would seem the sky was permanently illuminated. And, in a testament to the power of human activity to shape the weather, storms over the ocean are also enhanced over shipping lanes. Aerosol particles emitted in the exhaust of ships appear to be changing the process of cloud formation.

As the climate crisis heats the atmosphere it seems reasonable to assume that thunderstorm activity will increase. A warmer atmosphere holds more water vapour and the additional heat provides more energy to drive deep convection within thunderclouds. Yet the reality is more complicated than this suggests.

A recent review of lightning studies now under peer review finds that projections ranged from an 11% decrease to a 44% increase in lightning per degree of global warming, with a mean increase across all projections of 7.5% per degree. Despite considerable uncertainty about how tropical regions will be affected, it also finds broad agreement lightning will increase in high latitudes.

Andrew Dowdy is associate professor in climate science in the School of Geography, Earth and Atmospheric Sciences at the University of Melbourne, and one of Australia’s leading experts on lightning. He says that while “it’s clear that in a warmer world, some of the conditions that are conducive to thunderstorms and lightning can be enhanced”, there are still “large uncertainties” when it comes to understanding how lightning will be affected by climate change.

Some of these uncertainties relate to the difficulty of modelling the fine-scale processes that cause lightning, others to the relative paucity of high-quality, long-term data relating to lightning; until the launch of satellites capable of measuring lightning from space in the 1990s it was necessary to rely on ground-based observations and regional radar. Nonetheless, by combining records relating to cyclones and fronts with thunderstorm data, Dowdy and his colleagues have been able to track the frequency of such events as far back as 1979. This has revealed an increase in such events along the eastern coasts of continents alongside a poleward shift in cyclone activity in the southern hemisphere.

Separate research by Dowdy has found that while thunderstorm activity has increased in eastern and south-easternAustralia, other areas, especially in the tropical north, have experienced a decline.

But lightning can strike without a storm.

Just last week, a report released by the Emergency Leaders for Climate Change in Australia warned that the number of fires started by dry lightning – lightning that strikes the ground without accompanying rain – was increasing. The advocacy group noted that forests in Australia’s south-east recorded 50% more dry lightning strikes in 2000–2016 than in the previous two decades, helping create a “step change in fire conditions”.

“Lightning is the natural ignition source of fires,” says Dowdy, who also notes that “lightning fires tend to burn larger areas on average compared to fires that are ignited by humans. And that’s because lightning can occur in remote places that are hard for response crews to get to, but they can also occur in large clusters.”

The connection between any increase in dry lightning and fire is not straightforward, however. In Tasmania the number of fires sparked by dry lightning events has increased significantly since the 1990s. The fires that devastated Tasmania’s remote north-west in 2025 were sparked by a massive lightning storm that saw more than 1,200 lightning strikes reach the ground in less than 24 hours. Yet while it was lightning that started the fires, the landscape was already primed to burn by a combination of unusually dry conditions, strong winds and high temperatures, a convergence of factors that is rapidly intensifying as the planet heats up.

“It’s clear that in a warmer world you get more dangerous conditions for fire weather in many places,” Dowdy says.

Similar mechanisms are at work elsewhere in the world, perhaps most visibly in the United States, where dry lightning is combining with increasingly dangerous fire conditions to create megablazes such as the August Complex blaze, which burned more than 4,000 square kilometres in northern California in 2020.

More intense fires are driving an increase in another form of lightning, however.

When fires grow ferocious enough they can begin to create their own weather, as the heat and moisture they release can combine into giant thunderheads known as pyrocumulonimbus (pyroCb). Turbocharged by the intense heat of the fires, these terrifying formations reach far higher than ordinary storm clouds, often boiling up into the stratosphere, creating a massive vortex which sucks the moisture released by the fire up into the upper reaches of the atmosphere at speeds that can exceed 200 km/h. There, in the swirling darkness of these monstrous structures, this moisture freezes, collides and creates lightning.

Until recently, pyroCb storms were relatively unusual, but in the past decade they have become increasingly frequent, not just in Australia but in the United States, Canada and Russia, and most recently Europe, where one was reported during the fires that devastated France in July and August of this year.

Jason Evans is a professor at the Climate Change Research Centre at the University of New South Wales. He says there has been a “massive increase” in the number of pyroCB events in Australia. In the black summer fires of 2019-2020, he notes, there were almost as many recorded as in the 40 years prior combined.

PyroCb are not just a symptom of our planet’s increasingly deranged fire cycle, they also create feedback loops, spreading and intensifying the fire, as lightning strikes and embers borne by the strong winds they generate start new fires. This process can extend across very wide areas: during Australia’s black Saturday fires in 2009 pyrogenic lightning from a 15-kilometre high pyroCb ignited new fires 100 kms ahead of the fire front.

Evans says that once a pyroCb “kicks off”, it’s “not containable. We can’t control it really at all. All we can do is get out of the way. They’re even too dangerous for the firefighting aircraft to try and get close enough to get their water on to.”

The spectacle of pyroCbs is just one more example of the way human activity is transforming the planet. Whereas we once were at the mercy of the lightning, now we are helping create it. What this will mean for us and our world remains unclear. For as the stories of the Bininj and others remind us, lightning has always embodied an uneasy duality. Simultaneously beautiful and terrible, feared as well as exalted, it can be both life giver and destroyer.

Standing in the way of slop bowls: the woman blocking food delivery robots

The Guardian Sat, 07 Nov 2026 14:00:12 GMT

Semi-retired professor Carolyn Marvin became a local celebrity facing down Philadelphia’s growing robot delivery army: ‘It’s my first amendment right to protest’

“One of you needs to be on the lookout for cops, while I block the robot, OK?”

It is a crisp fall morning in Philadelphia. Tucked away in a dingy alley, opposite a garage called Patriot Parking, 78-year-old Carolyn Marvin is laying out some ground rules for a robot-disrupting expedition. Once a suitable target is identified, we will follow it to a busy sidewalk and Marvin will stand in front of the robot, blocking its way. The photographer and I will take turns ensuring we’re not all carted off by the police.

If Marvin sounds like she’s done this before, it’s because she has. Many, many times. The semi-retired University of Pennsylvania (UPenn) communications professor has become something of a local celebrity after taking it upon herself to block the UberEats food delivery robots which have become a ubiquitous presence in the city’s downtown. She doesn’t do this every day – “I have a life” – but whenever a robot crosses her path she’ll stare it down as a protest against their incursion into public spaces.

Her antics have gone viral: so much so that some Philadelphians dressed up as Marvin and the robot for Halloween. But while she may have supporters, her protesting isn’t universally admired: a few weeks ago it got her in trouble with the law.

“I was coming back from my flu shot and I saw a robot,” she recounts. “Since I had some time, I stayed in front of it as it was a very highly trafficked area.” A crowd amassed and a spirited debate occurred. Some people agreed with Marvin’s argument that, along with taking people’s jobs, the delivery robots pose a hazard to people with mobility issues. Others were concerned that she was stopping someone from getting the food they’d ordered and paid for. Eventually the cops were called about “criminal mischief” involving a delivery robot and three officers showed up.

“They asked me to move and I said ‘no, it’s my first amendment to protest against corporations in the same public space the robots are occupying.’ So I don’t see any reason to stop that.” The police officers, presumably a bit befuddled by the small but serious professor, who was dressed in her trademark blue visor, continued to try to get her to move along. Marvin just kept staring at the robot.

“So then they came up from behind me, took the food I was holding out of my hands, handcuffed me and hustled me over to a police car,” says Marvin. “I tried to make it hard for them but there were three of them and one of me. But I kept arguing with them. I think they weren’t sure what they could arrest me for because it’s all brand new stuff. And they hesitated a long time because I think the first amendment argument probably made some sense to them.”

The police ended up writing Marvin a ticket for disorderly conduct, with the rationale that she was blocking a business. She is still waiting for her court hearing date, but intends to contest the charges vigorously. “The wheels of justice grind slow, but I’ll go make my arguments,” she says. And one imagines these arguments will be convincing. Marvin has written a celebrated book, When Old Technologies Were New: Thinking About Electric Communication in the Late Nineteenth Century, about the social impact of electronic media. She is a formidable thinker who, in 1985, became the first woman to receive tenure at UPenn’s Annenberg School and now has an endowed chair named after at the Ivy League university.

*

A pending court date has not slowed Marvin down. Which is why she agreed to allow me to shadow her today, while she goes about her robot-disrupting business. I’ve picked our rendezvous spot because I’ve noticed that a number of the delivery machines congregate here while waiting for orders. We can trail them the moment they set off on their mission.

It’s unclear exactly how many food delivery robots there are in Philadelphia. Avride, the Texas-based company behind the machines, would only tell me that the number fluctuates according to demand. But there are only two in the alley when we arrive around brunch time. One of them is flashing Halloween graphics on the screen that operates as its “face” and another has little zzz on it, indicating that it’s sleeping. I’ve got to admit, they look cute. And, of course, that’s by design. “Humanizing the robots is important, because they are a completely new entity,” a spokesperson for Avride told me when I called them for an interview a couple of days earlier. “We want people to feel comfortable around the robots and not to feel scared about some weird box travelling down the sidewalk.”

The humanization didn’t fool Marvin, but it seems to have worked on other people. Avride, which operates almost 1,000 food delivery machines on more than 25 different college campuses and a growing number of urban locations including Jersey City and Austin, says it used to get concerned emails from people who’d see a robot in hibernation mode and assume it was lost or broken. Avride then added the zzz visuals to communicate the robot was waiting for an order, and now the emails have stopped. I ask the Avride spokespeople if they have they heard about Carolyn Marvin? There is a little pause. “We are all well aware of this lady, yes.”

As we wait for the robots to get moving, I start to wonder if the professor’s notoriety might have prompted Avride to install Marvin-mode software which disables the machines if they detect her presence. We’ve been hanging around for about 40 minutes and nothing is happening. Eventually, I hear a beeping noise and one of the robots whirs into an action. Someone had put an order in and robot 1617 was going from its holding pen to a nearby restaurant to pick up the food and deliver it.

While it may be equipped with all sorts of sophisticated cameras, sensors, and AI-powered software, the poor robot didn’t have the instincts to realize its mission was about to be thwarted. We chase it down the alley and, as soon as 1617 turns on to Walnut Street, a main thoroughfare, Marvin blocks its pathway and stares it down.

For the first few minutes people politely ignore the professor-robot standoff, although I do notice one woman rolling her eyes as she passes. But then the compliments and questions start rolling in. One elderly woman thanks Marvin profusely. A middle-aged man dressed in a nice suit cheers her on and says “someone’s got to do it!” Another man says he appreciates the efforts and “the gig economy sucks for everyone.”

“OMG,” a young passerby called Cadence says as she recognizes Marvin and her trademark blue visor. “It’s the queen! I feel like I met a celebrity!” Cadence, a 22-year-old recent graduate, is on board with the professor’s protest. “AI and robotics are supposed to make life easier for us and help us do the things we enjoy, not take the jobs of other people,” she effuses. “I will support any small business that doesn’t use AI. I appreciate what is made by humans.”

Passing kids, meanwhile, seem less concerned about the gig economy, and more interested in the robots’ cute faces. Every toddler who goes by points at them with delight. A couple of kids who pass have a heated discussion about whether the robot looks like a dog or a cat. (It looks like neither.) The only child we come across who isn’t enthralled looks around seven years old and yells “clanker!” at it. “I’ve watched enough movies to know that these things are going to hunt us down!” he says.

The people cheering Marvin on aren’t outliers: these protests have struck a chord with people because of a growing distrust around AI and automation. According to a recent study by Pew Research, a majority of Americans are deeply skeptical of AI; more adults are expecting it to have a negative impact than a positive one. And while I’m not sure if other people are blocking food delivery robots, we’re certainly seeing a rise in protests against datacenters and other symbols of automation. A few weeks ago in Philadelphia I passed a woman standing in front of a Waymo self-driving taxi (which is being tested in the city with human safety drivers) blocking its path and yelling “LAME-O”.

Despite this antipathy, robots are gradually being normalized. Pennsylvania legalized delivery robots via Act 106 of 2020, defining them as “pedestrians” and they’re slowly becoming part of the landscape. When Avride’s robots first appeared in Philadelphia back in March people would gawk at them and take selfies. Now most people just ignore them. And this same phenomenon is happening all across the world. While it isn’t clear exactly how many food delivery robots are in operation there are a number of companies besides Avride which operate these machines in the US, including Serve Robotics, which is one of the biggest players, with a fleet of 2,000 deployed robots.

While the automation industry has big plans to grow their fleets of robots, Marvin stages these protests because she wants to remind people that they have a say in all of this. They have a right to weigh in on whether private robots should be allowed on public streets.

“I’m very supportive of the kinds of things that AI is doing in terms of medical breakthroughs,” Marvin says. “And I think robots are fine on factory floors, but they don’t belong in public space. I take the position that this isn’t inevitable. But you have to have the will to do something. In Toronto they banned delivery robots from sidewalks in 2021. And I think, you know, the question is: who is public infrastructure designed to serve?”

The robot in front of Marvin isn’t (yet) smart enough to answer to this question. But it does seem to have clocked that it’s not going to be able to get to the restaurant to pick up its food today. After repeatedly trying to get around the professor it seems to have gone into hibernation mode. Eventually Marvin, who has to go to campus and prepare for a class, steps aside. The robot powers back up and trundles home to its garage. I know it’s only a computer with wheels, but I could swear it looked dejected. Marvin, on the other hand, looks triumphant.

Will Pete Hegseth be the blue tsunami’s next victim?

The Guardian Sat, 07 Nov 2026 13:00:12 GMT

The ‘secretary of war’ and his shameful history are facing bipartisan scrutiny

Can you smell the schadenfreude in the air?

Watching some of the worst people in the world get their comeuppance this week has been deeply satisfying. And the show isn’t over yet. While the midterms have wrapped up, the blame game is only just getting started, with Republicans desperate to find scapegoats for their shellacking.

He may be a big, strong, testosterone-obsessed warrior, but I suspect Pete Hegseth is panicking right now. When it comes to scapegoats, the defence secretary (or “war secretary” as he prefers to identify as) is an obvious choice. The disastrous US-Israeli war on Iran played a key role in the midterm upset, as even JD Vance has admitted, and Hegseth was one of its main architects.

The Democrats have already declared war on the former Fox News personality. “In the majority, one of the first things we’re going to do is run Pete Hegseth out of town,” Hakeem Jeffries announced at a campaign rally before the midterms.

It’s not just the Democrats; many of Hegseth’s peers are eager to give him the boot.

The outgoing Republican senator Thom Tillis told CBS News on Tuesday night that Hegseth has a “reckoning” coming. Meanwhile, the (also outgoing) Republican congressman Thomas Massie told Bloomberg News he will “definitely” reintroduce articles of impeachment against Hegseth next week. (Massie has already tried to impeach Hegseth for starting the war in Iran without congressional approval.)

In a Wednesday post on Twitter/X, Massie wrote: “There is one contingency in which I won’t reintroduce the articles of impeachment: Hegseth resigns.”

There is little chance that Hegseth will unilaterally decide to make a dignified exit. On Thursday, the defense secretary posted a longwinded video in which, after rambling about DEI and trans people, he asserted that he wasn’t going anywhere.

“A disgruntled, defeated congressman [aka Massie], along with all his Democrat allies, has also dropped sham articles of impeachment against yours truly, just like they tried against President Trump twice,” Hegseth said. “Didn’t work against President Trump, and it won’t work with me. You can rest assured of that.”

This little performance did not quieten his critics.

“@PeteHegseth, cabinet secretaries shouldn’t be wasting taxpayer dollars on campaign style videos,” Tillis wrote on social media in response. “This is about you: the incompetence you’ve displayed, the bad advice you’ve given to president, and your shameful and embarrassing episodes from firing our top generals to texting war plans to reporters.”

There have been rather a lot of shameful and embarrassing episodes in Hegseth’s career, haven’t there?

There are all the allegations about his previous drunk and disorderly conduct, for example. And the settlement he paid to a woman who accused him of raping her in 2017. And the time his own mother called him an “abuser of women”. (He’s denied any wrongdoing.) And the New Yorker’s report that, in 2015, Hegseth was accused of drunkenly chanting “Kill All Muslims! Kill All Muslims!” (Hegseth’s lawyer told the New Yorker that they weren’t going to comment on these “outlandish claims”.) And the time he accidentally sent top secret war plans in a Signal group chat that included a reporter from the Atlantic. And then, of course, there are all the alleged war crimes he’s responsible for.

Hegseth loves to rail against “DEI hires”, but imagine for a moment if a woman was texting classified information to the wrong people and battling scandal after scandal. There’s no way she’d still be heading up the Pentagon. As has been widely observed, Trump seems to like getting rid of his high-level female officials when they embarrass him, while holding on to his mediocre men.

Indeed, while the secretary of war may be on the defensive now, there’s always the depressing possibility that his sex – and his sycophancy towards the president – may end up saving him. Particularly as Trump is publicly standing by his man for the moment.

When asked on Wednesday if he was considering replacing Hegseth, Trump told reporters: “No, I think ⁠he’s doing a very good job.” Behind the scenes, of course, it could be a different story. NBC News reported on Wednesday that Trump has told some of his allies that he’s considering replacing the defense secretary.

But even if Hegseth is able to cling on to the sinking ship until it finally goes down, I take solace in the fact that he must be feeling very uncomfortable right now. And I am clinging on to hope that he will have a very public downfall.

This is, let’s not forget, a man who wanted to livestream an execution via firing squad. While that thankfully never happened, perhaps we’ll all get to watch a live stream of Hegseth getting fired.

Nancy Lacore was in the navy for 35 years before the three-star admiral was ousted by Hegseth without cause amid a broader purge. In response, she mounted a bid for Congress that made Hegseth’s incompetence a key talking point. At the time of writing, the race hasn’t been officially called, but it looks like she’s managed to flip a traditionally Republican seat. Wouldn’t it be poetic if she plays a part in firing Pete?

“Eighteen- to 29-year-old young white men with no college degrees swung 40 points to the Democrats, and I don’t think it’s all because they’re socialists,” the podcaster Tim Pool told Fox News. “I think it’s because many of them want to burn the Republican party down.” Go ahead, guys!

Part of Brand’s defence was the claim: “Not one of [the victims] resisted or screamed or even tried to leave.” Speaking after the trial, the victims’ commissioner for England and Wales, Claire Waxman, emphasized how dangerous these sorts of misconceptions about sexual assault are. “The idea that rape victims must scream, physically resist or immediately report an offence is a well-established rape myth, rooted in outdated and harmful assumptions about how victims are expected to behave,” she said. “Justice must be grounded in evidence, not misconceptions.”

Just when you think the US is getting a smidgen more sane, you see something like this.

Israeli militants killed five teenage students at al-Mughayyir school in the West Bank last academic year, one at the school gates. In response to parents being afraid to send their kids back to the classroom, the school has had to build bigger fences. Meanwhile, “settlers” continue their violent pogroms on the village, and far too many US politicians continue to excuse and enable this violence.

A Guardian investigation has found that groups such as Crunchy Moms (which has more than 490,000 members) are hives of anti-vaccine content and medical misinformation. Most alarmingly: Meta “appears to have helped spread such ideas by promoting Crunchy Moms into users’ feeds, even when they do not seek it out”.

While the midterms were on everyone’s mind this week, an alligator in North Carolina was just thinking about brunch. Surveillance cameras caught the creature strolling into the back of a bagel shop, startling the customers. The police were called and the gator was removed. The gator insists he did nothing wrong and is the victim of a schmear campaign.

Arwa Mahadwi is a Guardian columnist

Great British Railways: new dawn for a new network but with plenty of old problems to fix

The Guardian Sat, 07 Nov 2026 13:00:11 GMT

Experts predict a baptism of fire for GBR in 2027, with likely issues ranging from clapped-out trains and track to extreme weather-related stress

The glad tidings brought by the minister were that the wait was almost over: the establishment of Great British Railways could be wrapped up by Christmas, at least in law. But with a renationalised industry facing fresh storms in 2027, some in the railway world are wondering if they should be careful what they wish for.

The legislation that will rip up how rail has been run, anticipated for the best part of a decade, is being chewed over in its final stages in the House of Lords. It now has, the rail minister, Peter Hendy, told an industry conference in London this week, “a fair chance of getting royal assent” before parliament’s winter break, allowing a new arm’s-length body with overall control of Britain’s railway, spanning the track and train services.

Great Western Railway will come into the government stable in December, with the remaining private train operations, East Midland Railway, Avanti and CrossCountry, due to be nationalised next year.

There will be plenty to fix, as politicians and rail bosses acknowledged. Lord Hendy opened the Railway Industry Association’s conference by describing every train in the north of England as “clapped out”; Jeremy Westlake, the chief executive of infrastructure manager Network Rail, concluded the event by bringing up the two derailments in 24 hours at the peak of a summer of delays.

Some of the solutions may appear easier within an integrated, nationalised industry. The site of the future Great British Railways (GBR) HQ in Derby has now been picked, even if it remains unclear how many of rail’s leaders fancy decamping there, and exactly where the power will lie.

It won’t be, said Hendy, an all-powerful “Kremlin in Derby”, with control instead largely given to regional managing directors, something so far instigated at South Western and Southeastern. For Hendy, the rewards of the new structure will be a single point of accountability, and the end of a “culture of blame” under privatisation where contracts pitted operators against Network Rail, especially in times of disruption or delay.

Personifying for now the GBR ideal of track and train in harmony are Westlake and Alex Hynes, the chief executive of DFTO, the state operator managing the renationalised train services, who discussed their bromance in another joint appearance on stage at the London conference. Hynes said he had told train staff to “go find your new best friend on the trackside … We try to role-model it.”

It remains to be seen if either will be for the chop next year, when the newly appointed chair of GBR, John Kingman, picks one overall integrated boss. The flip side of the road to reform and integration for some, especially non-frontline managerial staff, has been prolonged uncertainty, as roles merge or disappear.

But GBR should mean being able to move resources more easily around the railway, be it people or trains. Hendy cited Great Western’s problems with former Transport for Wales trains, which had deteriorated after being replaced in service: “There’s nothing more stupid than watching some trains halfway through their lives that have been parked in a field … miserably failing on a daily basis because the industry wasn’t coherent enough. You can’t believe how stupid that is.”

Likewise, he said, most train companies “have been desperately short of drivers … That’s crackers. We can fix that – and I think it’s really important to fix those basic things. They will take time.”

Some, though, wonder where the GBR legislation will land rail under future governments. One of the missions was to end the micromanagement of rail by central government: when the 73-year-old Hendy, a railwayman and politician, eventually steps away, the separation – or lack of it – may become clearer.

Hendy said GBR would at last give the railway a long-term strategy; opponents argue it does not bind it clearly enough. Others are worried that the Treasury could step in more than ever, threatening rail’s limited financial independence. Darren Caplan, the chief executive of the Railway Industry Association, said his organisation remained “very concerned that a future secretary of state could reopen five-year funding settlements, making funding even less certain”.

Richard Holden, the Conservative shadow transport secretary, warned that rail could “lose out to the competing demands of that day [and] have to get in the queue. Will a new train win out over a new hospital? I doubt it.”

Olly Glover, the transport spokesperson for the Lib Dems, who are more positive about the bill but also voted against it in its current form, said: “They’ve raised a lot of expectation as a result of so-called nationalisation. But the truth of it is the benefits will take time and are only going to materialise if the Treasury is willing to sanction more spending.”

Money has been tight, even though the railway hopes fare revenues are finally on track to match pre-pandemic income in the coming years. For now, the state of the railway has reflected spending on renewing it: cut from nearly £5bn a year to less than £4bn in the last five years, according to the regulator, the Office of Rail and Road. It was, said the ORR’s interim CEO, Feras Alshaker, “expected that its reliability would decline in the period”.

As record levels of compensation for delayed journeys this summer show, it certainly has. That level was compounded by the extreme temperatures and changing climate; but as several speakers at this week’s conference pointed out, the outlook is for much worse as GBR takes shape, with a “super El Niño” event likely to test the infrastructure as never before.

In defense of feral children

The Guardian Sat, 07 Nov 2026 13:00:11 GMT

Adults complain and say kids should occupy more space in the world. Then when they do, the world tells them to quiet down

On the Maine island where I live, childhood ends when you’re old enough to catch the 7.15am ferry to school.

We live year-round on Peaks Island, a small island accessible only by boat about 3 miles off the coast of Portland. There is an elementary school here, but no middle or high school. So, once island children reach sixth grade, they begin commuting to the mainland by ferry. In many ways, it is a rite of passage.

When my son Theo started middle school, I was thrilled for him – and a little heartbroken. Suddenly, he was across the bay all day, reachable only by boat or cellphone (which he didn’t have). Theo has always belonged to our island as much as he has belonged to me. After years of rinsing sand from his socks and pulling twigs from his hair, sending him away each morning felt a little like prying him loose from his natural habitat.

Now his school days stretch from the 7.15am ferry until the boat deposits him back on the island at 7.35pm, after sports practice. That means less time roaming the woods and shoreline, and more time indoors being shaped into someone civilized. I have always subscribed to Henry David Thoreau’s idea that “all good things are wild and free”, and lately I find myself wanting my children to stay that way a lot of bit longer.

Fortunately, my son’s daily commute across Casco Bay suggests he has not yet been entirely domesticated.

The ferry is essentially our island’s school bus, except that tourists, commuters, construction workers, dogs, bicycles and people hauling groceries share the ride. Each morning, my son and his gaggle of friends pile into a corner of the cabin with their backpacks and cereal-bar wrappers, trading jokes and half-awake grievances at a volume best described as gull-adjacent. One of the boys is deaf in one ear, so the others naturally speak louder to make sure he doesn’t miss the plot.

It is a bright, goofy and very noisy pocket of preteen life. At least, that is how I see it.

But for a while, another regular passenger saw things differently. The boys didn’t know her name, so inevitably they nicknamed her “Ferry Karen”. My son began coming home with reports of their latest encounters with her. She sat rigidly in her seat, neck craned forward like a heron preparing to strike, and shushed them with clockwork regularity. Too loud! Too boisterous! Too much!

The ferry engine groaned. Gulls shrieked overhead. Waves slapped the hull. And somehow it was the children who were making too much noise.

The boys, good-hearted as they are, tried to lower their voices. Before long, they boarded each morning already bracing themselves, their joy bridled by the expectation that someone would tell them to quiet down before they had even warmed their hands.

When I heard about this, something defiant sparked in me. Maybe it was the mother in me. Or maybe it was the recognition that the world these children are inheriting is already asking an awful lot of them. School shootings, artificial intelligence, political turmoil, economic anxiety, academic pressure … we have handed children a frightening world, and then somehow still have the nerve to ask them to be quieter in it.

These kids already spend most of their weekdays indoors, where bells regulate their movements and adults regulate their voices. The ferry ride is one of the few unsupervised stretches left in their day: 20 minutes on the ocean suspended between island and mainland when they can be loud, loose, ridiculous and wholly themselves. Meanwhile, the adults complaining about kids these days are frequently staring into their phones as though doom-scrolling were a civic duty.

If anyone commuting is modeling questionable behavior, perhaps it isn’t the children being exuberantly alive. Perhaps it’s the grownups hunched over their screens like Dickensian clerks auditing the apocalypse.

To be clear, I am not arguing for children swinging from the ferry rafters or terrorizing commuters before coffee. Kids should learn that public spaces belong to other people, too. But that lesson works both ways. Lately I’ve been wondering whether the problem isn’t simply that parents have forgotten how to let children go. Maybe the rest of us have forgotten how to let children arrive.

Parents worry about their kids’ safety, anxiety, loneliness, resilience, their dependence on phones, their inability to tolerate boredom. We lament that children don’t roam neighborhoods or knock on doors or disappear on bicycles until dinner, the way children supposedly once did. So we tell them: get off your phones! Go outside! Be independent! Figure things out! Take risks!

And then, when they actually appear in the world without us, the rest of the world tells them to quiet down.

Children used to occupy much more of public life: sidewalks and buses, corner stores and vacant lots, parks and stoops and malls. Increasingly, childhood happens in places specifically designated for children – schools, camps, organized sports, scheduled playdates, bedrooms – or on screens. Their lives are supervised, programmed and transported from one adult-approved location to another.

That isn’t entirely the fault of anxious parents. Parents are responding to the world around them. Giving a child independence requires a surrounding culture willing to receive that child. But we seem to want independent children who somehow don’t inconvenience anybody with their independence. We want children in the world, provided they don’t take up too much of it. That may be the contradiction we need to examine.

Years ago, my neighbor May told me something I have carried with me ever since. “When a child is born on Peaks Island,” she said, “it is all our child.” (She was only about 15 herself at the time when she said this.) What she meant was that children here are raised not only by their parents but, in small ways, by everybody. Like the neighbors who let them cut through their yards. The deckhands who hold the ferry as they kids are racing to catch the morning boat. The checkout clerk at our little grocery store who know which candy they’ll choose before they even reach the counter (and remind them to brush their teeth). There is very little anonymity on an island of 1 sq mile.

Paradoxically, this watchful web of familiarity gives children tremendous freedom. Because everyone knows them, everyone is quietly looking out for them. Kids can roam freely, and roam freely they do. Island kids climb rocks and trees, they jump from docks and poke around tide pools without helicopter supervision. “Good thing we live on an island,” we parents say to one another when they wander home with wet sneakers and pockets full of mussel shells, they tear around on bicycles and disappear into the woods only to return when they’re hungry or when the sun has set.

They are gloriously feral. But they are also startlingly capable. By middle school, many of them know how to talk to adults without shrinking, how to read a ferry schedule, how to navigate a city bus, how to get themselves from point A to point B without an adult narrating every step like a GPS with anxiety.

When May told me that every island child was “all our child”, she was giving the adults around her a job, even if these kids weren’t biologically or legally “theirs”. Perhaps that job isn’t always to correct them; sometimes the job is simply to make enough room and to protect the spark that makes children tear down the road on bicycles at speeds that terrify their neighbors. To let them get muddy. To let them argue and reconcile without immediately refereeing. To allow them to grow in every direction, not just the polite ones.

And maybe this isn’t only an island proposition. Maybe wherever children live – in apartment buildings or suburbs, on city blocks or dirt roads – the adults around them can choose to create a little more territory in which childhood is allowed to remain untamed.

So the next time you encounter a cluster of children laughing too loudly on a bus, a sidewalk or a subway platform, consider it less a nuisance than a small daily miracle, the sound of children alive and unedited, the future refusing to sit still, lips sealed.

Look up from our phones, look out the window, and remember what it felt like to be on the verge of everything.

‘Mind-blowing’: dark-sky fans gather on Exmoor to see what light pollution hides

The Guardian Sat, 07 Nov 2026 13:00:11 GMT

The UK is 14th most light-polluted country, but in south-west England the veil is lifted at the dark skies festival

“It’s just mind-blowing,” says the astronomer and teacher Jo Richardson. She is standing in Exmoor national park talking about Saturn, the first planet she ever saw through a telescope.

But it is not the cosmic colour of the planet that Richardson is drawn to, nor its mysteries – it is the vastness. “Saturn, on average, is 800m miles away,” she says, the equivalent to travelling the circumference of the Earth 32,000 times. “You can see it through a telescope here. That’s just nuts.”

Richardson is on Exmoor to spread the word. She is here for the 10th dark skies festival, celebrating the park as Europe’s first designated international dark skies reserve. Throughout October, people travelled from across England’s south-west to see the wonder of the night sky and learn about space, guided by astronomers and ecologists from the national park.

Bringing people to the darkness of Exmoor encourages them to consider the light pollution that prevents them seeing the cosmic show at home, Richardson says. “It’s not about shutting all the lights off all the time, it’s about just using them wisely,” she says, the faint glow of Tiverton, the nearest town, emerging on the horizon as the sun sets. “It’s all about education, making people think about their environment and how to protect it.”

Throughout the evening, families are taught about the cosmos via fireside question and answers, peeks through the telescope and bioluminescence walks through the woods. “Sometimes it just generates that spark,” says Richardson’s husband, Peter, also an astronomer. Together, the pair run Space Detectives, which delivers space science workshops, presentations and courses for adults and children. “We’ve had youngsters go through our clubs that are now working as professional astronomers,” he adds.

Research has shown that the night sky becomes 10% brighter every year because of growing light pollution. According to the Light Pollution Map, the UK is the 14th most light-polluted country in Europe, with microstates such as Vatican City and Monaco making up the top five.

Light pollution is measured by the Bortle scale, the nine-level numeric chart that measures brightness. A nine is lit up like central London, while a one is the remotest locations on Earth such as the Atacama desert in Chile. The darkest zone of Exmoor is a two. “[A] one sky is proper jaw-dropping,” says Peter Richardson. “You can see the Milky Way and you can see dust lanes and everything with your naked eye. It’s quite incredible.”

The darkness is also important for the local wildlife, says Kate Lacey, an ecologist at Exmoor National Park Authority. Her work focuses on protecting the park’s nocturnal environment, including the rare bechstein’s and barbastelle bats that live on Exmoor. They rely on darkness for hunting, navigation and migration.

Protecting salmon populations is also on her to-do list. “Salmon migrate upstream and Exmoor is quite an important spawning ground for salmon,” Lacey says. “They get disrupted by artificial light. It confuses them, and then they’re less likely to survive.”

As the night goes on, clouds blanket Exmoor’s sky, obscuring the stars and bringing the event to a close. But the organisers hope the experience will stay with visitors long after they leave. They want people to continue to look up at the sky and think about how light pollution threatens what they can see.

“The night sky is a sense of wonder for people that not everyone gets to experience,” says Lacey. “It’s inspired science, it’s inspired art, it’s inspired religion. It’s just so important.”

‘A footballing alien’: Mamadou Sangaré soars to Premier League heights

The Guardian Sat, 07 Nov 2026 12:00:13 GMT

Brentford’s Mali midfielder stood out when he was six and has shone in the Premier League since £39m transfer

“When I first saw him, I thought to myself: ‘Who on earth is this player?’ laughs Youness Bengelloun as he remembers Mamadou Sangaré. With the transfer window in full swing in July 2025, the former Manchester City scout and agent was not expecting to come face to face with a “footballing alien”, but that proved the case during a visit to Rapid Vienna’s training ground. A few weeks later, Sangaré moved to Lens for around €5m. “He was impressive and what struck me was his technique and his work rate,” Bengelloun says.

That’s more or less the impression Sangaré has made at every club he’s played for, including Brentford, for whom the Mali midfielder signed, from Lens, for a club-record £39m at the start of August. The 24-year-old excelled in his debut against Tottenham a few weeks later, dominating the centre of the pitch and providing the assist for Keane Lewis-Potter’s opening goal, and has featured in every game this season, with Brighton up next. “I gave him his debut for Mali in September 2024, against Mozambique. He made an immediate impact,” says Sangaré’s former international manager Tom Saintfiet. “He’s every manager’s dream player.”

Sangaré’s rise began at Association Sportive Aboubacar Coulibaly (ASAC). A small club based in the Faladié neighbourhood of Bamako, Mali’s capital, became a home from home at the age of six. Even then, his strength of character, work ethic and desire to succeed were clear, and immediately impressed his coach at the time, Bakary Coulibaly. “He lived not far from the ASAC pitch, so he’d come and play every day,” Coulibaly says. “Right from the start I could see that Mamadou had great potential. He played as a right midfielder and was already technically better than the others.

“What surprised me most about Mamadou was that he always wanted to win. Even then he was very demanding of himself and his teammates and acted like a leader. When the team was struggling he was always looking for a solution to help us win.”

Setting high standards and taking personal responsibility are sides of Sangaré that Saintfiet recognises. “He manages everything in his professional life,” says the 53-year-old Belgian. “He controls his time for eating, sleeping, training … some people go to nightclubs to clear their heads, but he lives like a professional 24 hours a day.

“I remember one day, Yves Bissouma asked Mamadou what his favourite position on the pitch was. Mamadou answered that he wanted his own. I’ll never forget that moment because it shows he had enormous confidence in his own abilities. But he’s not arrogant; he’s very shy. Very laid-back.”

Saintfiet, who managed Mali from 2024 to 2026, adds: “When I think of Mamadou, I think first and foremost of his personality. He’s never nervous, he always stays calm. He’s always in control of the situation. When he receives the ball surrounded by three players, he’ll keep his cool and he’ll manage to find the pass to get out of it”.

Sangaré progressed from ASAC to Yeelen Olympique before leaving Mali for Europe in September 2020, joining RB Salzburg after catching the eye of scouts from the Austrian club via video footage. There came various loan spells before a permanent move to Rapid Vienna in July 2024, and then on to Lens the following August, with Sangaré’s one and only season at the French club a memorable one. Not only did he play a key role in Lens winning the Coupe de France but, in the process, he also picked up the Marc-Vivien Foé award, which recognises the best African player in Ligue 1.

Last season Sangaré took part in his first Africa Cup of Nations, where he helped Mali reach the quarter-finals. “The match during which he was the most impressive was against the Comoros [in the group stages],” says his fellow Mali midfielder, Lassana Coulibaly. “The first time we had seen him in training we all noticed he had that extra something. But in that match he was absolutely incredible”.

Saintfiet was impressed with Sangaré’s performance against the hosts Morocco, also in the group stage, and especially by his attitude beforehand. “I asked him to play on the right flank so we could field five midfielders. When you ask certain players to play in different positions, they often tell you it’s not their natural role and that they don’t feel comfortable. But when I spoke to Mamadou about it he immediately said: ‘OK coach, I’ll play wherever you want for the good of the team. I’ll do my best. He is a loyal player who has always done everything he could to help me.”

Brentford are the latest recipients of Sangaré’s capabilities, on and off the pitch, and Saintfiet is sure they won’t be the last. “I reckon he can play at an even higher level,” he says. “He won’t stop at Brentford.”

Gotta buy ’em all: how Pokémon card collecting became race against scalpers

The Guardian Sat, 07 Nov 2026 12:00:11 GMT

Fans trying to access latest releases are being priced out in a cut-throat market driven by crypto-like hype

The runaway demand for Pokemon cards is because they are being hyped “like crypto”, according to one young fan who had spent the night queueing outside a London store to make sure he did not miss out on the latest card release.

Before its 10am opening on Friday, the line outside the pop culture store Forbidden Planet in central London snaked past five others and, despite its strict sales policy, was probably “50/50” fans and resellers, said Kai, who had been there since 3am.

The 25-year-old has loved Pokémon since he was a child but the immense rise in reselling and scalping in recent years means fans like him are being priced out. “The cards used to be cheap but they have ballooned in price,” he says.

Kai blames the fact that “people in the crypto space have got into Pokémon” for fuelling the now rabid interest in buying cards for profit, and even gambling, with fans targeted by livestreams to bid on cards.

The signs on the door of Forbidden Planet spell out the rules. Like other stores, it limits high-demand products – in this case the £49.99 Delta Reign “elite trainer” box – to one a customer. (The set will be selling with big markups on eBay by the end of the day.)

It also has what it calls a “supplier-requested unsealing policy”. This approach deters some resellers because an opened product cannot be sold on as brand new.

“It’s calmer here,” said Kai of the queue of more than 120 people. “The people and workers are nice here.”

Like others in the queue he has (Pokémon) war stories of fights and overwhelmed security staff.

The clamour for cards has the most determined buyers zooming from store to store by e-bike. Others reportedly get around purchase limits by changing clothes or paying cash for other people’s hauls.

The traders were identifiable by their multiple shopping bags, said Kai, who added that “as a collector there is no reason to have that many”.

Some stores, such as Argos, only sell the trading cards online. On Amazon, high-demand lines are sold by an “invite-only” process designed to combat scalper bots.

With tattoos of his favourite Pokémon, Gengar and Dragonite , on his leg and arm, Anthony, 26, started collecting when he was five. He secured the third queue spot after coming straight from his waiting shift at 1am.

He admits to doing “everything” – buying, selling and exchanging cards – and using the sale proceeds to subsidise his collection.

Like Luke, second in the queue, and Hiep, who secured first place at 11pm, he wanted to buy the expensive elite trainer sets. Luke, 30, said nostalgia around Pokémon’s 30th anniversary this year was the “straw that broke me”.

He had a binder with placeholders for missing cards. It was an “expensive” hobby with scalpers being the reason “people like us turn up so early”.

Frustrated parents are increasingly found lurking in Reddit threads and Facebook groups looking for advice on how to buy cards for their children.

Even though Pokémon produces about 10bn cards a year, Calvin Innes, a fandom and pop culture strategist, said the demand had “outrun the machines, so everything else – bots, scalpers, queues etc – sits on the fact that there is a hard supply limit”.

“It’s not impossible for kids to get cards but the buying experience has gotten really ugly,” said Innes, author of Fandom Power: Marketing in the Age of Nerd Culture. “As a father of three kids who are all into Pokémon, it sucks.”

While elite trainer and booster box sets, plus Pokémon Center exclusives, were the hardest products to get, Innes said single packs and blisters were more accessible, although smaller high street retailers sold out quickly.

He also advised parents to buy singles from a UK card shop, singles marketplace, such as Cardmarket, or top-rated sellers on eBay UK.

Another option for parents was to go to a prerelease or league event at a game shop. Innes said they typically cost £25-£30 and the child usually got guaranteed cards, and the opportunity to play the game.

Daniel Garnett, who owns the Hull Pops Gaming Centre in Hessle, East Yorkshire, runs a free kids club and said he tries to keep product back for regular players. “We teach kids all about the Pokémon game, about the cards and how to play. We also have a qualified Pokémon judge that helps out.

“Sadly, however, about a month ago, we had lots of parents bring their kids in purely to buy product, and had no intention of playing or staying for the session.”

Israel took a beating in the US midterms

The Guardian Sat, 07 Nov 2026 12:00:11 GMT

In a reversal of longstanding assumptions, strong criticism of Israel’s actions may have helped put candidates over the top

“You took a chance on the unlikeliest of candidates,” Abdul El-Sayed told a Detroit crowd on Wednesday, declaring victory in Michigan’s hard-fought, often ugly, Senate race. In what was predicted to be a squeaker, the Democrat beat his Republican opponent, Mike Rogers, by a healthy seven points.

In some ways, El-Sayed was an unlikely candidate. At 34, in his first run for elected office, he set his sights almost cockily on a US Senate seat. He ran on what has become an uncontroversial affordability platform but also championed the socialist-adjacent Medicare for All.

But what was generally believed to qualify him as an unlikely candidate – and an even unlikelier winner – was his uncompromising criticism of Israel’s policies toward Palestine and Palestinians.

The assumption that El-Sayed’s Israel politics would doom his chances shaped the campaigns of his pro-Zionist Democratic primary rival, Haley Stevens, and the pro-Israel Rogers. It was certainly the wager that the rightwing American Israel Public Affairs Committee, or Aipac, placed when it wasted nearly $30m – its biggest investment ever in a single race – trying to defeat El-Sayed.

We don’t know yet, but his strong criticism of Israel may have put El-Sayed, and other Democrats, over the top. And like the Republicans, Israel and its prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, took a beating in the US midterms.

Six candidates endorsed by the Democratic Socialists of America, a prominent antagonist to rightwing Zionism, won Congressional races in part by foregrounding their primary opponents’ links to Aipac and their own refusal to take its funds. They all were running in bright-blue districts where the winner of the Democratic primary is the winner of the general election.

In Colorado, Melat Kiros, a 29-year-old lawyer, handily beat primary rival Diana DeGette, the 15-term incumbent backed by a Super Pac with Aipac links. In a New York district comprising portions of upper Manhattan and the Bronx, Darializa Avila Chevalier took down the once invincible Adriano Espaillat, who also had help from a Super Pac with ties to the group. The publication City and State New York predicted that Chevalier, a graduate student leader in Columbia University’s anti-Gaza war encampments, would be “the most pro-Palestine member of Congress”.

Where there was no sunlight between the candidates on the Israel question, some candidates used artificial light. In Brooklyn’s “commie corridor”, the victory of former state assembly member and artist Claire Valdez over the principled progressive Antonio Reynoso was tainted by her unsubstantiated charges that a mysterious Pac supporting him was funded by Aipac. It was in fact funded by one of New York’s teachers’ unions.

The Times of Israel noted pointedly that Pennsylvania’s Chris Rabb had the endorsement of the “far-left online streamer Hasan Piker”, whose support plagued El-Sayed in Michigan. But Rabb’s support did not come only from the extremes. Along with the DSA, the Maryland representative Jaimie Raskin, a Jew, endorsed Rabb, as did the respectable, radical Jewish Voice for Peace.

Rabb won without pulling any political punches. Last week he posted on X: “The Nakba never ended,” referring to the 1948 expulsion of Palestinians to establish a Jewish state on their land. In Michigan, Donavan McKinney defiantly labeled the last section of his plank “Palestine”.

More nuanced Israel politics also were in play. In Ohio, both Democrat Sherrod Brown, the winner, and Republican John Husted got help from pro-Israel organizations, but with different politics. The liberal Zionist J Street, which backed Brown, is critical of Israeli government policies and supports a two-state solution. Aipac stood with Husted.

In Georgia, the Jewish Democratic senator Jon Ossoff mapped a position that must have nettled voters on both sides. Expressing a commitment to Israel’s security and also to valuing “the lives of innocent Palestinians”, he voted in the Senate for some US military aid to Israel while opposing certain weapons transfers. That said, the choice was probably uncomplicated for Georgia’s Jews. Mike Collins, the Republican whom Ossoff trounced 59% to 41%, has ties to promoters of white nationalism and antisemitism.

Brad Lander, a lifer in New York City left-Democratic politics, has maintained his Jewish and progressive bona fides by displaying sympathy for both Israeli Jews and Palestinians. But he is not a slave to any official progressive stance.

He launched his primary campaign by vowing he would not be “doing Aipac’s bidding” and challenging the incumbent Dan Goldman, an unwavering Zionist and recipient of Aipac funds, to do what he had refused to do: call the Gaza war genocide and support the Block the Bombs Act, which would limit arms sales to Israel. Still, Lander quit the DSA after 30 years of membership when it publicized a patently pro-Hamas rally the day after the Hamas-led massacre of Israeli civilians on 7 October 2023. He picked up the endorsement of the Working Families party.

Their politics run from radical to liberal. But what all these winners have in common is their rejection of Israel’s wars and occupation and their support of Palestinian self-determination.

In many places, Israel probably had little effect on the elections. While its military continues to commit what the UN calls crimes against humanity in the occupied territories, Israel is off the front pages of US newspapers. Voters in poll after poll placed foreign policy way down their lists of concerns. Trump may be wrong that “people agree with what [he’s] doing in Iran”, but he might be right that it’s the consequent high gas prices that trouble them most.

In the president’s cold heart, Israel still has a place, and he believes the feeling is mutual. “I’m at 99% approval rating in Israel – can you believe it?” he mused on Fox & Friends. (Actually, no. Pew found his numbers were not even close.) Then Trump dreamed out loud: “If people get tired of me in the US, I’ll move to Israel and become prime minister.”

He’s certainly lost patience with the prime minister that country has now. Before election day, Trump said he’d cease sending $4bn annually in aid to Israel. While Maga’s ship is foundering, maybe its captain hopes to ride the ripple of the blue wave that’s cooling Americans’ sentiment toward Israel.

Judith Levine is a frequent contributor to the Guardian. Her Substack is Today in Fascism

‘Life is like a heartbeat. It’s up and down, up and down’: Michelle Yeoh on casting cliches, marriage at 60 and playing a robot in Blade Runner 2099

The Guardian Sat, 07 Nov 2026 12:00:10 GMT

Ballet dancer, action hero, Bond girl ... The actor won an Oscar for Everything Everywhere All At Once but she’s been through some challenges on the way

Before agreeing to appear in Blade Runner 2099, Michelle Yeoh received a letter – “an amazing letter, a love letter” – from Silka Luisa, the project’s creator, imploring her to be involved. Yeoh, who is 64, has played grandes dames, action heroes and a low-income Chinese-American battling the tax authorities in an infinite multiverse, but Blade Runner was different. The sci-fi series, a follow-up of sorts to Ridley Scott’s 1982 movie classic and its 2017 sequel, features both humans and replicants, their bioengineered antagonists, and Yeoh was adamant: “I don’t want to be human.” After working on ideas of what a synthetic human might look like, the result is Olwen, a terrifying individual with “a very cold, steely look in her eyes. And the way she moves – it’s not robotic. She’s sort of fluid. Like a dragon. Like a serpent.”

Yeoh is an actor who likes to figure things out for herself and, in the prep stages for Blade Runner 2099, the key question she thought about while building her character was, “What is it to be human? Are you born with humanity or does it come from the things you go through?”

Appearing via video link from New York, Yeoh exudes high-energy enthusiasm in plain white T-shirt, scraped back hair and huge, dark-framed glasses, all of which give her a cheerful, just-out-of-rehearsal air. She talks a mile a minute – about her family, the show, her holiday last summer on Luc Besson’s island in the Bahamas – and if her exuberance comes as a mild surprise, it’s because in recent years, much of Yeoh’s acting has been characterised by stillness. Her roles as Eleanor Young, the icy matriarch in the 2018 hit movie Crazy Rich Asians, and the crushed figure of Evelyn Wang, owner of a failing laundromat in Everything Everywhere All at Once (for which she won an Oscar in 2023, the first Asian woman to win for best actress), turn on tiny facial adjustments and furious or haughty looks, suggesting a performer who favours the minimalist approach.

As fans of Yeoh will know, however, the actor started out as a dancer, moved to martial arts movies in the 80s and is as robustly physical as any in Hollywood. An action star at heart, Yeoh is quick on her feet and unprecious in her outlook – so much so that, on occasion, she has found Hollywood a bit cautious compared with the wild west of the Hong Kong film industry she came up in as a young woman. “I’m tiny, I’m petite, five foot four,” she says, yet her ability to change her affect through movement is so intense, so persuasive, that, placed alongside Hunter Schafer, her much taller co-star in Blade Runner, “somehow you feel I loom over her”.

Schafer plays Cora, Yeoh’s sidekick Blade Runner – that is, a replicant cop with the LAPD – tasked with bringing a missing colleague back to base. The story’s complicating factors are that Cora is a human pretending to be a replicant, and Yeoh’s character, Olwen, is staring down her own imminent, preprogrammed death. The show is set 50 years after the last instalment of the Blade Runner franchise, in a world in which the replicants are running things and humans occupy a permanent serf-class. It’s chillingly timely, given recent instances of AI slipping its reins, and the challenge for Yeoh, she says, went beyond existential questions about what it means to be human into the practicalities of how to present a character created in a lab. “They had no childhood,” she says, “so you feel you’re dealing with someone who has no concept of private space. They’re in your face and if they want something, they take it. With Olwen, I wanted it so you don’t know where she is or what she’s going to do next, and everyone is terrified.”

Yeoh’s own childhood, in a middle-class Malaysian Chinese family, was one in which her ambitions, intellectual and professional, were broadly encouraged. Her father, Datuk Yeoh Kian-teik, was a prominent lawyer and businessman who had trained in England and her mother, Janet, a former beauty queen who would have an enormous influence on Yeoh’s career. In some ways, it was a highly conventional background, and when Yeoh expressed a desire to pursue dance as a career, her parents thought it entirely suitable that “I’d learn my ballet, graduate as a teacher, then come home and start my own ballet school. They were happy.”

In other ways, however, her background was more interesting and diverse than the average. The city she grew up in, Ipoh, is the capital of a Malaysian state 200km north of Kuala Lumpur and was a thriving, cosmopolitan place. This somehow made the world appear more accessible and when, at 15, she won a place to study ballet at the Hammond school in Chester, it made her decision to leave home so young seem less outlandish. She says she travelled, unaccompanied, to England, where she had plenty of cousins, but it remains surprising that her family permitted her not only to cross the world alone, but to live in student accommodation 7,000 miles away.

Yeoh says these kinds of ambitions were built into her upbringing. “I was always a bit of an adventurer, which my parents instilled in us. My dad has a philosophy that education is precious, but you can decide what you want to do. He never said I had to do the big five: lawyer, doctor, accountant, that kind of thing.”

At that point, Yeoh had no desire to be an actor; her sights were set on performing in ballet. It has been an interesting facet of her life and career that she has been able to absorb sudden changes of fortune; to pivot to new experiences with relative ease. Her energy, it seems to me, is primarily playful, whether she is flying through the air in Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon or swishing her ankle-length trenchcoat as a replicant in Blade Runner. (“They are almost naughty,” she says, of the non-humans, “like something playing with its food.”)

As a result, when Yeoh’s performance becomes still, it has a particular power. There is a scene in the Blade Runner 2099 pilot in which Yeoh’s character is informed she must go after and eliminate an old replicant with whom she was close and who has apparently gone rogue. Olwen stares silently at her superior, before saying, “I have never killed one of my own.” And in that moment of stillness, a muscle in her cheek twitches. It’s a remarkable piece of acting, discreet as a poker tell. How on earth, I ask, did she do it? Yeoh smiles, glittering. “Years of practice, my dear. Years and years.”

The experiences in England set up a great fork in the road for Yeoh, who had to tear up her plans and start again. While at the school, she injured her back and was told dancing professionally was out of the question. She compares that moment to looking in a “mirror that shatters … as a silly 17-year-old, it was the end of my dream.” Looking back, she feels lucky to have been in the care of the principal, Mrs Hammond, “an older, wiser lady who said, ‘Calm down, crazy little girl. It’s not the end of the world! You can still be involved in dance.’” Accordingly, after doing A-levels, Yeoh went to what is now Manchester Metropolitan University to study for a degree in creative arts, with an emphasis on dance’s history and choreography. “At the end of the day, if that’s my next best choice, I’ll take it!”

Yeoh makes the bounce-back sound easy. Surely she had a big crash somewhere in there? She insists that, after the initial shock, she quickly rationalised her way into her former state of cheerfulness, telling herself that, after all, the new degree course “still involved the world I loved … And now when I look back, those experiences actually helped me doing martial arts.”

As a child, she had been a real jock, a champion squash player and an athlete. “I ran, I did high jump, I love the outdoors, the physical challenge. All of which helped with action movies.” That pivot was a few years off, however, and after her degree Yeoh moved home to Malaysia and wondered what to do next. She thought of opening a dance school with a friend, but her mother had other ideas. Behind Yeoh’s back – “The number of things she has done behind my back is countless” – Janet sent headshots of her daughter to the judging panel for Miss Malaysia, a competition Yeoh ended up winning in 1983 at 21. She went along with it “to get her off my back”, but when invited to compete at a further beauty contest in Australia, Yeoh put her foot down. “I said, no, I’m not doing it, I’m going back to England.”

Why not seize the opportunity to travel? Because, while “I love dancing on stage, I don’t love speaking on stage. I panic, I’m sweating, my knees are shaking. Going to Comic Con is scary as hell. I always think I’m going to make a fool of myself.” Still, Janet’s will was greater and off she went to Australia, which was just as well: the exposure brought Yeoh to the attention of a TV station in Hong Kong looking for fresh, Chinese-language acting talent. She jumped at the opportunity and landed in a strange and “terrifying” situation.

Yeoh is fond of pointing out she’s adventurous, but this was something else: finding herself cast in a movie in a language in which she wasn’t entirely fluent and couldn’t read at all. “I still can’t. Fortunately at that time in Hong Kong they didn’t have much of a script,” she says, laughing, and in the early days of filming titles such as Yes, Madam!, a cop thriller, and the action comedy The Owl vs Bumbo, she would be fed lines by the assistant director and simply repeat what she’d heard. The turnaround time on these films was phenomenal: “I remember one where we finished shooting on Monday morning after filming all night, and by Friday night it was in the cinemas. They’re editing as they go along.”

It was a speed that suited Yeoh: “It toughens you up and makes you think on your feet. It’s like being in a standup show.” As her martial arts skills improved, she swiftly became a star, churning out title after title until she met the billionaire businessman Dickson Poon. He hired her to star in a commercial for one of his ventures and within a few years they were married.
