Yeoh has spoken about this marriage as an amicable failure that lasted four years, her divorce in 1992 freeing her up to return to acting; while married to Poon, she stopped working, a hangover from the more conservative elements of her background, and not something she repeated with her second husband. For the past 22 years, she has been in a relationship with Jean Todt, former head of Ferrari, whom she met in 2004 and was engaged to for 19 years before marrying in 2023. Todt has told her it was love at first sight, when he saw her “walking down some steps in Shanghai in 2004”. The pair went on to meet in Paris, for a while maintaining a long-distance relationship. (Todt, now 80, needed his friends’ help “teaching him how to text” to sustain this.) “I really liked the guy,” Yeoh says. “Very straightforward, honest, all that.” Two months after meeting, Todt proposed and, as “we got on very well”, she accepted.

Why marry at all, after such a long engagement? It was Covid, she says, that finally shunted them over the line: during lockdown, they realised Yeoh, a Malaysian passport holder, had no automatic right to travel to see Todt at their home base in Switzerland unless they were married. They tied the knot there before she took off again to film Blade Runner in Prague, Avatar 4 in the US and forthcoming movie The Surgeon in Ireland.

The hiatus taken by Yeoh during her first marriage didn’t harm her career; quite the opposite. Returning to the Hong Kong cinema scene, her celebrity rose over the next five years as the industry exploded, until, in 1997, she caught the eye of Hollywood casting directors hiring for a new Bond movie. As her first American film, this was the turning point for Yeoh, although in the first instance her experiences on the set of Tomorrow Never Dies – in which she played Wai Lin, the Chinese intelligence agent and martial artist who teams up with Pierce Brosnan to bring down Jonathan Pryce’s media mogul – were bafflingly slow compared with the world she was used to. Worse, she was prohibited from doing even the simplest of stunts. “I was an established action hero, and the first thing the director said was, you are not here because you know how to do action. You are here because you are an actress. We don’t want you to get hurt.” On the first day of filming, Yeoh was scripted to jump less than a foot down a step and to her amazement was told she wasn’t allowed to. “I’d say, are you guys pulling my leg?” But they weren’t. When the producers hired her stunt team to fly in from Hong Kong, they were amazed to be sent models of the set with which to plan their scenes. One day, as Yeoh walked past the green room, she was horrified to see them lying down. She went off: “What the hell?! They bring you all the way here and you’re lying around! Go and work!” They told her they’d already presented six options to the producers and had time for a nap because the Hollywood machine was so slow.

In the wake of Bond, a less confident actor might have felt caught between two cinematic cultures. Not Yeoh. “I never compared the two by thinking this side or that is better.” She did, however, have strong feelings about the amount of garbage she was offered after, when American cinema had no idea what to do with an Asian star. For two years she didn’t work, “not for the lack of offers” but because all the scripts that came in were “very stereotypical Asian roles”. The question a casting director or producer would ask before offering her a role, she says, was “‘Why is an Asian face in this room? Are we in Chinatown?’ There weren’t that many roles that had anything to say. I was fortunate, because I already had a very strong career in Hong Kong that had saved me enough money to have the power to say no. I didn’t want to endorse the stereotypes of our culture.”

What broke the drought and changed Yeoh’s fortunes again was being cast, in 1999, in Ang Lee’s Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon, as Yu Shu Lien, a master warrior and skilled martial artist. The film was a huge success, grossing more than $200m worldwide and proving, she laughs, that “Americans do know how to read subtitles”.

Since then, Yeoh says, the issue of racial stereotyping in casting has fluctuated wildly. For a while, “looking east was fun. It was exciting. And we had Quentin Tarantino, who liked the movies that came out of Asia, which made a big difference. Then Jackie Chan came, Jet Li, Chow Yun-fat, and the directors – John Woo, Tsui Hark, Johnny Chu. They pushed open the doors. But still they were regarded as ‘Chinese’ directors. Not quite there, yet. And it’s taken a long time.”

What moved the needle, she believes, was John M Chu’s Crazy Rich Asians, based on the bestselling novel by Kevin Kwan, which tells the story of an American Chinese girl who falls in love with the son of a billionaire. The action unfolds in Singapore and features an entirely Asian cast – a first for a mainstream US romantic comedy – in which Yeoh reigned supreme as the hero’s icy and terrifyingly elegant mother-in-law, Eleanor Young. The fact it was a huge hit, Yeoh says, “really changed things”.

Since its release, Yeoh has been cast in movies across every genre, from Star Trek to Minions to her turn in the Agatha Christie adaptation A Haunting in Venice, and as Madame Morrible in Wicked. Her greatest performance in the last five years was as Evelyn Wang, the put-upon matriarch of a failing laundromat – and other iterations in a series of alternative universes – in the indie film Everything Everywhere All at Once. Acting is so nebulous, I wonder if winning the Oscar confirmed something in her mind? “I know what you mean – life is like a heartbeat; it’s up and down, up and down. So you reassure yourself it’s OK, you did your best, but there’s never any guarantee. Any award, especially the Oscar, is a confirmation from your peers. When we started out with Everything Everywhere, we just wanted to tell a story people could understand, in the language of the younger generation, and that’s why it was so fearless. Because an older person would look at it and say, what is that? What are you smoking? Or whatever.”

It’s characteristic that, when presented with the script by directors Daniel Kwan and Daniel Scheinert, known as the Daniels, Yeoh did not have this killjoy recoil. Quite the opposite; her first thought was, “It’s so relatable, because it’s about a family in America dealing with things we all understand so well. Tax. The generation gap. Miscommunication. Love and family.”

It’s about something else, too, a more esoteric theme Yeoh perhaps understands better than most. It happened to her as a teenager, a reluctant beauty queen, and when she left Hong Kong for America, so when she encountered the notion in the Daniels’ script, with its description of a multiverse in which all versions of our lives take place simultaneously, she knew what they were saying, “that every time you make a decision, things change”. And if all the alternative futures evaporate in that moment, that is perfectly fine with Michelle Yeoh.

Blade Runner 2099 starts on Prime Video on 25 November.

Trump faces criticism for ‘dangerous’ Stephen Miller appointment as White House chief of staff

The Guardian Sat, 07 Nov 2026 10:00:08 GMT

Democrats and Republicans blast promotion of ‘xenophobe’ who led administration’s immigration crackdown in wake of US midterm elections

Democratic lawmakers decried Stephen Miller as a “hatemonger”, a “xenophobe” and “vile” after Donald Trump appointed his most trusted adviser as White House chief of staff.

On Friday afternoon, the US president abruptly announced via his Truth Social platform that Miller – the architect of his sweeping immigration crackdown – would replace Susie Wiles, whom he confirmed had been ousted.

The announcement came just days after voters overwhelmingly elected Democrats in the US midterm elections, a sharp rebuke of Trump’s agenda that ended his Republican party’s control of US Congress.

“For Trump to promote this hatemonger shows he has learned nothing,” Dick Durbin, a Democratic senator from Illinois, wrote on X. Chuck Schumer, who is expected to become Senate majority leader, said Trump “learned nothing from his historic defeat” and “couldn’t have made a worse choice” in elevating Miller.

Hakeem Jeffries, the top Democrat in the House of Representatives, who is widely expected to become the chamber’s first Black speaker, called Miller “a dangerous xenophobe and reckless extremist who has American blood on his hands”, and demanded he be fired.

Chris Van Hollen, a Democratic senator from Maryland, called Trump’s decision to elevate Miller “another kick in the teeth to the American people” and “a sign of Trump’s contempt for the voters”.

Miller, who has been serving as Trump’s deputy chief of staff, has become one of the most controversial figures in the administration. An author of the rightwing Project 2025 manifesto, Miller often makes TV appearances to attack Trump’s opponents or bolster policies such as ending birthright citizenship and suggesting the US could invade Greenland.

As a policy adviser, Miller is credited as the architect of Trump’s mass deportation agenda, which Democrats pointed to in denouncing his promotion.

Gavin Newsom, the outgoing California governor, called Miller “one of the most vile thugs to ever slither into the Oval Office” and said the move was “an insult to every American who voted for change” on Tuesday.

But Trump’s Republican allies and aides celebrated the announcement. Steven Cheung, the White House communications director, called Miller a “Trump OG”, and said: “There is no bigger advocate for the Trump agenda than Stephen.”

Mike Lee, a senator from Utah, said Miller had been “a staunch defender of law and order against illegal invasions and leftist lawlessness”. Eric Schmitt, a senator from Missouri, insisted Miller was exactly what the country needed. “Our country is at a pivotal point and Stephen Miller understands exactly what is at stake,” Schmitt wrote on X.

Cabinet members including JD Vance, defense secretary Pete Hegseth, health secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr and secretary of state Marco Rubio also praised Miller’s record.

Not all Republicans were pleased by the appointment, however.

Congressman Marlin Stutzman, an Indiana Republican who held his seat, argued Miller “should be fired” earlier this week amid anger over the administration’s deportation drive. Asked on Friday what he made of Trump’s choice to promote Miller instead, Stutzman told Semafor it was a “horrible decision”.

Miles Taylor, who served as chief of staff at the Department of Homeland Security during Trump’s first term, and later joined the ranks of anti-Trump Republicans, said: “I spent two years working with Stephen Miller. His appointment as White House chief of staff is among the most dangerous personnel decisions in the history of our republic. I say that without reservation.”

Asked about such criticism on Friday, the White House hailed Miller as a “key player” delivering Trump’s agenda. “He has spearheaded the administration’s crime crackdown including in DC and Memphis, record setting deregulation, unleashed American energy, dismantled drug cartels, and secured our border,” it said in a statement. “In his new role, he will continue to deliver historic successes for the American people.”

Accepting his new role, Miller thanked Trump and said he was “honored beyond words” to serve. “The mission now is more clear than ever: Fight with all of our soul to support our President and defend this magnificent Republic,” Miller wrote on X.

Narrative threads: How to write a Booker-shortlisted novel, by Marlon James, Douglas Stuart, Elizabeth Strout and more

The Guardian Sat, 07 Nov 2026 09:00:06 GMT

A trip to the Scottish islands, a psychological experiment, a chance encounter in a drugstore… the finalists for this year’s Booker prize reveal their inspirations

Who knows where a novel really comes from? I spend years gathering loose threads and then, when I feel like the cloth will hold, I start to weave them into a narrative. I suppose I began internalising John of John back in 1994, the year I went to college and chose to become a weaver myself.

But it was in 2019, in the anxious period waiting for Shuggie Bain to be published, that I really found the thread for John of John. I decided I would go to the Western Isles. It was a place I had been longing to see all my life and I had a vague idea that I might set a novel there about an adult son who has been called home to a crofting community to care for his difficult father. I reasoned that even if a novel didn’t emerge from the trip, at least I would have seen more of my own country.

I was drawn to the Western Isles for many reasons. I was keen to see the Harris tweed weavers, but I’d also just finished writing Young Mungo, a novel about sectarian violence where young Glaswegians seemed intent on destroying beauty, and so without being able to articulate it, I had set out seeking a spirit of gentleness, to write about creativity within working-class lives – about beauty, and colour, and nature, and music.

People have a romantic notion of the islands – and perhaps I had a little too. Although they are stunning, they are very real, very practical places, where it can be difficult to earn a living and raise a family, where managing your relationship within a community is of the utmost importance.

I started in Vatersay and, after slowly travelling up the archipelago, I finally arrived on the Isle of Harris. It was there, in the home of a local woman, that I saw what my third novel might become.

We were sitting at her kitchen table, talking about her involvement in the local church. I mentioned that I’d been struck by the number of spinsters and bachelors I’d met on my trip. It seemed unusual given that crofts seemed to benefit from larger families. When I asked her why she thought some folk had never married, she replied that they had probably just “missed their moment”. I agreed that it must be tricky to find love in a settlement with so few people, and then I ventured that it would be harder still if some of these older people had been gay. The woman looked at me with such cool horror that I realised, in that moment, that the novel was going to be less about a son returning home, and more about the father he had left behind; a weaver who was tied to the land, a man who had never been able to find love, or any sense of himself, in the only place where he belonged.

A woman works in the drugstore in the town in which I live in Maine, and one day almost two years ago, she whispered to me – no one else was in the store – “I just want it over!” She cupped both hands on the sides of her mouth and said: “The election.” I told her I felt the same. She said, looking around nervously: “I never, ever say anything about it to anyone, but I just want it over.” I told her I knew what she meant, and off I went. I have no idea who she voted for, but her pain was palpable. As was mine.

The Things We Never Say is a tribute to people such as her, people who are distressed about the way things are, and have been for a few years, in our country, the United States of America. We live it, breathe it, it is everywhere among us, and while people will talk to like-minded people (sometimes) there is much that people will not say to each other about our current situation.

Not only was this true as I was writing the book, it is even more true now; the book shows the decline of our democracy. And through it all we continue living our daily lives. We go to work, we shop for groceries, we take walks with friends and laugh, we go to our quilting clubs, and all around us terrible things are happening, and most of us are not talking about it.

I have spoken publicly about my inspiration for Artie Dam, the protagonist, how I found an old photo in an obituary and saw a splendid ordinary face … This is all true, and it gave me the visuals I needed for him, but the book itself came forth because of what is happening in our country. I made Artie a high school history teacher because he would have had – perhaps – a deeper understanding of what was going to happen, and in fact, has happened.

I interwove his personal story – because we all have a personal story as we move through our time in history – and I wanted his inner life to somehow reflect what was happening in his outer life. Artie’s time in history has caught up with him, and this is his story. It is our story.

There is a blind man in Mallorca who could tell this story better than I could. What he might not have in art he has in truth, and he could tell you about his life before he went blind, his hopes when he still lived in Jamaica, the night that took his vision, the mob that nearly took his life, and the last thing he saw: the man who took his eyes out. All alleged of course. The blind man was gay – is gay – and the last thing he saw was what Jamaican men do to gay people. But until three years ago I thought this man the stuff of urban legend, a story that shook my young gay self down to the bone and sent me hurling into the closet with the door slammed shut.

The thing is I knew it happened. The rumour was that on a night in the early 90s, a mob descended on a group of gay men in Kingston, gathered at either a support group or a branch of Jamaica Aids support, and beat them within an inch of their lives. That among the mob was law enforcement, men in business and a very famous musician. All alleged, of course. There has never been a written record of it, no police report, no news article, no lead in the nightly news, and so I was convinced it happened.

Rumours are ephemeral, which is why in Jamaica they are almost always true. We know that you pay a price for standing on fact. Espousing a truth means making yourself a target. Speaking truth to power in the end attracts power to stop it. Because it is the kind of news that fades, the kind of news that is untraceable, the rumour speaker knows that he has the safety of knowing that his truth will never come back to expose or convict him. So, he speaks it freely. They killed a gay man. One of the mob was Jamaica’s biggest reggae singer. The gay men were getting safe sex advice. The gay men might have been having sex. The men were all black. The men were a mix of black and white. The men all had Aids. All alleged of course.

I tend to make novels out of stories that haunt me. The stories that haunt the most sometimes tell me the least, leaving me with gaps and leaps, and holes that stop the tale from adding up. This is where I feel most useful as a novelist; as something between a historian and a journalist, making real the lives of imagined people. Or filling in the other dimensions of a one-dimensional event. Or, most importantly, conjuring what might have been the consequences of a singular, sometimes forgotten action. It might not be exactly as the blind man in Mallorca would tell it, or it might be totally different. But a story can be real if not factually true, and sometimes that is truer than reality itself.

Poetry had left me and I missed writing. Bolstered by publishing a short work of creative nonfiction about my childhood as a competitive trampolinist, I started working on two separate short stories, testing if fiction was something I could do.

One story was about a young attendant to a dying king, and another about a lonely woman using replica food in her home to create scenes and their resident spirits, with the ultimate goal of cohabiting with them. At a point it became clear to me that she was working her way towards the young attendant, and that I was writing one book and not two separate stories at all.

A year or so before that I said to two of my friends, while visiting the Royal Magdalene Almshouses in Glastonbury and feeling transported by one of the dressed bedrooms, that I was interested in writing about staging and replica.

Thirty years before that I squeezed a plastic grape in a sofa showroom.

I had no idea what would happen in the book when I started writing it, or how it would end. Iris Murdoch once said, “One should sit quietly and let the thing invent itself”, and I took that as a mantra, letting the book emerge. It turns out that can be quite messy, and it took a while to find its final form. Initially the chapters were alternately contemporary and historical. At one point I cut and rewrote half of it. Some decisions, like the short chapters, were instinctive. Others were the work of much stylistic experimentation. All the usual messy business (I assume, having only done it once) of writing a novel.

On that journey, what surprised me most was that the wider world fed more into the writing of the medieval part of the book than it did the present-day sections. I was already thinking about power and empire, but writing at the height of the genocide in Gaza and watching in horror the results of unchallenged, untethered absolute power, certainly shaped the writing of the king and many of the characters around him. Before this, I assumed that novels exist in a state of purity in the mind, untouched by current events. I’m sure that’s sometimes true, but in my case the contemporary and medieval worlds had to be in conversation.

It was March 2021, and I had chronic neck and back pain from spending eight hours a day teaching on Zoom during the lockdowns. I was also temporarily head of my department (which anyone in academia will know to be a completely thankless and enervating role). I had given myself a night off to work on some poems because I go absolutely spare when I’m not writing. It was about 10pm, I probably had a glass of wine next to me, and I was looking for interesting phrases in social psychology articles. I had 12 tabs open, when I found, in a footnote, a brief precis of the black bag experiment (University of Oregon, 1967). It struck me as beautiful and ridiculous. I wasn’t really interested in the findings of the experiment, which focused more on others’ gradually more affectionate reactions to black bag over time. What obsessed me was the experience of portraying black bag: what kind of actor would leap at the chance to do it? The fact that it was a pretty neat symbol of the status of the artist in the 21st century … The fact that I wasn’t averse to the idea of doing it myself because, ugh, just being a person at all is so wearying.

It was a really lucky and completely arbitrary find and I felt utterly rejuvenated by it as a concept. I like writing that has some kind of constraint (like Georges Perec’s novel A Void, composed without a single letter “e”), a rule that starts to generate the work; that becomes its own inspiration. But this was a constraint for a character within the book, and that struck me as even better. Within minutes of reading about it I felt like I was black bag, my constant inner monologue turned into even more of a bathysphere than usual.

I immediately abandoned the poem I was working on and started writing a first-person scene where an out-of-work actor talks to a psychology lecturer about the role of black bag. It was pretty much all I wrote from that point on. I wrote BLACK BAG on the front of a notebook and vowed to do as little research as possible.

I always start writing from an interest in form, rather than from ideas for characters or scenes or stories. They come later. As soon as I find the form, I look for its weak points so I can break it. The two forms that interested me when I began to think about The End of Everything were the UK novel of catastrophe after the second world war, expressed best in John Wyndham’s The Day of the Triffids and its outbreak of ambulatory carnivorous vegetables; and the novel of the alien invasion of Earth epitomised by HG Wells’s classic The War of the Worlds.

In both, the disaster is bounded, understandable and, most importantly, solved. This is not necessarily true of disasters in the real world; they’re constant, unmanageable, entangled with one another and with global politics; and wherever possible they go unacknowledged by people whose comforts are not immediately threatened. The classic disaster stories burst in on a fictional population, rag it about, and then, having taught the reader a lesson, recede. They encourage us to feel good by presenting unpredictable upheaval followed briskly by the defeat of the threat and a return to some form of the author’s preferred cultural ground state.

I wanted this book to offer a different shape: a catastrophe the nature of which is impossible to parse, and which continues unabated for the foreseeable future. In short, actual change. Nested inside the novel are various parodies, pastiches and political metaphors; a certain amount of grotesque humour. The End of Everything is about trying to live as if nothing has gone wrong. It’s a disaster story in which the disaster is the failure to comprehend. It’s an alien invasion narrative in which the aliens arrive not as Wells’s invaders from Mars but as incomers from another dimension, paralleling the gentrification of places like the UK’s south-east coast. Their motives are so unhuman that we aren’t sure even they know how – or why – they came.

As a favour – and with a whispered You’re welcome! Enjoy! – I’ve passed on to the reader some of the puzzlement and confusion of the characters in the book as they face a future with the alien. I hope, though, that the issues are transparent: the collapse of rationality that comes with Trumpism and the internet, and which consciously confounds the ability to make a factual statement about anything; humanity’s inexplicable attempt to break down and abandon the environment it can’t live without; the loss of any sense that we actually know how to manage the world except via a Netflix empowerment fantasy.

In an early film of The Day of the Triffids, the triffids are defeated by spraying salt water on them; in the novel itself, the hero and his dependents ignore the issue of giant carnivorous plants and retreat to the Isle of Wight, where they return to the ground state by starting an allotment. We don’t have those options.

Moscow has shuttered Novaya Gazeta – we told the truth and we paid the price

The Guardian Sat, 07 Nov 2026 08:00:05 GMT

Russia’s best-known independent newspaper was my home for 17 years. It’s being shut down, but the spirit of its journalism will live on

Novaya Gazeta – Russia’s most prominent independent newspaper – is being shut down. On 29 October, two things became known: Novaya was being evicted from its newsroom, and banks would stop processing readers’ donations to Novaya (its only legal income). Insiders spoke of the risk of Novaya being declared an extremist organisation – then any employee could be jailed: a journalist, an editor, an accountant, a cleaner. Closing was safer.

Novaya Gazeta is a second family to me and to many journalists now scattered around the Earth. For me it is my first family, too – my adopted sister also worked at Novaya, and it’s funny how alike we turned out.

I bought Novaya for the first time when I was 14. I opened it to an article by Anna Politkovskaya about the “cleansing” of the Chechen village of Mesker-Yurt by Russian soldiers. Thirty-six people were killed; one man was crucified. None of it made sense to me. I considered myself well informed; like everyone around me, I knew exactly what was happening in Chechnya. Our soldiers were heroically protecting civilians from terrorists.

The more I read, the more I realised that I knew nothing about my own country. I was angry at Novaya. It took away the truth I shared with everyone else. I couldn’t ignore it – the words would not be forgotten. Later, I understood that this is exactly what journalism should be: it should drag you back to reality, even when you don’t want to go. A few years later, I was working at the paper.

I came to Novaya at 17 with no connections, not knowing how to turn on a computer – and I stayed for 17 years. Novaya rarely hired established journalists – it took very young kids and nurtured them. The youngest people in the newsroom were 15, the oldest close to 80. It was one big, intergenerational school. Today, people from Novaya work at almost every independent Russian outlet.

The paper wrote about the most important things in a way that turned the words themselves into events: Beslan, the purge of gay men in Chechnya, Malaysia Airlines flight MH17, corruption, the wars in Chechnya, Georgia, Syria and Ukraine, torture, organised crime, the environment, terrorism – and the people living very different lives across our vast country.

In 1993, just a few months after Novaya Gazeta was established, Boris Yeltsin, then the president, dissolved the Supreme Soviet, our country’s parliament. The army shelled the White House in Moscow using tanks. Officially, 158 people died; unofficial estimates are higher. Novaya’s special issue carried reports from the White House, from the streets and hospitals under the headline: “As long as we divide even the dead into our own and our enemies, the war will go on.” That was the paper’s true motto.

Dmitry Muratov, one of Novaya Gazeta’s founders and editors-in-chief, liked to say: “The work only begins once the text is published.” When I wrote about a former orphanage kid wrongly convicted of murder, Novaya Gazeta found him a lawyer, and for several years we went to the hearings until he was acquitted. Novaya’s investigations became the basis of criminal cases, lives were saved (Anna Politkovskaya organised the evacuation of 89 elderly people abandoned in a nursing home in Grozny).

In the paper’s 33 years, six of its people were killed: Igor Domnikov, Yuri Shchekochikhin, Politkovskaya, Stanislav Markelov, Anastasia Baburova, Natalia Estemirova. In most cases, those who ordered the killings were never found or punished. Many Novaya journalists received threats. Many were beaten. Someone splashed a chemical in Muratov’s face; his eyes were saved.

When Russia’s full-scale war against Ukraine began in February 2022, Novaya Gazeta came out in Russian and Ukrainian with a clear message on the front page: “We refuse to see the Ukrainian people as our enemies.” A month later, Novaya had to suspend publication; the authorities took away its licence and printing the paper became impossible. The website was blocked. Social networks were blocked too, for the whole country. In April of this year, the newsroom was searched and equipment was seized; at the same time, the investigative journalist Oleg Roldugin was arrested, and he is now awaiting trial. On 4 September, the Ministry of Justice declared Novaya a “foreign agent” – along with 106 of its contributors.

Many now say it was a miracle that Novaya Gazeta kept working inside Russia for four and a half years of war, when almost all independent media had moved their newsrooms abroad. This miracle was made possible by the daily choices of people I love and of those I have not met yet. They were afraid to come to the newsroom – but they came every single day. They went to the occupied territories, investigated, documented the repression, talked to people as people, without simplifying, generalising, or looking away. Many kept prison bags in their hallways – clothes and medicine packed in case of arrest. Everyone learned their lawyer’s number by heart. Everyone gave their neighbours a set of keys so – if anything happened – someone would water the plants and feed the cats.

For my colleagues, I feel gratitude and love, fear, endless admiration and endless pain. For the Russian state that set out to kill Novaya Gazeta and has now killed it, I feel nothing. The drive to know the truth (even when it hurts terribly) is built into every human heart, written into our biology; it is a condition of our survival. That is why Novaya will be eternal, even when every one of us is gone.

Elena Kostyuchenko is a Russian journalist and the author of I Love Russia: Reporting from a Lost Country

Pineapple on pizza is an insult to our great Italian cuisine – and here’s why we secretly love it

The Guardian Sat, 07 Nov 2026 07:00:06 GMT

Of course an Italian chef would rather be sacked than make this. Defending our food against such blasphemy makes us feel like better people

Luca Cesari is a food historian and author of The History of Pizza

You may have smiled at the news a few days ago: the Italian chef Davide Tamburella was sacked by a Brisbane restaurant after refusing to put pineapple on a pizza. Never mind that Queensland grows almost all of Australia’s pineapples. Tamburella would not give way to his customers or his boss, insisting that the combination was an insult to Italian culture.

Strange as it may sound, he is not the first. In 2017, Maurizio Landi, a chef from Bologna, was sacked by a bistro near Lyon after resisting pressure to cook his pasta for longer and to serve spaghetti bolognese, a dish that does not exist in his home town. For anyone who doesn’t know, Bologna is the only city in the world where ragù is eaten solely with tagliatelle, and putting it on spaghetti borders on an outrage.

Why would Italians rather lose their jobs than question their culinary certainties? The answer lies somewhere between anthropology and history. Food fashions are changing faster than ever. There are more chefs on television than grandmothers cooking at home, and Italians can sense the dangers hanging over their beloved cuisine.

It is a bit as if Renaissance paintings were crumbling before our eyes while we stand by, powerless. Yet there is one crucial difference between the Sistine Chapel and a pizza. Michelangelo’s frescoes have looked the same for half a millennium, whereas a pizza from a century ago was nothing like the one we eat today.

Some of the most glaring sins against Italian recipes are simply old ways of eating that Italians themselves no longer recognise. Overcooked pasta and pasta as a side dish are two of them. Leaf through old recipe books and you will find that pasta was eaten soft for centuries, while macaroni with cheese was served alongside meat dishes from the middle ages onwards.

But it takes far less to drive an Italian mad. One spoonful of cream in a carbonara is enough to get you thrown out of the country. A pity, then, that this too is an old habit, introduced in the 1960s by a few Roman cooks and kept up for at least 40 years, a small detail everyone seems to have forgotten.

Then there is grated cheese on pasta with fish, an outrage to many Italians, who stand ready to scientifically prove that cheese ruins the taste of fish, while forgetting such ultra-traditional pasta dishes as mussels with pecorino.

No list of extreme pairings would be complete without the cappuccino, which foreigners order at the end of a meal under the horrified gaze of the waiters. Ask for a caffè macchiato, which is a cappuccino in miniature, and nobody bats an eyelid. Not all Italians are so rigid, and even pineapple on pizza has its admirers among the great pizza makers.

A few years ago, Gino Sorbillo, one of the world’s most respected pizzaioli, opened the door to it, though only on a white pizza with no tomato, which would otherwise make it too acidic. Franco Pepe, considered by many the best pizza maker in the world, came up with the AnaNascosta (“hidden pineapple”), a cone of pizza filled with pineapple, San Daniele ham and Grana Padano fondue, making the heretical match respectable. And this summer, Berberè, a pizzeria chain with five sites in London, launched a pizza with a spiced pineapple sauce, to break with the prejudice once and for all.

Pineapple is only the latest blasphemy to land on a pizza. An article headlined “Neapolitan pizza”, in the Morning Post of 17 December 1860, reads: “There are other modes of preparing the pizza, by the substitution of freshly caught anchovies, or slices of sausage, or mushrooms for the cream and grated cheese; but the highest authorities on these points treat with disdain all such modern innovations, and protest that a pizza compounded after that fashion has no right to the name at all.”

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

after newsletter promotion

The toppings change, but the “authorities” will always have something to say about what can go on a pizza. It is hard to see why all the hatred should fall on pineapple, when Italian pizzerias offer frankfurters and chips, speck and mascarpone, tuna and onion, and the traditional pizza of Pesaro, in the Marche region, is a margherita with hard-boiled eggs and mayonnaise.

The truth is that we Italians don’t need pineapple pizza to eat. We need it to despise. It stands for everything we fight against to keep our traditions intact, and loathing it makes us feel like better people, on the right side of the barricade.

Luca Cesari is a food historian and the author of The History of Pizza

The end of Maga as we know it

The Guardian Sat, 07 Nov 2026 06:00:05 GMT

The Republican party will regroup after their shellacking in the US midterm elections, but it won’t look the same

Walking by a tattoo studio and medical spa on the pretty main street of Round Rock, in Texas Hill Country, Tarik Bakir recalled voting for Barack Obama in 2008 and Donald Trump in 2024. But when it came to the 2026 midterm elections, he was firmly back in the Democrats’ column.

“I’m not happy with the Iran war,” said Bakir, 41, a financial adviser who served with the US military in Afghanistan. “The economy’s OK, but not great. This election was a rebuttal to Trump. This time people said they didn’t like him, or his policies.”

Once a reliably Republican suburb north of Austin, Round Rock is the birthplace of James Talarico, whose victory this week in a US Senate election – Democrats’ first in Texas since 1988, the year before Talarico was born – symbolised a nationwide “blue-nami” that swept away Trump’s Maga (Make America Great Again) coalition.

It was the most sweeping midterm repudiation of a sitting president since the Watergate election of 1974. Unlike typical midterms, where losses are concentrated in swing districts or isolated suburban pockets, the 2026 midterms saw the Republican floor drop out across deep-red strongholds, suburban corridors and rural heartlands alike.

Democrats stormed once impregnable fortresses such as Kansas and South Carolina, taking control of both chambers of Congress and redrawing the political map. In Texas, for decades a bedrock of conservatism, the senator Ted Cruz is now the last statewide Republican still standing.

For Trump, it was a scathing rebuke after a madcap campaign that left some wondering: if the president had deliberately tried to sabotage his own party’s chances, what, precisely, would he have done any differently?

The president heaped praise on Ohio senator Jon Husted’s “ass” but, in the words of Cruz, his party got an “ass-kicking”. Florida governor Ron DeSantis called it “close to an extinction-level event for Republicans in many parts of the country”.

Patrick Gaspard, a former official in Barack Obama’s White House, said: “Anyone who says that they were not surprised is lying. This busted all of the models across all demographics and geography. You would think that 2024 was the last century, not just two years ago.”

Why did Maga fall apart so fast, and in such colossal fashion? The short answer is that costs, corruption and conflict with Iran left Trump supporters feeling betrayed.

Frank Luntz, a veteran pollster and strategist, hosted a focus group on the eve of the election with people who voted for Trump in 2024, but would be voting for Democrats in 2026.

Affordability issues were “hurting Trump voters more than others because they are more likely to be paycheck-to-paycheck voters”, said Luntz. “They are more likely to have no money at the end of the week, and very little money at the end of the month, and so they were susceptible to food and fuel prices more than the average voter.”

“They were promised in 2024 that prices would come down, and we wouldn’t have forever wars, that we would drain the swamp,” Luntz added. “They looked in 2026 and they felt not nearly enough had been accomplished on this and so they wanted to punish Republicans. This is not about rewarding Democrats. This was about holding Republicans accountable for these voters believing what they were promised.”

Instead of focusing on the economic pressures hurting many of his own supporters, like farmers struggling to pay for diesel and fertiliser, Trump diverted his public commentary towards vanity projects, legal grievances and high-profile spats.

“He lost the plot,” according to Luntz. “He was talking about topics that they didn’t fully understand and didn’t care about. He wasn’t talking about the things that mattered most to them and in the end they took it out on the Republican party.”

Gaspard, a distinguished senior fellow at the Center for American Progress thinktank in Washington, agrees that the Maga coalition fractured because Trump violated every pledge made to working-class voters – from sweeping tariffs on foreign goods and an unpopular military conflict in Iran to cryptocurrency self-enrichment schemes and federal immigration overreach that terrorised local communities.

The result has broken the psychological chokehold Trump exerted over his party, Gaspard believes. “We’re seeing it already. When your approval hits the low 30s, politicians think about survival,” he said. “What happened creates a permission structure finally for Republicans to develop a spine to move away from him on their political choices, their policy choices and how they navigate their cultural choices as well.”

He added: “Donald Trump can’t act as if he wasn’t present at the scene of the crime. He personally picked the candidates in Texas and South Carolina. His fingerprints are all around it, and he can’t proclaim his innocence.”

Republicans lost most of Trump’s gains with Latino voters in 2024, according to an Associated Press voter poll, while only about one in 10 Black men voted Republican in their local House race, down from roughly one in four who backed Trump in 2024. Voters under 30, who had been roughly evenly divided between Trump and Kamala Harris two years ago, backed Democratic House candidates by about seven-to-three this time.

Gaspard noted that the collapse extended to Trump’s prized demographic strongholds: “When you end up in an election where the Republican party ended up splitting men 50/50 with Democrats, that is a death knell for the manosphere, the bro platforms that they saw as their firewalls.”

Some observers were quick to pronounce the death of Maga and the end of the Trump era. But the past decade of US politics has been characterised by whiplash elections with both parties lurching between triumph and disaster. Trump was written off after his defeat in 2020 only to bounce back four years later. He still has more than 800 days left in office.

Charlie Sykes, a conservative author and broadcaster, said: “Is this the end of Maga? No. As long as Donald Trump is in the White House, it’s still a danger. But it’s been badly wounded and, like a cornered ferret, it can still be quite dangerous. But this is a collapse of generational significance across the map and it has to deliver a massive shock to a Republican party that has been in thrall to Donald Trump for 10 years.”

Sykes, author of How the Right Lost Its Mind, added: “It takes a massive defeat like this for a political party to come to its senses. That’s what history tells us. It’s not because of op-ed pieces or commentators, or critical podcasts. It’s losing on this kind of epic level.”

The populist right may have lost some recent battles in Brazil, Serbia and Hungary, where close Maga ally Viktor Orbán was defeated, but it has hardly lost the war. From Argentina to India, its leaders remain in power, while in France, Germany and Britain its movements are challenging the established political order.

Bill Galston, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution thinktank in Washington, cautioned against assuming that the midterms marked the permanent demise of populist conservatism, comparing its persistence to illiberal movements in Europe.

He said: “I would hesitate to say that it’s the end of Maga, any more than the defeat of Viktor Orbán means the permanent defeat of illiberal democracy, any more than Donald Tusk’s comeback in Poland means that the forces arrayed against him have gone away.

“Maga has deep social roots in the American population. It expresses something that’s real and isn’t going away. But the question is whether it will be as dominant as it has been for more than a decade inside the Republican party in the United States and around the world. I think the answer to that question is no.”

Galston does believe that the midterms have created a vacuum within the Republican party and an opening for a reform candidate to challenge the Maga orthodoxy before 2028.

“These questions are never settled in the abstract,” he continued. “They’re settled when someone steps forward and says: ‘I stand for something different,’ and then convinces enough people that that is the right thing to stand for. That’s the way Donald Trump took the party away from the Reaganites.

“I don’t think we’re going back to the status quo ante, but is somebody going to stand up with a coherent counter-agenda? I don’t know who that would be but there’s a market opportunity.”

Trump responded to his humiliation at the ballot box like a man in denial. The following morning, he retreated to his safe space, the construction site of a new White House ballroom, and concentrated on signing a structural beam rather than addressing the electoral defeat. “Trump is still your president,” read an official White House social media post superimposed over an image of the 80-year-old, glowering into the camera.

But the race to succeed him has been blown wide open by the Republican debacle. Newt Gingrich, a former speaker of the House, wrote on social media: “The scale of the Republican defeat is so great that it makes the race for the GOP presidential nomination wide open.”

The biggest loser was the vice-president, JD Vance, who responded by posting an essay-length message on X, publicly identifying Trump’s deeply unpopular war in Iran as the catalyst for the defeat. “The reason we lost is the war,” he wrote in what many saw as a calculated move to align himself with rightwing podcasters – and to put daylight between himself and his boss.

Tara Setmayer, a former Republican communications director on Capitol Hill, said: “It’s going to be very challenging for JD Vance, because he’s hitched his wagon to Donald Trump so closely as his vice-president. But he’s going to try: he’s a professional political chameleon. I don’t think he has the chops to do it. He’s not very good at this.”

Other Republican contenders for 2028 could include DeSantis; Marco Rubio, the secretary of state; Nikki Haley, the former US ambassador to the United Nations; Utah governor Spencer Cox; and former Virginia governor Glenn Youngkin. Winning the nomination may depend on harnessing Maga populism while also presenting a new vision.

“Trump is a toxic brand, underwater with every demographic, including his own base,” added Setmayer. “It’s fair to say it’s the end of Maga as we know it under Donald Trump. Be prepared for it to morph into something else with the same basic foundation.”

For Democrats, the challenge meanwhile will be to turn an anti-Trump coalition into a positive political programme. The midterms highlighted a new wave of young, dynamic leaders including Talarico in Texas, Jon Ossoff in Georgia and Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan, a progressive and the first Muslim elected to the Senate. His victory could encourage the representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez to throw her hat into the ring in 2028.

Galston believes that the sweeping wins across deep-red states have effectively rendered traditional debates over candidate “electability” obsolete in the upcoming Democratic primary contest.

“There was something for everyone,” he said. “The arguments over electability have been mooted because it turns out that different kinds of Democrats can win in different kinds of places. That’s good news because, rather than shadow-boxing about electability, Democrats can actually have the discussion that they need substantively.”

They will be aware that Trump has an unearthly survival instinct. He has weathered controversies, impeachments, assassination attempts, criminal charges and electoral defeats and is not yet halfway through his second term. But this week’s national reckoning suggests that, after pulling off a comeback for the ages in 2024, he has squandered his last shreds of political capital.

Back in Round Rock in Texas, the epicentre of this week’s electoral tremors, there was little sympathy for the president.

On Main Street, Billy Joe Wilson, 47, who was wearing a long beard, tattooed arms and a bright yellow T-shirt, said: “The guy’s given us six years now of who he is and we keep believing him, and yet everything he says is going the opposite way: gas is up, diesel is up, cost of goods is up. Our economy’s hurting.”

Wilson, who runs bars and restaurants in the area, added: “Texas was a big supporter of the Republican party and Trump. But my generation got tired of realising that we’re getting screwed in the deal. We want to make sure that our kids or grandkids are set up to be successful, not living under a rule where the rich eat the poor.”

The PM’s small measures aim to help the public take back control – and we know how powerful that can be

The Guardian Sat, 07 Nov 2026 06:00:05 GMT

E-bikes, noisy headphones, flytipping: Burnham is weighing in on areas that make a difference to how people feel about life

Imagine waking up one morning to find a humiliating video of you, filmed without your knowledge or control, plastered all over social media. Maybe you were sweating at the gym; or maybe at work, in a bar, or walking down the street, where you never realised the stranger hassling you for your number was covertly filming for his social media channel dedicated to shaming women who won’t date him.

This week ministers hinted at a potential crackdown on so-called pervert glasses, wifi-enabled spectacles that let the wearer capture video of people around them, after multiple reports of men using them to harass women. (Though a small flashing light on the frame is meant to warn that the user is filming, it’s easily missed and worryingly easily disabled.) If so, it would be a small win, admittedly, in the context of what feels like an endless losing battle against big tech. But it would give young women back some small sense of control in life, and that matters perhaps more than we think.

When Andy Burnham declared war last month on people listening to loud music on the bus without headphones, he was mocked for fiddling while Rome burns. What next, jail time for finishing off the milk and putting the empty carton carefully back in the fridge? But if anything, the prime minister has since doubled down on sweating the small stuff. In a week in which unknown forces have been disrupting food supplies and grounding flights across Europe, Burnham found time to weigh in personally over thoughtless idiots abandoning hire bikes in the middle of city pavements – a genuine problem for blind people and people trying to get round them with pushchairs or wheelchairs, but usually the sort of crackdown left to junior ministers – and on the attempt to save Poundland shops for the nation. It wasn’t until I spoke to the former Starmer strategist Claire Ainsley about her new book, Control: How We Lost it and How to Take it Back, that something clicked into place: all these policies are about exerting control, in situations where we feel it’s been taken away from us.

In the book, she writes that the classic advice given to people in anxious times is to focus on what you can do – small things over which everyone has mastery – and worry about the rest later, when you can ideally tackle it in a calmer frame of mind. And that’s essentially how Burnham is approaching Britain, an anxious country with much to be anxious about currently. There may be little its prime minister can realistically do about Donald Trump (that’s one for American voters, who made a promising start this week), Vladimir Putin, oil prices or a stock market slump that may or may not herald the beginning of the AI bubble bursting. But combating small acts of selfishness, that make a surprisingly big subliminal difference to how people feel about their lives, their high streets, the public realm through which they move, are very much in his wheelhouse.

The freedom to just unlock a Lime bike and cycle away undoubtedly changed city life for the better, but with it came a whiff of anarchy. Hire bike riders have earned their reputation for jumping red lights, zooming along pavements, knocking over pedestrians and abandoning their bikes wherever it suits them when they’re done. But transport secretary Heidi Alexander’s consultation will also look at illegal and antisocial riding, picking up on persistent reports from outside big cities of something darker and more intimidating; packs of balaclava-wearing young men burning through housing estates on dirt bikes and e-scooters that aren’t legal on roads, yelling abuse at anyone trying to stop them, fuelling a sense that the police have lost control of the neighbourhood. This kind of antisocial behaviour isn’t new – 20 years ago it was teenage joyriders stealing cars – but when it leaves parents feeling it’s not safe to take their kids to the park, it’s corrosive on a much deeper level. In parliament recently, the Darlington MP Lola McEvoy described illegal e-bike riders running amok in her constituency as a “visible degradation of our collective social contract”.

The summer’s crackdown on fly-tipping, again personally fronted by the prime minister, fits a similar pattern: his new Makerfield constituency was home for years to an illegal dump full of rotting, rat-infested rubbish that despite his best efforts the previous MP Josh Simons couldn’t get anyone in authority to shift, until it caught fire and a nearby primary school had to close. In her book, Ainsley quotes Simons describing the first year in office for many new Labour MPs as “a crash course in state failure”.

If all Andy Burnham can ultimately offer the country is petty crackdowns while the world goes to hell in a handcart, then his project is doomed to fail. (Keir Starmer used to talk before the last election about small steps to win back the confidence of voters angry with politicians, and look what happened to him.) But “take back control” was a powerful slogan for Vote Leave for good reason. If Labour could somehow creatively reinterpret it to mean a country where the state actually works, big tech can no longer operate with no thought for the human consequences, predators don’t have licence to behave as they please and pensioners have a fighting chance of making it down a pavement – well, isn’t that what we used to call governing?

From Rise of the Rockstar Chefs to La Bola Negra: the week in rave reviews

The Guardian Sat, 07 Nov 2026 06:00:04 GMT

Gordon Ramsay and Marco Pierre White reunite to beef it out, while the poetic Spanish saga recounts the hidden history of gay sexuality. Here’s the pick of the week’s culture, taken from the Guardian’s best-rated reviews

BBC iPlayer; available now

Summed up in a sentence After detailing their journeys to culinary stardom and their infamous feud, Marco Pierre White and Gordon Ramsay are reunited to beef it out (and Heston Blumenthal is there, too). From Wild Horse Nine to Kings of Leon: your complete entertainment guide for the week ahead

The Guardian Sat, 07 Nov 2026 06:00:04 GMT

John Malkovich and Sam Rockwell team up in a typically offbeat Martin McDonagh comedy, and the Followill brothers reach album No 10 in rustic mode

Wild Horse Nine Out now John Malkovich looks set to be nominated for an Oscar for his portrayal of an ageing CIA agent with terminal cancer who is sent to Easter Island with his younger colleague (Sam Rockwell) in this dark comedy drama from Martin McDonagh (The Banshees of Inisherin).

La Bola Negra Out now Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi were inspired by Lorca’s unfinished four-page fragment of the same name to create this epic Spanish queer drama spanning three timelines, with an international cast including singer-songwriter Guitarricadelafuente, Penélope Cruz and Glenn Close.

I Play Rocky Out now Back in 1975, a struggling actor by the name of Sylvester Stallone wasn’t getting the parts he wanted – so he gave himself three days to write a juicy role. The result was Rocky and the character was so good he had to fight to play it. Anthony Ippolito stars as Stallone in this feelgood dramatisation of the story behind one of cinema’s most famous roles.

One in a Million Out now Winner of the audience award at the Sundance film festival, this documentary follows a girl across an extraordinary decade in her life: from her childhood in Syria to adult life in Germany. Directed by Itab Azzam and Jack MacInnes. Catherine Bray

Simple Things festival Various venues, Bristol, 7 November For the first time in its 12-year history, Bristol’s festival celebrating boundary-pushing music has employed guest curators in the shape of Squid, Shabaka, Jeremy Deller and Cobrah. Alongside their picks are the likes of Hannah Diamond, My New Band Believe and the Avalanches. Michael Cragg

London jazz festival Various venues, 13 to 22 November This ever imaginative 10-day festival’s opening night includes spectaculars such as the star-packed John Coltrane centenary celebration (Barbican Hall) and vocal showcase Jazz Voice (Royal Festival Hall), while small-band gems such as saxophonist Jean Toussaint’s JT5 (also Friday, World Heart Beat Embassy Gardens) will be happening all over town. John Fordham

SBTV20 The O2, London, Wednesday The great and the good of the UK grime scene will appear at this 20th-anniversary celebration of the pioneering music platform SBTV. The event, which features Chip, Ms Banks and Tinie Tempah, will also honour the legacy of SBTV’s founder, Jamal Edwards MBE, who died in 2022. MC

Elgar’s Dream of Gerontius The Glasshouse, Gateshead, 8 November The epic oratorio at the heart of the 2025 film The Choral is a blockbuster even without Ralph Fiennes and co. The Royal Northern Sinfonia, local amateurs and a vast choir perform this choral favourite with top-flight soloists Sarah Connolly, Benjamin Hulett and Roderick Williams. Dinis Sousa conducts. Flora Willson

Constantinople to Istanbul: One City, Two Empires V&A, London, 7 November to 9 May This big, ambitious exhibition looks at 1,600 years of art, design, antiquities and rarities such as the 11th-century Enkolpion of Constantinos, from a city that acts as a cultural bridge between Europe and Asia, east and west, and Islam and Christianity.

Georg Wilson Gainsborough’s House, Sudbury, 8 November to 18 April Young painter Georg Wilson takes an ecological, folkloric, atmospheric approach to landscape painting, which means she should fit in perfectly in the historic surrounds of Thomas Gainsborough’s old gaff.

Ade Adesina City Art Centre, Edinburgh, 7 November to 11 April Aberdeen-based printmaker Ade Adesina uses woodcuts, etchings, linocuts and screenprints to tackle big themes of colonial history and the climate crisis, all with dramatic starkness and intense detail.

Katie Shannon Goldsmith’s Centre for Contemporary Art, London, to 13 December The latest artist to take over GCCA’s experimental Episodes series, where they give a platform to young creatives, is Katie Shannon, with a new body of work looking at lost musical histories and “feminist rereadings of time and space”. Eddy Frankel

The Adam and Joe Show Royal Albert Hall, London, 11 November; Beacon Hall, Bristol, 5 December It has been 30 years since Buxton and Cornish’s cult comedy series was first broadcast. To celebrate, the duo revisit its highlights – toy movies; BaaadDad et al. Rachel Aroesti

Cloud 9 National Theatre: Lyttelton, London, to 13 January Dominic Cooke revives Caryl Churchill’s typically inventive, time-bending, mind-boggling play. It begins in Victorian colonial Africa then jumps to 70s London, with the cast performing theatrical gymnastics along the way. Miriam Gillinson

Owain & Henry Wales Millennium Centre: Donald Gordon theatre, Cardiff, to 28 November Michael Sheen stars as Owain Glyndŵr, a Welsh lord who rebelled against Henry IV after being declared an outlaw. Written by Olivier winner Gary Owen with a cast including Sophie Melville, Linus Roache and Rakie Ayola. MG

Humanhood: Vortex Sadler’s Wells East, London, 10 to 14 November Hypnotic movement from the Birmingham-Barcelona-based duo Humanhood and their company. Artistic directors Julia Robert and Rudi Cole have developed a method that’s somewhere between dance and a spiritual practice. Lyndsey Winship

Sign up to Inside Saturday

The only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.

after newsletter promotion

12 12 12 Apple TV, 13 November A heist: 12 months to plan, 12 hours to execute and 12 days to see whether you’ve got away with it. That’s according to this neat, numbersy cat-and-mouse thriller starring Jamie Dornan as the criminal mastermind behind a Zurich bank vault robbery and Anthony Mackie as the FBI agent on his tail.

Hunting Alice Bell Channel 4, 11 November, 9pm The Guardian’s film critic Peter Bradshaw and his schoolmate David Baddiel once co-starred in a sitcom; now they’ve reunited to create this internet vigilante thriller about a group of women who are all rumoured to be the accomplice of an infamous serial killer (Simon Pegg) living under a new identity.

The Good Daughter Sky Atlantic & Now, 12 November, 9pm Rose Byrne lends her exceptional acting chops to Karin Slaughter’s own adaptation of her characteristically disturbing 2017 novel about the secret truths behind a horrific attack that continues to haunt two sisters. Brendan Gleeson and The White Lotus’s Meghann Fahy also star.

Cunk on Cinema BBC Two & iPlayer, 12 November, 10pm It has been 13 years since “computer typist” Philomena Cunk first appeared as a talking head on Charlie Brooker’s Weekly Wipe; since then Diane Morgan’s alter ego has found fame as a very confused documentarian. Her latest series sees her grill doyens of the film industry in bewildering style. RA

The Devil’s Due PC; out 10 November It’s a classic story: you’ve lost a card game with the devil, and now you must make your way out of hell by defeating all of his minions at poker. Inventive cheating and a characterful collage-esque look make this a trip to hell worth considering.

Shrek 2: Remastered All platforms; out 10 November I’m not sure anyone expected this rerelease of the 2004 movie tie-in, which was surprise-announced just a few weeks ago, but it’s here to capitalise on the run of Shrek nostalgia that has already resulted in an immersive experience, a musical and several Shrek-themed raves. Keza MacDonald

Kings of Leon – O My Beloved Out now On their 10th album, the Followills get reflective. Self-produced, rustic and rooted in nostalgia, O My Beloved looks back at their career, their family life and the moments that shaped them, with the sweet, country-tinged My Whole World a painting of domestic bliss.

Shygirl – Swallow! Out now The artist born Blane Muise channels the likes of the Prodigy, William Orbit-era Madonna and the more interesting aspects of indie on this second album. Songs such as lead single Alyse also bolt on plush string arrangements, creating a sound that feels both decadent and dirty.

Skepta – The Fork and Knife Out now Seven years after his last album, the rapper and producer returns with a record rooted in the sounds of modern Britain. Absorbing everything from grime to house to jungle, its lyrics explore identity and strength via tracks such as the dark-hued Pandora’s Box, while the Fred Again-produced Victory Lap is pure party.

La Roux – Old Flames Out now Never one to be rushed, 00s electropop survivor Elly Jackson, AKA La Roux, follows up 2020’s occasionally brittle Supervision with this warmer album. The minimalist throb of Babyline stands out on a record focused on fresh starts. MC

Talking Common Podcast This engaging new series from author Josh Connolly departs from the usual self-help format and looks for answers to personal problems in community solutions. Guests include the musician Sonny Green on breaking the generational cycle of addiction issues.

International Intrigue Online This daily newsletter briefing from former diplomats is one of the most concise and thorough rundowns of complex geopolitical issues available. Recent topics feature the race for a new UN chief and the EU’s Arctic Strategy.

The Life Scientific BBC World Service, Monday, 8.32pm Associate professor of chemistry Asel Sartbaeva reveals how her research into silica materials has the potential to free lifesaving vaccines from needing to be constantly refrigerated and therefore reducing their risk of becoming spoiled in transit. Blind date: ‘I told her I don’t like the theatre. In retrospect, I can see why a playwright would be offended’

The Guardian Sat, 07 Nov 2026 06:00:02 GMT

William, 28, a PhD candidate, meets Abigail, 24, a theatre artist

What were you hoping for? To have a spark of some kind.

First impressions? She looked very glamorous and suited the smart restaurant far more than I did.

What did you talk about? Our love of Robert Pattinson. The play she’s working on. Shucking oysters. She asked lots of questions, so I’m worried I dominated. She did a palm reading on me too and it said I’m not a good writer.

Most awkward moment? When I told her I don’t like theatre. In retrospect, I can see why a playwright and actor would be offended by that.

Good table manners? I’m gonna go for “impeccable”. She was very friendly and chatty to the staff too.

Best thing about Abigail? She has a lovely smile and a great sense of humour. I laughed a lot.

Would you introduce Abigail to your friends? Lots of my friends are performers, so they would have loads to talk about.

Blind date is Saturday’s dating column: every week, two strangers are paired up for dinner and drinks, and then spill the beans to us, answering a set of questions. This runs, with a photograph we take of each dater before the date, in Saturday magazine (in the UK) and online at theguardian. com every Saturday. It’s been running since 2009 – you can read all about how we put it together here. What questions will I be asked?We ask about age, location, occupation, hobbies, interests and the type of person you are looking to meet. If you do not think these questions cover everything you would like to know, tell us what’s on your mind.

Can I choose who I match with?No, it’s a blind date! But we do ask you a bit about your interests, preferences, etc – the more you tell us, the better the match is likely to be.

Can I pick the photograph?No, but don't worry: we'll choose the nicest ones.

What personal details will appear?Your first name, job and age.

How should I answer?Honestly but respectfully. Be mindful of how it will read to your date, and that Blind date reaches a large audience, in print and online.

Will I see the other person’s answers?No. We may edit yours and theirs for a range of reasons, including length, and we may ask you for more details.

Will you find me The One?We’ll try! Marriage! Babies!

Can I do it in my home town?Only if it’s in the UK. Many of our applicants live in London, but we would love to hear from people living elsewhere.

How to applyEmail blind. date@theguardian. com

Describe Abigail in three words Funny, kind-hearted, genuine.

What do you think Abigail made of you? I hope she thought I was kind and easy to talk to. I realised I wasn’t making much eye contact at one point, so “awkward” may be a safer bet. Funny would be a lovely addition.

Did you go on somewhere? We stayed at the restaurant until closing. Then she walked me back to King’s Cross so I could catch a train back to Cambridge, which was very kind.

And … did you kiss? I would never say.

If you could change one thing about the date, what would it be? I forgot the bathroom was a push door and thought I had locked myself in.

Marks out of 10? 9/10.

Would you meet again? We’ve shared numbers.

What were you hoping for? Love, obviously.

First impressions? Polite, gentle. Nervous in a sweet way. He was very concerned about being underdressed, but he looked lovely.

What did you talk about? Standup comedy. Socialism. Academia. His disdain for contemporary British theatre and my adoration of it.

Most awkward moment? He seemed keen to show off his American accent at a few points.

Good table manners? Yes, knows his way round a wine list too!

Best thing about William? He has lived a fantastically varied life of travels and extracurriculars. It’s good to meet people who have life by the horns.

Would you introduce William to your friends? I’d consider it. But he said he loves lying to strangers. That gives a woman pause.

Describe William in three words Charming, roguish, amiable.

What do you think William made of you? I gave him a flirty palm reading and I’m worried he thinks I’ve got a hand fetish.

Did you go on somewhere? I don’t kiss and tell …

And … did you kiss? … see above.

If you could change one thing about the date, what would it be? I would have stolen his gorgeous thick-rimmed emerald green glasses.

Marks out of 10? 7/10.

Would you meet again? I fear his love line looked a bit unsteady. But he’s got my phone number if he’d like to tempt fate.

Abigail and William ate at Kobe, London W1. Fancy a blind date? Email blind. date@theguardian. com

Freezer meltdowns and airline hoaxes are a taste of things to come. Hoping for the best is no longer an option

The Guardian Sat, 07 Nov 2026 05:00:02 GMT

Acts of greyzone aggression aim to spread panic. Europe has to show the saboteurs that we are resilient

It was as though a ghostly hand had switched the settings on supermarket freezers across Europe from “freeze” to “defrost”. From Finland to Ireland, they suddenly began heating up, many reaching 50C and food worth millions of euros had to be thrown away. But no actual hand was needed to cause the meltdown. This was a cyber-attack, or rather a chain of attacks. Like pretty much everything else in 2026, supermarket freezers are digitally enabled. That makes them smarter and more efficient, but like everything else that is connected to the internet, it also makes them more vulnerable.

Russian hacktivists claimed they were behind some of the supermarket sabotage, but no one knows for sure. It could also be Iran, Iranian proxies, North Korea – or unaffiliated bedroom hackers. When Transport for London suffered a devastating hack two years ago, the culprits turned out to be two British teenagers. Governments regularly warn retailers and other companies about cyber-attacks and even provide cyber-defence training to businesses. The lessons of costly ransomware and cyber-attacks also mean many big organisations and retailers have become much better at keeping their payments and logistics systems safe.

But freezers present a new vulnerability. In Sweden, for example, some of the stores that were attacked this week hadn’t connected their freezers to national retailers’ systems, which have centralised protection. Now they’ve learned their lesson the hard way.

Hybrid warfare – or, to use the defence term, greyzone aggression – refers to an array of hostile acts by a country’s adversaries that fall short of full-on military conflict. Cyber-hackers also this week attempted to meddle with fridges at French blood banks, while hoax bomb threats forced commercial airliners across Europe to divert, make emergency landings or require fighter jet escort to safety.

This comes after at least two years of sporadic Kremlin-suspected arson attacks on factories, explosives-laden drones flown into airports and drone incursions into countries’ airspace. There is constant GPS interference in the skies around the Baltic Sea, highly suspicious damage to subsea cables and pipelines, disinformation spread by bot farms and repeated acts of cyber-aggression.

Saboteurs and hackers usually have two aims: the first is to disrupt, but they also want to psychologically destabilise the target societies by spreading fear. It is fortunate then that the aviation hoaxes and freezer incidents coincide with a renewed conversation across Europe about resilience. It is as if the hackers wanted to showcase the need for preparedness projects such as the UK government’s new Be Ready campaign, which launched last month.

The British campaign, which instructs people on such things as stockpiling for emergencies whether caused by climate change or state-sponsored terrorism, had been in the works for months. Ministers hesitated however, fearing that citizens would respond with cynicism or ridicule, or just wouldn’t follow the advice.

Such campaigns are commonplace elsewhere. Earthquake zones such as Tokyo and San Francisco have had them for decades. “Make a Plan. Gather Supplies. Get Connected. Get Trained,” are the San Francisco city government’s pillars of instruction.

The newest version of Sweden’s official booklet In Case of Crisis or War, distributed to every home since 2018, is even more comprehensive, with clear language about everything from civil defence duties, how to volunteer (give blood or team up with neighbours for mutual support), to what items always to have at home, and how to find out if a crisis is real or a fake warning by bots.

For several years, I have been calling on the UK to follow Sweden’s lead and send a similar instruction leaflet to UK households, only to be told by officials that doing so would cause too much panic and frighten people. A House of Lords committee heard from the chair of the UK National Preparedness Commission in March that “the bulk of the UK population is blissfully unaware” of some of the risks they face.

It turns out that British people are less cynical than their leaders had assumed. Perhaps a few minds were also changed by Covid-19, which dramatically illustrated how vulnerable globalised and open societies are to all manner of threats.

Sign up to This is Europe

The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment

after newsletter promotion

Either way, within a week of the Be Ready campaign launching, the retailer Robert Dyas reported that weekly sales of radios had shot up by 160%. Maplin reported that sales of radios had nearly doubled and sales of power banks had more than doubled, while torch sales had soared to nearly four times the usual figure.

The puddles of defrosted ice in the supermarket aisles and stress for air travellers this week show that we need to be prepared for a very wide range of threats including power and water outages. We have already seen what happens to our complex food supply chains when global shipping lanes are suddenly disrupted. Iran’s obstruction of the strait of Hormuz following US airstrikes has given us painful food inflation and costly global oil and fertiliser shortages.

But what if the ships importing the food we eat can no longer make it to our ports? No industrialised nation grows all the food it consumes. What if the internet goes down? It’s not impossible. Even companies with the best cyber defence could fall victim to sabotage of the subsea data cables that transmit nearly all our connectivity.

This week has been a nasty preview of what could happen in future with alarming regularity. Severe disruption will come our way so simply hoping for the best is not an option. The good news is that by accepting that we need to prepare, and demonstrating that we remain strong in times of crisis, we can signal to Vladimir Putin and other rogue actors that disrupting our services is unwelcome, but ultimately it is futile.

Elisabeth Braw is a Swedish security expert and the author of The Undersea War: The International Battle for Supremacy at the Bottom of the World
