What’s the point? Ten years after the Paris treaty, are climate talks getting anywhere?

The Guardian Sat, 07 Nov 2026 05:00:02 GMT

Its key temperature goal has been missed but experts say the agreement is still proving a vital moral compass for progress

It was a curious way of conducting negotiations. Ahead of the 2025 climate summit, in the Amazonian port of Belém last year, the Brazilian hosts had taken off the table the issue that most had assumed would be at its heart: concrete plans from each country laying out exactly what they would be doing to cut their greenhouse gas emissions.

Brazil was insisting, instead, that these plans – the bedrock of the Paris agreement – were the business of national governments and not up for negotiation. “In that case, it will be a very short Cop,” one seasoned global south negotiator told the Guardian shortly before, reflecting a widespread unease. “There is nothing to negotiate.”

“They have decided that there is no appetite for negotiation, with the US out of Paris,” said another developing country diplomat. “Countries won’t engage.”

The summit ended with a deal, although few loved it. But, as the faultlines from the Brazilian decision deepen going into this year’s summit, it is clear that the Paris agreement, and climate action around the world, has reached an impasse.

And it is not just Cop insiders who are worried. For many outside the vast white air-conditioned conference halls, the question, as this year’s summit begins, will be: what is the point?

Those same governments have pledged year after year since the Paris agreement was signed in 2015 – and entered into force a year later – to limit global heating to 1.5C above preindustrial levels. Yet temperatures for two years have exceeded that threshold, and the UN revealed a few weeks ago that its most optimistic estimate was now for about 1.7 to 1.8C of heating.

There could be no clearer evidence that the Paris agreement, on the face of it, has failed. It is impossible not to wonder whether the Cop process itself is just not fit for purpose.

The charge sheet against Paris is long, with the central issue being the failure to achieve its goal. Beyond that immediate failure, the negotiation processes are endlessly convoluted and cause their own problems. It took more than five years just to negotiate the Paris “rulebook” under which the treaty is interpreted and put into effect.

The convention that all resolutions must pass by consensus has given bad actors free rein. Donald Trump’s allies – in Saudi Arabia, Russia, Venezuela and some other petrostates – frequently veto measures and obstruct progress.

It took more than 30 years of negotiation since the UN framework convention on climate change was signed in 1992 for fossil fuels even to be addressed directly. This was at Cop28 in Dubai in 2023, where countries agreed for the first time to “transition away from fossil fuels” but failed to set a timeframe or any policies to back up the resolution.

The US, the world’s biggest economy and responsible for about one in every eight tonnes of carbon dioxide emitted today, has withdrawn from Paris under President Trump.

Even parts of the developed world which support the process have mostly failed to come up with convincing plans: Australia, co-host of Cop31, has set no end to fossil fuel exports; its fellow co-host Turkey plans to increase its carbon output. The UK is opening a gasfield and mulling a new oilfield, Germany has dropped its electric vehicle sales targets and scrapped a renewable heating law. Meanwhile, most rich countries are reducing their contributions to climate finance for the poor.

Most of all, the slow pace of the Paris timetable might have seemed fine in 2015, when temperatures were rising at 0.2C a decade. Today, the rate of rise is 0.4C a decade and still accelerating.

“The structures of Cops and Paris are labyrinthine, bureaucratic, and ultimately dispiriting,” said Paul Bledsoe, a former Clinton White House climate adviser, now with the American University. “It may be time to streamline them to focus more deliberately on national emissions reduction goals.”

As ordinary people watch these failures outside and inside the process, some are losing faith. The Paris agreement was a sensation, celebrated around the world. In the years since, the aura of Cop has faded, as meetings seem to disintegrate into arguments over wording and compromise.

“A lot of the commitments, the promises that were made, just turned out to be a bunch of hot air,” said Juan Carlos Monterrey, former climate envoy for Panama, now chief executive of the Vanglabs consultancy. “Under that measure, we have failed.”

Johan Rockström, director of the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research, said: “The fact that global warming is accelerating, that we inevitably will be breaching the 1.5C limit within three to five years, that tipping points are coming closer fast, that Earth’s resilience is showing worrying signs of decline, and that we still allow ourselves to follow a global path that will take us to a catastrophic 2.6C-3C, and that this is allowed to happen within the framework of the Paris agreement, cannot be considered as anything but a global failure.”

But, like most involved in international climate efforts, both refuse to concede that Paris is done for. “On the other hand,” said Rockström, “Paris is all we have. And we know that the global climate crisis can only, in the end, be solved if all countries in the world simultaneously move away from planet-damaging heat injection.”

Monterrey agrees. The most important fact about the Paris agreement, and the Cop process, he says, is that they exist. “Paris is our moral compass. It has told us where we should go. The speed of travel is not what it needs to be, but Paris has set the direction.”

This year’s Cop is the first to have a split presidency and host. Being held in Turkey but presided over by Australia, Cop31 is a messy compromise between two countries whose other chief point of commonality is an admiration for coal.

Unexpectedly, however, the skies are a little brighter over this year’s meeting than anyone might have expected. Brazil has decisively re-elected Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva who has already overseen the biggest reductions in deforestation for decades.

The US midterms delivered a drubbing for the right, while in Serbia and Hungary this year democracy has won out over authoritarianism. Though the far right is still on the march across much of Europe, and autocrats still rule in most of the countries with the biggest fossil fuel industries and highest emissions, the replacement or weakening of anti-climate authoritarians by pro-climate parties is a positive sign. Globally, a large majority of people support climate action.

Action beyond the framework of Cop is marching on. After the failure of last year’s Cop30 in Brazil to provide a strong statement on phasing out fossil fuels, a group of nearly 60 countries held an alternative meeting in Colombia in April and agreed to draw up their own national roadmaps for the “transition away from fossil fuels”.

Three major countries have so far done so: France, Germany and the Netherlands. Bledsoe wants to use this model for more side agreements on the “super pollutants” such as methane, refrigerant chemicals called HFCs, ground-level ozone, nitrous oxide and black carbon, or soot.

Cutting methane by 40% could alone hold down temperatures by about 0.3C in the next decade, and deeper cuts beyond that could yield a 0.5C decrease by 2100.

“Paris was never intended to do all the hard work itself,” Bledsoe said. “We need to use the G7, the G20 and other forums too, and we need to elevate the climate to the level of national security concern, and see it as an economic threat.”

While the failures of Paris might seem obvious, its “moral compass” has also translated into greater success in the real world than many people realise.

“The solar panels on my roof and the BYD Dolphin [electric car] my neighbour drives are exhibit one and exhibit two of Paris’s success,” said Claudio Angelo, of the Observatório do Clima thinktank. “Will Paris prevent overshoot of 1.5C? No way. Will it prevent 2C of warming? Unlikely. But the transformation it has triggered can’t be exaggerated.”

Perhaps the clinching argument lies in China, the world’s biggest emitter of greenhouse gases and second-largest economy.

“China is taking multilateral climate efforts more seriously than many other countries, and certainly more seriously than it did a few years ago,” said Li Shuo, director of the China climate hub at the Asia Society Policy Institute. “The reason is simple: its economic stakes have grown enormously. If the world abandons decarbonisation, where will China sell its solar panels and electric vehicles?”

And, stung by high fossil fuel prices, many developing-country consumers are grasping clean technology without waiting for assistance. In Pakistan, plagued by blackouts and grid supply issues, rooftop solar panels have taken off, now making up about a quarter of electricity use in the country. Similarly, drivers in Vietnam are increasingly opting for cheap electric vehicles from China, which now make up more than 40% of its car sales.

Meanwhile, the conference hosts themselves, from unpromising beginnings, have brought forward one of the biggest new ideas in the last decade for putting the world on track to lower emissions – changing fuel sources for cars and heating to electricity. The electricity should be from clean sources where possible – but its efficiency means that even if the energy source is fossil-based, it still uses less power.

Jan Rosenow, professor of energy and climate policy at Oxford University, estimates that the superior efficiency of electricity over fossil fuels will mean that the world’s total final energy use can be halved by switching to electric for everything – meaning we need to generate a lot less, too.

If countries can agree a target at Cop31 of deriving 35% of final energy use from electricity by 2035, up from 23% today, that would be a major boost to decarbonisation efforts. Adair Turner, former chair of the UK’s climate change committee and now co-chair of the Energy Transitions Commission thinktank, said: “Electrification is the single most important thing you have to do [to reach net zero emissions].”

Cops provide a place where countries can come together to share experiences, to seek advice, to find support and fellowship. “That’s very valuable,” said Ilana Seid, ambassador of Palau and chair of the Pacific Small Island Developing States. And in a world in which the bulk of current and future emissions, and fossil fuel production, comes from non-democracies or authoritarian states, Cops also provides one of the few forums where they can be held to account.

That “societal pressure” is crucial, said Seid. “We small islands and vulnerable nations are on the frontline. For us, this is existential. We are all very committed to Paris.”

After all, despite all the doubts, the power of a decision at Cop should not be underestimated. While “coalitions of the willing” are a “good thing” according to Nick Stern, the economist, the universality of the Paris agreement and Cops give them a unique authority.

Sue Biniaz, a former US climate negotiator, said: “Any time you have a consensus decision, it sends a signal to investors, to people who finance things, and to countries. I think that’s true these days with the geopolitics of the world – if something can be agreed by the whole world, it’s impactful.”

Cop31 may bring progress on electrification, on climate finance and on the transition that countries, rich and poor, need to make to a low-carbon world. But we already know that whatever the summit produces, it will not be enough.

However flawed yet substantive they are, Cops last only a fortnight, while efforts to tackle the climate crisis will require such wholesale transformation of our economies and societies that they should top governments’ agendas all year.

“Imagine you have lost your loved one without having their bodies to bring back home. Lost livelihood where you spent your whole life to accumulate those assets. We faced a horrific situation,” said Sujeeta Mathema, executive director of ActionAid Nepal, who was quickly on the scene to help people after the catastrophic glacier collapse there.

“It feels like living with grief, fear and uncertainty about the future. The devastation is not just physical; it is deeply emotional and psychological.”

People are traumatised, she says, and deeply feel the injustice of how the climate crisis is created by the rich while hurting the most vulnerable. But Cop can still be a place of hope, Mathema adds.

“Cop is an important space for us to raise our voice, clearly putting our agenda. Cop can help prevent such disasters if the commitments come off paper and are put into action.”

Russell Brand suspected to have attacked at least 10 other women

The Guardian Sat, 07 Nov 2026 00:00:47 GMT

Met police chief says ‘many more’ victims could come forward, as actor and comedian awaits sentencing

Police are bracing themselves for more victims of Russell Brand to come forward, with at least 10 more women suspected of having been attacked by the disgraced star.

Brand, 51, will be sentenced on Monday to what is expected to be a lengthy jail sentence for rape and sexual assaults after he abused his fame to become a “predator” targeting women, and got away with it for years.

The fallout from Brand’s case saw the government pledge to examine calls to crack down on “rape myths” in trials.

The Guardian also understands that next week the Metropolitan police team that built the case against Brand will start sifting through reports and intelligence about other potential victims.

The Met commissioner, Sir Mark Rowley, said there could be “many more” victims, but declined to say how many, with some intelligence about further victims being third-hand and some further suspected victims reluctant to face the criminal justice system.

Sources say it is feared the number of further victims is at least in “double digits”, with 10 currently seen as a minimum.

The Met police said on Thursday that Brand was under investigation for two further rape allegations. Detectives have sent files to specialist rape prosecutors and are in discussions with them over the material.

Rowley said: “We’ve got two other victims who’ve come forward who want to tell their story, and so two rape cases we’re investigating. I wouldn’t be surprised if many, many more come forward, and we’re open to that.”

Rowley declined on LBC Radio to confirm the new allegations would reach “double figures”, and said: “I’m not going to guess on this, but we’ve seen in the past with high-profile individuals who are brought to justice that it does often bring out a flood of other cases. Let’s see where this one goes.”

Brand’s trial, which spanned claims of attacks from 1999 to 2009, saw women asked by the defence barrister why they had not screamed during attacks.

Since the end of the trial there has been a debate about rape myths. A No 10 source said the prime minister, Andy Burnham, believed calls from the victims’ commissioner, Claire Waxman, for a legal duty that would require judges to issue directions to juries on rape myths and misconceptions, should be examined.

A Ministry of Justice spokesperson said: “Rape myths have absolutely no place in our courts and victims should never feel as though they are the ones on trial.

“Judges are already able to give directions to counter rape myths … we will also carefully consider the victims’ commissioner’s proposals as we continue to strengthen protections for victims.”

Siobhan Blake, the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) lead for rape and serious sexual offences, said: “The focus must be the actions of the perpetrator and not the behaviour of the victim.

“We know that there is no typical response to sexual assault and myths that victims should scream and fight back are outdated. Some people may freeze or feel unable to speak about it for months or even years, but this is not a barrier to justice.”

Brand now faces years of imprisonment and the growing prospect of a fresh trial over further allegations.

He was convicted on Thursday of raping a young fan at his luxury London townhouse in 2009, continuing despite her pleas for him to stop. He had picked her out of a crowd. He was also found guilty of sexually assaulting three women in separate incidents at a radio station, a recording studio and a bar.

Victims are expected to tell of the impact his crimes had on them in court on Monday.

Brand became an international star, acting in Hollywood films, and in latter years an online influencer, but was dogged by whispers and allegations about his danger to women. He was accused of treating women as a “disposable commodity” and a “means to an end” to satisfy his voracious sexual appetite.

The government says it is committed to reducing violence against women and girls by half.

Burnham told Times Radio: “It’s horrifying what Russell Brand has done. And I’d firstly like to praise the bravery of the women, the victims in the case, who’ve come forward and had the courage to speak out.

“But yes, the journalists too, who supported those who had been abused by Russell Brand. So all of them deserve our praise for having that courage to come forward.”

Later on the BBC, Burnham was asked about a statement of support for Brand in 2014 as the star faced media criticism, and said: “Well, over a decade ago, and all I can say is I had no idea of the full extent of what he was doing or what he went on to do. His crimes are horrific.”

Burnham told Times Radio he will look at making changes to rape trials so that they “do not leave the woman feeling like she is on trial”.

He said: “We need to constantly look at the way rape trials are conducted to make sure that they do not leave the woman feeling like she is on trial in court, as has been the experience of people in the past … we need to encourage more women to come forward to report rape.”

The comedian Katherine Ryan, who warned of a “predator” in the entertainment industry before Brand’s trial, said she felt relief at his conviction.

“They came forward despite Russell Brand having fame, power, money and a legion of fans ready to attack them,” she said.

“I will never be someone who, like, dances on graves. There has been some justice done today. There’s a level of relief, but there’s grief alongside relief.”

Bear Grylls, who baptised Brand when he converted to Christianity in 2024, said the star’s faith seemed genuine and added: “It is right that justice has now been served. I can’t imagine how hard this time has been for the victims, the heroes of the day.”

Brand was cleared of two further charges of rape and one allegation of attempted indecent assault.

Brand’s victims told how he “snapped” – changing from charming to nasty – as he raped and sexually assaulted them before gaslighting them into believing nothing was wrong.

The Guardian view on the AI backlash: Silicon Valley’s political power is cracking

The Guardian Fri, 06 Nov 2026 23:45:52 GMT

Tech stocks have lost trillions while voters have rejected the industry’s political champions. The billionaire-led boom is facing a democratic reckoning

This week’s midterms showed that the political bill for the AI boom is falling due. The Democratic sweep intensified fears over runaway spending, mounting debt and resistance to datacentres, sending tech shares tumbling. On Thursday Wall Street suffered its worst day since the pandemic as $3.2tn was wiped from markets. Anthropic, developer of the Claude chatbot, is hoping to float within the next fortnight for $1.5tn (£1.1tn), but it may not now get even a trillion dollars. The dominant AI chipmaker Nvidia saw its value crash by more than $400bn. The world’s richest man, Elon Musk, lost $113bn in two days.

While a few very rich people may be a little less wealthy, the sell-off may not be a bad thing. It brings a needed dose of reality to an industry whose spending plans and valuations depend on heroic expectations of future profits. That is a view held by many influential figures – from Goldman Sachs’ research boss to Nobel laureate Daron Acemoğlu. AI may transform the economy. That does not guarantee investors will earn back the sums being poured into it.

Donald Trump is the other big loser. He rejected concerns about AI and the need to impose stricter rules despite most Americans wanting more safeguards. He called concerns about the potential dangers of AI development a “hoax”. Republicans paid a price for his refusal to listen. Mr Trump argued computing capacity was a national asset that needed to expand rapidly, while dismissing resistance to the infrastructure and the companies building it. The US president was deaf to voter frustration over electricity prices, water demand and disruption. Democrats could campaign against those costs falling on residents while the gains went to tech billionaires and their companies, which donated money to Mr Trump’s favoured causes.

Mr Musk’s SpaceX, a combined space, satellite-connectivity and AI group, warned in its June 2026 prospectus that new regulations could derail its growth plans. He spent $200m in Texas for Republicans as Democrats took aim at AI datacentres in a state where there was rising voter discontent over the industry’s rapid expansion. Mr Musk could not buy this election. Democrats won a US senate seat, the state governorship and wiped out every other statewide Republican office, taking the Texas house with a comfortable margin. Across the US, the blue wave saw wins for Democrats who have been critical of datacentre construction and pledged to slow or pause their rollout.

Democrats say they intend to make AI companies answerable for the environmental and societal costs of their infrastructure buildup as well as the harm their products cause. The new Congress is likely to be much more ready to shield voters from rising prices caused by datacentre expansion, ensure independent safety testing for advanced AI and clarify liability for possible harms. Democrats’ willingness to take public fears about AI seriously is welcome. People need confidence that elected governments can protect their livelihoods and communities.

Whatever happens to tech stocks, the genie of AI won’t be put back into its lamp. This year alone the technology was given as the reason 120,000 Americans lost their jobs. Politicians ought to strengthen workers’ bargaining power and ensure that productivity gains are fairly shared. Just letting the markets decide will only deepen the economic insecurity and political distrust that is corroding democracy.

Five Great Reads: What now for Trump, a cruise from hell, and manhood enhancements

The Guardian Fri, 06 Nov 2026 21:06:45 GMT

The Guardian’s weekend wrap of essential reads from the past seven days, selected by Miles Herbert and Jacqui Housden

Get this in your inbox every weekend. Sign up for Five Great Reads here

Hello and welcome to the weekend.

We went big this week. In this selection of reads from across the Guardian, big wins are dissected, big questions are asked, big bowls are taste-tested and dreams of being bigger are realised. Enjoy.

A blue wave has swept through the US. In what appears a remarkable repudiation of Trumpism, voters handed Democrats control over the House of Representatives and the Senate. Our Washington DC bureau chief, David Smith, called it an “extinction-level event” and one famous Democrat proclaimed it was “morning again in America”.

But how will Trump and the Republican party respond to having his power diminished to a veto pen? Will it eat away at his “cult-like” control over the GOP, and will conservatives conclude Trump is now a creature of the political past?

​What happens next? Come January, Democrats will have the power to significantly impede Trump’s agenda. Progressive lawmakers will be “a bulwark against Trump’s expansion of executive power”, with the ability to block legislation in Congress as well as launch investigations into Trump’s family business and the Epstein files.

​Notable quote: “A wounded Trump who feels he has nothing to lose over the next two years might turn out to be the most reckless and dangerous of all.” – David Smith

​How long will it take to read: Two minutes.

​Further reading: Why Democrats turned towards the politics of affordability, and the Republicans hopeful of succeeding Trump read through the tea leaves.

The recent rise in diagnoses of autism has brought with it a heated debate. From supposed “overdiagnosis” to whether some people are prioritised over others, the controversy has become a new front in the culture wars. But what do the experts make of it all? John Harris sat down with some key figures to find out.

Different conclusions: Dame Uta Frith, who helped come up with the accepted understanding of autism, once agreed with the idea of a broad autistic spectrum; now she has come to the conclusion that many people diagnosed as adults are different from those whose condition was obvious in their early years. “Some of them, I think, are being wrongly influenced by social media to believe that they’re autistic, because it’s a possible way to explain your difficulties,” she tells Harris. Another expert, Simon Baron-Cohen, now thinks the catch-all term “autistic spectrum disorder” – or “autistic spectrum condition” – is proving increasingly problematic.

But there is strong disagreement: One is from Mary Doherty, an Irish anaesthetist and one of the founders of Autistic Doctors International, who believes there is potential harm done by “invalidating people’s life experience”. “If you are autistic, understanding your autistic nature is life-changing,” she says. “It’s so damaging to deny that to people, particularly people who are already at risk of mental health problems.”

How long will it take to read: 10 to 11 minutes.

Further reading: How the Beatles heped my autistic son find his voice.

It’s the epic story of the Odyssey – but not that one. In 2024, the owners of the MV Odyssey cruise ship made a tempting (but not cheap) offer: a four-year voyage at sea, in which one could escape the troubles of a land-based world in which Donald Trump had just been elected president. But things did not go to plan.

From haven to hellhole: Even with the best planning and even the best prices, it turned out there was no escaping the US president and his knock-on effects on fuel prices amid his disastrous war in Iran. Instead of being a haven, the ship became a microcosm for the global economic turmoil, leading to passengers being “unceremoniously” dropped in Cambodia.

Notable quote: “People were shellshocked, numb, crying,” said one passenger. “People were angry. They were hysterical.”

How long will it take to read: Four minutes

Further reading: ‘They have schedules to follow’: how fast ferries can threaten endangered whales in the Mediterranean.

Sign up to Five Great Reads

Each week our editors select five of the most interesting, entertaining and thoughtful reads published by Guardian Australia and our international colleagues. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Saturday morning

after newsletter promotion

Interest in penile-enhancement is on the rise, and it is now a booming industry. Manhood, a new documentary from film-maker Daniel Lombroso (formerly of The Atlantic and The New Yorker), investigates the latest phenomenon tied to men’s obsession with their members.

While the subject matter may invite humour, Lombroso centres the film on the male self-esteem issues driving the enhancement trend, highlights the patience and tender attention afforded to the fragile men seeking treatment and portrays it as another form of gender affirming care: “So many of these things are funny and self-evident, especially to smart viewers. It’s fun to have these tough conversations and not tell people exactly how to feel in every moment,” Lombroso says.

​The economics of enhancement: one penis practitioner featured heavily in the documentary, Bill Moore, wants enlargement procedures to be “as common as Botox”. Moore’s company, which advertises its offerings as “girth enhancement”, now has 32 locations across the country. Moore offers “career-changing, sex-life turbocharging, depression-curing” procedures for up to $20,000 out of his office in a Dallas strip mall.

​Notable quote: “Everybody wants a boat that’s one foot longer” – Penis enlargement patient

​How long will it take to read: A modest three minutes (no need to extend it).

​Further reading: How toxic masculinity is reshaping young men’s faces, and a look back at the “original looksmaxxer”.

Max Veenhuyzen says the people of Darwin take their laksa seriously. He must be right, because the city in Australia’s far north hosts the Darwin international laksa festival – a celebration of multiculturalism and food that brings together chefs and foodies from across the country. More than 50 different vendors entered the competition, with only one walking away the winner.

The Golden Bowl: Vendors compete for the top prize – a gaudy laksa dish-shaped trophy – as chosen by a panel of judges who secretly visit the restaurants and blind taste the dish on stage.

Notable quote: “Can I get some tissues on stage, please?” – Golden Bowl judge and self-taught chef Junda Khoo as he struggles to taste-test finalists in the Darwin heat.

Who went home the winner? Angkor Takeaway walked away champions, with the judges unanimously awarding Cheata Ouch’s bowl the accolades on account of its seasoning and diverse body.

How long will it take to read? Just under two minutes, leaving you plenty of time to make and enjoy your own bowl of laksa.

Further reading: How to cook the perfect laksa.

Nations Championship, Rugby League World Cup and NFL action – follow with us

The Guardian Fri, 06 Nov 2026 20:33:58 GMT

Here’s how to follow along with our coverage – the finest writing and up-to-the-minute reports

There will be plenty to talk about in the world of football on Saturday morning. As well as building up to Saturday’s four Premier League games, David Tindall will be looking at the fallout from Frank Lampard’s return to Everton with Coventry on Friday night and reaction to Thomas Tuchel’s last England squad of the year. With finals weekend of the inaugural Nations Championship coming up at the end of the month, England would love to be back at Twickenham on the Sunday, you would imagine, when the top team in the north plays the top team from the south. What, though, if Steve Borthwick’s side lose to Australia? They might still get a Sunday match – but in the fourth v fourth warm-up against, say, France or South Africa. England need a clean sweep and South Africa to beat France next weekend in order to make the grand finale, and Daniel Gallan will take you through their efforts live while Robert Kitson, Andy Bull and Gerard Meagher report from south-west London.

It’s the last Premier League game before an international break that could open up the managerial merry-go-round, despite being the old-style two-weeker rather than the three-week one that straddled September and October. Michael Carrick will be trying to build on Manchester United’s thrilling comeback against Roma, while Unai Emery will hope Aston Villa can respond to his latest defeat at the Camp Nou. Tim de Lisle will have all the live updates, while Jamie Jackson and Will Unwin report from Old Trafford.

It’s so nice they named it thrice: the grand prix venue can be referred to as the city of São Paulo; as the Autódromo José Carlos Pace; or perhaps most famously by the neighbourhood it sits in, Interlagos. If it wasn’t for that pesky kid, then this could be a title race for the ages: Max Verstappen is two points ahead of Lewis Hamilton, who is nine ahead of George Russell, with Charles Leclerc five more back. And even Lando Norris is within a win of Leclerc, and has twice as many race victories as the Monégasque and Hamilton. Daniel Harris is on the live blog, while Giles Richards reports.

It’s week nine, no one can go unbeaten now, and Graham Searles will have news of the crop of 1pm eastern, 6pm GMT kick-offs. They include the meeting of two table-toppers, though it’s fair to say the AFC West’s 6-and-2 Broncos are in better shape than the NFC South’s 3-and-4 Panthers, who are hosts. The Guardian view on Russell Brand: his conviction sends a powerful message

The Guardian Fri, 06 Nov 2026 17:57:08 GMT

The brave women who testified against the star have struck a blow against the sexual entitlement that he personified

The conviction of Russell Brand for one rape and three sexual assaults on Thursday would never have happened were it not for the remarkable courage of his victims. There was no guarantee, before the trial, that he would be found guilty; two more rape charges and one of attempted indecent assault ended in acquittal. The women who testified about what Brand did to them between 2004 and 2009 are owed a debt of gratitude by everyone who believes that sexual predators should pay a price for their crimes, even when they are celebrities. On Monday, Brand will receive what the judge said would be a “significant” jail sentence.

The message sent by his rape conviction is particularly powerful. His sexual encounter with “Woman E”, who was 21 at the time, began as a consensual one, before he turned it into an anal rape that left her with psychological and physical injuries. A single case is unlikely to alter a culture of male sexual entitlement, in which it is viewed as acceptable to push women over boundaries that they do not want to cross. But the jury’s acceptance of her version of events – which was supported by multiple witnesses – can still be viewed as a step forward. Far too many women are disbelieved, or not taken seriously, when they make allegations about abuse by partners.

Nearly 10 years after the #MeToo movement, serious problems in the entertainment industries around sexual misconduct and abuse of power – as well as insecure working conditions that make it hard for junior colleagues to speak out – are widely recognised. Brand, who was a highly in-demand media figure from about 2007, picked “Woman E” out of an audience, while one of the sexual assaults he was convicted of took place in Choice FM’s studios, and another of his victims was a Channel 4 colleague. When he initiated a relationship with “Alice” (a pseudonym), she was a 16-year-old schoolgirl and he was on the verge of stardom (his alleged conduct towards her has not led to criminal charges, but was featured in the 2023 Dispatches programme that prompted the police investigation).

Internal reviews led to apologies from the BBC and Channel 4, after the revelations on Dispatches and in the Times and Sunday Times. But it would be naive to claim that the culture that enabled Brand, who was also once a Guardian sports columnist, is no more. His particular shapeshifting, from outrageous Essex boy to anti-establishment commentator to born-again Christian, would be unlikely to fool people a second time. But as the times change, so do the ruses and roles that predators adopt. It is frankly disturbing to be reminded now of just how brazen Brand was about his vicious behaviour (spitting on, choking and humiliating women) in his bestselling memoirs and on the radio. On Thursday, Pan Macmillan announced that it would stop publishing his books – including a British Book Awards biography of the year.

Two further rape complaints are being examined by police. Brand’s barrister, Ian Winter KC, has referred himself to the Bar Standards Board after an extraordinary exchange with a reporter that he initiated outside court, after the verdict. But whether or not more charges are brought, and whatever the wider impact of Brand’s disgrace, the women who testified should be proud of their part in exposing him.

Russell Brand has finally faced justice. But other abusers in comedy are still hiding in plain sight

The Guardian Fri, 06 Nov 2026 17:35:46 GMT

I love my industry but it contains people who leave a secret trail of pain and devastation totally at odds with their stage and screen personas

Sarah Solemani is an actor, writer and activist who starred in the Bafta-winning comedy Him & Her

I’ve worked in comedy in some capacity for several decades, and I include in that a year in a call centre in north Finchley run by a man who embraced the early stages of hair transplant technology, which was serious LOLS until the company was shut down by HMRC. Acting funny and writing funny has got me far. From winning the best sitcom Bafta for Him & Her, to playing Bridget Jones’s best friend, to writing monologues for Goldie Hawn, who held me like a newborn in her house and insisted we had met in a previous life. I also get to work on new projects with my favourite directors, such as Tom George of This Country, where we make each other laugh from the beginning of the day to the end. Lucky me.

Unluckily, working in comedy has also, for some strange reason, brought me into the close orbit of more than your average number of sexual predators, several of whom are still merrily working. Recently I had to pull a project from a company when I was informed it was common knowledge that a high-level exec was known for allegedly raping a colleague. Another famous comic had to pull a project when I informed them a legend they were working with was also an alleged rapist. That was two rape-related conversations in the same week without a punchline.

If you think there’s dissonance in the pursuits, you’d be right. On one level – the higher level, you might say – we are trying to make work that brings joy and amusement to the deserving masses. Then, in the secret, unfunny world, we are sending clandestine, time-consuming warnings about rapists and trying to covertly deal with the fallout. Are male comedians more likely to be rapists than say, firefighters or coastguards? We don’t have the data on that (but you can bet some poor, out-of-work female comedian is researching it as we speak instead of what she should be doing: WRITING JOKES).

Before he was a conspiracist YouTuber or even a Hollywood star, Russell Brand was a comedian, taking shows up to Edinburgh and building a following on the comedy circuit. For years, it has been common knowledge in comedy circles and beyond that he hurt many, many women. Brand has now been found guilty of raping a fan and sexually assaulting three other women. Thanks to the gargantuan bravery of the four women who came forward, he is unlikely to harm again. From my understanding it was those within the comedy community, and one famous female comedian in particular, who helped the survivors bring about justice.

Brand will serve a “significant custodial term” but the British comedy community knows there are more sexual abusers working on sets right now. They may not be tried in their lifetime. But we know. And they know. Female and working-class young talent have also only been made more vulnerable by slashes to comedy budgets and a dearth of TV commissions. I will never forgive myself for introducing one comedy producer to promising new talent, only to find out he had abused them in his flat, offering them London accommodation for their gigs and auditions.

The criminal justice system served the victims of Brand. For the majority of others, it does not: it’s “he said v she said”, and he said wins because the burden of proof is not on him. The informal network of reporting and taking action are crucial to protect women and vulnerable people.

Brand has been brought to justice, but his damage to the culture runs deep. If only he had been the ultimate radical comedian and admitted the harm he had done. If only he had led the way through remorse and rehabilitation, rather than doubling down and putting the women through the pain and humiliation of a criminal trial. If only we had been spared the changing of his shamanic cloaks, and him settling on his current Christian charade, and instead witnessed a man surrendering to true repair and redemption. That would have finally been an act of his worth watching.

Sarah Solemani is an actor, writer and activist

Autism, masking, and building a more inclusive world

The Guardian Fri, 06 Nov 2026 16:39:31 GMT

Readers respond to an article by John Harris on the rise in the number of people labelled autistic over the last 20 years

John Harris’s article addresses all the main issues that are being debated around autism (‘The term is becoming unrecognisable’: have the experts who believed in a single autism spectrum changed their minds?, 1 November). However, I feel it did not go far enough to broaden our understanding of the challenges experienced by autistic people who do not have a learning disability.

From a young age I sensed that I was experiencing the world differently to other people. I was bullied, and worked hard to fit in. I was fortunate as structurally I had a stable life that mitigated some of the more challenging aspects of my life. Things started to get less manageable when I entered adulthood and left home.

Since the age of 25 I have experienced bouts of depression and ongoing anxiety, often resulting in breakdowns, or what I now understand to be autistic burnouts. Throughout adulthood I have seen numerous medical professionals and repeatedly been directed towards therapies, designed to deal with anxiety and depression, which have had limited success in addressing my life challenges.

Despite having a postgraduate education, I have struggled to hold down many jobs and have had to leave most due to stress. I have ongoing relationship problems. I don’t have children, partly due to reluctance and health issues. I suffer from fatigue and sleep issues.

I was finally diagnosed with autistic spectrum disorder at the age of 53. My diagnosis has allowed me to understand my life; what has been harder is getting other people (including health professionals) to understand how challenging it is for me. If there were more stories published that went beyond accounts of obsessional collecting behaviours or discussing whether people make eye contact, perhaps there could be a greater understanding of what autism can look like, informing experts on how to support people appropriately and how to categorise it. Louise King London

Having spent years working adjacent to mental health services, I have come across many people with “classic” autism. I remember when Asperger’s was dropped and “autism spectrum disorders” came into use, I initially mistook the “spectrum” as a continuum we are all on. I know I was wrong, but I wonder if this framework holds a broader social truth – a spectrum with classic autistic people at the far end, Asperger’s a little way along and most people between the middle and the opposite end.

I’m not autistic, but I’m socially uncomfortable. I can confidently present to an audience of hundreds and my grasp of language is good – but I hate using the phone, don’t like meeting people, avoid parties and need my own space a lot. I think that makes me an introvert, but that’s another term that has been adopted as an “identity” rather than a defined classification. As psychiatrists and psychologists taught me, most diagnoses are essentially descriptions; if a description sounds like you, is long-lasting and is a significant problem for your functioning, then you get that label. What this idea misses is that almost everyone finds some aspects of life functionally difficult.

Rather than continuously expanding clinical classifications to grant people validity, perhaps we should focus on creating a society where anyone (or their advocates) can declare what they struggle with, and have our communities and services respond with appropriate flexibility and understanding. Salli Ward Market Harborough, Leicestershire

John Harris quotes Uta Frith calling masking “completely unfalsifiable”, then moves on as if no one had tried to falsify it.

People have. Will Mandy’s group at University College London built the standard masking questionnaire and has spent years publishing its weaknesses, which is what good science looks like. Meng-Chuan Lai and colleagues measured masking by comparing how autistic adults present in a clinical interview with how they perform on social-cognition tests, a gap no one can produce simply by saying they mask.

At Birkbeck, University of London, Jagdeep Wadhwa-Brown is now recording neural activity in autistic adults during social tasks, alongside their own accounts of masking. The study is at an early stage, but it is exactly the kind of test Frith says cannot be done. The neuroscientist Francesca Happé has described watching the mask slip in a tired house guest. That is an observation, not a feeling.

Between us, every week we assess people who present with what is sometimes called “internalised” autism: people who make eye contact, hold down demanding jobs and have spent decades being told, like Abigail Stow (who featured in Harris’s article), that they “can’t possibly be autistic”. The measures need work, and the researchers say so. But “the measure needs work” and “the phenomenon does not exist” are different claims, and only one was put to readers. Dr Louise Legg Counselling psychologist, London Dr Emma Bede Clinical psychologist, London

Like the Danes, we need to pay for the society we want

The Guardian Fri, 06 Nov 2026 16:37:15 GMT

Karin Blak responds to an article about children’s homes in crisis and what can be learned from the Danish system

As a Dane who went through Danish children’s services, and later worked in Sure Start centres as a family therapist in England, I found your article particularly resonant (English children’s homes are in crisis. Does Denmark hold the answers?, 1 November). Adopting similar care here requires two changes: our attitude to paying tax and our electoral system.

Denmark’s basic national income-tax rate and average municipal income-tax rate together amount to about 37%, almost twice England’s 20% basic rate. Although allowances and other contributions make this an imperfect comparison, we need to acknowledge Danes’ willingness to pay for the quality of services that underpin a stable society. Tax-funded services benefit us at every level of society, including care we hope neither we nor our families will ever need.

But funding alone is not enough. Working in Sure Start centres, I saw the gradual dismantling of a service that should have been the pride of the country. Children’s services need sustained investment, experienced staff and policies that last beyond the next election. When successive governments dismantle or redirect their predecessors’ work, vulnerable children bear the consequences.

Denmark’s proportional electoral system requires parties to work together. I believe proportional representation at Westminster would help us build the broader agreements needed to sustain social provision through changes of government. It would not guarantee good care, but it would help improvements endure.

We need the willingness to pay for the society we want, and a political system that encourages parties to take responsibility for its future together. Children who have already experienced instability and neglect deserve that much. Karin Blak Market Harborough, Leicestershire

John Smedley will always be in vogue

The Guardian Fri, 06 Nov 2026 16:36:12 GMT

Tim Heavisides recalls his fondness for the historic fashion firm and his enduring attachment to a black jumper

Re your report (Fashion and tradition: how John Smedley is innovating in a tough market, 1 November), I was fortunate to grow up with a mum who was interested in good quality clothes and fashion, and who, when I was 17, bought me a black rollneck top. Think Roger Moore. Think Illya Kuryakin (The Man from U. N. C. L. E.). Think of me in the lower sixth at a rural grammar school in Wiltshire, who missed going to the Bath blues festival at Shepton Mallet in 1970. I also missed the Isle of Wight ferry once.

I recall going on a school trip to see the film Kanał by the Polish director Andrzej Wajda. There were girls on the coach from the girls’ high school. Shock horror. What should I wear? My black polo top, of course. It would be perfect with my tweed sports jacket. And then Mum uttered those immortal words: “It’s made by John Smedley. You can wear it with anything.”

She was right. She had good taste and she wanted me to have good taste. So thanks, Mum, and thanks John Smedley (and Bill Nighy). Tim Heavisides Church Stretton, Shropshire

Trump Asks Dana White of U. F. C. to Be His Press Secretary

The New York Times November 07, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

On social media, the president offered the now-vacant job of White House press secretary to Dana White, the organization’s C. E. O., and told him to bring along fighters as aides.

By Erica L. Green

Erica Green, a White House correspondent, reported from Palm Beach, Fla.

President Trump said on Saturday that he had offered Dana White, the chief executive of the Ultimate Fighting Championship and a longtime friend, the role of White House press secretary.

Mr. Trump made the announcement in a social media post in which he pleaded with Mr. White — a “violent Fighter and Warrior” — to take the job. The president said he had also requested that Mr. White bring with him a number of U. F. C. fighters to serve as aides who could respond to attacks against the administration.

“I have requested that he bring with him assistants, even though some are not from our Country, of Islam Makhachev, Khabib Nurmagomedov, Justin Gaethje, Daniel Cormier, Amanda Nunes, and Kayla Harris,” Mr. Trump wrote. “We need these people to defend us against the Lunatic Left. Dana will be a Press Secretary like none other. Dana, please take the job!”

It was unclear if Mr. Trump’s out-of-the-blue offer to Mr. White was a formal one or a projection of defiance after his midterm election losses — or perhaps both.

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment. A U. F. C. spokeswoman did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Mr. Trump’s announcement came as he signaled that he was preparing for political battle against Democrats when they take control of Congress next year, after Republicans lost control of the House and Senate in the midterm elections.

Mr. Trump announced on Friday that he was elevating Stephen Miller, his combative domestic policy architect, as his new chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles. The president had blamed Ms. Wiles for the sweeping election defeats.

“He’s a great fighter,” Mr. Trump said of Mr. Miller on Friday. “He’s been with me right from the beginning.”

Mr. Trump has been without a White House press secretary since mid-October, when Katie Zacharia, a pundit who Mr. Trump chose to replace Karoline Leavitt, was forced out after just five days.

Ms. Leavitt stepped down in August, shortly after returning from maternity leave, citing the need to spend more time with her young children.

Mr. Trump has projected defiance after an initial conciliatory reaction to the Republican wipeout earlier in the week, when he maintained that he would simply block Democratic efforts for the next two years.

On social media on Saturday, Mr. Trump began to lash out at Democrats he said were making “threats” against members of his administration, including impeachment and imprisonment, and against Republicans in general.

Mr. Trump, who has made retribution against his political foes a priority of his second term, called on the Justice Department to investigate the threats. He labeled them “weaponization and lawfare at another level.”

“The threats being made by the Democrat Party against innocent Republican Donors and Party Members are absolutely unprecedented, and totally illegal,” he wrote. “Please report them to the Department of Justice, IMMEDIATELY! If you would like, send them directly to me, your President.”

Earlier this year, Mr. White, who has had a decades-long friendship with Mr. Trump, hosted a mixed martial arts cage fight on the South Lawn of the White House. The bouts fell on Flag Day, and the president’s 80th birthday.

Mr. Trump has supported the U. F. C. and Mr. White, and has regularly attended the league’s fights during his presidency.

Erica L. Green is a White House correspondent for The Times, covering President Trump and his administration.

With So Much New Blood in the Senate, the Average Age Is Falling. To 63.

The New York Times November 07, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Incoming senators are nearly 15 years younger than departing ones, on average. But the chamber’s overall age isn’t shifting much.

By Francesca Paris and C. J. Robinson

When the new Senate convenes in January, it will welcome some (relatively) young new legislators. A few are even millennials, including James Talarico of Texas, 37, and Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan, 42, two Democrats who may have energized young voters to turn out.

But their effect on the average age of the Senate — which has crept up over the last few decades — will be small. The senators of the 120th Congress will be less than a year younger, on average, than the Senate’s current members were at the start of the 119th Congress two years ago. That’s because so many sitting senators are old, and getting older.

Incoming senators are much younger than the existing Senate …

… but the average age of a senator will fall only a little, compared with two years ago

The data assumes Democratic victories in Alaska and Mississippi. Members that were actively serving terms as of Nov. 6 were included for the 119th Congress. For the top chart, numbers are based on senators’ ages as of January 2027. For the bottom chart, ages are calculated based on the date each Congress convened or will convene.

These numbers assume that Mary Peltola and Scott Colom will win their races in Alaska and Mississippi; they were both ahead in the vote count Saturday. (If both lose, the Senate’s average age will land at 63.6.)

Voter complaints about an aging Congress were part of the discussion as the midterm primaries played out. Polls show a majority of Americans support age limits for elected officials, but voters have continued to choose older politicians. In congressional primary races where an incumbent 65 or older faced a challenger, often a younger candidate, the incumbent almost always won, according to a New York Times analysis.

Still, some older members of the Senate are headed out the door, and the new senators-elect are, on average, much younger. The age difference between incoming and departing senators is nearly 15 years.

But new members make up only about a fifth of the next Senate, in part because only about a third of the members are up for re-election every two years.

And the aging of returning senators over the past two years has erased most of the effect brought by incoming younger senators. If all current Senate members had remained, the average age would have risen above 66.

This remains one of the oldest Senates

Ages calculated based on the day that a particular Senate convened. For years prior to the 119th Congress, members who were serving at the start of a term were included.

Democrats, in particular, will contribute to the age decline. Of the incoming senators, the average age for Democrats is 53; for Republicans, it’s 58.

Mr. Talarico, the youngest incoming senator, will be part of the small percentage of senators under the age of 40 sworn in since 1900 — including Joe Biden, who took the oath of office soon after he turned 30. (Barack Obama was 43 when he was sworn in.)

The oldest incoming senator — who is also a former senator — is Sherrod Brown of Ohio, who will turn 74 on Monday.

About the data

Senators’ ages were calculated based on the day that Congress first convened (or, for the 120th Congress, will convene).

For the Senate of the 119th Congress, we used only the members who were serving as of early November, excluding those who left — such as JD Vance (to become vice president), Marco Rubio (to become secretary of state) and Lindsey Graham (who died in July). Their replacements were included to get an accurate picture of the differences between incoming and departing members. For earlier years, for simplicity, we used the members who started each term.

Additional reporting by Karen Yourish, Elena Shao, Ashley Wu and Matt Zdun.

Francesca Paris is a Times reporter working with data and graphics for The Upshot.

C. J. Robinson is a reporting fellow at The Upshot and a member of the 2026-27 Times Fellowship, a program for journalists early in their careers.

Eisenkot Seeks to Oust Netanyahu as Prime Minister. Here’s How.

The New York Times November 07, 2026

Israel’s Election

Advertisement

Supported by

news analysis

Gadi Eisenkot gets the chance to form a new government, replacing Benjamin Netanyahu as prime minister. But the obstacles are formidable.

By David M. Halbfinger

Reporting from Jerusalem

Gadi Eisenkot, Israel’s former military chief, has been given a chance to form a new government, after he was recommended for the task by parties that won 67 seats in the 120-seat Parliament.

But completing that mission and replacing Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu may well be the toughest assignment of Mr. Eisenkot’s career so far.

The ideologically and ethnically diverse factions that recommended him for prime minister include left-wing, right-wing, centrist and predominantly Arab parties. Most would have to break seemingly ironclad campaign promises to unite behind Mr. Eisenkot, no matter how he arranges them into a governing coalition.

But the pressure is on him and his allies to do just that because the alternatives, in their view, are far worse.

A failure to form a government could send Israel to another round of elections. It would leave Mr. Netanyahu in his job as prime minister in the meantime, with all of the advantages of incumbency. And the opposition would be unlikely to perform as well as it did in October, when thousands of expatriate Israelis flew home to vote.

A unity government in which Mr. Eisenkot and Mr. Netanyahu share power, such as by taking turns as premier, seemed far-fetched before Election Day and seems unthinkable now. Some of Mr. Eisenkot’s campaign promises left wiggle room, but he was adamant in saying that Mr. Netanyahu, as the person with ultimate responsibility for defending the country on Oct. 7, 2023, when it suffered its worst attack in history, was unfit to continue in government.

Since the election, Mr. Netanyahu’s efforts to delegitimize the result — by accusing Arab parties of stealing votes — have hardened those views. And the lopsided result of the U. S. midterm elections underscored the urgency of replacing Mr. Netanyahu, opposition leaders have argued: Israel’s standing with lawmakers in both the Democratic and Republican parties is so dismal, and Mr. Netanyahu so deeply loathed, that only a new prime minister could possibly begin to repair it.

“Israel is already in the midst of a dangerous diplomatic tsunami,” Mr. Eisenkot said on Friday. He added that a situation in which Mr. Netanyahu “continues to exercise authority over Israel’s security system and law enforcement agencies is dangerous and must not be allowed to continue for even one more day.”

But what kind of government can Mr. Eisenkot form?

He starts with 48 members of Parliament, thanks to his own center-right Yashar party (21), Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid’s centrist Together party (12), Yair Golan and the left-wing Democrats party (8), and Avigdor Liberman’s right-wing but secular Yisrael Beiteinu (Israel Our Home) party (7).

That is more than Mr. Netanyahu’s coalition can count on: After an ultra-Orthodox party, United Torah Judaism, refused to recommend him for prime minister, Mr. Netanyahu’s coalition has only 46 seats.

To form a bigger coalition, let alone a majority in Parliament, Mr. Eisenkot’s options include partnering with the ultra-Orthodox parties, which together have 13 seats, or the Arab parties, which won a record 19 seats. Either route is deeply problematic, according to opposition lawmakers, operatives and advisers, most of whom insisted on anonymity to discuss coalition talks.

Here is a look at Mr. Eisenkot’s possible path forward, and at one major roadblock standing in his way.

Until a new government is formed, Mr. Netanyahu remains a caretaker prime minister. But Parliament is another story. Lawmakers will be sworn in on Tuesday, and Mr. Eisenkot is working to arrange for the election of a new speaker to replace Amir Ohana, a Netanyahu loyalist.

If he is successful, that could put Mr. Eisenkot’s allies in charge of key legislative committees. And it could allow his anti-Netanyahu bloc to begin enacting legislation — fulfilling key campaign promises and demonstrating Mr. Eisenkot’s ability to get things done.

The lowest-hanging fruit, insiders say, would be to repeal laws passed by Mr. Netanyahu’s coalition, such as controversial judicial changes allowing more political control over the appointment of judges and curbing the attorney general’s powers.

Equally important would be to deliver on a core campaign promise by all the opposition leaders to establish a national commission of inquiry to investigate the security failures that preceded the Oct. 7 attack.

Mr. Eisenkot this past week began speaking of the need to form a “national emergency government” — an important rhetorical shift.

“If it’s an emergency, you do things you wouldn’t do otherwise,” said Nimrod Novik, a senior fellow of the Israel Policy Forum who was an adviser to Shimon Peres when he was prime minister.

The Arab parties’ 19 seats would give Mr. Eisenkot a solid majority, but bringing them into a government could cost him other allies.

For now, the question is moot: The Joint List, an amalgam of three smaller Arab parties that together won 11 seats, has ruled out joining a government, though it could provide support from the outside and enable a minority government to function. The United Arab List, or Raam, which won eight seats, has not. But Mr. Eisenkot has insisted that any party joining his government must declare Hamas a terrorist organization.

Raam’s leader, Mansour Abbas, has refused to do so, though he condemns all terrorist acts. But he did say on Thursday that Hamas and all other Palestinian factions should be disarmed.

Even if Mr. Abbas were to satisfy Mr. Eisenkot, however, Mr. Liberman, the Yisrael Beiteinu leader, has repeatedly ruled out a government that includes Arab parties or even relies on their support from the outside.

That leaves relying on the ultra-Orthodox, or Haredi, parties.

This, too, is fraught with peril. The most important issue for the Haredim is to protect their young men, who now account for about one in four draft-age teenagers, from conscription into the military and punishment for draft evasion. But with the Israeli Army overstretched, a core campaign promise of Mr. Eisenkot and his opposition allies was to compel Haredi men to share the sacrifice of defending the country.

Mr. Liberman has now chosen to break that promise but not his vow to keep Arab parties out of the government.

On Friday, he wrote on social media that while he remained dead set on replacing Mr. Netanyahu, avoiding new elections and spurning any partnership with the Arab parties, “on all other issues, it is permissible and desirable to be flexible and compromise, and to understand that you cannot have it all. This includes the issue of the conscription law as well.”

Mr. Eisenkot was not entirely absolutist in his campaign rhetoric about drafting the ultra-Orthodox, but Mr. Bennett, of the Together party, was adamant about it and would have to accept going back on that pledge.

Mr. Eisenkot could also find it difficult to strike a deal with the Haredi party leaders, who are far more experienced at coalition negotiations than he is, and whose voters have grown steadily more right-wing and nationalist in recent years.

David Makovsky, an analyst at the Washington Institute for Near East Policy, said the fact that United Torah Judaism had declined to recommend Mr. Netanyahu for prime minister was a positive sign. “It means the store is open,” he said. “But how much they’re willing to go against their base, which is really right-wing — that’s the $64,000 question.”

With 48 votes to Mr. Netanyahu’s 46, Mr. Eisenkot said on Friday that he planned to form a minority government, at least initially. That would mean that the Arab and ultra-Orthodox parties abstain from the vote to form the government.

But he also said he would invite every political party — without exceptions — to join his government, now or later, provided it embraced his terms: recognizing Israel as a Jewish and democratic state, accepting the values in the Israeli Declaration of Independence, requiring universal national military or civilian service, and agreeing that Hamas is a terrorist organization that must be dismantled.

Mr. Liberman, however, is again standing in the way. On Friday, he ruled out forming a government with anything less than a 61-seat majority.

Gayil Talshir, a political science lecturer at The Hebrew University of Jerusalem who is advising the opposition, said it was unclear whether Mr. Liberman really wanted Mr. Eisenkot to be successful.

Mr. Liberman has complained publicly that Mr. Eisenkot ended his campaign by cannibalizing support for his allies in a way that Mr. Liberman contends cost both Yisrael Beiteinu and the anti-Netanyahu bloc several seats.

Ms. Talshir said Mr. Liberman may fear the wrath of his right-wing voters if he agrees to a partnership with Arab parties.

He also may be angling to take a shot at becoming prime minister himself.

Should Mr. Eisenkot fail to form a government, Mr. Netanyahu would be given a chance next. But if he failed, there would be a short period before new elections are called in which anyone in Parliament — including Mr. Liberman — could become prime minister by enlisting the support of 60 other lawmakers.

On Friday, Mr. Eisenkot appeared to allude to Mr. Liberman’s resistance — and possible ulterior motives.

“Anyone who seeks to delay or sabotage the formation of a government for personal rather than substantive reasons,” he wrote on social media before the start of the Sabbath, “will be remembered by history as someone who failed to rise to the occasion and failed to act to save Israel in a time of national emergency. They will not be forgiven.”

Adam Rasgon contributed reporting from Tel Aviv.

David M. Halbfinger is The Times’s Jerusalem bureau chief, leading coverage of Israel, Gaza and the West Bank. He also held that post from 2017 to 2021. He was the politics editor from 2021 to 2025.

Gadi Eisenkot, a former military chief, hopes to succeed Benjamin Netanyahu as prime minister by cobbling together a coalition after an inconclusive election.

By Ephrat Livni and Aaron Boxerman

Israel’s president on Saturday selected Gadi Eisenkot, the leading rival of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, to try to form a new government, handing him the daunting task of forging a parliamentary coalition after an indecisive national election last month.

Isaac Herzog, the Israeli president, said he had held “in-depth talks” with both Mr. Netanyahu and Mr. Eisenkot before making his decision. He ultimately tapped Mr. Eisenkot, a center-right former Israeli military chief, after more members of Parliament supported Mr. Eisenkot than Mr. Netanyahu during consultations over the past week.

The announcement gives Mr. Eisenkot a long-awaited chance to fulfill his pledge to unseat Mr. Netanyahu and steer Israel in a new direction, but he will have to navigate significant obstacles to form a government. He has up to six weeks to build a coalition before the president passes the opportunity to another candidate, most likely Mr. Netanyahu.

The election on Oct. 27 left all sides short of an outright 61-seat majority in Parliament. Mr. Netanyahu’s coalition won 53 seats; Mr. Eisenkot and his Zionist allies secured 48; and two Arab parties took a record 19.

Now that Mr. Eisenkot has received a mandate to form a government, he faces a series of difficult choices. He could join forces with the two Arab-led parties, but some of the right-wing Jewish parties in his bloc have said they would not enter a government that relied on their support. Mr. Eisenkot has also stipulated conditions that the Arab parties have yet to meet, such as publicly labeling Hamas as a terrorist organization.

Mr. Eisenkot said on Friday that he would work to establish a “national emergency government” to eject Mr. Netanyahu as soon as possible. That would probably mean forming a minority government, with support from some parties that would not formally join his coalition. Mr. Eisenkot has said other parties could join “at a later stage.”

“We must urgently establish stable, responsible leadership, prevent another round of elections and put an end to outgoing Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s determination to cling to office,” Mr. Eisenkot said.

Mr. Netanyahu has been prime minister for almost 19 years in all, through multiple periods dating back to 1996.

On Saturday, Mr. Netanyahu attacked a prospective government led by Mr. Eisenkot that would rely on the Arab parties. He claimed it would unleash “fires and flames we will see in the streets” and compared it to “national suicide.”

“This is a matter of our very existence. Israel simply will not survive under such a government,” Mr. Netanyahu said.

If Mr. Eisenkot fails to form a government, Mr. Herzog can select another candidate, who will then have four weeks to do so. If neither succeeds, Parliament could ask Mr. Herzog to grant the mandate to a third lawmaker, who would have 14 days to make a last-ditch attempt.

If the candidates all fail, Parliament would be dissolved, and new elections would be held. Mr. Herzog and Mr. Eisenkot have said they hope to stave off that prospect.

Mr. Netanyahu will serve as the caretaker prime minister until a new government is formed. Political analysts say remaining in power by forcing a new round of elections would be a victory for him, even if he is not able to form a government this time around.

Since the vote, Mr. Netanyahu and his hard-line allies have repeatedly attacked the results, saying that the election was “stolen by Arab parties.” Israeli election officials have insisted there is no proof of widespread fraud.

The selection of Mr. Eisenkot had been expected for several days, after Mr. Herzog consulted with leaders and officials of the 11 parties that won seats in Parliament. Mr. Eisenkot received a clear majority, with most parties backing him; he got the support of 67 lawmakers, compared with 46 for Mr. Netanyahu.

Mr. Eisenkot, a soft-spoken former general, campaigned on the promise of keeping Israel secure while leading it away from policies that have brought it to the brink of becoming a pariah state. He has also paid a painful personal price to which many Israelis can relate: His son and two nephews died in the war in Gaza that followed the Hamas-led Oct. 7, 2023, attacks on Israel.

Many in Mr. Eisenkot’s camp saw the vote as a referendum on the prime minister’s failure to prevent the Oct. 7 attacks and on Israel’s growing international isolation over the subsequent war in Gaza.

Still, Mr. Netanyahu cannot be counted out. A consummate political survivor and Israel’s longest-serving leader, he overcame widespread criticism in Israel and fury abroad to outperform many of the polls. His Likud party secured 27 seats, down from 30 in the last election in 2022 but still more than any other political party.

Mr. Eisenkot has articulated four principles he said parties must meet to be included in a governing coalition: recognizing Israel as a Jewish and democratic state; supporting the Israeli Declaration of Independence; backing universal national service; and labeling Hamas as a terrorist organization that must be dismantled.

Mr. Eisenkot may need to rely on Raam and the Joint List alliance, two Arab-led parties, to support a minority government. Raam has accepted most of the conditions and has condemned all terrorist acts but has not called Hamas a terrorist group. The Joint List includes leftists and Palestinian nationalists who reject Israel’s founding ideal of a “Jewish democracy.”

Mr. Eisenkot could also try to woo some of Mr. Netanyahu’s ultra-Orthodox allies. But many of the former general’s supporters could view that as a betrayal if he had to compromise on a push to force ultra-Orthodox religious students to serve in the military, given that he campaigned on ending their longstanding exemption from conscription.

Ephrat Livni is a Times reporter covering news around the world. She is based in New York.

Aaron Boxerman is a Times reporter covering Israel and Gaza. He is based in Jerusalem.

Unfazed by Midterm Rebuke, Miller Is Poised to Push the Limits of Trump’s Power

The New York Times November 07, 2026
