The president’s new chief of staff has already demonstrated his intention to forge ahead with an agenda that many voters rejected.

Credit... Eric Lee/The New York Times

Supported by

By Zolan Kanno-Youngs and Hamed Aleaziz

Zolan Kanno-Youngs covers the White House, and Hamed Aleaziz covers the Department of Homeland Security. They have reported on Stephen Miller’s policymaking since the first Trump administration.

Republicans called for President Trump to scale back the policies many blamed for their midterm blowout. Mr. Trump ruminated about deals with Democrats.

Stephen Miller was unfazed.

A day after the elections, as votes were still being counted and the Democrats’ victory margin seemed to increase by the hour, the longtime Trump aide and MAGA stalwart convened one of his regular calls with national security officials to get an update on immigration policy.

There was no talk of the results of the midterms or suggestion of scaling back the hard-line immigration approach that contributed to Republicans’ steep losses, according to people with knowledge of the call, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe a private discussion. Instead, Mr. Miller continued to push the officials to carry out an agenda that has in the past year included ramping up deportations, driving down border crossings and removing immigrants to faraway nations they were not from.

In other words, the architect of some of the administration’s most divisive policies demonstrated that he would aggressively pursue more of the agenda that many voters rejected on Tuesday.

Now, after being named Friday as White House chief of staff, Mr. Miller is poised to help oversee what is likely to be a combative final two years of Mr. Trump’s term. And as Democrats vow to investigate the very policies that Mr. Miller helped devise, Mr. Miller, the ultimate Trump loyalist, is in a prime position to continue his longtime pursuit of limiting checks on executive power.

If Mr. Miller’s predecessor, Susie Wiles, preferred to stay behind the scenes while trying to temper Mr. Miller’s brusque approach to issues like immigration, the president on Friday signaled that he was ready to more fully empower a hard-nosed lieutenant who had proved his loyalty and was happy to be a visible spokesman for the president and his agenda.

“He’s a great fighter,” Mr. Trump said on Friday after landing in Florida. “He’s been with me right from the beginning.”

“He’s very loyal,” the president added.

For Mr. Miller, 41, his new role is the culmination of a rise from Senate aide to speechwriter in Mr. Trump’s 2016 campaign to the most powerful policy staff member in the modern history of the presidency.

In addition to helping oversee the militarized crackdown of the U. S.-Mexico border, he set in motion the suspension of U. S. refugee programs and the deadly deportation crackdowns on American streets.

But his influence during Mr. Trump’s second term has extended beyond immigration policy. He also pushed Mr. Trump’s lethal strikes on civilian boats in the Caribbean that the administration claimed were carrying drugs. He helped use the powers of the federal government to target political opponents and universities, and oversaw the federal crackdown in the District of Columbia.

Mr. Miller, whom the White House declined to make available for an interview, has pushed Republicans in Congress to resist compromises with Democrats, such as efforts to rein in Immigration and Customs Enforcement. He was heavily involved in the efforts to assert more federal control over elections, including at one point earlier this year circulating a draft executive order to try to limit mail voting, a version of which Mr. Trump ultimately signed.

Marc Short, who served as chief of staff to Vice President Mike Pence, said Mr. Miller was “intertwined” with Mr. Trump.

“I don’t think it can be underestimated,” he said. “Most of the shots are being called from Stephen’s office in the West Wing.”

During the immigration operation in Minneapolis, which drew the ire of many Americans after federal agents shot and killed two U. S. citizens in January, he discussed with Mr. Trump invoking the Insurrection Act.

The 1807 law gives the president broad authority, under some conditions, to use the military to quell widespread domestic unrest. Taking that step would allow the federal government to deploy active-duty troops inside the country. Mr. Trump has declined to rule out such a move in the past, but has yet to go to that extreme.

Mr. Miller “was kind of already running the White House in so many ways, so you can expect more of the same from the White House that you were probably already pissed off and frustrated about,” said former Representative Marjorie Taylor Greene, the Trump ally turned critic, in a video posted to X. “Only this time he’s going to go into a hyper, hyper mode because they’re about to get investigated in every way possible by the Democrats who are going to control the all powerful House and Senate committees.”

Democrats on Friday indicated that, as they prepare to scrutinize the White House, Mr. Miller himself is squarely in their sights. Representative Robert Garcia, who is set to lead the House Oversight Committee, called Mr. Miller the “architect of the unconstitutional ICE raids that have terrorized our communities.”

A White House spokeswoman, Lauren Bis, described Mr. Miller in a statement as a “key player in delivering on President Trump’s America First agenda since Day 1.”

“He has spearheaded the administration’s crime crackdown, including in D. C. and Memphis, record-setting deregulation, unleashed American energy, dismantled drug cartels, and secured our border,” Ms. Bis added. “In his new role, he will continue to deliver historic successes for the American people.”

Mr. Miller has shown no interest in compromising with congressional Democrats and was already preparing for a fight over congressional subpoenas and investigations, The Times reported Friday.

To the extent that he has dealt with Democrats in the past, he has mostly lobbed insults, as he did earlier this month when he ridiculed the Democratic candidate slate as “extremists, freaks and America-hating lunatics.”

His expressions of admiration for Mr. Trump are often over the top.

“If it wasn’t for President Trump, the United States of America would not exist right now,” Mr. Miller said at a gala at Mr. Trump’s Florida residence on Friday, adding: “I swear to you and I pledge to you, Mr. President, my absolute loyalty, my unwavering commitment and my total devotion to your success and the success of this country.”

On the global stage, Mr. Miller has suggested the administration’s preferred approach is through brute force, defending the administration’s seizure of the Venezuelan leader Nicolas Maduro and Mr. Trump’s threats against Greenland.

But throughout his time in the Trump White House, Mr. Miller has maneuvered in a way to preserve his power in the face of crises. Many of Mr. Trump’s allies are aware that the Iran war has become politically untenable and alienated members of the president’s base. Mr. Miller also understands the war has become a political crisis and believes the president needs to prioritize policies that are more popular with his supporters, The Times reported on Friday.

The policies Mr. Miller has helped craft have in many ways sought to redefine what it means to be American.

He has long believed that the United States thrived after instituting strict immigration policies in the 1920s blocking off whole sections of the globe. He has argued that loosening those laws hurt the country, calling the landmark 1965 law that paved the way for more Hispanic and Asian immigrants “the single-largest experiment on a society, on a civilization that had ever been conducted in human history.” Decades of data have shown immigrants’ effects on U. S. society include having lower crime rates and use of public benefits than that of native-born Americans.

As a young Senate aide, Mr. Miller was known for sending late-night emails attacking immigration to the United States, including by referring to white nationalist websites.

In Mr. Trump’s first term, Mr. Miller played a part in some of the president’s more polarizing policies, including the separation of migrant families at the border and his travel ban on several predominantly Muslim countries.

Mr. Miller was among the cadre of aides who remained steadfast in supporting Mr. Trump, even after the Jan. 6, 2021, Capitol attack — devoting the ensuing four years to planning a return to power.

In the four years Mr. Trump was out of office, Mr. Miller helped recruit like-minded right-wing lawyers likely to carry out Mr. Trump’s agenda without contest. He mapped out Mr. Trump’s second-term agenda, overseeing the team drafting the dozens of executive orders that Mr. Trump would sign immediately after returning to the White House.

Mr. Miller’s approach has at times prompted internal pushback.

Mr. Miller and Ms. Wiles debated over how wide to “cast the net” on immigration enforcement, Lindsey Graham, the longtime Trump ally and South Carolina senator, said in an interview this year before his death. The debate centered on critical questions of “how far to go, what to do, when to do it” and what methods to use, he said.

For many, it went too far. Along with the economic fallout over the war in Iran, Mr. Trump’s deportation campaign emerged as one of the most emotionally charged issues driving midterm voters to the polls in many areas of the nation.

Mr. Miller has drawn criticism from members of his party at times this year, including after federal agents shot and killed two Minneapolis residents, Renee Good and Alex Pretti. Senator Thom Tillis, Republican of North Carolina, told CNN that Mr. Miller had “been repeatedly responsible for embarrassment for the president of the United States by acting too quickly, speaking first and thinking later.”

Rather than losing clout after Minneapolis, Mr. Miller adjusted his tactics.

He pivoted from highly publicized immigration raids in cities to imposing policies that squeezed the lives of undocumented immigrants as well as those with legal status. He has targeted those with refugee status, particularly Somalis.

By the summer, just months after the chaos of Minneapolis seemed to mark a challenge to Mr. Miller’s influence, the administration was once again ramping up immigration arrests in pursuit of Mr. Trump’s mass deportation goals.

Mr. Miller’s new job did not mean that the criticism from some Republicans would end, particularly on the immigration policies that led to so much political upheaval. Representative Marlin Stutzman, Republican of Indiana, told Fox News on Friday that Mr. Miller’s promotion was a “horrible decision.”

Earlier in the week, Mr. Stutzman had said the midterm losses should have moved Mr. Trump to distance himself from Mr. Miller.

“It looked bad on us, the deportation effort,” Mr. Stutzman said while addressing a crowd at the Republican headquarters in Allen County. He said the President Barack Obama had also surged deportations, “but he didn’t go out and talk about it in the way that, you know, we did.”

“Frankly,” he said, “I think Stephen Miller should be fired.”

Zolan Kanno-Youngs is a White House correspondent for The Times, covering President Trump and his administration.

Hamed Aleaziz covers the Department of Homeland Security and immigration policy for The Times.

Here Are Five Signals We Might Be on the Road to Recovery

The New York Times November 07, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Lydia Polgreen

By Lydia Polgreen

Opinion Columnist

Two years ago, Donald Trump’s return to office felt like a diagnosis, a confirmation of some terrible disease. Now, after the spectacular reversal in the midterms, the body politic looks rather different. My sense is that America may be in remission, even if we are a long way from a cure. Trump, after all, is still president. Here are five signals from the Democrats’ extraordinary string of victories that, taken together, could push the country toward recovery.

In 2012 a young artist named Cat Frazier posted an intentionally janky GIF she had designed. “lol nothing matters,” it read, in spinning blue-green letters. It became her first viral GIF, capturing the irony-soaked ennui of the post-financial-crisis 2010s. When Trump first ran for president, the GIF became a go-to response to the madness of his candidacy. His mendacity, his crudeness, his total disregard for any of the norms of presidential behavior — it seemed he could get away with anything. To those in his thrall, it was all a big lol, and nothing mattered.

Fast-forward to 2026, and suddenly a lot of things matter, and no one is laughing. For much of his political career, Trump has relied on an almost supernatural ability to defy the hard facts of material reality: His lies about trivial things, like the size of the crowd at his first inauguration, or quite serious things, like Mexico paying for the border wall, never seemed to catch up with him — no matter how much they were fact-checked. Now, reality has reasserted itself.

Trump’s insistence that other countries would pay for his ruinous tariffs was disproved by the sharply rising prices of imported goods and the falling prices of some key American exports that faced retaliatory tariffs. His administration’s insistence that DOGE could cut trillions of dollars from the federal budget by eliminating countless programs ran straight into the reality of Americans’ reliance on those programs — and actually increased rather than decreased the federal budget and deficit.

The fantasy of a quick, spectacular military strike to topple the government of Iran gave way to a world of pain for American consumers. No spin can change the fact that filling your gas tank costs, on average, about 40 percent more today than it did when the war began. Democratic victories in deep-red heartland states like Kansas and Iowa make a lot more sense when you know that the prices of diesel and fertilizer, so crucial to farmers, have gone up by about 70 percent and 20 percent respectively in the past year — and that tariffs have sapped export demand and increased the costs of farm machinery.

Americans know their own wallets. They see the high mortgage rates and the frozen housing market. They know that, Trump’s dismissal notwithstanding, the affordability crisis is no hoax. They can see and feel how a very small number of people at the summit of the economy have grown unfathomably rich as workers’ share of the pie has shrunk ever smaller. No amount of anti-woke point scoring can distract from the stark arithmetic of daily life. The Trumpian reality distortion field is long gone.

Democrats long assumed that as the country grew less white, their base would grow. The 2024 election was painful proof of that assumption’s flimsiness: Latino and Asian voters swung hard toward Trump and the Republican Party, cementing his narrow victory. Then Republicans made the mistake of assuming these voters were now a permanent part of their coalition. The 2026 midterms demonstrated the folly of that assumption, too, as those voters, like many other Americans, boomeranged left.

This was hardly a surprise. Trump’s cruel and indiscriminate immigration crackdowns squandered any opportunity to solidify his party’s gains among these groups. What’s more, these voters were as much if not more affected by the economic carnage wreaked by Trump’s tariffs and the heedless war in Iran. A snapback of support was more or less assured.

Somewhat less examined is the role of internal migration in reshaping the political map. Republican leaders in Texas and Florida love to boast that their low taxes and plentiful housing draw millions of blue state transplants frustrated by the high cost of living in places like California and New York. But those new arrivals don’t suddenly become conservative Republicans.

Consider Texas. It added 2.47 million residents from 2020 to 2025, with Dallas-Fort Worth and Houston accounting for some two-thirds of the increase. The state’s four biggest metropolitan areas absorbed about 85 percent of that growth. Many of these new arrivals were people who came from blue states and brought with them expectations about tax-supported government services, even if they were frustrated by high taxes in the places they left. They doubtless played a vital role in the victories of Democrats across the state.

Indeed, the influx across the Sun Belt has helped turn deep red states into purple ones — from Southern states like Georgia and the Carolinas to Western states like Arizona and Nevada. Similar internal migration trends are playing out in the Mountain West, too, as blue staters move inland from the Pacific to Montana, Idaho and Utah. In some blue states and cities, meanwhile, voters have grown frustrated with Democrats’ governance, eroding the huge margins they once enjoyed. It is notable that deep-blue Oregon’s governor won re-election by a similar margin as Gina Hinojosa, the shocking Democratic victor in the Texas governor’s race.

As people move around the country, seeking new opportunities and lower costs, they inevitably transform the states they move to — just as the states they leave behind are reshaped by their departures. All of this movement may point to a political landscape that is less polarized along ethnic, racial and geographic lines. For American democracy, that can only be salutary.

Who can forget the tagline of the mega-viral advertisement Trump’s campaign dropped in the closing stretch of the 2024 campaign? “Kamala is for they/them. Trump is for you.” True or not, it cemented the Republicans’ message that Democrats were obsessed with obscure identity politics. Kamala Harris, they argued, was more worried about making sure incarcerated transgender people received gender-affirming surgeries at taxpayer expense than about helping ordinary Americans pay their bills. As a line of attack, it worked.

The Trump administration, with the help of a conservative supermajority on the Supreme Court, has delivered on its promise to make life hellish for transgender people in many parts of the country, enacting draconian policies such as requiring transgender people to put their sex at birth on their passports. Republicans have all but eliminated access to gender-affirming care for young people in most red states and the administration sharply curtailed it in blue states, too, by threatening large hospitals with funding cuts and investigations.

It is not just trans people. Affirmative action and diversity, equity and inclusion have been banned or eliminated through coercive pressure on the major institutions of public life. Universities across the country have gutted humanities programs that carry even a whiff of anything deemed woke. Pete Hegseth has been purging the top ranks of the U. S. military of women and people of color. Billionaire tech oligarchs jettisoned their diversity programs, reveling in a new macho energy unleashed by Trump’s second term.

This rapid and breathtaking victory, however, has come at a cost. In the midterms, Republicans spent millions of dollars on scaremongering advertisements about boys playing in girls’ sports, to little effect. In the aftermath, no less a culture warrior than Gov. Ron DeSantis of Florida declared the battle over. “Four years ago, we were in the peak woke era,” he said on Wednesday. He added, “Now the issues are different.” These culture war victories left Republicans with few boogeymen with which to whip up their base.

Scaremongering about immigrant invasions falls flat when the border is practically sealed and masked Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents are hunting down people in the streets and shipping them off to prisons in El Salvador and war-torn Central African nations. Parents in Texas, a state with some of the harshest laws restricting trans care for minors, have little reason to fear that their children will receive transgender surgeries at school, no matter how much money Elon Musk and his ilk spent to convince them otherwise.

Not long ago, liberal concerns about the basic rights of trans people to dignity and racial equality were mocked as luxury beliefs. In these hard times, it seems that the Republicans’ obsessions with nonexistent cultural threats are the real luxuries.

Under these conditions, it has become clear that Americans relish smashmouth politics and abject cruelty much less than Trump and his administration anticipated. Nothing illustrated this more clearly than the immediate and almost universal horror that followed when Vivek Ramaswamy, the Republican candidate for governor of Ohio, aired a vile ad featuring the estranged mother of his opponent Amy Acton, calling her a liar and casting doubt on Acton’s well-documented experience of sexual abuse at the hands of her stepfather.

Ohio’s Republican governor harshly criticized the ad, as did many other members of his party. Trump and Vice President JD Vance, on the other hand, praised Ramaswamy for having the courage to smear a victim of child sexual abuse. Ramaswamy, ever the opportunist, doubled down on the ad, paying to broadcast it statewide, only to pull it in the final days of the campaign when it became clear that voters found it repulsive. Ramaswamy, who ran for president in 2024 and was banking on a win this year to boost his chances in a future presidential run, lost by eight percentage points. The revulsion was a tell: Even if Trump could get away with that kind of nastiness, no one else could.

But there were signs of revulsion much earlier. I saw it in Springfield, Ohio, where a community in a county Trump won by more than 20 points in 2020 rallied around its Haitian residents after Vance absurdly accused them of eating pets. I saw it in Minneapolis this January, when the Trump administration unleashed a ruthless operation to round up undocumented immigrants. When federal agents gunned down Renee Good and Alex Pretti, millions of people recoiled at the blood of their fellow citizens running in the frozen streets of an American city.

It has been heartening to see some of the crudest Republican candidates go down to defeat, even in districts they had been heavily favored to win. Brandon Herrera, a vile gun influencer who trafficked in Nazi imagery and disgusting misogyny, was running for an open House seat in Texas. The previous incumbent, a Republican, won by nearly 25 points in 2024. Herrera lost by eight — and to a woman, to boot.

I’m not naïve. A country whose people brought children and picnic baskets to watch the lynching of Black men clearly has a long and deep history of not just tolerating but celebrating brutality. Yet it has slowly become clear that under today’s economic and political conditions, displays of wanton cruelty fail to motivate anyone but the hardest core of Trump’s base. The rest of us live in the real world, fretting about gas prices, the relentless march of artificial intelligence, war in the Middle East and more.

When Zohran Mamdani was elected mayor of New York last year, Republicans were thrilled. A democratic socialist, he looked like the perfect cudgel for Republicans eager to hammer home the message that Democrats were too far to the left, both economically and culturally. His strident criticism of Israel, unabashed embrace of democratic socialism and immigrant and Muslim identity made him the perfect foil for Trumpian reaction: He was a foreign and dangerous radical, an insurgent who had invaded and occupied America’s glittering metropolis.

So Republicans were aghast when Trump, who had condemned Mamdani in racist and Islamophobic terms during the mayoral campaign, suddenly seemed utterly charmed by the handsome and affable young mayor. The boogeyman became a bestie. This unlikely and one-sided bromance derailed a key part of the Republican midterm strategy, as demonization by association would take in the president, too.

What happened with Democrats was quieter but even more interesting. Mamdani became something of a model for many successful Democrats across the ideological spectrum. Many adopted his sunny affect and his snappy social-video-driven messaging. They also put the central issue of his mayoral campaign — affordability — at the heart of their campaigns. Speaking after the Democratic blowout victory, he was clearly thrilled. But he sounded a warning to his fellow lawmakers in waiting.

“It is not enough to simply win power,” Mamdani said. “We must use it. And the American people will know the difference between hollow words and hard work. For years, we’ve had the debate. Now, it’s time for us and the Democratic Party to deliver.”

One of the reasons that Mamdani is so popular is that he does the basic things New Yorkers want. But he also aims high in trying to improve their lives in new ways, from expanding preschool to giving away opera tickets, from freezing rents to holding scavenger hunts. He is always doing something to try to make life in New York better and always making sure everyone knows about it. His immediate predecessor, like Trump, was entertaining, corrupt and a bit of a clown. For all his smiles, Mamdani is deadly serious about delivering.

There is a lesson here for the incoming Democratic majority in Congress and all these new Democratic governors. The Trump circus stopped entertaining Americans once the bill for his disastrous decisions came due. Democrats will need to use their power to improve people’s lives, quickly and visibly. That won’t be easy, of course. But Trump loves winners and hates losers. Improbable as his promotion of the hard-liner Stephen Miller to the White House chief of staff makes it seem, the Trumpiest move imaginable now would be for him to step away from the smoldering wreck of the G. O. P., opening the door to legacy-burnishing deals with ascendant Democrats.

That would really be a shot in the arm.

Democrats need to remember why they even still exist: they are a voice for working people and the poor. That is the focus, not raking in donations from corporations and Israel's US enforcers just to stay in power and do nothing. Many of the newly elected candidates understand this, whether they are moderate or progressive or socialist. Those who do not, including current leadership, will be next to go.

You make great points. I would add that the Democrats work best as a coalition of state and city organizations. This goes back to the New Deal/Fair Deal days. This time it worked out as an array of locally-tailored candidates vs. a vulnerable national target.

More Than 50 Killed in Yemen in One of the Deadliest 24 Hours of the War

The New York Times November 07, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Strikes show the heavy toll since fighting between the Houthis and the Saudi-backed government reignited in August, with civilians paying a heavy price.

By Shuaib Almosawa and Ismaeel Naar

Shuaib Almosawa reported from Sanaa, Yemen, and Ismaeel Naar from Dubai, United Arab Emirates.

More than 50 people have been killed in Yemen over the past 24 hours, in what appeared to be one of the deadliest stretches since the conflict between the Iran-backed Houthis and the government of Yemen backed by Saudi Arabia reignited in recent months.

Houthi officials said airstrikes tore through the village of al-Shariya, in the Bani Hushaysh district east of the capital, Sanaa, on Saturday. Anees al-Asbahi, a spokesman for the Houthi-run Health Ministry, said at least 27 people were killed and 30 others wounded, most of them women and children, and blamed Saudi warplanes. The Saudi government did not immediately respond to questions about the strikes.

The attack in Sanaa took place a day after strikes on a crowded market in Taiz Province killed at least 30 people, according to a Houthi-run news agency. The warring parties traded blame for the attack. The authorities in government-held Taiz, Yemen’s third-largest city, said the Houthis were responsible, but officials for the Iran-backed group blamed Saudi Arabia.

The past few days’ high toll underscores the growing ferocity of the war since it resumed in August. Almost 1,800 people had been killed by the end of October and more than 300,000 people had been displaced, the World Health Organization said last week. Aid agencies have warned that hospitals in Yemen are running short of medical supplies.

The United Nations has repeatedly warned that the fighting is returning to the levels seen a decade ago, before a cease-fire was signed in 2022. A Saudi-led coalition waged a yearslong air campaign against the Houthis after the group seized control of Sanaa and ousted the government in 2014. The conflict contributed to hundreds of thousands of deaths from violence, hunger and disease, causing one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises.

Independently verifying casualties inside Yemen is difficult. The Houthis require journalists to obtain permits before visiting strike sites, and Saudi officials have disclosed little about a campaign. Each side has repeatedly accused the other of targeting civilians.

The war resumed when the fragile truce unraveled over the summer after the Houthis accused Saudi Arabia of carrying out an airstrike on Sanaa’s airport.

Since then, the Houthis have taken control of Yemen’s Red Sea coast and threatened Saudi shipping through the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a key trade route. A Saudi-led bombing campaign has not shifted the Houthis from the territory they have held in northern Yemen or on the Red Sea.

The Houthis have also struck deep inside Saudi Arabia. The Saudi-led coalition said on Saturday that it had intercepted and destroyed a Houthi cruise missile aimed at the Riyadh region, the latest attack in a monthslong barrage that has included a hit on the main international airport in the Saudi capital, killing more than a dozen people and wounding hundreds. That attack forced Saudi Arabia to postpone a string of marquee events, including its flagship investment conference and a summit with European leaders.

Houthi officials vowed retaliation for the latest deaths. Yahya Saree, the Houthi military spokesman, said the group would avenge their dead “against the killer of children and women.”

Saeed Al-Batati contributed reporting from al-Mukalla, Yemen.

Ismaeel Naar is an international reporter for The Times, covering the Gulf states. He is based in Dubai, United Arab Emirates.

Schumer, Once Besieged, Is on Track to Remain Leader After Election Blowout

The New York Times November 07, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

The Democratic leader still faces skeptics in his ranks and hostility from some activists, but aides say he has enough commitments of support to be elected majority leader.

By Carl Hulse

Reporting from Capitol Hill

Last year, Democratic interest groups and voters berated Senator Chuck Schumer of New York, the minority leader, for backing off a spending fight with President Trump rather than forcing a government shutdown early in his term.

Activists called for Mr. Schumer’s ouster. Some Democratic lawmakers seethed. Protesters jeered outside his Brooklyn home. The outcry reached such a pitch that he postponed public appearances to promote a new book he had written and hunkered down amid questions about whether he could continue as the Democratic leader.

Twenty months later and in the wake of a sweeping electoral victory he engineered and funded, Mr. Schumer’s aides say he has locked down another term in that post, having secured commitments of support from enough Democratic senators to be elected majority leader in a private vote scheduled for next month.

Senate Democrats have gained at least seven and potentially nine seats to capture the largest majority they have enjoyed since Barack Obama’s presidency.

None of it has quelled the outcry from the left against Mr. Schumer, 75, who was viewed favorably in a May New York Times/Siena poll by only about one-third of Democrats. Among Democrats in the Senate, there is still some resistance to his continuing at the top — including by some of the newly elected members — but no Democrat has emerged to challenge him.

Between that implosion in March 2025 and the midterm exuberance, Mr. Schumer and his political team engaged in an all-out, $550-million push to put more Senate seats in play and increase their chances of regaining the majority — an investment that paid off handsomely.

But even the stubbornly optimistic Mr. Schumer did not foresee the extent of the Democratic victory or the Republican collapse.

“I did not,” Mr. Schumer said in an interview. “But I was confident we would get it back. My confidence did not waver in that.”

Not everyone had such certainty, given the Senate map for 2026. Democrats began the election cycle with six fewer seats in their caucus than Republicans had. It was a hole that threatened to get deeper.

Just one Republican seat — that of five-term incumbent Susan Collins in Maine — was up for re-election in a state that went for Kamala Harris in the presidential election. And Ms. Collins had proved in previous elections that she would not go easily.

Mr. Schumer set out to find candidates he believed could be competitive and who matched a winning profile in red states, drawing scorn from progressive activists who said his choices were too old and too moderate. His first target was Roy Cooper, the outgoing Democratic governor of North Carolina. Mr. Schumer said he called him immediately upon the expiration of his term as governor on Jan. 1, 2025.

Mr. Cooper initially demurred because he was embarking on a fellowship that was to run through May. The Democratic leader marked June 1 on his calendar to pester Mr. Cooper again. In late May, Mr. Cooper called Mr. Schumer instead.

“He said he was ready to go,” Mr. Schumer recounted. It was a critical get. Mr. Cooper won easily in a race that never really seemed in doubt, allowing Democrats to focus time and money elsewhere and giving them one sure pickup to start. And Georgia, the most endangered Democratic seat on paper, fell off the map as Senator Jon Ossoff showed early strength and Republicans there feuded and nominated a weak challenger.

Next up was Sherrod Brown, the three-term Ohio Democrat who lost in 2024, felled after a barrage of cryptocurrency industry money was spent against him. Mr. Schumer put on the hard sell, visiting the state three times to amiably work over Mr. Brown and his wife, the writer Connie Schultz. His closing message was a guilt trip: “If we lose the Senate by one vote, you and Connie won’t enjoy your retirement,” Mr. Schumer warned.

The next day, he was in. Senate Majority PAC, the political action committee allied with Mr. Schumer, spent $150 million helping Mr. Brown to victory.

Over a series of dinners, Mr. Schumer successfully enticed a strong challenger in Alaska: Mary Peltola, who had won statewide races for the House before being defeated in a re-election campaign. She is ahead of the Republican incumbent senator, Dan Sullivan, in the count there.

He also encouraged Josh Turek to enter the Senate contest in Iowa, then poured $67 million into his winning race. A veteran Democratic strategist told Mr. Schumer to take a look at Adam Hamilton in Kansas, and he became enamored, and would eventually spend $14 million in the upset win against Senator Roger Marshall.

The Democratic primary in Maine was a mess, and Mr. Schumer’s initial recruit, Gov. Janet Mills, dropped out. But the PAC affiliated with him pushed a steady anti-Collins message with $65 million in spending that was focused on her, not the Democratic contender.

Michigan was tricky for Mr. Schumer as he leaned toward the centrist Representative Haley Stevens while her ultraprogressive primary opponent, Abdul El-Sayed, was among a group of candidates who said they would not back Mr. Schumer for leader. Still, the day after Mr. El-Sayed won the primary, Mr. Schumer began injecting funds to help him win.

“We never hesitated,” he said. “We put in from Day 1.” Michigan ended up as a top state for spending by the Schumer-affiliated super PAC, essentially tied with Iowa and behind only Ohio.

And in a race that was seen by many as a pipe dream, Mr. Schumer recruited Scott Colom, a Black prosecutor, to oppose Senator Cindy Hyde Smith, the Republican incumbent, hosting Mr. Colom and his father, a well-known Mississippi Republican, for lunch in Brooklyn. Mr. Colom is slightly ahead in what would be a monumental upset.

At the same time, Mr. Schumer and Senate Democrats were setting legislative traps on the Senate floor, forcing Republicans to take tough votes on unpopular tariffs and the war with Iran. The second time a spending dispute threatened a shutdown, Mr. Schumer did not hesitate to force one as Democrats dug in against ending subsidies for health insurance under the Affordable Care Act.

The shutdown eventually ended, but Democrats won individual votes on protecting the health care aid, which Republicans opposed. When the subsidies expired at the end of last year, Mr. Schumer had new fuel for a message that Republicans had ignored rising costs on Americans and made the problem worse.

“In retrospect, even though we hated shutting down the government, it helped us,” Mr. Schumer said.

Then, after the president initiated the war against Iran, Democrats forced Republicans on the record repeatedly in support of the war and its accompanying increases in fuel and fertilizer prices that were ravaging the economy in agriculture-reliant states. Democrats also resisted Mr. Trump’s push to enact a restrictive voting law that they feared would suppress eligible voters inclined to support them.

The mix of legislative strategy, solid recruitment, missteps by Republicans and a dismal approval rating for Mr. Trump added up to a Democratic rout, marking the third time Mr. Schumer had overseen a successful effort to retake the Senate majority after wins in 2006 and 2020.

Even with Tuesday’s remarkable showing, Mr. Schumer’s future as leader is being questioned. Senator Chris Van Hollen, Democrat of Maryland, has publicly urged a discussion about the direction of the party’s leadership, though Mr. Van Hollen himself has shown more interest in a presidential bid.

“I am pretty confident that he is going to be re-elected as leader,” Senator Chris Coons, Democrat of Delaware, said of Mr. Schumer, given his “particular talent” of recruiting good candidates, raising lots of money and advising candidates on messaging. “He revels in winning elections. That makes a good case of why he should continue in leadership.”

But Mr. Coons said Democrats should have a “big conversation about what future leadership should look like,” and take an expansive approach that allows more voices to be heard.

Mr. Schumer said he intends to capitalize on this year’s success in Republican-leaning territory to fortify and expand the Democratic electoral presence.

“We’re going to make a durable majority by delivering and by focusing on good Democrats who are now in office in red states,” Mr. Schumer said. “I spent decades working to change the Senate map. The election proved we could. Now we have to make sure what we built lasts.”

A picture caption with an earlier version of this article misstated the status of Scott Colom’s candidacy for Senate in Mississippi. The ballots were still being counted on Saturday; he had not won the race.

We acknowledge mistakes in our reporting with corrections. If you spot an error, please let us know at corrections@nytimes. com. Learn more.

Carl Hulse is the chief Washington correspondent for The Times, primarily writing about Congress and national political races and issues. He has nearly four decades of experience reporting in the nation’s capital.

How Cardiologists’ High Hopes for Two Drugs Were Dashed

The New York Times November 07, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

By every measure, the drugs were no better than placebos, full data revealed on Saturday. Was it the fault of the design of the studies, or our very hypotheses about heart disease?

By Gina Kolata

Cardiologists have been on edge for months, waiting for the details surrounding recent reports of the stunning failures of two new heart drugs.

The drugs — pelacarsen and ziltivekimab — were widely expected to usher in a new era in preventing heart disease. Companies, betting on the drugs’ promise, made huge investments in developing them.

So when doctors saw preliminary announcements that the drugs were not helping patients in large clinical trials, many felt blindsided, although still hopeful that there was more to the story than they knew.

“The whole cardiovascular community was gobsmacked,” said Dr. Karol Watson, a director of UCLA’s preventive cardiology program.

Were the drugs close to succeeding, just barely missing a statistically significant benefit? Or were there at least subgroups of patients who were helped?

Now the answers are in. There was not a shred of evidence that the drugs helped anyone. By every measure, they were no better than placebos.

The results, Dr. Watson noted, “are about as neutral as they can be.” The full data were presented on Saturday morning at the annual meeting of the American Heart Association and in simultaneous publications in The New England Journal of Medicine.

One drug, pelacarsen, by Novartis, is known to make levels of the Lp(a) blood protein plunge. The protein is widely believed to cause heart attacks and strokes. The other, ziltivekimab, by Novo Nordisk, stops inflammation, thought to be a major component of plaques in arteries. Neither drug made a dent in heart disease outcomes during these clinical trials.

Dr. Paul Ridker of Mass General Brigham, who was the principal investigator for the inflammation trial — known as the Zeus study — had been a true believer.

He was convinced by suggestive evidence that squelching inflammation could protect people from heart disease. There was, he said, an earlier encouraging study involving an experimental anti-inflammatory drug made by Novartis, as well as studies indicating that colchicine, an anti-inflammatory drug used to treat gout, could also be protective.

Until the day he saw the results, Dr. Ridker said in a recent interview, he had thought the Zeus study was “a brilliant idea,” bound to show that the Novo drug, ziltivekimab, which blocks an inflammatory protein called il-6, was effective. The participants all had severe heart disease, advanced kidney disease and a blood protein that is a marker of inflammation.

Instead of protecting patients in Zeus, though, Dr. Ridker announced on Saturday that no one had been helped by the drug. Every subgroup of patients in the 6,376-patient study fared the same. Those taking the drug did no better than those taking a placebo, even though the drug did reduce inflammation.

“Did we pick the wrong target, the wrong patient population?” Dr. Ridker said.

Or did the patients have heart disease that was so advanced it could not be helped? “Maybe the horse was out of the barn,” he said.

Others in the field are wondering if the hypothesis itself was wrong. Maybe inflammation is a sign of disease, not a cause, as white hair is a sign of aging.

Novo announced in September that it was stopping two other studies of ziltivekimab that involved patients with heart failure. An independent committee determined that the drug was not helping them. The company is continuing to test its drug in patients who have had a heart attack. That study will conclude next year.

Dr. Ridker, who proposed the link between inflammation and heart disease more than a quarter-century ago, has not given up hope. He noted that there was genetic and epidemiological evidence as well as evidence from animal studies that a different protein in the same inflammation pathway should protect against heart attacks and strokes.

“We already know this is going to work,” Dr. Ridker said. Now, he added, the question is: “How do we find the right drug for the right patient?”

The principal investigator for Horizon, the Lp(a) study, is Dr. Steven Nissen of the Cleveland Clinic. He said his concern was that the study’s disappointing results would lead patients to drop out of two other studies testing drugs that reduce Lp(a) levels.

“A single trial doesn’t necessarily give us all the answers,” Dr. Nissen said. And, he added, high levels of Lp(a) are “a powerful risk factor.” It remains possible, he said, that patients in the Horizon trial had heart disease so advanced that it was too late for the Novartis drug to help.

Another hypothesis was that the patients’ other risk factors — blood pressure and L. D. L. cholesterol — were so well controlled that their risk was about as low as it could go, said Dr. Roger Blumenthal, director of the Johns Hopkins Ciccarone Center for the Prevention of Cardiovascular Disease. Reducing Lp(a) levels could not lower it further.

Dr. Ridker had another idea. All the Horizon patients were taking anti-clotting medications. Lp(a) is thought to cause heart disease by promoting blood clots. Perhaps the anti-clotting medications diluted the drug’s effects.

But the bottom line was that, for whatever reasons, the Novartis drug had utterly failed.

“Was there anything that we could point a finger to that said, ‘Yeah, there’s a benefit’?” Dr. Nissen asked.

No, he added, “there was nothing.”

Gina Kolata reports on diseases and treatments, how treatments are discovered and tested, and how they affect people.

Connections: Sports Edition

Connections: Soccer Edition

Connections Coach

After publishing a book about the 1939 classic “The Women,” the actress and writer talks about her film career and her role in #MeToo.

Douglas says she has learned to be “very strong and very direct.”Credit... Jillian Freyer for The New York Times

Supported by

By Maureen Dowd

Reporting from Haddam, Conn.

At the dawn of feminism, I assumed that cat fights would soon be history.

We were all going to be sisters, supporting each other and keeping our claws sheathed.

How naïve I was.

As they fought for equality, women were competing not only for mates but for jobs, desperately trying to infiltrate the room where it happens. Even the pioneers of feminism, Gloria Steinem and Betty Friedan, feuded.

But cat fights, as it turns out, are great for business. From “Dynasty” to the “Real Housewives,” “The Bachelor” and “Love Island” franchises, from “Mean Girls” to “Bridesmaids,” women scratching each other’s eyes out has been an amazing moneymaker, mostly for the men who still largely run the entertainment industry.

Cat fights are big in politics, too. Witness the tabloid delight in the “Democrat fight” between Nancy Pelosi and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez in 2019 and the recent hair-pulling at the White House, with President Trump’s recently ousted chief of staff, the “ice maiden” Susie Wiles, sparring with the West Wing aide Natalie Harp and the short-lived press secretary Katie Zacharia.

So, naturally, I wanted to go to Connecticut to talk with Illeana Douglas about the biggest cat fight movie of all time and one that helped popularize the term — Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer’s 1939 classic, “The Women,” based on the Clare Boothe Luce Broadway hit of the same name. (Luce, the wife of Henry Luce, the founder of the Time-Life magazine empire, later became a congresswoman from Connecticut.)

Douglas, a 65-year-old actress, writer and director, has a glossy new book, “Jungle Red!”, on the making of the movie — the only lavish studio film, she says, ever produced with no men onscreen — and the rivalries offscreen among the famous actresses.

Even the animals in the film, dogs and horses, were female. George Cukor, the director, told the press that male visitors were barred from the set — an order defied by Joan Crawford.

“In all the publicity and in the press, they had people coming to the set, like, ‘This is going to be the world’s best catfight,’” Douglas said. “So from the very beginning, they set it up.”

In case anyone possibly missed the point, Cukor’s opening credits included animals corresponding to the film’s main characters — a leopard for Crawford and a hissing black cat for Rosalind Russell, while Norma Shearer and Joan Fontaine were prey, a doe and a lamb.

Crawford embraced her inner predatory feline. “I wanted this role more than anything in my life,” she said. “I like playing bitches. There’s a little bitch in all of us.”

Douglas and I are sitting in her renovated kitchen of her colonial farmhouse, which looks like one of the dreamy film sets depicted in her earlier book, “Connecticut in the Movies.” She grew up mostly in nearby Old Saybrook, where Katharine Hepburn also lived.

She made pancakes with maple syrup and turkey sausage and reminisced about her grandfather, the urbane Melvyn Douglas, who starred in Ernst Lubitsch’s “Ninotchka” with Greta Garbo and “The Candidate” with Robert Redford.

He went on to win two late-in-life supporting actor Oscars for “Hud” with Paul Newman and “Being There” with Peter Sellers. Melvyn’s second wife was the actress and politician Helen Gahagan Douglas, who lost the 1950 Senate race to Richard Nixon in California, after Nixon smeared her as a Communist sympathizer.

Illeana Douglas had memorable film roles in “GoodFellas,” “Cape Fear,” “To Die For,” “Grace of My Heart” and “Ghost World,” as well as the TV shows “Six Feet Under” and “Law & Order: SVU.” She played Gary Shandling’s girlfriend toward the end of “The Larry Sanders Show” and hosted a show on female filmmakers for Turner Classic Movies.

Her house is filled with gorgeous movie posters, including her grandfather’s Hollywood classics “A Woman’s Face” (with Crawford), “That Uncertain Feeling” (with Merle Oberon) and “Ninotchka.” There’s also a picture of her former boyfriend of eight years, Martin Scorsese, and a library of books about Hollywood.

Douglas was a nepo baby, given her legendary grandfather, but she had to work her way up. After attending the American Academy of Dramatic Arts in New York for a year, she was an assistant to the notorious publicist Peggy Siegal, decades before Siegel got tarred in the Jeffrey Epstein scandal.

“People would jokingly say, ‘You work for the devil’s publicist,’” she recalled. “And I would say, ‘Oh, that’s why it’s so hot in the office.’ My job consisted of calling people like Walter Cronkite on the phone and inviting him to a party.”

Scorsese was editing “The Last Temptation of Christ” nearby and needed someone to dub in screams for Mary Magdalene. Douglas pitched in and the two began dating.

Douglas has complained that she always gets asked about Scorsese, but he never gets asked about her.

“Would you want to be identified with one relationship you had in your life?” she asked me. “Except for privately, I never get to talk about other great relationships I’ve had and influences I’ve had on them.”

What influence did she have on Scorsese?

She said that during the filming of the 1990 movie “GoodFellas,” she suggested making the scene with all the wives a Mary Kay party, after Scorsese couldn’t get the rights to make it a Tupperware party. “And a lot of the improv lines that we were coming up with that day at my house went into the movie,” she said.

Douglas was married to the late Jonathan Axelrod, a producer and writer, for three years until their divorce in 2001. Would she want to remarry?

“No,” she said flatly. “I used to always want to be married, but unfortunately I don’t think there’s anything in it for women. Having been married once, I don’t think it’s a good idea.”

The title of Douglas’s book comes from a signature line in “The Women,” when Shearer’s character, Mary Haines, resolves to go on the offensive against Crawford’s Crystal Allen, a vampy shopgirl who has stolen her husband. Haines gets in fighting trim by growing her nails into “claws” and having them painted a fierce shade: “Jungle red!” she cries, showing off her manicure as violins swell.

When Douglas recounted the scene, I noticed that her nails were done up in the same deep shade.

The stars of “The Women” did not care for each other offscreen either. Crawford felt that Shearer got all the good roles because of her marriage to MGM’s “Wonder Boy” executive, Irving Thalberg, who died in 1936. Crawford mockingly called Shearer, the classy first lady of MGM, “the Widow Thalberg.”

As Anita Loos, the screenwriter, put it: “Norma and Joan could never have been personal friends — they came from different worlds. Norma thought Joan crude and pushy, and Joan considered Norma overbearing and uppity — but they both knew the ‘feud’ was good copy, and so they helped it along.”

Things came to a delicious head when Crawford read lines with Shearer while engaging in her cacophonous hobby, knitting. Norma genteelly asked Joan to put away the clacking knitting needles, but the whole point was needling Norma, so Joan didn’t.

As the movie’s hair stylist, Sydney Guilaroff, recalled, “Crawford went home, drank six martinis and fired off a telegram to Norma informing her in no uncertain terms exactly what she thought of her.” At Cukor’s insistence, Crawford sent an apology telegram to Shearer, but she doubled down by listing all the slights she felt she had endured.

After that, Crawford bailed on the first day of shooting with Shearer, saying she had arsenic poisoning. She also skipped the cast luncheon after the film wrapped, sending word that she had ironing to do.

“So many people say Norma and I don’t like each other,” Crawford purred to the gossip columnist Hedda Hopper. “Who are we to disagree with the majority opinion?”

Cukor, who was known in Hollywood to be gay, had something to prove. He had recently been fired as the director of “Gone With the Wind” after Clark Gable fretted that his approach was too feminine, favoring Vivien Leigh.

“I thought it was kind of interesting that he got fired from ‘Gone with the Wind’ for being gay and then hired for ‘The Women’ because he was gay,” Douglas told me.

Rosalind Russell soared as Mary’s backbiting friend, playing the role as high camp. “I relate, obviously, to Rosalind Russell, who was stuck in these second leads, but she persisted,” said Douglas, who has played her share of supporting roles.

Tensions bristled between Russell and her fellow cast member Paulette Goddard, a longtime girlfriend of Charlie Chaplin who showed up at the soundstage each day in her custom Rolls-Royce. “There was no sisterhood,” Goddard said.

The mutual antipathy spilled over into what the producer Hunt Stromberg hailed as “the greatest catfight of all time,” a fight scene at a ranch in Reno, Nev., which escalated to the point that a doctor was called to patch up Goddard after Russell bit her.

It should have been a mere stage bite, Douglas writes, “but during one of the takes, Russell sank her teeth right into Goddard’s thigh. Loos, who was watching the scene, said, ‘Blood began dripping from her leg.’”

“The Women” was such a hit that studio suits began inserting cat fights in other movies, Douglas noted, saying, “‘Oh, it worked with Rosalind Russell. Let’s see Marlene Dietrich now!’”

Douglas added dryly: “You know, if Nicole Kidman and Sandra Bullock had had a catfight in ‘Practical Magic,’ it would have done so much better.”

Some people objected to Luce’s portrayal of women in “The Women.” Eleanor Roosevelt dismissed it as unpleasant.

But Douglas said she was relieved, when she saw screenings of the film with younger women, that they got into the fur-is-flying spirit and were not put off by female characters who devote so much energy to discussing husbands, ex-husbands and suitors. (The movie’s tag line was “It’s all about the men!”)

Douglas acknowledged that some women these days might be skeptical of a movie centered on female characters who talk so much about men. “But what should they be talking about?” she said. “Their diet?” And when you think about it, the girls in “Girls” and “Sex and the City” talk a lot about men, too.

“As soon as the leopard comes on and you see Joan Crawford, the audience starts laughing,” Douglas said. She added: “People seem to be relieved, like, ‘Oh, OK, we can just laugh at women all being bitches.’ ”

She said she follows the Elaine May rule, that there’s no point trying to disarm men who think you’re scary-smart by trying to be likable. (That’s where Hillary Clinton went wrong in her debate with a lurking Donald Trump; as she recently acknowledged, she should have just turned around and said, “Back up, you creep!”)

“You wrap yourself up like a pretzel trying to please people and navigate and then you can’t take it anymore,” Douglas said. “It’s better to just be unlikable from the get-go.”

She said that all the actresses in “The Women” “used the tools in their tool kit to scare the hell” out of Cukor and the producers.

“That’s why I wrote the whole book,” Douglas said. “But I think we’re so afraid of it because we want to be liked. But I absolutely know that you get more done with men if they’re afraid of you.”

She continued: “And, yes, people are going to dislike you. And, yes, unfortunately, a lot of times it’s women. ‘Who do you think you are, standing up for yourself?’ That’s what I do find a little odd in the female empowerment game — that we don’t celebrate other women becoming successful.

“I do think that women are way too sensitive to criticism. And that has ended many of my friendships.” Douglas said, adding, “Women will stop being friends with you simply because you confront them about something they did that hurt your feelings.”

Douglas made headlines in 2018 when she told Ronan Farrow of The New Yorker about being assaulted and retaliated against by Les Moonves, then the powerful head of CBS. Moonves admitted to trying to kiss Douglas in his office but denied her other allegations. He ended up losing his job and his severance after revelations by Douglas and other women.

“I was attacked by Les Moonves when I was doing a television show,” she recalled. “And, again, nobody talked about it, but it was something that everybody in my life knew, and we even sort of comically talked about it.

She added: “So I’m glad I stood up for myself. It was extremely cathartic.

She said that making her case against Moonves “did put the nail in the coffin of the predatory behavior at the top level.” But she added, “I don’t think that the #MeToo movement did anything for the relationships between men and women. If anything, it’s like men solidified, and women became terrified.”

She noted “an odd unnaturalness” between men and women in Hollywood meetings these days.

“There always is going to be that weird, awkward thing of, ‘Is she going to say I attacked her?’ or ‘Is he going to say … ?” she said.

Now she’s working on a book about Hollywood in the ’90s.

Back then, she recalled, “There was this environment where you were told to go in — the agents, the managers, everybody’s involved in it — you’re supposed to go in and wear a short skirt, and you’re supposed to flirt with the leading actor, to a certain extent, to get the part.”

The casting couch was installed on the first day of Hollywood. As Douglas writes in her book, Louis B. Mayer, the head of MGM, would tell Crawford he felt paternal toward her. “Mayer would always say, ‘I feel about you like I feel about one of my own daughters,’” Crawford said, “‘but usually, when he was saying it, he would have his hand on my tit.’”

Douglas said that when her grandfather got to MGM in the 1930s, “he said they gave you a list of people that you could take out to dinner, and then people you could have sex with.”

She felt that the #MeToo movement “did seem to be hijacked away from what the initial scream of pain was.”

“I’m like, wait a minute,” she said. “Can we focus? And so, part of the reason that I had friends who wanted me to come forward was to put it back on track to workplace harassment.”

Given the comebacks of several men in the entertainment industry who had been banished for sexual misconduct, and given the recent purging of women executives at studios, what is her advice for young women trying to make it in Hollywood?

“I think they should be a bitch right off the bat,” she said. “You don’t have to be mean. You don’t have to say, ‘Your hair is receding’ or anything like that. But I think that being very strong and very direct always works better.”

An earlier version of this article included a photo and caption, relying on information provided by Getty, that misidentified one of the actors. The still from the movie “The Women” showed Rosalind Russell sitting next to Joan Crawford, not Norma Shearer. It has been replaced.

Maureen Dowd is an Opinion columnist for The Times. She won the 1999 Pulitzer Prize for distinguished commentary. She is the author, most recently, of “Notorious.”

Turning Point Bet on the Midterms and Lost. Some Republicans Are Furious.

The New York Times November 07, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Candidates backed by the right-wing activist group did not fare well, and the results set off recriminations from establishment Republicans.

By Reis Thebault and Sejal Govindarao

Reis Thebault reported from Phoenix.

Turning Point USA bet big on Arizona.

Leaders of the right-wing activist organization founded by Charlie Kirk said the state’s contest for governor was “the most important race in America.”

The group’s handpicked candidate, Representative Andy Biggs, a MAGA-aligned Republican, was one of the last politicians Mr. Kirk personally endorsed before his assassination last year. Its political arm spent nearly $20 million to support Mr. Biggs’s campaign.

But on Tuesday, Turning Point’s bet went bust.

In the group’s home state, where registered Republicans outnumber Democrats, Mr. Biggs lost to Gov. Katie Hobbs by more than 10 percentage points, and Democrats thumped Turning Point’s chosen candidates for statewide and congressional races. The same happened in Nevada and New Hampshire, states where the group hoped to build conservative power and lay a foundation for the 2028 presidential contest.

Instead of vindicating a polarizing organization that has pitched itself as the future of the G. O. P., Tuesday’s results set off recriminations from establishment Republicans who have been exiled by Turning Point’s political machine.

“Turning Point is driving us to extinction,” said Gina Swoboda, the former Arizona Republican Party chairwoman who has feuded with the group. “They have become a destructive force in Republican politics.”

In the days since Republicans’ blowout loss, Turning Point leaders have been left to sift through the rubble of the “red wall” they had pledged to build in Arizona, Nevada and New Hampshire, states they view as critical battlegrounds. Despite the group’s significant investment, the only high-profile candidate in those three states who won with its backing was Kelly Ayotte, the incumbent governor of New Hampshire.

Turning Point and its allies have defended the group’s strategy, blaming Republican losses on a brutal national political environment stemming from President Trump’s deeply unpopular war with Iran. And they note that many other Republican candidates who ran without Turning Point’s backing lost by similar margins.

“I think it’s clear that we were up against a national wave that impacted every state,” Andrew Kolvet, Turning Point’s spokesman, said in a statement. “One of the mistakes you can make after a result like we had Tuesday is to learn the wrong lessons. Any suggestion that a more moderate candidate would have fared better is plain wrong.”

In a social media post, Erika Kirk, Mr. Kirk’s widow and Turning Point’s chief executive, said it was clear voters were “concerned about the state of the economy and the war in Iran.” The group’s leaders, she said, were poring over election results and would “spend the next two years making the case for how conservative, free market solutions, and a renewed focus on our country’s founding principles can address the problems the American people face.”

Turning Point, which is headquartered in Phoenix, has thousands of chapters at high schools and college campuses across the country, but its leadership has long considered Arizona to be the most important battleground for setting up national Republican victories. The group has honed its get-out-the-vote operations there and worked to remake the state’s G. O. P. in its image, championing hard-right primary challengers while muscling out the type of moderate Republicans exemplified by the late Senator John McCain.

But Arizona’s general election voters have repeatedly passed over Turning Point-supported candidates like Kari Lake and Blake Masters, allowing Democrats to take control of most major statewide offices and both U. S. Senate seats, even as Mr. Trump won the state in 2024.

This year, some Republicans warned that Turning Point had not learned from past mistakes. One misstep came in April, when the group’s unusual involvement in an obscure public utility election prompted a backlash that allowed a slate of liberal candidates to triumph.

And as the midterms approached, Turning Point elevated some candidates despite warnings from fellow Republicans that most voters would see them as too extreme.

The group’s operatives helped clear the primary field for Mr. Biggs by relentlessly attacking his chief competitor, the more moderate Karrin Taylor Robson, who dropped out early in the race after lagging in polls.

And Turning Point sparred publicly with Ms. Swoboda, who first planned to run in one of the state’s most competitive House districts before pivoting to an unsuccessful bid for secretary of state. Turning Point worked against her in each primary contest.

Both of the group’s favored candidates in those races lost on Tuesday — Jay Feely, a former N. F. L. kicker, for Arizona’s First Congressional District, and Alexander Kolodin, an election-denying lawmaker, for secretary of state.

Ms. Swoboda and other longtime Turning Point opponents could barely contain their schadenfreude this week. She likened the group’s relationship to the Republican Party as akin to “a parasite on a host.”

“It’d be one thing if you were a parasite that could function in a symbiotic way,” Ms. Swoboda said. “But if you’re a tick that keeps sucking on a host until the host is dead, then you’re useless and a negative.”

Some Turning Point critics argue that more moderate candidates would have performed better. Others struggled to think of a Republican who could have withstood the blue tide that swept the country.

“It might be satisfying to me to say Turning Point snatched defeat from jaws of victory,” said Stephen Richer, a Republican and former Maricopa County recorder who lost his 2024 primary to a candidate backed by Turning Point. But, he said, “President Trump owns this loss.”

Still, Mr. Richer said, Turning Point has “missed the message” several cycles in a row.

Mr. Kolvet said those denouncing Turning Point were “irrelevant, disgruntled local political malcontents.”

But even some Republican base voters have grown tired of the combative political environment the group has fostered.

“This whole nonsense about insulting other conservatives because they don’t agree 100 percent with their views is really dumb, and it’s cost us dearly here,” Tom Abood, a real estate developer who has voted for Mr. Trump three times, said after casting his ballot for Republicans on Tuesday in the suburb of Paradise Valley. “It should be an easy slam dunk win in this state.”

On the day after the election, Turning Point staff members arrived early at their office near the foothills of Phoenix’s South Mountain Preserve to take stock.

The shift to Democrats among young men — who had moved sharply right in 2024 — was especially concerning, said Alex Clark, who hosts a health and wellness podcast for Turning Point and was at the office that day.

College-age voters should be the group’s top priority going forward, Ms. Clark said, and Turning Point should invest in more polling on campuses to keep tabs on the constituency before it drifts further left.

“That should be a really sobering reality for the G. O. P., that if you do not work to rebuild trust with these voters by 2028, you will have built a super-Democrat party,” Ms. Clark said.

Mrs. Kirk has already endorsed Vice President JD Vance for president in 2028. But Ms. Clark said Turning Point would be wise not to tie itself too closely to any one president. The group should promote conservative values while remaining neutral in 2028 and beyond, she said.

“The base could turn on a president, conservative or not, at any time,” Ms. Clark said. “You don’t want to be stuck in the middle of that.”

The group’s leaders say they plan to analyze state-level polling, redouble their efforts on college campuses and strategize about how to best allocate their resources ahead of 2028.

Sean Noble, who was Mr. Biggs’s top campaign strategist, saw a silver lining for Turning Point in the sweeping Republican defeat. The group now has a chance to become the leading voice of resistance to new Democratic leadership on Capitol Hill, he said. Mr. Noble compared the moment to the early 1990s, when Rush Limbaugh surged in popularity and became a hero to grass-roots conservatives.

“One of the best things that could have happened for Turning Point,” Mr. Noble said, “is they now have the foil of Democrats in charge of Congress.”

Reis Thebault is a Phoenix-based reporter for The Times, covering the American Southwest.

Sejal Govindarao is a national reporter and a member of the 2026-27 Times Fellowship, a program for journalists early in their careers.
