Trump’s D. C. Construction Blitz May Be About to Get Tougher

The New York Times November 07, 2026

The president has bulldozed through obstacles as he has sought to remake the face of Washington. But newly empowered Democrats and angry judges are setting up a high-stakes showdown.

Credit... Alex Kent/The New York Times

Supported by

By Luke Broadwater and Emily Badger

Reporting from Washington

Since his party’s midterm election drubbing, President Trump has publicly retreated deeper into the big, bold and often-gilded Washington construction projects he sees as a lasting legacy. The construction, he said this week, is “relaxing.”

That serenity may not last long. In two short months, Democrats, concerned at the way Mr. Trump has seemingly brushed aside federal law in pursuit of his projects, will take control of Congress and have new powers to begin focusing on them, too. Federal judges also have become increasingly fed up.

The result is a looming high-stakes showdown over Mr. Trump’s glitzy building agenda, one that could alter the face of Washington for years to come.

The Trump administration is rushing to push as many projects as far along as possible before January, under the theory that lawmakers and the courts will be less inclined to halt or undo what is already done. That is a lesson Mr. Trump learned in his career as a real estate developer, and one he applied early in his term to abruptly demolish the White House’s East Wing and to build a luxury ballroom in its place.

“President Trump is moving at lightning speed because we don’t have time to waste in our mission to make America greater than ever before,” said Davis Ingle, a White House spokesman.

But Representative Jamie Raskin, a Maryland Democrat who is set to be the chairman of the Judiciary Committee, said Democrats are considering how best to assert their new powers. Under consideration: language prohibiting the projects in federal spending bills or other must-pass legislation, intense oversight and lawsuits.

“These were illegal, unauthorized projects, just like the demolition of the East Wing, and Congress will assert its authority over federal government properties by denying funds for any more illegal purposes, which amount to criminal vandalism,” Mr. Raskin said.

For the better part of two years, Mr. Trump has attempted to build as he pleased throughout the nation’s capital, brushing aside concerns that he was circumventing Congress, the public, building codes, his own architects and numerous federal laws. He has bypassed or stacked review panels, reinterpreted decades-old statutes and moved at a pace seemingly intended to outrun the oversight of courts.

Some of those projects are finished: the paved-over Rose Garden, the White House helipad, the gilded Oval Office. On Thursday, the president took steps to make that last change permanent.

But most of his most prized projects remain unbuilt or unfinished. And what happens over the coming months could determine whether they stay that way.

Construction on the president’s planned triumphal arch was due to start this week, but a federal judge has temporarily halted it while litigation proceeds. Other projects have not broken ground: a Garden of Heroes (which Mr. Trump this week said would have as many as 500 statues), an elite-level golf course in East Potomac Park and a promenade behind the Lincoln Memorial. His renovation of the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts remains in limbo. Even his signature project, the White House ballroom, needs at least another year of work, the president has said.

Congress has many tools to stymie the president’s projects outside the court system. But Republicans have declined to use them.

“That could mean a joint resolution barring construction,” said Andrea Katz, a law professor at Washington University in St. Louis. “It could mean an appropriations rider: ‘No funds shall be appropriated for any of the following construction projects.’ Obviously, they could do oversight.”

Stanley M. Brand, the former top lawyer in the House, said either chamber could vote to sue to enforce Congress’s constitutional role and block any projects it has not expressly authorized. It could also vigorously exercise its oversight role, conducting investigations that could cover anyone involved in the building blitz. That could include issuing subpoenas to donors or officials involved in spending decisions.

“If you authorize money for a purpose that’s not included in the appropriations law, you can be subject to suit and criminal penalties,” Mr. Brand said.

To be sure, not all of Mr. Trump’s construction projects are likely to spark congressional investigations. For instance, repairs to Washington’s fountains have drawn mostly praise by those who live nearby. Democrats argue that, regardless of the merit of any individual project, Mr. Trump must follow the law when carrying out building plans.

The president’s dominance of the planning commission that must approve his projects is also set to end with the new Congress, as many of his projects are still winding through review. Two members of the National Capital Planning Commission represent congressional committee chairs who will become Democrats in January, leaving the president in control of only half of the commission’s members.

Crucially, tied votes fail under the commission’s bylaws. And it is already too late for the president’s appointees to change those rules by the end of the year. That means that approvals for the president’s projects could grind to a halt after the commission’s December meeting.

The rush to build, and the newfound limitations on the president’s building power, were laid bare during a roller-coaster Thursday evening that began at the commission.

Mr. Trump’s allies on the panel hurried through a marathon session to issue final approval for his planned 250-foot arch along the Potomac, between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery. The president hoped to begin work that same night.

“As I understand it, the project proponent is under a time constraint and wants the decision today,” said Stuart Levenbach, the Trump-appointed vice chairman of the panel.

He left unstated what that time constraint was. But the outcome of the election loomed over the meeting — and was invoked by several people testifying who implored the commissioners to recognize widespread opposition to the project.

After the commission’s late-night vote, the administration immediately alerted the Federal District Court judge overseeing a lawsuit seeking to block the arch, Tanya S. Chutkan, of the outcome, and then of its final decision to begin construction. She halted the project minutes later.

On Friday morning, with no construction underway, allies of the president rolled out a slickly produced website promoting the arch. The website is credited to the United States Triumphal Arch Foundation. That group, incorporated in Delaware earlier this year, lists its president as Randy Evans, a lawyer who served as ambassador to Luxembourg during Mr. Trump’s first term. It is not listed in the I. R. S.’s database of tax-exempt charities. Mr. Evans did not respond to questions sent by The New York Times on Friday evening.

Representative Don Beyer, a Virginia Democrat whose district includes Arlington National Cemetery and Ronald Reagan National Airport, hailed the ruling halting the arch but said that “this fight is not over.”

“While this decision prevents Donald Trump from immediately implementing his plans to create a monument to his own ego, the courts and Congress must put in place permanent safeguards to stop the Trump administration from violating the law and proceeding with this project,” he added.

Before Democrats in Congress can do that, opponents of the president’s projects fear a rush of construction.

“I’m expecting between now and the seating of the next Congress a worst-case scenario,” said Charles Birnbaum, the president of the Cultural Landscape Foundation, which has sued over the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, the Kennedy Center and the Garden of Heroes.

Just as the administration quickly tore down more than 400 trees in East Potomac Park over Columbus Day weekend, Mr. Birnbaum is warily eyeing the holidays, when Washington empties out.

“There will be no gatekeepers present,” he said, “and they’re going to try and create an air of inevitability.”

The administration is already pushing forward with the president’s next priorities. Initial plans for the luxury golf course in East Potomac Park are scheduled to come before the Commission of Fine Arts, an advisory body, this month and then the planning commission in December. And the government has said it plans to close most of the park on Nov. 15.

The administration has also submitted to the fine arts commission this month plans for significant changes to West Potomac Park, a strip of land just south of the National Mall where Mr. Trump has proposed the Garden of Heroes. The submitted plans make no mention of the garden, but plaintiffs suing to block it have noted in court that they bear a “striking resemblance” to public renderings of it.

“This is not the Garden of Heroes,” a National Park Service official insisted last month in a meeting with outside groups consulting on the project.

But judges have increasingly lost patience with similar government pronouncements — that it is just doing “routine maintenance” on the golf course, that it is merely mulling ideas about what to build.

“What we saw with the ballroom is that they are fine pushing the boundaries of what the court has said, and they seem to be fine angering the judges,” said Phil Mendelson, the Democratic chairman of the D. C. Council, who sits on the planning commission and has on several occasions been the only vote opposing the president’s projects. “But I think their ability to keep doing that is going to get more difficult.”

He said he expects that the incoming Washington mayor, Janeese Lewis George, will confront the administration more forcefully than the current mayor, Muriel E. Bowser, has. Ms. Bowser has largely adopted a nonconfrontational stance with the president during his second term, given Washington’s limited self-governance and vulnerability to interference from the president and Republican-controlled Congress.

Three members of the planning commission who represent Ms. Bowser or were appointed by her have followed that strategy, too, abstaining from some votes that might anger the president. All of them voted, using muted language, to oppose the arch on Thursday, another sign of the coming change.

Even if the restraining order on the arch is lifted, it is unlikely that the government can get far with the project before January. A construction timeline outlined by the government said it would take two to three months to prepare the site, stage equipment and excavate. That is all before the foundation work could begin.

David A. Fahrenthold contributed reporting.

Luke Broadwater covers the White House for The Times.

Emily Badger writes about cities and urban policy for The Times from Washington. She’s particularly interested in housing, transportation and inequality — and how they’re all connected.

How Elon Musk Frittered Away Nearly $500 Million on the Midterms

The New York Times November 06, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Behind the scenes, the world’s richest person spent a record amount over two years to bend the country’s politics to his will. He couldn’t.

By Theodore Schleifer

Theodore Schleifer extensively covered Elon Musk’s political work in the 2024 and 2026 elections.

The world’s richest person had face-planted — and was now trying to turn back time.

Elon Musk spent nearly half a billion dollars during the midterm cycle, the most in any election period for a donor who wasn’t a candidate himself.

2023-24 $290 mil.

2025-26 $474 mil.

America PAC $216 mil.

Senate Leadership Fund $168 mil.

Congressional Leadership Fund $30 mil.

Other Republican groups $44 mil.

State groups $16 mil.

2023-24 $290 mil.

2025-26 $474 mil.

America PAC $216 mil.

Senate Leadership Fund $168 mil.

Congressional Leadership Fund $30 mil.

Other Republican groups $44 mil.

State groups $16 mil.

Source: Federal Election Commission.

Lily Boyce/The New York Tiimes

He hoped to defend Republican control of Congress and rescue Ken Paxton, the party’s embattled nominee for Senate in Texas. Instead, Democrats won shockingly large House and Senate majorities, and Mr. Paxton was trounced by James Talarico, who seemed to bother Mr. Musk like no other Democratic candidate.

When the devastating result became clear, Mr. Musk deleted an X post that had encouraged Republicans to turn out, and tried to joke his way out of how badly the night had gone for him. “Guess my election-interfering space lasers didn’t work this time,” he wrote early Wednesday.

It was a stunning failure. Now the onetime trillionaire is all but certain to face investigatory scrutiny and financial pressure with newly empowered Democrats in control of Congress and top state offices in Texas, where he lives and operates many of his businesses. Mr. Musk, who moved there from California in part to escape the regulatory environment, will soon be represented by a senator who has said he wants to “tax trillionaires out of existence.”

The political influence of Mr. Musk, who has become by far the Republican Party’s biggest megadonor, is now in serious question.

How he arrived at this point is a story of an unpredictable tycoon who was never in denial about Republicans’ predicament this year, but who was also characteristically starry-eyed about his ability to help the party beat the odds.

In interviews, nearly 30 people with insight into Mr. Musk’s political operation — most of whom spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss private conversations — recounted how he came to spend so much on the midterms, how tensions grew between his team and President Trump’s advisers, and how his varied and often last-ditch strategies fizzled.

There is now some finger-pointing in Mr. Musk’s broader orbit about who is responsible for what went wrong and whether he should have spent so much, particularly in Texas. Some advisers to Mr. Musk’s super PAC, America PAC, had argued internally that the group should be more focused on persuasion (winning over new voters) than on turnout (encouraging past Republican voters to cast ballots again).

But in private conversations, Mr. Musk has rejected that argument, saying that spending money to persuade Americans to vote for a certain candidate is a waste. Plenty of other groups spend money on that. The real return on investment, he has told people, comes from getting out the vote with door-knockers — something that Mr. Musk believes he is better at than anybody else.

Many elections come down to turnout. But not this one.

If Mr. Paxton had won in Texas, according to two people with knowledge of his planned victory speech, he intended to issue a big thank-you to Mr. Musk.

The public message of appreciation, of course, went undelivered.

Mr. Musk, the chief executive of Tesla and SpaceX, went through a politically tumultuous 2025. He served as a powerful adviser to the Trump White House before the two men fell out spectacularly over the president’s domestic policy bill. By early this year, he and Mr. Trump had warmed back up to each other, but it was unclear even to Mr. Musk’s advisers whether he planned to lift a finger to help Republicans in the midterms.

Mr. Musk began the year in a mood that did not seem aligned with Senate Republicans. He whipped up a frenzy against Senator John Thune of South Dakota, the majority leader, because he had not forced through a major bill of voting restrictions. At a meeting in January at a Tesla factory near Austin, Mr. Thune tried to walk a patient Mr. Musk through why he didn’t have the votes to pass the measure, two people with knowledge of the discussion said. The meeting seemed to go well. But Mr. Musk continued his online rampage.

In private conversations, Mr. Musk was all over the place about whether he wanted to spend heavily on politics.

He was unnerved by his first foray into midterm-cycle spending, a 2025 judicial election in Wisconsin in which he spent $47 million only for his candidate to lose. Mr. Musk’s lesson was that he should not make himself the face of his campaign efforts.

His mind also seemed elsewhere, on A. I. and SpaceX. Early this year, he told a billionaire peer that he was not terribly optimistic about the Republican Party’s political standing or its chances in 2028. Throughout the year, he did not seem to want to talk much about the midterms, beyond voicing concern that a left-wing politician like Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York could eventually become president.

He could be erratic. In January, Mr. Musk donated $10 million to support Nate Morris, a long-shot candidate for the Senate in Kentucky — a move that blindsided his own team, which had no heads-up. Several people close to Mr. Musk thought the donation to Mr. Morris, a friend of Vice President JD Vance’s, was a mistake, and Mr. Morris dropped out before the primary.

In May, as Mr. Musk rode aboard Air Force One on a trip to China, James Blair, Mr. Trump’s top political adviser, told Mr. Musk he hoped the billionaire would help Republicans in the midterms again, according to two people with knowledge of the discussion. Mr. Musk, whose super PAC spent hundreds of millions in 2024 to return Mr. Trump to office, said that yes, he was in for Round 2 — and told Mr. Blair to send him ideas.

Mr. Blair sketched out a request for a Musk-led door-knocking program costing about $100 million. The Musk team was taken aback. Such money might be pocket change for Mr. Musk, who is worth hundreds of billions, but it was far more than America PAC had been prepared to spend.

Mr. Musk eventually assented — and went even further, authorizing spending for a program beyond door-knocking that would cost $100 million to $120 million.

But at times the Musk team grew frustrated with the Trump team, according to three people with knowledge of the interactions. The Musk crew was deferential but sometimes felt resentful or used by the Trump operation. The Musk team also believed that the polling from Mr. Trump’s super PAC, MAGA Inc., was inconsistent and that the group was too slow to engage in races.

Asked for comment, an America PAC official said the relationship was strong.

Mr. Musk’s budget for his super PAC eventually grew to $150 million or $160 million — because of Texas.

The state wasn’t even on the initial list of six Senate races that Mr. Musk had in mind. But over the summer, Mr. Musk’s advisers began to tell close allies that he planned to allocate an eye-popping amount to Texas, primarily to help the state’s Republican candidates for the U. S. House.

Mr. Musk’s team saw how Texas was trending politically, and he found himself at a crossroads. He hardly knew Mr. Paxton well, and the two barely speak, according to two people with knowledge of their relationship. But he grew preoccupied with Mr. Talarico. Should he spend a fortune to beat him?

In mid-August, Mr. Paxton’s team was desperate and needed cash immediately. He had struggled mightily to raise money and was facing the strongest Democratic fund-raiser in the country, who had been pounding him with negative ads.

An extraordinary plan came together. The head of Mr. Paxton’s super PAC, Sam Cooper, hosted a fund-raising call alongside Mr. Paxton and Senator Ted Cruz of Texas, a fellow Republican. In dire terms, Mr. Cooper urged some of the party’s biggest Texas donors to give money to save Mr. Paxton before it was too late.

Listening, with some alarm, was Mr. Musk’s top political adviser, Chris Young. Soon after, he began negotiating with Alex Latcham, the head of the Thune-aligned super PAC for Senate Republicans. They agreed to split a $15 million ad reservation to help Mr. Paxton — and then things snowballed. They swapped spending proposals, and Mr. Young got Mr. Musk’s sign-off to send another $158 million to Mr. Latcham’s group for a Paxton rescue mission that began in mid-September.

Despite cutting some of the biggest checks ever recorded in American politics, Mr. Musk operated during those negotiations with the remove that defined all of his midterm engagement. Mr. Thune, too, was effectively absent: He was informed afterward that his Texas money problem, so to speak, had been solved. In private conversations with donors, Mr. Thune mostly stayed mum about Mr. Musk’s role.

Mr. Musk was now firmly in the persuasion game he had dismissed: Mr. Latcham’s super PAC ran ads to try to win over voters by focusing on transgender and crime-related issues.

The Musk team thought that its spending for Mr. Paxton had worked and had chipped 10 percentage points off Mr. Talarico’s favorability numbers.

Some allies of Mr. Musk were also nervous about what would happen to his companies if Gov. Greg Abbott and other top Republican state officials were to lose re-election. So the billionaire spent $12.5 million on state politics, too. All that Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick needed to do to get his $500,000 was simply call Mr. Young and ask.

Mr. Abbott, Mr. Patrick and all the other Republican statewide candidates in Texas lost.

“Elon tried to spend a whole bunch of money in his home state and not only lost the Senate, but the governorship and all the rest,” Reid Hoffman, a major donor to Mr. Talarico and a business rival of Mr. Musk’s, said in an interview. “Clearly, his ability to spend money to win an election has been multiply disproven.”

As Election Day approached, Mr. Musk’s advisers feared a blue wave and were skittish about being blamed. They came to see the midterms as an inescapable referendum on Mr. Trump and his second-term actions, especially his decision to go to war with Iran. How much power did they really have?

Mr. Musk’s team believed that its turnout operation could act like a special-teams unit in football — helping Republicans gain a few extra percentage points that could make the difference in a close race.

Mr. Musk expressed to at least one friend that he thought of his turnout work as effectively a civic duty and not political at all.

At the same time, Mr. Musk’s super PAC sent texts to voters that used A. I. to create personalized videos of Mr. Trump using their first names to encourage them to turn out. (“We need voters like you, Kathleen.”)

The operation that Mr. Musk assembled was enormous, bigger than what he had in 2024. Thousands of paid canvassers were dispatched to knock on millions of doors of Republican-leaning Americans who were seen as less likely to vote yet could be encouraged to do so. But as Republicans’ polling grew uglier in the final weeks, America PAC began knocking on the doors of likelier and likelier voters, drifting away from its original job.

Some Republicans wished that the Musk field operation had begun earlier — it did not kick fully into gear until around Labor Day.

Around then, Mr. Musk’s super PAC decided to scale up drastically in Texas. The group knocked on roughly 1.7 million doors there over the final three weeks of September. But it may have been too late: In some key Texas markets, the super PAC did not meet all of its door-knocking targets, in part because it could not find enough labor, according to people with knowledge of the figures.

Asked for comment, the America PAC official said the group had routinely raised its target numbers.

The Musk operation tried to do things as cost-effectively as possible — paying some canvassing firms about $4.50 a door, a relatively low amount, with canvassers earning their pay per door rather than per hour. Those firms in turn paid most canvassers roughly $2 or $2.50 per door.

Slides from one America PAC training presentation for door-knockers that were obtained by The New York Times pulled back the curtain on its approach.

The trainers made no mention of Mr. Musk, telling canvassers only that America PAC was an “independent organization” that was “working to make sure that people who love America get out to vote in the November election to defend our American values and weaken the far-left agenda knocking on our door.”

The super PAC also used digital tools to try to crack down on fraud among its canvassers, a rampant problem in the industry. The slides warned that if canvassers “in any way cheat or commit fraud, we will report you to local law enforcement and assist them in your prosecution.”

In Texas, these door knockers focused heavily on transgender issues. Mr. Musk’s team saw this as essential to turning out right-wing voters against Mr. Talarico, but some advisers thought that focus was a tactical mistake.

Last Friday, in America PAC’s final internal poll of the Senate race, Mr. Talarico held a six-point advantage over Mr. Paxton.

On Tuesday, after more than $210 million in spending from Mr. Musk to help Mr. Paxton, the results finally arrived. Mr. Talarico won by 12 points.

Theodore Schleifer is a Times reporter covering billionaires and their impact on the world.

The Best VPNs to Protect Yourself Online

Wired November 05, 2026

Hundreds of VPNs are at your disposal. They all want you to believe they’re the best VPN you can buy. All of them claim to have the biggest network or a no-logging policy. And they all promise your internet traffic is safe on the network of servers they’ve rented. Only some of them are telling the truth.

VPNs are only growing in popularity due to age-verification laws in the UK and in several states in the US. Even if you don’t want a VPN, you might need one. If you’re hesitant, I get it. VPN providers have been deep in murky waters for years, constantly caught lying about their practices, handing over user data that was never supposed to be logged, and serving as safe havens for large cybercriminal organizations.

I wanted to find the VPN services that actually work; the ones that keep their promises even in the face of potential prosecution, and the ones that have a proven track record of reliable performance. Some of the picks in this guide aren’t conventional, and some of the services I suggest you avoid might be controversial. But these are the top VPNs I’d use day to day.

Read our other VPN guides, including how to set up a VPN on your router and how to use a VPN to watch Netflix when you travel abroad.

If your looking to get a VPN deal, Proton, our top VPN pick (read more below), is running an early Black Friday sale: 75 percent off the regular price for two years. You can get Proton VPN Plus for $2.49 a month (regularly $10 a month); billed at $60 for 24 months. VPN Plus protects up to 10 devices and gives you access to more than 20,000 servers, plus it blocks ads, trackers, and malware. You can also snag one year of Proton Unlimited for $6.50 a month (regularly $13 a month); billed at $78 for 12 months, which adds Proton’s mail, calendar, and password manager software, plus 500 GB of cloud storage. We don’t know when this deal expires, but we imagine it will last through Cyber Monday.

What Does a VPN Do? And How Does It Work?

VPN stands for virtual private network. A VPN provides a tunnel through which all of your internet traffic passes. Instead of connecting to your internet service provider's servers, you connect to a VPN's server before connecting to the broader internet. Because most VPN services operate this way, your browsing data isn't stored, essentially making you anonymous online.

The linchpin in this system is a VPN protocol. Today, nearly all internet traffic is encrypted, but that encryption happens only after you've established a connection with a website. A VPN protocol encrypts traffic before it reaches the VPN server, adding extra security on untrusted networks like public Wi-Fi at a coffee shop or airport. It doesn't help much on your personal network unless there is an intruder.

What Are VPNs Used For?

Although VPNs are often marketed as security tools, they serve a better purpose for privacy and bypassing geo-restrictions. By anonymizing your traffic through a VPN server, your browsing can't be traced back to you. The internet is full of cookies, and you might be surprised by how much of your traffic online is tracked via browser fingerprinting. That includes hiding what sites you visit (and what you do on those sites) from your internet service provider (ISP).

By routing your traffic through a server in another location, you can also bypass geo-restrictions online, such as the content libraries available in different countries on Netflix or checking product availability in other regions of the world.

VPNs can also be important when connecting to public Wi-Fi. If you're doing anything remotely sensitive on your computer at a coffee shop, a VPN is a good idea to protect your personal data.

How Much Do VPNs Cost?

VPN prices vary widely, but most providers cost around $10 per month for a monthly plan. Pricing changes if you buy several months at once, and it gets even more complicated with full security suites, such as those offered by Nord Security and Proton.

Most prominent VPN services offer multi-month or even multiyear discounts. These plans are often the best way to get your foot in the door, but some VPNs have recently faced class-action lawsuits over their auto-renewal practices. Although a handful of lawsuits have been filed, that doesn't mean these services necessarily engaged in illegal practices.

Free VPNs exist, as well, but you should avoid most of them. Some restrictive free plans from Proton and Windscribe are useful, but you should approach most free VPNs with skepticism.

VPN Terms and Features, Explained

You'll come across a few of these terms in this guide as you generally shop for a VPN. Here's what they mean.

Double-hop: Connecting to two (or more) VPN servers in succession. This provides an extra layer of privacy if someone traces your network path, but it will vastly reduce speeds.

Split tunneling: Allows you to choose which apps use the VPN tunnel. Useful if you want some apps (like your browser) to use the VPN tunnel but not others.

Kill switch: A security feature in VPNs that will disable your internet connection if the VPN connection drops. A kill switch can prevent internet traffic from leaking if the VPN fails.

IP and domain block list: A list of IP addresses or domain names that are blocked inside the VPN tunnel. Some VPNs offer Domain Name System (DNS) blocking, too, which can block ads served from particular DNS servers.

Static IP: Most VPNs assign you a random IP address, or even rotate the IP address while you’re connected. If you need external access to your network with a network-wide VPN, you'll need a static IP address.

Port forwarding: Allows you to forward a port on your private network, bypassing the VPN tunnel. Useful when you need external network access with a network-wide VPN, such as running a media server.

NetShield: A feature specific to Proton VPN that blocks ads and trackers while connected to the VPN. Other services, such as Windscribe and NordVPN, offer similar features.

Dark web monitoring: A feature available in some VPNs, such as NordVPN and ProtonVPN, that will monitor the dark web for your email address or other personal information. You'll be notified if the information shows up on the dark web or as part of a breach.

DAITA: A feature of Mullvad VPN that will introduce background noise to your connection, combating AI-assisted network analysis. Windscribe, NordVPN, and ProtonVPN offer similar features.

Are VPNs Illegal?

Short of a few exceptions, VPNs are legal around the world. That includes the US, UK, Canada, Australia, the EU, South Africa, and many countries in Central and South America. Places such as North Korea and Turkmenistan have VPN bans in place, but due to the extreme censorship in those countries, it's hard to verify what laws are on the books (and how they're enforced). You can probably guess the North Korean government's stance on bypassing censorship, though.

For everyone else, VPN legality only comes into play based on which VPN you use and what you use it for. Countries such as India and Russia call for compliance with the government, forcing providers like NordVPN to shut down servers in those regions. And, regardless of what country you're in, engaging in illegal activity while connected to a VPN is still illegal.

Proton

Proton (Yearly)

Proton (2 Year)

Proton (Free)

Proton VPN (9/10, WIRED Recommends) is the best VPN you can buy. Its Plus service was the fastest I tested across the US and UK. It has a generous free plan if you'd like to try it out first. The features are unmatched, and the pricing is excellent, especially if you bundle Proton VPN with the company's other software (Proton Unlimited). After testing all of these services, Proton is what I personally use now.

What sent Proton over the edge was its commitment to transparency. It has maintained a transparency report since 2017, undergone third-party audits annually since 2022, and open-sourced its applications five years ago. That last bit is huge, as bugs within the application can pose a security risk, and handing those applications over to the open-source community can surface those bugs much faster. There are no real compromises here, with features like split tunneling, port forwarding, and double-hop connections.

Proton is a rare example of a VPN service that gets it. Every VPN engages in the same marketing practices, touting their security, speed, and privacy. But Proton puts its money where its mouth is, all while offering a remarkably easy-to-use and feature-rich VPN application.

Black Friday is a good time to sign up for Proton VPN. The company is offering 75 percent off the regular price for two years.

NordVPN

NordVPN (2-Year)

NordVPN (1-Year)

NordVPN (Monthly)

NordVPN has a long history, and it's one of the most prominent VPN services on the market. It comes with one of the largest VPN networks available, enough features to make Surfshark blush, and decent (though not the best) speeds. It's a little more expensive than I'd hoped for, but that's the price you pay for such an extensive network and feature set.

That feature set is where NordVPN stands apart. Its Basic plan will get you access to the VPN, but I recommend going with at least the Plus plan. It opens up an ad blocker and gives you access to one of the best password managers around, NordPass.

Nord backs up security and privacy credentials with independent audits of the company’s no-log policy and the service’s security. Like Proton, Nord lets you scale up your protection with encrypted cloud storage, but Nord leans further into security while Proton focuses on privacy-focused productivity. With NordVPN, you can upgrade to unlock NordProtect, an identity theft protection service, as well as Incogni to remove your data online.

These extras wouldn't mean much on their own, but the core of NordVPN is still an excellent VPN service. It's been on the bleeding edge of VPN security and features for years, and that hasn't changed.

Windscribe

Windscribe (Pro, Yearly)

Shop at

Windscribe (Free)

You should generally avoid free VPNs, but Windscribe is one of the few worth considering. You get 10 GB of data across 10 server locations and unlimited connections, and you can even unlock more data if you refer friends or post on social media about Windscribe. There are a few similar offers from services like Proton, but Windscribe provides a pleasant on-ramp for subscribing.

If you do decide to pay, you can build your own plan. Unlimited data runs an extra $3 per month, and you can add server locations for an extra $1 per server per month. It's fantastic. Most people don't need VPN servers in Ghana, Cambodia, and Peru, so rather than charge for all those locations, you can pick out your locations piecemeal. If you want everything, that's available at a discounted rate, too.

The pricing model is what sets Windscribe apart, but it's an excellent VPN in its own right. It offers additional packet obfuscation to combat network analysis, and it's loaded with features like split tunneling and port forwarding. It's fast, too, dropping just 15.6 percent of my speed when connected in the US.

Like the other providers I've included, Windscribe has undergone a third-party audit. But unlike the other options, it's also been taken to court. Windscribe CEO Yegor Sak was personally charged with a crime in Greece in relation to a user's activity on Windscribe-operated servers, essentially tying activity on the network to Sak personally. It was dismissed. VPNs are subpoenaed all the time, but the fact that Windscribe wasn't able to produce logs even when the CEO of the company was facing criminal prosecution speaks volumes.

Windscribe added random hashed login in December 2025, which makes it possible to create an anonymous account. Windscribe doesn’t record the random hash, so if you lose it, you’ll also lose account access—but it can help to keep your identity private. This is similar to how Mullvad and IVPN handle accounts. Windscribe accepts cryptocurrency payments as well.

Mullvad

Mullvad VPN (Monthly)

Any VPN worth its salt claims a no-logs policy, but almost all of them keep some logs. Those logs shouldn't have anything to do with your browsing data, and they should be anonymized, but most VPNs need to at least keep logs of information like your email and payment method. But not Mullvad.

Mullvad doesn't do multi-year subscriptions, referral links, or social sign-on. You generate an account number to sign up, and you add time to that account with the payment method of your choice, including a credit card, PayPal, crypto, or cold, hard cash (via mail). If you want to go through the hassle, you can stay fully anonymous in the eyes of Mullvad. If that wasn't enough, Mullvad even claims it was raided by Swedish police and still didn't produce logs.

It's not as fast as Proton, Windscribe, or Surfshark, but it's not bad, either—around a 24 percent drop in the US compared to 19 percent with Surfshark—and it lacks some features like port forwarding. But the pricing is good at roughly $6 a month, depending on exchange rates (Mullvad charges a flat €5 regardless of location).

Mullvad is on the cutting edge of privacy, too, building RAM-only servers starting in 2022 and introducing defense against AI-guided traffic analysis (DAITA) last year. DAITA protects against AI traffic analysis, introducing network noise and sending consistent packet sizes to obfuscate your encrypted traffic further.

Bitdefender

Bitdefender

While the built-in, free Bitdefender VPN is usable, it's too limited for what most people will want. The company's paid option, Bitdefender VPN Premium, gets you support for up to 10 devices, and it's plenty reliable and fast—without the data restrictions. Its biggest draw is its first-year price: it's only $30, which is a great value for a VPN like this. It goes up to $70 after the first year, though, which is a bit more expensive than ProtonVPN. But that first-year price comes out to just $2.92 per month, making it an especially good VPN for beginners to try.

Our VPN reviewer, Matthew Smith, was also impressed by the app experience, which is supported on Windows, Mac, iOS, and Android. It's clean, and all the important information is right up front—including the kill switch. A couple of platforms are missing, such as TVs and Linux, so be aware of that. So, while Bitdefender VPN Premium might not be the ultimate privacy tool, as it's missing some more of the advanced features, it's a user-friendly and dependable VPN with a killer first-year price. —Luke Larsen

ExpressVPN

ExpressVPN (2 Years)

ExpressVPN (Yearly)

ExpressVPN (Monthly)

ExpressVPN has had a rough few years, but it finally seems to be on solid footing. It was purchased a few years back for almost $1 billion by Kape Technologies, a firm that owns several VPNs, including CyberGhost and Private Internet Access. A revolving door of executives followed the sale, but ExpressVPN's leadership is solid enough now that it's worth recommending.

That's because the service itself hasn't degraded in the past few years. ExpressVPN is still insanely fast, packed with features, and dead-simple to use across desktop and mobile. It can go toe-to-toe with the top dogs, and it's always been able to. That hasn't changed.

However, I'm recommending it here due to recent changes ExpressVPN made to its membership options. Its core service is still intact, offering 10 simultaneous connections and full access to the ExpressVPN network. You can push higher, though, with the Advanced plan offering 12 connections and the Pro plan offering 14. The Advanced plan is best for most people, not only due to the higher connection limit but also because it comes with a password manager and 50 percent off one of ExpressVPN’s AirCove routers.

Surfshark: I've used Surfshark personally for a few years, and I'd still be using it if Proton didn't impress me so much. Surfshark is dead simple to use. It pops up and connects before swiftly getting out of my way so I can get on with my day. If you spring for a two-year plan, it's cheap. You can score over two years for around $54 with the Starter plan.

If you want to dig in deeper, you can. Surfshark is one of the most feature-rich VPNs I've used, sporting the basics like a double-hop connection and split tunneling, as well as an ad blocker and email masking. Like Proton, Surfshark offers other security tools like antivirus and dark web monitoring if you pick up a more expensive plan. Surfshark loses out just a bit when it comes to privacy, however. It has a no-logs policy, and it maintains a transparency report and a warrant canary, so it’s not bad in this regard. However, it doesn't have open-source applications, so you’ll need a bit more faith in Surfshark’s app security than with some other VPN services.

EventVPN: This is a free, ad-supported VPN from ExpressVPN. Ads and VPNs don't really mix, but EventVPN says it's able to offer a free service via Apple's App Tracking Transparency (ATT) and Identifier for Advertisers (IDFA), basically allowing it to serve ads without harvesting your personal data. The problem is the pervasiveness of ads. A banner lives at the top of the app at all times, and you'll need to sit through a 30-second ad each time you connect or disconnect; a big problem when some servers post unreasonably slow speeds. I'll admit EventVPN is a unique concept, but I see nothing better than ProtonVPN or Windscribe for a free VPN service. And when it comes to the inconvenience of sitting through ads, it's straight-up worse.

IVPN: This privacy-focused VPN provider is similar to Mullvad. It does not ask you to create an account with a username, password, and email, but instead generates a random ID, which you use to log in. That helps preserve your anonymity, since that information can’t be tied to your usage even if IVPN suffered a security incident. IVPN also accepts cryptocurrency payments (Bitcoin and Monero). Unlike Mullvad, IVPN offers one-year, two-year, and three-year plan options, as well as an unusual weekly option, which might be nice if you want a VPN while on vacation (IVPN standard is $2 per week). These can be more affordable than Mullvad’s monthly fee. However, IVPN lacks some privacy features you will find with Mullvad, such as RAM-less servers. IVPN scheduled a security audit for 2025, but as of January 2026, the results have not been posted. IVPN also has a tight two-device limit on the Standard plan. The Pro plan raises that to seven, but the Pro plan’s price is $10 per month, so it’s more expensive than Mullvad, which has a five-device limit. That remains true even if you go with a multi-year IVPN plan. Still, IVPN is a fine alternative if you want annual plan options. And while most VPN apps serve their purpose, I do think IVPN’s app is both more attractive and easier to use than Mullvad’s. —Matthew S. Smith

Private Internet Access (PIA): With its long history in the VPN space, PIA has maintained a track record of defending user privacy—even in the face of actual criminal activity. In 2016, a criminal complaint was filed in Florida against Preston Alexander McWaters for threats made online. McWaters was eventually convicted and sentenced to 42 months in prison. Investigators traced the online threats back to PIA's servers and subpoenaed the company. As the complaint reads, “A subpoena was sent to [Private Internet Access], and the only information they could provide is that the cluster of IP addresses being used was from the east coast of the United States.” According to the complaint, McWaters engaged in several other identifying activities, but PIA wasn't among them. Despite such a clear view of a VPN provider upholding its no-logging policy, PIA didn't impress me during my tests. It delivered the worst speeds out of any VPN I tested, with more than a 50 percent drop on the closest US server. (Windscribe, for context, only dropped 15.6 percent of my speed.)

MysteriumVPN: This is the go-to dVPN, or decentralized VPN, as far as I can tell. The concept of a decentralized VPN has existed for a while, but it's really gained traction over the last couple of years. The idea is to have a network of residential IP addresses that make up the network, routing your traffic through normal IP addresses to get around the increasingly common block lists for VPN servers. Mysterium accomplishes this network with MystNodes. It's a crypto node. People buy the node to earn crypto, and they're put into the Mysterium network. It's not inherently bad, but routing your traffic through a single residential IP is a little worrisome. Even without the decentralized kick, Mysterium was slow, and it doesn't maintain any sort of privacy materials, be it a third-party audit, warranty canary, or transparency report.

PrivadoVPN: A popular option to recommend as a free VPN, offering a decent free service, with a handful of full-speed servers and 10 GB of data per month. You'll have to suffer through four—yes, four—redirects begging you to pay for a subscription before signing up, but the free plan works. The problem is how new PrivadoVPN is. There's no transparency report or audit available, and although the speeds are decent, they aren't as good as Proton, Windscribe, or Surfshark. PrivadoVPN isn't bad, but it's hard to recommend when Proton and Windscribe exist with free plans that are equally as good.

You'll find dozens of free VPNs all claiming to protect your privacy. Most of them don't. There are plenty of VPNs I don’t recommend, but these are a few I've tested that are worth mentioning.

Hola is an infamous name in the VPN industry, but it's been close to a decade since its very public debacle. Hola is free, and it's able to stay free because it uses a peer-to-peer network. Hola also owns Bright Data (formerly Luminati), which is a data collection company. In 2015, Hola sold access to the network of its free users (via Luminati), which was used in a distributed denial-of-service attack on 8chan. It's been a decade since that incident, but Hola still operates in a similar way. If you don't pay, you could be used as an exit node in Bright Data's network, and the privacy policy makes it clear that Hola logs data about your usage, including your IP address, the pages you visit, and timestamps.

X-VPN is available on desktop, but it primarily shows up in results on the Apple App Store and Google Play, targeting mobile users with a free offering. X-VPN hasn't done anything explicitly wrong like Hola, but it has way too many inconsistencies to recommend. For starters, it uses a proprietary VPN protocol, which it obfuscates within the app. Proprietary protocols like NordVPN's NordLynx and ExpressVPN's Lightway are based on existing, open-source protocols. Further, X-VPN was highlighted in a Tech Transparency Project report about free VPNs with links to the Chinese government; X-VPN is based in Hong Kong. There's no smoking gun with X-VPN, but there doesn't need to be. The speeds aren't the best, the app lacks basic features like split tunneling, and the pricing for a paid plan is in line with top providers.

Functionally, a VPN should do two things: keep your internet speed reasonably fast, and actually protect your browsing data. That's where I focused my testing. Extra features, a comfy UI, and customization settings are great, but they don't matter if the core service is broken.

Speed testing requires spot-checking, as the time of day, the network you're connected to, and the specific VPN server you're using can all influence speeds. Because of that, I always set a baseline speed on my unprotected connection directly before recording results, and I ran the test three times across both US and UK servers. With those baseline drops, I spot-checked at different times of the day over the course of a week to see if the speed decrease was similar.

Security is a bit more involved. For starters, I checked for DNS, WebRTC, and IP leaks every time I connected to a server using Browser Leaks. I also ran brief tests sniffing my connection with Wireshark to ensure all of the packets being sent were secured with the VPN protocol in use.

On the privacy front, the top-recommended services included on this list have been independently audited, and they all maintain some sort of transparency report. In most cases, there's a proper report, but in others, such as Windscribe, that transparency is exposed through legal proceedings.

Ads in Chatbots Have Arrived. Here’s What’s Working—and What’s Not

Wired November 05, 2026

Anthropic is holding firm on the pledge made in its Super Bowl commercial this year to keep Claude ad-free. The company’s recent IPO filing didn’t even mention the possibility of selling ads to make money from the AI chatbot. It’s easy to maintain the high ground with about $112 billion in investor cash.

The chatbot industry, though, may find selling ads necessary to defray the high costs of generating AI responses. OpenAI is all in, with over 100,000 customers advertising in ChatGPT since ads debuted there in February. Last week, Google expanded ads in its search chatbot AI Mode to 10 more countries beyond the US and declared that users “find them highly relevant.” Advertisers are far from satisfied with the experience, but they expect it to improve.

Ads stand to be particularly vital for the long-term viability of niche chatbot platforms, which can’t rely on the same degree of venture capital largesse as the top AI labs or the massive revenues of tech giants. I recently spoke with Koah Labs, one of a number of new ad technology companies focused on AI experiences. The San Francisco startup markets itself as bringing ads to over 200 apps, such as DeepAI, which offers tools for creative queries, and Liner, which focuses on providing citations in AI answers. It works with brands like telehealth giant Hims and flower delivery service UrbanStems.

Koah has attracted just a tenth of the advertisers OpenAI has, but CEO Nic Baird still believes he’s getting a good sense of what’s working and what’s fuzzy as chatbots take over from traditional search engines—and what their rise will mean for your AI experiences.

Ads composed partly by AI rather than fully by a human generate double the clicks, Baird says. It’s difficult to assess exactly why, but AI-generated marketing copy likely feels more natural next to the output of an AI model.

Because ads shown by Koah are grounded in product details and imagery supplied by the advertiser, users don’t seem to be encountering AI-hallucinated, erroneous information. But some advertisers, such as drugmakers, face government requirements on what they must—or cannot—say in ads, Baird says. These companies default to more human control over their ads, generating weaker results, according to Baird.

Since ads with dull messages or that feel like clutter could drive users away, the onus is on ad tech companies to find a middle ground that’s engaging to users without triggering risk-averse brands. That balance might be harder to strike when a human is out of the loop.

Google searches for “help with stress” are likely to bring up ads for therapists. Chatbots can get more creative, in Baird’s view. For instance, ads for spas have performed well within Koah’s network when shown after users’ prompts related to “stress,” he says.

The key difference, according to Baird, is that Koah can select and customize the ad based on “not only the prompt, or the Google search, but also the response from the AI platform, which brings context from the rest of the conversation thus far.” In addition, chatbot prompts tend to be at least double the length of Google queries, giving Koah more information to determine a relevant ad.

Baird claims users are accustomed to navigating through multiple topics within a chatbot conversation, which could make them more receptive to adjacent marketing than they are in traditional search. Koah says users are clicking on about 3 percent of ads, about on par with the performance of the more mature Google ads system.

When called on to show an ad, Koah generally receives a user’s entire conversation up to that point to help inform what it displays. While traditional search queries generally look for specific information, people often use chatbots as not just conversation partners but confidants. It’s unclear whether users will accept the privacy trade-offs that come with personalized chatbot ads as they begin to proliferate.

Baird says Koah anonymizes the queries it receives and stores them in a de-identified way, but he declined to comment any further on the data collection and storage. While acknowledging that personalization can become intrusive, he argues that there are benefits for users and advertisers alike as the tech matures. Nonsensitive information about chatbot discussions, for instance, could inform personalized content on the page that loads after an ad click. Perhaps someone expressed interest in a specific feature, or the AI model didn’t highlight a particular downside of a competing product. The advertiser could fill in the gap.

Koah doesn’t have data on whether people actually want these customized pages, but the tech industry has long argued that people prefer when ad experiences feel relevant. Having the conversation history also could benefit advertisers when Koah enables retargeting, or repeating, an ad to the same user.

By Koah’s estimate, one out of every four chatbot queries about a retailer or brand concerns a return, exchange, or other support issue. Baird believes chatbots provide an opportunity not replicated easily elsewhere for advertisers to address what they might politely call a “customer success” matter.

He expects manufacturers and retailers will eventually target disappointed customers to remind them about warranties, engage them in an AI-intermediated support, and potentially steer them away from a more costly customer service interaction. It’s possible that the AI chatbot’s response may provide users with similar help, but buying an ad guarantees companies get their message across.

The ideal outcome is users reaching resolution they can live with more swiftly than through other means. In the worst case, it's a wasted ad buy and a more irate consumer.

None of the apps Koah currently serves ads in offer users AI agents that can shop on their own. However, apps like Instinct and Meta’s Muse are starting to take over shopping chores for some users. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg recently said Muse could become the company’s biggest source of revenue but suggested it would come from transaction fees rather than ads.

That doesn’t mean advertising will be entirely cut out from bot-dominated ecommerce, with initial studies suggesting that ads could influence AI agents.

Baird expects an opportunity to give “the user's agent the best possible recommendation, and that’s going to be a combination of a great discount, a really relevant product,” and an easy digital path to make the purchase. The chatbot must make “abundantly clear” to the agent what content is sponsored or else risk losing user trust, Baird says.

It’s also possible the chatbot ad market fizzles out before agents take hold if more AI developers adopt Anthropic’s stance. Kevin Baragona, CEO of DeepAI, says while ad revenue has been meaningful, he’s not committed to it because the experience just doesn’t feel right yet in terms of privacy, design, and more.

“I don’t think the ads are working terribly well for anyone,” he says.

The Blue Tsunami Swept Doctors and Scientists Into Office

Wired November 05, 2026

What do Michigan senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed, South Carolina senator-elect Annie Andrews, Ohio governor-elect Amy Acton, and North Carolina representative-elect Jamie Ager have in common, beyond their victories in this week’s midterm elections?

Each is either a doctor or a scientist. And each had the backing of the political action committee 314 Action Fund, which focuses on electing pro-science voices to public office.

“We really benefit by having those data-driven, fact-based decisionmakers actually in a position at the governing table,” says Shaughnessy Naughton, a chemist and former congressional candidate who founded 314 Action after losing her race in 2016. This cycle, the PAC spent above $30 million donating to and supporting various campaigns, including fundraising for specific races. It raised $3.6 million for pediatrician Andrews in the fight over what had been Lindsay Graham’s Senate seat in South Carolina, for example, and another $3 million for physician Acton’s campaign in the hotly contested Ohio governor race, according to Naughton.

The organization’s success rate topped 80 percent this cycle for congressional candidates, with 14 of 17 of its candidates in the US House of Representatives winning their races and hundreds of successful down-ballot candidates. Nine of these races flipped seats from Republican to Democrat. Victorious congressional candidates who flipped their districts this year include an oncology nurse-practitioner, a mathematician, a microbiologist, a nuclear engineer, and an agricultural scientist. “It did turn out to be a health care election,” Naughton says.

Richard Frank, the director of the Brookings Institute’s Center on Health Policy, notes that health care workers and scientists have always been part of the makeup of Congress, but not to this degree. “What is unusual,” he says, “is just how many came in one wave.” He sees the spike in this type of candidate as a direct result of the hostility toward medical and technical expertise from the Trump administration. “Science has been under attack,” Frank says. “It’s not surprising that scientists have recognized that, and some of them went out and ran for Congress.”

The rise of the science candidate has several causes, according to historian Kristoffer Shields, who runs Rutgers University’s Eagleton Institute of Politics. “Some of it certainly is a reaction to what's been happening at the federal level, the defunding of a lot of laboratories and scientific exploration,” he says. But he also sees this as a legacy of the pandemic, when many health care workers started thinking about how politics impacts public health.

Earlier this year, El-Sayed emphasized to WIRED that his candidacy was focused on public health, noting that the cyclospora outbreak that sickened Americans over the summer likely stemmed from the Trump administration’s choices. “We DOGE’d our whole service that keeps the lettuce safe,” he said at the time, referencing the so-called Department of Government Efficiency directing mass layoffs at the Food and Drug Administration.

In 2024, 314 Action’s past acceptance of funding from groups with ties to the pro-Israel lobbying group AIPAC came under scrutiny. The organization no longer accepts AIPAC funding and supported candidates like El-Sayed who were vocally critical of the Israeli government. Unlike some other political committees that aim to put doctors in office, like the American Medical Association’s PAC, 314 Action specifically focuses on electing Democratic health and science experts; it is forthright about its opposition to the Trump administration’s approach to public health.

That so many of these politicians are advocates for the importance of public health and scientific expertise suggests that the election was, in part, a rejection of current health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s MAHA movement, which promotes medical misinformation, including anti-vaccine sentiment. Many of the winning candidates with scientific and technical backgrounds have explicitly discussed how their concerns about the state of health care policy drove them to enter the race. “I am appalled seeing infectious diseases spreading through our communities that we had once declared eradicated,” microbiologist Jasmine Clark, the incoming representative from Georgia, told The Guardian earlier this year.

Clark was first supported by 314 Action when she ran for Georgia’s House of Representatives eight years ago. “She was in the first class of scientists that we helped elect in that 2018 cycle and now has made that move up to the federal level,” says Naughton.

Shields sees the straightforward communication style favored by doctors and scientists as another asset that has made them strong candidates. Some of this year’s winners are especially direct. In recent interviews, South Carolina’s Annie Andrews has referred to RFK Jr. as her “archnemesis” and promised to hold him accountable.

314 Action has also been clear that rebuking RFK Jr.’s agenda is a core part of its goals. In 2025, it launched its Guardians of Public Health initiative to recruit health care experts to run for public office. “We thought it was important to speak directly to doctors and people in public health, like nurses, to say that we have this program and we need you to step up to run, because we have a madman running the Health and Human Services cabinet,” Naughton says.

The push for pro-science public servants isn’t over; 314 Action is starting its next recruitment round later this month.

Reddit Founder Says Building Social Media Apps Is ‘Not Cool Anymore’

Wired November 05, 2026

Alexis Ohanian wants to figure out the future of user-generated content. According to the Reddit cofounder, building social media apps is “not cool anymore” and so much of the internet has been compromised.

“I'm expecting some better version of the group chat to be that new version of UGC,” Ohanian told WIRED senior correspondent Lauren Goode at the inaugural WIRED World Fair.

Ohanian has a complicated relationship with the internet. He resigned from Reddit in 2020, following the killing of George Floyd, to make room for a Black board member and to pressure the company to reform its content moderation policies. The social site had been notorious for hosting violent and harmful rhetoric. Ohanian reflects on recently learning someone with a Reddit tattoo—once a sign of the site’s success to Ohanian—had since covered it up: “I don’t blame him.”

He now runs venture capital firm Seven Seven Six, which has over $1.3 billion in assets under management. He focuses on sports, where he finds real-life communities “in the age of AI slop” and a “manipulated” internet.

Ohanian is a proponent of the “Dead Internet Theory”—the idea that a lot of online activity and content is being generated by bots. Large language models have turbocharged this, with AI agents outrunning human users. “The internet that I grew up on … that was really built for humans first; user interfaces and experiences are going to go away,” said Ohanian, “because more of the internet is going to get created for these agents to use, [rather] than for people.”

In some ways, the advance in generative AI has been lucrative for sites like Reddit, which has licensed its vast archive of human conversations to companies including Google and OpenAI to train AI models. “Platforms like ours became very, very valuable to LLMs,” Ohanian said.

But the technology has also undermined the business. Reddit shares plunged 29 percent last week after the platform warned that Google’s AI-powered search was hurting referral traffic. Ohanian also worries the commercialisation of these conversations means they are full of “bullshit.” “The internet has gotten so manipulated because it is so incredibly valuable to do so,” he said.

Reddit recently said it would require users to sign in to fight third-party scraping and keep up user engagement. While Ohanian declined to say whether he agrees with the move, “there has to be provable humanity on the internet without being creepy.”

An early Anthropic investor, Ohanian is nonetheless optimistic about the potential benefits of AI. He is especially excited to see medical breakthroughs from the technology. “There is still a very real chance that this technology can cause a lot of harm for sure,” he said. “I think we have to be sober about how we're building and what we're doing, but I still can't help but see all of the things that can get so demonstrably better.”

Area Man Feels Joy Online for First Time in Years

Wired November 05, 2026

When The Onion made a bid to buy conspiracy theorist Alex Jones’ Infowars two years ago, Donald Trump had just won his second presidential election—and, for many, things were looking dark.

“You guys remember ... how fucking hopeless we felt?” Onion CEO Ben Collins asked an audience at the WIRED World Fair Wednesday in Miami. At the time, he asked his partner, researcher and journalist Kat Abughazaleh, if she was up for walking “into a fucking burning building” by trying to take over Jones’ media empire. Her reply, according to Collins, was “Yeah. Nobody else is going to do this.”

Although The Onion is still in an ongoing legal battle over Infowars—it won the media network in a bankruptcy auction, but a federal judge in Texas struck the deal down—Collins is feeling more hopeful in light of the Democrats’ midterm wins.

“I want people to feel hope today because things changed last night,” he said. “We have an attorney general in Texas who might make a different decision.”

Collins joined comedian Patti Harrison, who stars in The Onion’s parody Infowars show, in a panel about the role of satire in society and politics. Collins also cagily spoke about The Onion’s interest in sports—comments that made more sense on Thursday when he posted on Bluesky, “The Onion is extremely close to buying an honest-to-goodness, Division 1 college football bowl series bowl game. Yes, we're trying to pull off The Onion Bowl.”

During the conversation, the pair discussed a lot of what has caused that sense of hopelessness in the Trump era: Jones’ disinformation campaign against the parents of Sandy Hook school shooting victims; ICE raids; Democrats abandoning trans rights. But they also talked, albeit in measured tones, about the value in fighting back with humor.

“Comedy is a good pill-in-the-cheese way to sort of introduce ideas to people,” Harrison said, noting that though she had let out “a huge sigh of relief” over the midterms, there’s a large swath of the population that is still “truly radicalized.” “They’re still out there drinking Mountain Dew,” she added, perhaps a nod to a nonsensical joke Vice President JD Vance made about how his love for Diet Mountain Dew could be viewed as “racist.”

Collins, who was previously an extremism reporter, extolled the virtues of being able to state things plainly via a satirical site. And he noted that many of The Onion’s headlines—including “almost everything that we say about RFK [Jr.]”—end up coming true.

“We don’t need three sources to write down the perfect sentence about what's wrong in the United States,” Collins said. “We're allowed to get to the heart of the matter a lot faster.”

Both also reflected on the internet being a lifeline for them while growing up in small towns. For Harrison, MySpace offered her a chance to talk to “other weird people” who were into “weird stuff” she had no access to in a rural, Christian, white community.

“I don't think social media is intrinsically bad,” she said. “I think the version of it that we have is truly abusive and evil.” The algorithmic era of being online means that sometimes her content gets pushed on people who don’t get it; when she recently dressed up as Elon Musk in a black MAGA hat for a WIRED cover, a lot of people told her it was “so fucked up.”

But she said comedy is still thriving online and it is possible to “de-algorithmize our internet.”

Collins’ take was harsher. He referred to the current iteration of the internet as a “joy vacuum” that “takes away anything that could be fun.” However, spaces like The Onion offer catharsis. “You kind of need to find ways to stay sane when things are so messed up,” he said.

For now, he says, the most fun he has is “playing around in the real world,” including The Onion’s writers’ room or just hanging out with friends. Then again, he adds, “I do hope that some benevolent-ass companies come soon and try to fix it.”
